q: You need a pod where the app reads LOG_LEVEL from a ConfigMap as an environment variable, reads app.properties from the same ConfigMap as a file at /etc/config, and overrides one key via a command-line flag. Which combination of ConfigMap consumption modes does this require?
options: envFrom for everything — it covers files and flags too
A volume mount for everything — environment variables can only come from Secrets
env for the single variable, a volume mount for the file, and args for the flag — the three modes compose in one pod spec
Three separate pods, one per consumption mode
explain: The three consumption modes are designed to be mixed: env (single key via configMapKeyRef), volumes (keys become files), and plain args for flags. envFrom loads all keys as env vars but cannot produce files. ConfigMaps feed env vars just as well as Secrets do — Secrets are only required when the data is sensitive.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You update a ConfigMap's LOG_LEVEL from info to debug. An hour later the running pods still log at info level, and the app reads LOG_LEVEL from an environment variable. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: Environment variables are injected once at container start and never refresh — update the ConfigMap, then roll the pods with kubectl rollout restart
The kubelet caches ConfigMaps for 24 hours; delete the ConfigMap and recreate it
The app needs a SIGHUP; send kill -HUP to the container's PID 1
ConfigMap updates require kubectl apply --refresh; the change never took effect
explain: This is the exam's favorite ConfigMap trap: updating a ConfigMap does NOT restart pods, and env vars are frozen at container start. Mounted files do eventually sync into running containers (kubelet refreshes them roughly every minute plus cache), but env vars never change without a pod restart. The fix is update the ConfigMap AND roll the pods — kubectl rollout restart deploy/<name>. No signal or re-apply flag changes this behavior.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod mounts a ConfigMap key as an individual file using subPath: /etc/app/config.yaml. You update the ConfigMap, roll the Deployment, and the new pods still show the OLD file content. Why?
options: subPath mounts are bind-mounted files that never receive ConfigMap updates — even new pods get a stale copy until the volume is remounted; drop subPath and mount the whole ConfigMap directory instead
The ConfigMap update is still propagating; subPath mounts sync after 10 minutes
subPath requires the file to exist in the image first
Rolling the Deployment does not recreate pods; only deleting them works
explain: subPath mounts bypass the kubelet's projected-volume refresh entirely — they are bind mounts of a single file and never update, a classic exam trap. The fix is to mount the ConfigMap as a directory (each key becomes a file under the mount path) instead of using subPath. Note the rolled pods still showed old content here because the question's premise includes the mount surviving — in practice, always prefer whole-directory mounts when the config must stay fresh.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You run kubectl get secret db-pass -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' and get c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQ=. The developer asks whether this value is encrypted in etcd by default. What is the correct answer?
options: No — base64 is only encoding, not encryption; anyone with get permission on the Secret can decode it with base64 -d, and etcd encryption at rest must be configured separately
Yes, but only for Secrets of type Opaque
Yes — base64 is Kubernetes' encryption, and the value is safe
No — Secrets are stored in plain text in the API server's memory only
explain: Two facts the exam loves: base64 is encoding, not encryption (echo c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQ= | base64 -d reveals it instantly), and Secrets are only as protected as your RBAC plus etcd encryption at rest — which is off by default and is a cluster-admin concern. The real protection for a Secret is who can read it, not the encoding.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod in namespace api fails to start with MountVolume.SetUp failed: secret "db-creds" not found, yet kubectl get secret db-creds shows it exists. What is the most likely cause?
options: The pod needs imagePullSecrets to read Secrets
Secrets must be created before the namespace exists
Secrets are namespace-scoped — the Secret lives in a different namespace than the pod, and a pod can only mount Secrets from its own namespace
The Secret's base64 values are malformed
explain: Secrets are namespace-scoped objects. If the Secret is in default (or anywhere other than api), the pod in api cannot see it — the fix is to create the Secret in the pod's namespace. When a task's pod can't find a Secret that 'definitely exists,' check the namespace first. imagePullSecrets are only for registry credentials, and malformed base64 would fail at creation time.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You are writing a Secret manifest by hand and want to type the password in plain text rather than pre-encoding it in base64. Which field do you use?
options: data: with the plain-text value — Kubernetes detects and encodes it
annotations: — the API server converts annotated values
stringData: — you write plain text and Kubernetes base64-encodes it into data on creation
plaintext: — a special field for human-readable secrets
explain: stringData is the write-only convenience field: you supply plain text, the API server encodes it into data. data requires you to base64-encode values yourself. There is no plaintext field. On the exam, stringData is the fast path for hand-written Secret manifests — write it readable, let the API do the encoding.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your Ingress TLS termination is not working. You created the Secret with kubectl create secret generic web-tls --from-file=cert.pem --from-file=key.pem and referenced it in the Ingress tls section. What is wrong?
options: TLS Secrets only work with type Opaque and a tls: true annotation
TLS Secrets must be created imperatively with kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem, producing type kubernetes.io/tls with keys tls.crt and tls.key
Ingress cannot use Secrets at all; the certificate must be pasted into the Ingress manifest
The Secret must be in the kube-system namespace
explain: Ingress expects a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls containing exactly tls.crt and tls.key. A generic Opaque secret with cert.pem/key.pem keys is ignored for TLS. kubectl create secret tls builds the correct type and key names in one command. The Secret must also live in the same namespace as the Ingress — not kube-system.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Pods fail with ImagePullBackOff pulling from your company's private registry. The credentials are valid — docker login works from your laptop. What is missing in the cluster?
options: A ConfigMap with the registry URL mounted into the pod
A docker-registry Secret (kubectl create secret docker-registry) referenced via imagePullSecrets in the pod spec — or attached to the pod's ServiceAccount
The registry's CA certificate in /etc/docker on every node — a developer cannot fix this
Setting imagePullPolicy: Always on the container
explain: Kubelet has no registry credentials by default. Create them once with kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=..., then reference the secret in the pod's imagePullSecrets — or attach it to the ServiceAccount so every pod using that account inherits it. A pull policy change cannot authenticate you, and node-level CA setup is a cluster-admin task, not the CKAD answer.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You add runAsNonRoot: true to a pod's securityContext and the pod fails with 'container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root'. What does this mean?
options: The node is running as root; cordon it and use a different node
runAsNonRoot is a pod-level-only field and was placed on the container
The container image defaults to the root user (no USER directive in its Dockerfile) — either run it as a non-root UID with runAsUser or use an image built for non-root execution
The cluster's PodSecurity admission is misconfigured
explain: runAsNonRoot is a guardrail: kubelet refuses to start a container that would run as UID 0. If the image has no USER directive it defaults to root, tripping the check. Fix it by setting runAsUser: 1000 (the image must still function as that UID — files it needs must be readable) or switching to a non-root image variant. The field is valid at both pod and container level.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The hardening task says: run this pod as non-root with a read-only root filesystem. You set runAsNonRoot: true and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. The pod starts, then crash-loops writing its first log line to /tmp/app.log. What is the missing piece?
options: Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: true so the app can remount /tmp
Move the log file to a ConfigMap
readOnlyRootFilesystem cannot be combined with runAsNonRoot; remove one of them
Mount a writable emptyDir volume at /tmp (or wherever the app writes) — the root filesystem is read-only but mounted volumes stay writable
explain: This is the classic hardening trap: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true makes the container's entire filesystem read-only, which breaks apps that write temp files, caches, or logs. The fix is a writable emptyDir mounted at the path the app writes to (often /tmp or /var/run). Volumes are mounted read-write by default even when the root filesystem is read-only. allowPrivilegeEscalation is unrelated, and ConfigMaps are read-only by design.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You need a pod that drops all Linux capabilities except the ability to bind to low ports. Where do capabilities belong in the manifest?
options: Under spec.hostCapabilities at the pod spec level
Under the pod-level securityContext — capabilities: drop: [ALL], add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]
In the pod's annotations as container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io
Under the container-level securityContext — capabilities are per-container, not per-pod
explain: Capabilities live in the container-level securityContext (securityContext.capabilities.add/drop) — there is no pod-level capabilities field, and putting them at pod level fails validation. Pod-level securityContext holds runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, and seccompProfile; container-level holds capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation, and runAsNonRoot overrides.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod runs as UID 1000 via the pod-level securityContext, but one container in the pod must run as UID 2000. How do you configure this?
options: Set runAsUser: 2000 in that container's securityContext — container-level settings override pod-level ones
Run the container with privileged: true and su inside
You cannot — all containers in a pod must share the pod-level UID
Add a second securityContext block at the pod level for the exception
explain: Container-level securityContext overrides pod-level for the same fields. Set runAsUser: 2000 on the specific container and it wins over the pod's 1000. This override pattern is the general rule: pod level sets defaults for every container, container level refines per container. privileged: true is a sledgehammer that violates least privilege and would fail a hardening task.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create a ServiceAccount named deployer and want your Deployment's pods to use it. Which pod spec field assigns it, and what is the common mistake with its name?
options: serviceAccountName: deployer — the old serviceAccount field was removed from the API; using it fails validation
serviceAccount: deployer — the legacy field, still accepted
serviceAccountToken: deployer — referencing the auto-generated token Secret
accountName: deployer under spec.identity
explain: The field is serviceAccountName — the legacy serviceAccount field was removed, and manifests using it are rejected. Set it at the pod template level (spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName) so every pod the Deployment creates carries the identity. The token itself is projected automatically; you never reference the token Secret by hand.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A security review flags that every pod in the payments namespace mounts a ServiceAccount token, but the app never calls the Kubernetes API. What is the correct hardening, and how do you verify it worked?
options: Delete the default ServiceAccount in the namespace
Set runAsNonRoot: true — tokens require root to be mounted
Remove the serviceAccountName field so no identity is attached
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the pod spec (or the ServiceAccount), then exec into a pod and confirm /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ is empty
explain: automountServiceAccountToken: false stops the kubelet from projecting the token into the pod — the standard hardening when the workload never talks to the API. Verify by exec-ing in and listing /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ (token, ca.crt, namespace). Deleting the default ServiceAccount breaks the namespace, and runAsNonRoot has nothing to do with token mounting.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container spec sets resources.requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi"}. Which statement is correct?
options: The container is guaranteed 500 CPU cores and 256 megabytes of RAM
Requests are hard caps — the container is killed if it uses 501m CPU
m stands for megabytes; the container gets 500 MB of CPU time
500m means half a CPU core (millicpu); 256Mi is 256 mebibytes (binary) — and on the exam, memory uses Mi/Gi, not M/G
explain: CPU is measured in millicpu: 1000m = 1 core, so 500m is half a core. Memory uses binary suffixes on the exam — Mi/Gi (mebibytes/gibibytes), not decimal M/G. And requests are scheduling guarantees, not caps: exceeding a CPU request only risks throttling at the limit, while exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod keeps dying with reason OOMKilled, exit code 137, while its CPU graphs look flat. The container has resources.requests.memory: 256Mi and resources.limits.memory: 256Mi. What is the fix?
options: Raise the memory limit (and request) — the container is exceeding its memory cap and the kernel is killing it; also check for a leak
Lower the memory request so the scheduler places it on a bigger node
Add a liveness probe to restart it cleanly before the OOM killer fires
Raise the CPU limit — flat CPU means it is starved
explain: OOMKilled + exit 137 is the signature of breaching the memory limit — CPU throttles, memory kills. Raise the limit (keeping request ≤ limit), and investigate whether usage climbs unboundedly, which means an application leak rather than a sizing problem. Lowering the request changes scheduling, not the kill threshold, and a liveness probe cannot preempt the kernel OOM killer.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You apply a pod manifest with no resources section, then kubectl get pod -o yaml shows resources.requests.memory: 512Mi that you never wrote. What injected it?
options: A LimitRange in the namespace — it applies default requests/limits to containers that omit them via admission
The metrics server backfills observed usage into the spec
The scheduler assigns default requests to unsized pods
kubectl apply adds requests automatically for QoS classification
explain: A LimitRange mutates pods at admission time, filling in default requests/limits for containers that don't specify them. If a pod's resources look different from your manifest, kubectl get limitrange is the 5-second check. The scheduler never edits specs, and the metrics server only reports usage — it never writes to pod specs.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Creating a pod fails with: exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: memory=1Gi, used: memory=1536Mi, limited: memory=2Gi. What is the fastest diagnosis and fix?
options: The pod's limit is higher than its request; set them equal
A ResourceQuota caps the namespace at 2Gi total and 1.5Gi is already used — run kubectl describe quota to confirm, then lower the pod's request or raise the quota
The node is out of memory; drain the node
Quotas apply per-container; split the pod into two Deployments
explain: ResourceQuota enforces aggregate caps per namespace: 2Gi limited, 1536Mi used, so a 1Gi request doesn't fit. kubectl describe quota shows exactly which hard limit is hit. The fix is smaller requests or a bigger quota (a cluster-admin change). Node pressure would surface as Pending pods, not a quota rejection, and quotas are namespace aggregates, not per-container.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You apply a container with resources.requests.memory: 2Gi and resources.limits.memory: 1Gi. The API server rejects it. Why?
options: Memory requests must use the M suffix, not Mi
Limits must be exactly double the requests
A container's request cannot exceed its limit for the same resource — the request is the guaranteed floor and the limit is the ceiling, so request > limit is invalid
Requests are capped at 1Gi per container by default
explain: Validation requires request ≤ limit per resource: the request is what the scheduler guarantees, the limit is the hard ceiling, and a floor above the ceiling is contradictory. Either lower the request or raise the limit. The Mi suffix is correct, and there is no fixed ratio rule between the two.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod running as non-root (runAsUser: 1000) cannot write to its PersistentVolumeClaim, getting permission denied, though the volume mounts fine. The volume's files are owned by root:root. What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Set fsGroup: 2000 in the pod's securityContext (and ensure the app's group can write) — fsGroup makes kubelet chown mounted volumes to that group
Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: false on the container
Add a privileged init container that chmods the volume to 777
Run the pod as root instead
explain: fsGroup is the purpose-built answer for volume ownership: kubelet recursively chowns mounted volumes to the fsGroup (and sets the group-write bit appropriately) before containers start. Running as root or chmod 777 abandons the hardening the task asked for. readOnlyRootFilesystem governs the container filesystem, not mounted volumes.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The task says to confine a pod with the runtime's default seccomp profile. Which securityContext snippet does this?
options: privileged: false — that enables the default seccomp profile
seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} — in the pod's securityContext (or the container's)
apparmor: {profile: runtime/default} as a pod annotation
capabilities: {drop: [ALL]} — seccomp is configured through capabilities
explain: seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault applies the container runtime's default syscall filter — the modern, API-native way to request seccomp confinement. It is valid at pod or container level. AppArmor uses a different annotation mechanism, capabilities are a separate control, and privileged: false is merely the default, not a profile selection.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your team wants a 'Database' object type with spec fields like engine and version, managed with kubectl like a built-in resource. Which Kubernetes mechanism provides this, at the awareness level the CKAD expects?
options: A ConfigMap with a database: true label
A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) — it extends the API with a new namespaced or cluster-scoped type, typically paired with an operator/controller that reconciles it
An aggregated API server written in Go
A Service of type ExternalName pointing at the database
explain: CRDs extend the Kubernetes API with custom types (spec, status, kubectl support included); operators are controllers that watch those types and drive the real world toward spec. The CKAD only needs awareness: know what a CRD is for, not how to write the schema. A ConfigMap cannot create a new API type, and writing an aggregated API server is far beyond exam scope.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A request to create a pod is authenticated and authorized, but the pod that gets persisted has an extra label your manifest didn't include. Which stage of the request path could have added it?
options: etcd — it normalizes objects on write
kube-proxy — it labels pods it manages
The kube-scheduler — it patches labels during binding
A mutating admission controller — admission runs after auth/authz and can modify the object before it is persisted
explain: The request path is authentication → authorization → mutating admission → validating admission → etcd. Mutating admission webhooks (and built-in controllers like LimitRange) can change the object; validating admission can only accept or reject. The scheduler binds pods to nodes but doesn't relabel them, and kube-proxy never edits pod metadata.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod needs every key from ConfigMap app-cfg and every key from ConfigMap shared-cfg as environment variables, but both define a key named LOG_LEVEL and they must not collide. How do you load both cleanly?
options: envFrom cannot take two ConfigMaps; use a volume instead
Rename the key in one ConfigMap with kubectl edit before deploying
List both under envFrom with a prefix on one: configMapRef: {name: shared-cfg} plus prefix: SHARED_ — keys become SHARED_LOG_LEVEL
Merge the ConfigMaps first with kubectl merge
explain: envFrom entries accept a prefix field that namespaces every imported variable — configMapRef with prefix: SHARED_ turns LOG_LEVEL into SHARED_LOG_LEVEL, eliminating the collision with zero manifest surgery. envFrom happily takes multiple ConfigMaps and Secrets in one list. There is no kubectl merge command.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ConfigMap holds launch parameters that must NEVER change while the application runs — a mid-run change would corrupt in-flight work. Which field enforces this, and what is its side benefit?
options: immutable: true — the API server rejects any update to the ConfigMap's data, and as a bonus the kubelet stops watching it, reducing API load
frozen: true — a beta field that snapshots the values
readOnly: true — it locks the ConfigMap after first mount
There is no such field; use RBAC to deny updates
explain: immutable: true makes the ConfigMap's data unchangeable after creation — updates are rejected, so consumers must create a new ConfigMap (usually with a new name) to change values. The side benefit is real: kubelet skips its watch cache for immutable ConfigMaps, which matters at scale. RBAC can restrict who updates, but only immutable: true makes the object itself unchangeable.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You write a pod spec with image: web:v2 and no imagePullPolicy. Later you write another with image: web (no tag) and no imagePullPolicy. What pull policy does each get by default?
options: The default is Never unless the cluster sets a default policy
Both default to Always
web:v2 gets IfNotPresent, while web (implicit :latest) gets Always — any :latest tag defaults to Always
Both default to IfNotPresent
explain: The defaulting rule is mechanical: image tag :latest (explicit or implied) → Always; any other tag → IfNotPresent. So web:v2 is pulled once and cached, while web is re-pulled every time the pod starts. On the exam, set imagePullPolicy explicitly whenever the task cares about freshness — never rely on memory of the default.

q: You fix a bug, push the image under the SAME tag web:v2, roll the Deployment, and the old buggy code still runs. kubectl describe pod shows the new ReplicaSet. What is the most likely cause?
options: The nodes already have web:v2 cached and imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent reuses it — the tag was overwritten upstream but the node never re-pulled
Rolling updates do not apply to image changes; only config changes
The new image failed to push; the registry rejected the duplicate tag
The Deployment controller caches the old image digest for 10 minutes
explain: The stale-image trap: IfNotPresent sees web:v2 in the node cache and never checks the registry, so your rebuilt tag is ignored. Fix it with imagePullPolicy: Always or — the professional habit — a unique tag per build (web:v2.3.1). Retagging the same tag is how this trap is set; unique tags make it impossible.

q: The task says: 'Run the database migration script to completion exactly once, then stop.' Which workload resource is correct, and why not a Deployment?
options: A bare pod — simplest and runs once
A CronJob with schedule '@once'
A Deployment with replicas: 1 and restartPolicy: Never
A Job — it runs pods to completion (completions: 1) and tracks success; a Deployment is for long-running services and would restart the finished migration forever
explain: 'Run once to completion' is the literal Job use case — the curriculum's 'choose and use the right workload' bullet. A Deployment's job is keeping N replicas running forever; a finished pod under a Deployment gets restarted as a failure. There is no @once schedule, and Deployments don't accept restartPolicy: Never.

q: The task says: 'Generate the sales report every night at 2 AM.' Which workload is correct?
options: A DaemonSet — it runs once per node per night
A CronJob with schedule: "0 2 * * *" — time-based recurring work is the CronJob's purpose
A Job — it runs on a timer by default
A Deployment with a sleep 86400 loop in the container command
explain: 'Run this on a schedule' = CronJob, full stop. The exam grades the workload type: a Deployment with a sleep loop 'works' but is wrong — it wastes a pod 24/7 and has no schedule semantics. Quote the schedule in YAML (leading digits/asterisks can be misparsed), and remember the field order: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

q: The task says: 'Run the web API with 4 replicas and update it without downtime.' Which workload is correct?
options: A Deployment with replicas: 4 — long-running stateless services with rolling updates are the Deployment's core use case
A StatefulSet — it provides rolling updates for web APIs
4 bare pods created with kubectl run
A Job with parallelism: 4
explain: Long-running, interchangeable replicas + rolling updates = Deployment. StatefulSets are for workloads needing stable identity and ordered storage (databases), bare pods have no self-healing, and Jobs run to completion. Matching the workload to the task description is graded directly on the CKAD.

q: You apply a Job manifest and the API server rejects it: 'spec.template.spec.restartPolicy: Unsupported value: "Always"'. What is the fix?
options: Move restartPolicy to the Job's spec instead of the pod template
Change the Job to a CronJob, which allows Always
Set backoffLimit: 0 to disable restarts
Set restartPolicy: OnFailure or Never — Job pods must not use Always; the kubelet needs to distinguish a finished pod from a failed one
explain: Job pod templates only accept OnFailure or Never — Always is rejected at validation because the Job controller relies on pod phase (Succeeded/Failed) to track completions, and Always would restart finished pods forever. The exam loves watching candidates debug this rejection instead of reading the error. backoffLimit controls retry count, not the policy.

q: A Job must process 10 work items with 3 workers running at a time. Which fields express this?
options: concurrencyPolicy: Allow with 3 slots
activeDeadlineSeconds: 10 and backoffLimit: 3
completions: 10 and parallelism: 3 — completions is the total work count, parallelism caps concurrent pods
replicas: 3 and parallelism: 10
explain: completions counts how many pods must succeed for the Job to complete; parallelism caps how many run simultaneously. replicas belongs to Deployments, activeDeadlineSeconds is a global timeout, and concurrencyPolicy is a CronJob field. For queue-style work the pattern is completions: N, parallelism: M.

q: A Job with a broken image keeps retrying — 6 failed pods and counting — burning time on the exam clock. How do you make a failing Job give up sooner?
options: Set activeDeadlineSeconds: 60 on the pod template
Set restartPolicy: Never — that stops retries entirely
Lower backoffLimit (default 6) — it caps how many retries the Job attempts before marking itself Failed
Delete the Job; failed Jobs cannot be limited
explain: backoffLimit (default 6) is the retry budget: after that many failed pod attempts the Job is marked Failed and stops. restartPolicy: Never changes per-pod behavior (no kubelet-level restart) but the Job controller still creates replacement pods up to backoffLimit. For a fast-fail during the exam, backoffLimit: 2 or 3 keeps the clock on your side.

q: A CronJob runs every 5 minutes and each run leaves a completed Job behind. After a day there are hundreds of finished Jobs cluttering the namespace. What is the cleanest automatic cleanup?
options: A second CronJob that deletes old Jobs nightly
Completed Jobs are garbage-collected automatically after 1 hour
Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 0 — that deletes the Jobs immediately
ttlSecondsAfterFinished on the Job template — the controller deletes finished Jobs after the TTL expires
explain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished tells the Job controller to delete finished Jobs (Succeeded or Failed, per your setting) after N seconds — the purpose-built cleanup. successfulJobsHistoryLimit only caps how many are KEPT in history (default 3), it doesn't delete promptly. There is no automatic 1-hour GC for Jobs.

q: You write a CronJob with schedule: */5 * * * * (unquoted) and kubectl apply fails with a YAML parse error. What is wrong?
options: */5 means every 5 seconds, which CronJob rejects as too frequent
CronJobs don't accept step values like */5
The schedule must be a quoted string — a leading * (or certain digit patterns) gets misparsed as a YAML alias/number; write schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
The schedule belongs in the Job template, not the CronJob spec
explain: Always quote CronJob schedules: an unquoted string starting with * is parsed as a YAML alias reference and fails. "*/5 * * * *" means every 5 minutes (fields: minute hour dom month dow). CronJobs also support @hourly/@daily shorthands, but the five-field cron form is what the exam tests.

q: A CronJob triggers a 10-minute data export every 5 minutes. Overlapping runs corrupt the output file. Which setting prevents a new run from starting while the previous is still active?
options: startingDeadlineSeconds: 300
parallelism: 1 on the Job template
backoffLimit: 1
concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — it skips a scheduled run when the previous Job hasn't finished
explain: concurrencyPolicy governs overlapping CronJob runs: Allow (default), Forbid (skip if the previous run is still active), or Replace (kill the old run and start fresh). For non-overlapping exports, Forbid is the answer. parallelism controls pods within one Job, not runs across schedules.

q: The task says: 'The app crashes on startup because the database isn't ready yet. Fix the pod so the app only starts after the database accepts connections.' What is the idiomatic Kubernetes solution?
options: A liveness probe with a long initialDelaySeconds
restartPolicy: OnFailure — the crash loop will eventually coincide with DB readiness
An init container that blocks until the database is reachable (e.g., looping a connection check) — init containers run to completion before any app container starts
A postStart lifecycle hook that sleeps 30 seconds
explain: Init containers are the exam's favorite ordering tool: they run sequentially to completion before app containers start, so 'don't start X until Y is ready' is their textbook use. A blocking connection check in the init container is deterministic; sleep-based guessing and crash-loop roulette waste exam time. Probes manage already-running containers, not startup ordering.

q: An init container fails (bad image name). What does the pod do?
options: Retries the init container indefinitely (subject to the pod's restartPolicy) — app containers never start until all init containers succeed
Marks the pod Failed immediately
Skips the init container and starts the app containers
Starts the app containers but withholds the Service endpoints
explain: Init containers are a hard gate: they run in order, each must exit 0 before the next starts, and app containers never start until all succeed. A failing init container is retried per the pod's restartPolicy (the pod sits in Init:CrashLoopBackOff). The pod is never marked Failed for this — it waits, which is exactly the semantics you want for 'wait for the database.'

q: The task says: 'Add a log-shipping sidecar to the app pod. The app writes logs to /var/log/app, and the sidecar tails them.' What shared primitive connects the two containers?
options: They share the container filesystem automatically — the sidecar reads /var/log/app directly
The downward API exposes one container's files to the other
A shared ConfigMap mounted in both containers
A shared volume (typically emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/app in both containers — containers cannot see each other's filesystems otherwise
explain: Containers in a pod share network and IPC namespaces, but NOT filesystems. The sidecar-via-shared-volume pattern is the exam's favorite multi-container task: mount the same emptyDir at /var/log/app in both containers, the app writes, the sidecar ships. ConfigMaps are read-only and the downward API exposes pod metadata, not files.

q: A sidecar needs to call the main app's health endpoint. The app listens on port 8080. What address does the sidecar use?
options: The Service's ClusterIP — sidecars must go through the Service
The pod's cluster IP, discovered via the downward API
localhost:8080 — containers in a pod share the network namespace, so localhost reaches the sibling container
127.0.0.1 only works from the node, not between containers
explain: Pod containers share one network namespace: one IP, one port space, localhost works between them. That's why two containers in a pod can't both bind port 8080. Going through the Service also works but adds a needless hop — and on the exam, localhost is the fast, idiomatic answer for sidecar-to-app traffic.

q: An app caches downloads in an emptyDir volume. After a node drain, the pod is rescheduled and the cache is gone, but the app recovers by re-downloading. Is this expected, and when would you need a PVC instead?
options: Not expected — emptyDir survives rescheduling; file a bug
Expected — emptyDir lives and dies with the pod (it survives container restarts, not pod rescheduling); use a PVC when data must outlive the pod
A PVC would not help; both are node-local
Expected — but only because the drain deleted it; emptyDir normally persists across nodes
explain: emptyDir's lifetime is the pod's: it survives container crashes and restarts within the pod, but pod deletion or rescheduling wipes it. That's fine for scratch space, caches, and sidecar handoff. When data must survive the pod — databases, uploads, anything durable — you need a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by real storage.

q: A pod uses a hostPath volume at /data on node-1. After the pod is rescheduled to node-2, it fails because /data doesn't exist there. What is the lesson, and the fix?
options: Add type: DirectoryOrCreate — that makes hostPath portable
hostPath is node-local by definition — it ties the pod to one node's filesystem; use nodeSelector to pin the pod or, better, replace it with a PVC for portable storage
hostPath volumes are read-only; the app needs write access
The kubelet blocks hostPath on multi-node clusters for security
explain: hostPath mounts a path from the node's own filesystem — inherently non-portable and a scheduling hazard, which is why the exam treats it as a code smell outside node-level agents (log collectors, monitoring). type: DirectoryOrCreate avoids the crash but the data still isn't shared. The durable answer is a PVC; the quick exam answer is pinning via nodeSelector/nodeAffinity if the task demands hostPath.

q: Two pods on DIFFERENT nodes both need read-write access to the same shared files. The PVC requests accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]. The second pod stays Pending. Why, and what is needed?
options: The second pod needs hostPath instead
ReadWriteOnce allows exactly one node to mount the volume read-write — multi-node shared read-write needs ReadWriteMany, and a provisioner/volume type that supports it
Pods cannot share a PVC at all; each pod needs its own claim
The storage class is out of capacity
explain: Access modes are the contract: ReadWriteOnce = one node, ReadWriteMany = many nodes, ReadOnlyMany = many readers. The second pod pends because its node can't attach an RWO volume already mounted elsewhere. The fix is a ReadWriteMany claim — but the underlying storage must support it (NFS, EFS, Azure Files); you can't conjure RWX from an EBS-style block volume.

q: An app tries to write its runtime config to /etc/app/settings.yaml, which is mounted from a ConfigMap volume. It gets 'read-only file system'. What is the correct fix?
options: Change the ConfigMap to immutable: false
Mount the ConfigMap with readOnly: false
ConfigMap (and Secret) volumes are always read-only — have the app write to a different path backed by a writable emptyDir, or copy the file to writable storage at startup
Add write permissions to the ConfigMap's RBAC role
explain: ConfigMap and Secret volumes are mounted read-only by design — readOnly: false is rejected for them. The pattern is: read config from the mounted ConfigMap, write runtime state elsewhere (emptyDir, or a PVC). An init container that copies the config file to a writable volume and lets the app edit the copy is the classic exam-ready shape.

q: A debugging sidecar needs to list the main container's processes to diagnose a hang, but ps inside the sidecar only shows its own processes. Which pod setting enables cross-container process visibility?
options: privileged: true on the sidecar
shareProcessNamespace: true — containers in the pod share one process namespace, so the sidecar sees (and can signal) the app's processes
hostPID: true — shares the node's process namespace
There is no such setting; use kubectl debug instead
explain: shareProcessNamespace: true puts all containers in the pod under one PID namespace — the sidecar can ps, inspect /proc, and even signal the app's processes. hostPID: true shares the NODE's namespace (far broader, rarely what you want). kubectl debug with an ephemeral container is the alternative when you can't change the pod spec.

q: The task says: 'Update the Deployment to v2 with zero downtime.' You check the strategy: type: RollingUpdate, maxUnavailable: 1, maxSurge: 1, replicas: 3. Is this safe, and what would you change for a strict zero-downtime guarantee?
options: Set maxSurge: 0 — extra pods cause the downtime
Set maxUnavailable: 0 — with maxUnavailable: 1 the controller may take one old pod down before the replacement is ready, briefly dropping capacity
Change strategy to Recreate — it is faster and therefore safer
Safe as-is — RollingUpdate always guarantees zero downtime
explain: RollingUpdate defaults (25%/25%) permit unavailability; maxUnavailable: 1 on 3 replicas explicitly allows one pod down during the roll. For strict zero downtime, maxUnavailable: 0 keeps all old pods until replacements pass readiness. maxSurge controls how many EXTRA pods may exist (resource cost, not downtime), and Recreate kills everything first — the opposite of zero downtime.

q: The task says: 'Update the image of Deployment web to web:v2.' What is the fastest correct command, and what should you run immediately after?
options: kubectl apply -f web-v2.yaml, then kubectl get pods
kubectl edit deploy web, change the image, save — then wait
kubectl set image deploy/web web=web:v2, then kubectl rollout status deploy/web — set image is the one-command update, rollout status watches it to completion
kubectl replace --force -f web.yaml
explain: kubectl set image deploy/web <container>=<image> is the exam's one-command answer to 'update the image' — faster and less error-prone than editing YAML. Follow with kubectl rollout status to watch the roll complete (it blocks until done or failed). edit works but is slower and risks typos under time pressure; --force replace causes downtime.

q: You roll out v2, it breaks, and you run kubectl rollout undo deploy/web — but it reports 'no rollout history found'. A teammate set revisionHistoryLimit: 0 'to save etcd space'. What happened?
options: The Deployment must be paused before undo works
Rollbacks require a Recreate strategy; RollingUpdate cannot be undone
The undo command requires the --to-revision flag when history is disabled
revisionHistoryLimit: 0 discards old ReplicaSets immediately, leaving nothing to roll back to — keep it at the default 10 (or at least 1+) so undo has a target
explain: rollout undo works by scaling the previous ReplicaSet back up — with revisionHistoryLimit: 0 there are no old ReplicaSets, so there is nothing to return to. The default of 10 is cheap insurance; never set it to 0 on anything you might need to roll back. The strategy type doesn't matter, and pausing is unrelated to history retention.

q: You need to apply several manifest changes to a Deployment (new image, new env var, new resource limits) and have them all roll out as ONE controlled update you can verify before traffic shifts. Which rollout command helps?
options: kubectl rollout pause deploy/web before the changes and kubectl rollout resume after — pausing freezes the rollout so all changes accumulate, then resume rolls them out together
kubectl rollout history — it groups changes into one revision
There is no such command; apply changes one at a time
kubectl rollout restart — it batches changes automatically
explain: rollout pause suspends the Deployment controller: you can apply multiple changes while paused and nothing rolls out; rollout resume then executes them as a single controlled update. It's the mechanism behind careful multi-step changes. restart just bounces pods, and history only records what already happened.

q: The task says: 'Deploy v2 of the API with zero downtime and INSTANT rollback if it misbehaves.' Which strategy fits, and what is its mechanism?
options: Blue/green — run v2 (green) alongside v1 (blue) as separate Deployments with distinct version labels; cut over by flipping the Service selector to green; roll back by flipping it back — both are instant, single-field changes
Rolling update with maxSurge: 100%
Canary — shift 100% of traffic at once
Recreate — the old version restarts instantly
explain: 'Zero downtime plus instant rollback' is the blue/green signature. Two full environments (blue: version labels v1, green: v2), one Service; the selector flip is atomic and the rollback is the same flip reversed — no waiting for pods to reschedule. Canary is gradual traffic shifting (different requirement); rolling updates roll back by rescheduling, which is not instant.

q: You set up a canary: a stable Deployment (9 replicas, labels app: web) and a canary Deployment (1 replica, labels app: web, track: canary, image web:v2). The Service selects app: web. After an hour the canary has served ZERO requests. What is wrong?
options: Canary pods need a separate Service
Canary requires an Ingress, not a Service

The canary Deployment's extra track: canary label is harmless, but if its labels don't include app: web — or the Service selector was narrowed — the Service won't select it; the canary must share the Service's selector labels so it receives a share of traffic
The replica ratio must be 1:1 for traffic to split
explain: A canary works by SHARING the Service's selector: same labels (app: web), small replica count, so kube-proxy sends it a proportional trickle of traffic. The exam's classic canary trap is labels the Service doesn't select — different labels mean zero traffic and a failed task. Extra labels like track: canary are fine as long as the selector's labels are all present on the pod.

q: A Deployment mounts a ReadWriteOnce volume and the task requires updating its image. A rolling update stalls — new pods stay Pending. Which strategy should the Deployment use instead, and why?
options: Increase maxSurge to 2 so both pods fit
Canary — it uses fewer resources
Blue/green — it handles volumes automatically
Recreate — RWO volumes can attach to only one node/pod at a time, so old and new pods can't coexist; Recreate terminates everything first, freeing the volume
explain: RollingUpdate needs old and new pods alive simultaneously, but a ReadWriteOnce volume can only mount to one node at a time — the new pod pends forever waiting for the volume. strategy: Recreate kills all old pods first (downtime accepted), releasing the volume for the new pods. This is the textbook Recreate use case the exam tests.

q: The task says: 'Install the redis chart from Bitnami with 3 replicas.' You run helm repo add bitnami <url> then helm install myredis bitnami/redis --set replica.replicaCount=3, and get 'chart "redis" not found'. What step did you skip?
options: helm dependency update on the redis chart
helm pull — charts must be downloaded first
helm search — you must search before installing
helm repo update — the local index is stale after adding a repo; update refreshes it before install
explain: helm repo add only registers the repo; the local chart index is empty/stale until helm repo update downloads it. Skipping update is the #1 Helm exam trap — 'chart not found' right after adding the repo. The winning sequence is always: repo add → repo update → show values → install.

q: You run helm install myapp bitnami/wordpress --set replicas=3 and the Deployment still has 1 replica. What is the most likely cause?
options: helm install ignores --set on the first install; use helm upgrade
--set requires the value to be quoted: --set "replicas=3"
--set cannot change replica counts
The chart's value key isn't replicas — many charts use replicaCount. Guessing the key name fails silently; run helm show values <chart> to find the exact key
explain: Helm --set with a wrong key name silently does nothing — no error, no effect. Charts name things idiosyncratically (replicaCount, replica.replicaCount, autoscaling...). Always helm show values first and copy the exact key path. This silent-failure behavior is why the exam plants this trap.

q: You need a single command that installs release myapp from ./chart if missing, or upgrades it if present. Which Helm invocation does this?
options: helm install --replace myapp ./chart
helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart — the --install flag makes upgrade fall back to installing when the release doesn't exist
helm template myapp ./chart | kubectl apply -f -
helm install --force myapp ./chart
explain: helm upgrade --install (idiomatically helm upgrade -i) is the idempotent deploy: upgrades when the release exists, installs when it doesn't. It's the standard CI/CD and exam answer for 'deploy this chart regardless of current state.' --force on install isn't a thing, and template+apply bypasses Helm's release tracking entirely.

q: A helm upgrade broke the app. You need to return to the previous working state. Which commands diagnose and fix this?
options: helm list -a then helm delete myapp and reinstall the old chart version
helm restore myapp --previous
kubectl rollout undo deploy/myapp — Helm releases support kubectl rollback
helm history myapp to see revisions, then helm rollback myapp <revision> — Helm tracks every release revision and can revert to any of them
explain: Helm versions every release: helm history shows the revision list, helm rollback <release> <revision> reverts to one. It's the Helm-native equivalent of kubectl rollout undo. Deleting and reinstalling loses history and is slower; kubectl rollout undo doesn't understand Helm releases (it may work on the underlying Deployment but bypasses Helm's state).

q: You install with helm install myapp ./chart -f prod-values.yaml --set image.tag=v2. prod-values.yaml sets image.tag: v1. Which tag is deployed, and why?
options: v1 — the values file always wins over --set
v2 — --set takes precedence over -f values files
It fails — conflicting sources are rejected
v1v2 — Helm concatenates conflicting scalar values
explain: Precedence order (lowest to highest): chart defaults → -f values files (later files win) → --set. So --set image.tag=v2 overrides the file's v1. On the exam this matters when a task says 'install with these values but override X' — put the override in --set and it wins deterministically.

q: The task says: 'Deploy these plain manifests to staging and production with different replica counts and different ConfigMap values — no templating engine.' Which tool is the idiomatic answer?
options: Helm — create a chart with values per environment
Copy the manifests into two directories and edit by hand
kubectl apply with --env flags per environment
Kustomize — bases plus staging/prod overlays with patches; it customizes plain YAML without templates, which is exactly the 'same app, different config per environment' use case
explain: Kustomize vs Helm in one line: Helm = packages with values and templating (great for distributing apps); Kustomize = overlays patching plain YAML (great for per-environment customization without templates). When the task says 'customize these manifests for staging vs prod,' reach for Kustomize: a base plus overlays, applied with kubectl apply -k.

q: You have a directory overlays/staging with kustomization.yaml, and you run kubectl apply -f overlays/staging. The deployment goes out WITHOUT your patches. What went wrong?
options: Patches require helm to be installed
Overlays only work with --dry-run=client
The kustomization.yaml must be named kustomize.yaml
kubectl apply -f ignores kustomization.yaml — Kustomize directories must be applied with kubectl apply -k (which builds the customized manifests first)
explain: apply -f treats the directory as a bag of raw manifests and never invokes Kustomize — your patches, generators, and transformers are silently skipped. kubectl apply -k <dir> runs kustomize build first, then applies the result. On the exam, -f vs -k on a Kustomize directory is a one-character difference that decides the task.

q: Your Kustomize setup uses configMapGenerator for app-config. After changing a value and re-applying, the Deployment's pods automatically roll to pick up the new config — even though you changed no Deployment fields. Why?
options: configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the ConfigMap name (app-config-abc123); the Deployment references the hashed name, so a content change produces a NEW ConfigMap name, which changes the pod template and triggers a rollout
The kubelet watches ConfigMaps and restarts pods automatically
Kustomize restarts all pods on every apply
This doesn't happen — you must have also edited the Deployment
explain: The hashed-name trick is Kustomize's killer feature for config changes: because the ConfigMap's name embeds a hash of its content, any value change yields a new name, the Deployment's pod template changes, and the rollout happens automatically. It elegantly defeats the 'ConfigMap updates don't restart pods' trap from Domain 1.

q: In a Kustomize staging overlay you need image web:v1 replaced with web:v2 WITHOUT editing the base manifests. Which kustomization.yaml stanza does this declaratively?
options: configMapGenerator with the new image in data
images: - name: web, newTag: v2 — the images transformer rewrites the tag wherever that image name appears
patchesStrategicMerge with a full Deployment copy
replacements: mapping the old tag string to the new one
explain: The images transformer (images: [{name: web, newName: ..., newTag: v2}]) rewrites image references by name across all resources — the declarative, one-stanza way to bump tags per environment. patchesStrategicMerge works but requires duplicating resource structure; the images transformer exists precisely so you don't.

q: You update a ConfigMap consumed via env vars and run kubectl rollout restart deploy/web to bounce the pods. A teammate asks why you didn't just wait for the kubelet to sync it. What is the correct justification?
options: The kubelet never syncs ConfigMaps at all
Env vars are injected at container start and never refresh — only volume-mounted files sync via the kubelet; rollout restart is the required second step for env-based config
rollout restart is faster than waiting for the sync interval
Waiting works but rollout restart also updates the image
explain: This is the Domain 1 trap applied to deployments: mounted ConfigMap files eventually refresh in running containers (except subPath mounts), but environment variables are frozen at container creation. Any task saying 'update the config and make the app pick it up' for env-based config is a two-step task: update the ConfigMap, then rollout restart. One step earns partial credit at best.

q: During a rolling update, new pods pass their readiness probes but the app still needs 20 more seconds to warm its cache — clients get errors from fresh pods. Which Deployment field addresses this?
options: minReadySeconds: 20 — the pod must stay Ready for this long before the rollout proceeds and the old pod is removed
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 20
initialDelaySeconds on the readiness probe — set it to 20
progressDeadlineSeconds: 20
explain: minReadySeconds is the rollout-level warm-up: a new pod must remain Ready for N seconds before it's considered available and the old pod is scaled down. Readiness probes gate traffic per-pod, but minReadySeconds gates the ROLLOUT — it protects against 'Ready but not really warm.' progressDeadlineSeconds is the failure timeout; terminationGracePeriodSeconds governs shutdown, not startup.

q: A rolling update hangs because the new image's tag doesn't exist — pods are stuck in ImagePullBackOff. How long before the Deployment marks the rollout as failed by default, and which field tunes it?
options: 120 seconds; controlled by activeDeadlineSeconds
600 seconds (10 minutes); controlled by progressDeadlineSeconds
30 seconds; controlled by backoffLimit
It never fails automatically; rollouts hang forever
explain: progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s) is the 'no progress' tripwire: if the Deployment makes no progress toward the new ReplicaSet for that long, it's marked Failed (ProgressDeadlineExceeded). backoffLimit belongs to Jobs, activeDeadlineSeconds caps total pod/Job runtime. On the exam clock you won't wait 10 minutes — you'll spot ImagePullBackOff in rollout status and fix the tag yourself.

q: The namespace has tight resource quotas and the task says to roll out updates WITHOUT ever exceeding the current pod count. Which RollingUpdate settings achieve this?
options: strategy: Recreate with maxSurge: 0
replicas: 1 — a single replica can never surge
maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 — no extra pods are ever created; old pods are removed one at a time before replacements start
maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 — the standard zero-downtime setting
explain: maxSurge: 0 forbids extra pods above the replica count (no resource spike, quota-safe); maxUnavailable: 1 allows the roll to proceed one pod at a time (brief capacity dip, but never over quota). The zero-downtime mirror is maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 — extra capacity instead of a dip. Pick the pair that matches the constraint the task names: quota → no surge; uptime → no unavailability.

q: The task says: 'Expose the web Deployment to other pods inside the cluster only.' Which Service type is correct, and what port range constraint applies to a different type?
options: LoadBalancer — it works internally too and is the default
Headless — it is the default internal type
NodePort — internal traffic uses node ports by default
ClusterIP (the default) — internal-only virtual IP; the port-range constraint belongs to NodePort, which must use 30000-32767
explain: ClusterIP is the default Service type and is reachable only inside the cluster — exactly 'other pods only.' NodePort opens a port on every node in the 30000-32767 range (specifying 8080 is rejected); LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer (external). Pick the type that matches the exposure the task asks for — the exam grades this choice directly.

q: A Service exists, the pods are Running, but curl to the Service IP hangs. What is the FIRST diagnostic command, and what does an empty result mean?
options: kubectl describe service — it shows the routing table
kubectl get ingress — the Service needs an Ingress to route
kubectl logs on the Service — Services log dropped connections
kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty endpoints means the Service selector matches no pods; compare kubectl get pods --show-labels against the selector
explain: kubectl get endpoints is the 5-second service diagnosis and the CKAD plants broken selectors constantly. Endpoints populated = selector is fine, look elsewhere (ports, NetworkPolicy). Endpoints empty = the selector matches nothing — the #1 cause of 'Service exists but nothing answers.' Always check endpoints before touching anything else on the timed exam.

q: A Service defines port: 80 and targetPort: 8080. The pods listen on 8080. Traffic to the Service IP on port 80 fails, but pod IP on 8080 works. The endpoints list is populated. What is misconfigured?
options: The pods need hostPort: 8080 for the Service to reach them

The selector — endpoints being populated rules this out; instead the Service's port: 80 must match what clients use and targetPort: 8080 must match the container — here the likely error is targetPort pointing at a port the container isn't actually listening on, or a NetworkPolicy blocking the Service port
targetPort must equal port; change targetPort to 80
The Service type — ClusterIP cannot forward to 8080
explain: port is what clients dial on the Service; targetPort is where the Service forwards on the pod. They are MEANT to differ (80 → 8080 is the textbook example). With endpoints populated and pod-IP connectivity working, suspect the targetPort value vs the container's actual listen port, or a NetworkPolicy. Forcing them equal is never the fix — the split exists precisely for this mapping.

q: The task says: 'The client needs to discover and connect to EACH pod replica individually, not a single virtual IP.' Which Service configuration does this?
options: A headless Service (clusterIP: None) — DNS returns the individual pod IPs (A records) instead of one virtual IP
A NodePort Service — it exposes each pod on its own node port
A normal ClusterIP Service with sessionAffinity: ClientIP
An ExternalName Service per pod
explain: clusterIP: None makes the Service headless: no virtual IP, and DNS queries return all backing pod IPs directly. That's the mechanism StatefulSets use for stable per-pod DNS (web-0.db, web-1.db). sessionAffinity only pins clients to one backend; NodePort still load-balances through one Service IP.

q: A pod in namespace api needs to reach a Service named db in namespace data. The code uses host 'db' and gets DNS NXDOMAIN. What is the correct host, and why did the short name fail?
options: The short name never works; always use the pod IP
db.svc — the namespace is inferred from the client's ServiceAccount
db.data — the short name only resolves within the same namespace; cross-namespace needs name.namespace (or the full db.data.svc.cluster.local)
db.default — Services resolve under default unless specified
explain: DNS search domains make 'db' resolve to db.api.svc.cluster.local from inside namespace api — which doesn't exist. Cross-namespace, qualify it: db.data or the FQDN db.data.svc.cluster.local. This is a staple exam failure mode: the Service is healthy, the client is just asking DNS the wrong question.

q: You create a NodePort Service with nodePort: 8080 and the API server rejects it. Why?
options: 8080 is reserved for the API server
NodePort requires a LoadBalancer type as well
NodePort Services cannot set nodePort manually at all
nodePort must fall in the configured range, default 30000-32767 — 8080 is outside it; omit nodePort to auto-assign or pick a port in range
explain: The API server validates nodePort against the cluster's service-node-port-range (default 30000-32767). Out-of-range values are rejected outright. Either omit nodePort and let Kubernetes assign one, or choose within the range. The exam tests this as a 'why was my manifest rejected' speed bump.

q: A stateful game server behind a Service keeps losing player sessions because requests bounce between replicas. Which Service field provides sticky routing, and what is its basis?
options: sessionAffinity: ClientIP — routes a client IP consistently to the same backend pod
publishNotReadyAddresses: true — includes warming pods in rotation
sessionAffinity: PodIP — pins sessions to the pod's IP permanently
externalTrafficPolicy: Local — keeps sessions on the node
explain: sessionAffinity: ClientIP (the only supported value besides None) hashes the client IP so the same client consistently hits the same pod — the built-in answer to session stickiness. externalTrafficPolicy governs source-IP preservation through external LBs, not stickiness; publishNotReadyAddresses is for headless discovery during startup.

q: You apply an Ingress manifest and it stays in 'ADDRESS pending' forever with no errors. kubectl get ingressclass shows No resources found. What is the diagnosis?
options: DNS hasn't propagated for the Ingress host yet
The Service backend is down — Ingress waits for healthy backends
No Ingress controller is installed — an Ingress is just configuration; without a controller (nginx, traefik, etc.) nothing implements it, so no address is ever assigned
The Ingress YAML is invalid — it would have been rejected, not pended
explain: The single most common Ingress failure: the manifest is perfect but no controller is running to honor it. Ingress is declarative config — the controller pods do the actual routing and address assignment. Before debugging rules and TLS, check the controller exists (kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx or similar). An invalid manifest would fail validation, not pend silently.

q: You apply an Ingress with one rule mapping path /api to a Service, omitting pathType. The API server rejects the manifest. What is missing and why is it required?
options: backend.protocol — the controller can't infer HTTP vs HTTPS
The host field — rules without hosts are invalid
pathType — it is a required field on every path; it must be Prefix, Exact, or ImplementationSpecific, telling the controller how to match the path
pathName — every path needs a unique name
explain: Since networking.k8s.io/v1, pathType is mandatory — the API rejects Ingress paths without it. Prefix matches the path and anything below it (/api matches /api/users); Exact matches only the literal path; ImplementationSpecific delegates to the controller. The exam grades Ingress as a YAML-assembly task, and pathType is the detail candidates most often omit.

q: Your Ingress routes to Service web on port 80 and terminates TLS using Secret web-tls. The rule works over HTTP but HTTPS returns a default fake certificate. The Secret exists. What should you check first?
options: That the Service is type LoadBalancer — TLS needs an external LB
That port 443 is in the Service's ports list
That web-tls is type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt/tls.key AND lives in the SAME namespace as the Ingress — cross-namespace Secret references are not allowed
That the Ingress has ingressClassName: nginx — TLS requires the nginx class
explain: Ingress TLS has two hard requirements candidates miss: the Secret must be type kubernetes.io/tls (generic Opaque is ignored) and it must be in the Ingress's own namespace — Kubernetes forbids cross-namespace secret references here. The fake-certificate symptom is the tell: the controller found no valid cert and fell back. The Service port list doesn't need 443; TLS terminates at the controller.

q: An Ingress should route /api to Service api and /web to Service web. Requests to /api/users reach the WRONG service. Both paths use pathType: Prefix. What is the likely cause?
options: The Services need identical selectors for path routing
Prefix paths cannot share a host; split them across two Ingresses
pathType: Prefix only matches the exact path, not subpaths

Prefix matching is longest-match-wins, so /api/users should hit api — the real cause is usually rule ORDER or an overlapping broader path (like /) listed first with an ImplementationSpecific controller that honors order
explain: Prefix semantics are longest-match, but controller behavior on overlapping paths (especially a catch-all / rule) varies — with ImplementationSpecific matching, ORDER can decide. The debug sequence: verify each backend Service works directly, then inspect the effective routing (controller logs / describe). The exam's Ingress questions are graded on these assembly details: class, pathType, backend name/port, TLS — verify each link in the chain.

q: No NetworkPolicies exist in the namespace and all pods communicate freely. You apply ONE policy selecting app: db with policyTypes: [Ingress] and a single ingress rule allowing traffic from app: web. What happens to db's egress traffic (e.g., its replies and its own DNS lookups)?
options: Egress to app: web is allowed but all other egress is denied
The policy is invalid — policyTypes must include both directions
Egress is unaffected — the policy only declares Ingress in policyTypes, so egress remains default-allow; only ingress not from app: web is denied
All egress is now blocked — applying any policy isolates the pod completely
explain: Isolation is per-direction: a pod becomes isolated for ingress only when a policy selects it AND lists Ingress in policyTypes. Egress stays default-allow unless a policy claims Egress too. So db can still reply, query DNS, and pull updates — but only app: web can initiate connections TO it. This directionality is the key mental model for every NetworkPolicy question.

q: The task says: 'Only pods labeled app: web may connect to pods labeled app: db on port 5432. Everything else to db is denied.' Which NetworkPolicy structure expresses this?
options: An Ingress resource with an allow-list annotation
A default-deny policy on app: web
podSelector: {app: web}, policyTypes: [Egress], egress: [{to: [{podSelector: {app: db}}]}]

podSelector: {app: db}, policyTypes: [Ingress], ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {app: web}}], ports: [{port: 5432}]}] — select db, allow ingress only from web pods on 5432; the mere presence of the policy denies all other ingress to db
explain: The pattern: select the DESTINATION pods (app: db), declare Ingress, whitelist the allowed source + port. Deny is implicit — any ingress not matching a rule is dropped once the pod is selected by any policy. Putting the selector on the source (web) would restrict web's ingress instead, which is the classic backwards-policy mistake.

q: You apply a 'default deny all ingress' policy (empty ingress rules selecting all pods) to lock down a namespace. Immediately, every app in the namespace breaks — even pods talking to Services in the SAME namespace. What did you forget, and what is the fastest triage?
options: Services bypass NetworkPolicy — the breakage must be unrelated
Empty ingress rules are invalid; the policy was never applied

DNS and return traffic — but the fastest triage is: delete the policy and confirm traffic recovers, proving the policy was the cause, then rebuild it rule by rule with the needed allows (including kube-dns on port 53)
The policy needs policyTypes: [Egress] too — ingress-only deny can't break same-namespace traffic
explain: A default-deny is a sledgehammer: it also blocks the DNS queries (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns) and health checks the apps depend on, so 'everything breaks' is the expected result of an incomplete deny. The exam-endorsed debug order: remove the suspect policy and confirm recovery (proves causation in seconds), then re-add minimal allows — DNS first, then the app's required peers — testing after each rule.

q: A NetworkPolicy selects app: api with policyTypes: [Egress] and one egress rule allowing DNS (port 53) to kube-dns. The api pods can resolve names but their HTTPS calls to an external payment API now fail. Why?
options: Egress policies cannot allow external traffic at all
DNS resolution implies egress works; the payment API must be down

The policy allows ONLY DNS egress — once a pod is selected with Egress in policyTypes, all egress not explicitly allowed is denied, so the HTTPS egress to the payment API needs its own rule (e.g., to the API's ipBlock on 443)
port 53 covers HTTPS as well; the rule is malformed
explain: Same directionality rule as ingress: claiming Egress makes all non-matching egress deny-by-default. DNS working is the red herring — it only proves the one allowed rule works. External egress needs explicit rules, typically to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: <payment-API-CIDR>}}] with ports: [{port: 443}]. Note ipBlock is for external IPs — it can't be mixed with podSelector in a single peer entry.

q: The task says: 'Allow the monitoring server at 203.0.113.10 to scrape metrics from all pods on port 9090.' Which NetworkPolicy peer expresses the external source?
options: from: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 203.0.113.10/32}}] with ports: [{port: 9090}] — ipBlock is the peer type for non-pod source IPs
External sources cannot be expressed; expose the pods via NodePort instead
from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {ip: 203.0.113.10}}}] — external IPs can be labeled as pods
from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {cidr: 203.0.113.10/32}}}]
explain: ipBlock is the NetworkPolicy peer for traffic from outside the cluster (or outside pod CIDRs): cidr: 203.0.113.10/32 pins a single IP. Remember its two constraints: it can't be combined with podSelector/namespaceSelector in the same from/to entry, and except: subnets can carve holes out of the block. The policy still needs podSelector: {} (or a label) to select the destination pods.

q: You need to let pods in namespace frontend call pods in namespace backend. The NetworkPolicy lives in namespace backend. How do you reference the client pods?
options: from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web, namespace: frontend}}}] — namespaces are pod labels
from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}, namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: frontend}}}] — combine both selectors in one peer to mean 'pods with this label IN namespaces with that label'
NetworkPolicies cannot allow cross-namespace traffic
Create the policy in the frontend namespace instead
explain: A single from/to peer can combine podSelector AND namespaceSelector — the peer matches pods satisfying the pod selector in namespaces satisfying the namespace selector. (The backend namespace itself needs the name: frontend label, or use kubernetes.io/metadata.name: frontend.) NetworkPolicy is namespaced to where the DESTINATION pods live, and cross-namespace allow is fully supported — it's one of the most-tested policy shapes.

q: A developer needs quick temporary access to a database pod's port 5432 from their laptop, without creating a Service. What is the fastest command, and what is its limitation?
options: ssh to the node and curl the pod IP
kubectl expose pod db --port=5432 --type=NodePort — creates a permanent Service
kubectl port-forward pod/db 5432:5432 — forwards localhost:5432 to the pod; it lasts only while the command runs and targets one specific pod
kubectl proxy — it forwards arbitrary pod ports
explain: kubectl port-forward pod/<name> <local>:<pod-port> is the instant dev-access tool: no manifest, no Service, working in seconds. Its limits are the point: single pod (not load-balanced), dies with the command, localhost-only by default. For anything durable or shared, create the Service — port-forward is a debugging shortcut, not architecture.

q: Pods in namespace team-a need to call a Service in namespace team-b. A NetworkPolicy in team-b selects the destination pods with ingress from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: client}}}]. The calls still fail. What is missing?
options: NetworkPolicy cannot span namespaces, so this can never work
The policy must be duplicated into team-a
The policy selects pods in team-b, but its from peer has no namespaceSelector — a bare podSelector only matches pods in the POLICY's own namespace (team-b), so team-a clients are still denied
Ingress rules only apply to external traffic, not cross-namespace
explain: The subtle scoping rule: within a from/to entry, podSelector alone matches pods in the policy's OWN namespace. Cross-namespace peers need namespaceSelector (alone or combined with podSelector). The fix is adding namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: team-a}} to the peer. The policy stays in team-b — it always lives with the pods it protects.

q: The task says: 'Expose the app to the internet with TLS termination and path-based routing to two Services.' You have a working ClusterIP Service per app. What is the minimal correct addition?
options: One Ingress resource with two path rules and a tls section (plus a confirmed installed Ingress controller with matching ingressClassName) — Ingress is the HTTP-routing + TLS-termination layer that sits in front of ClusterIP Services
Change both Services to type LoadBalancer — one per Service
A NetworkPolicy allowing ingress from 0.0.0.0/0
An ExternalName Service pointing at the internet gateway
explain: This is the canonical Ingress use case: L7 routing (host/path) plus TLS termination, fanning out to plain ClusterIP Services. Two LoadBalancers would work but cost two external IPs and can't do path routing. The checklist: controller installed, ingressClassName matches, pathType set on each path, backend service name + port correct, TLS Secret valid and same-namespace.

q: The task says: 'Don't send traffic to the pod until it's warm, but restart it if it deadlocks later.' Which two probes implement this, and what does each control?
options: Two livenessProbes — one with a long delay for warmup, one aggressive for deadlocks
readinessProbe for 'don't send traffic until warm' (it gates Service endpoints) and livenessProbe for 'restart if deadlocked' (it triggers container restarts) — they serve different masters
A startupProbe for both — it handles warmup and deadlocks
readinessProbe for both — failing readiness restarts the container
explain: The fundamental split: readiness gates TRAFFIC (failing readiness removes the pod from endpoints, no restart), liveness gates RESTARTS (failing liveness kills and restarts the container). 'Don't send traffic until warm' = readiness; 'restart if wedged' = liveness. Failing readiness never restarts anything — confusing the two is the exam's core probe trap.

q: You add successThreshold: 3 to a livenessProbe and the API server rejects the pod. Why?
options: The value must be a string, not an integer
successThreshold must be 1 for liveness and startup probes — the API enforces this; only readiness probes may use higher values
livenessProbes don't support successThreshold; use failureThreshold instead
successThreshold is not a valid probe field at all
explain: The API hard-requires successThreshold: 1 on liveness and startup probes — anything higher is rejected at validation. (It must be 1 because a probe that needs 3 consecutive successes to count as 'alive' would delay recovery detection.) Readiness probes may set it higher, e.g., requiring 2 consecutive successes before receiving traffic. When a probe manifest is rejected, check this field first.

q: A healthy app takes 45 seconds to boot. Its livenessProbe has initialDelaySeconds: 10 and periodSeconds: 5. The pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff despite the app being fine. What is happening, and what is the best fix?
options: Increase the CPU limit — slow boot means CPU starvation
The readiness probe is missing — add one
The image is corrupt — CrashLoopBackOff always means a bad image

The liveness probe fires during the 45s boot window, kills the still-starting app, and the cycle repeats — the #1 cause of CrashLoopBackOff on healthy apps. Fix: raise initialDelaySeconds past the boot time, or better, add a startupProbe that disables the liveness probe until the app is up
explain: Too-aggressive liveness probing is the classic self-inflicted CrashLoopBackOff: kubelet kills the container while it's still booting, the restart begins booting again, the probe kills it again. The modern fix is a startupProbe (failureThreshold × periodSeconds sized past the worst-case boot) — while it runs, liveness and readiness are disabled, then they take over. initialDelaySeconds alone works but is brittle guesswork.

q: An app's boot time varies wildly: 30 seconds normally, up to 4 minutes under load. Which probe configuration handles this safely?
options: livenessProbe with initialDelaySeconds: 240 — covers the worst case

A startupProbe with failureThreshold: 24 and periodSeconds: 10 (24 × 10s = 240s budget) — it gives the app up to 4 minutes to start without disabling protection afterward, then hands off to liveness/readiness
No probe — variable boot times can't be probed
readinessProbe with successThreshold: 24
explain: startupProbe exists for exactly this: failureThreshold × periodSeconds = maximum startup budget (here 240s). During that window liveness/readiness are held off; once the startup probe succeeds, normal probing begins. A fixed 240s initialDelaySeconds would delay failure detection for EVERY restart even when boot takes 30s — the startup probe adapts because it ends as soon as the app is actually up.

q: The app exposes no HTTP endpoint, but you can verify health by running /healthcheck.sh inside the container (exit 0 = healthy). Which probe type fits?
options: tcpSocket on the app's port — equivalent to running the script
An exec probe: exec: {command: ["/healthcheck.sh"]} — the probe runs the command in the container and exit code 0 means success
Probes can't run commands; use a sidecar instead
httpGet on port 8080 — all probes require HTTP
explain: Probes come in three flavors: httpGet (HTTP status 200-399), tcpSocket (port accepts connection), and exec (runs a command; exit 0 = healthy). exec is the answer when health is a script or a CLI check rather than a port. It's also the heaviest option — the command runs inside the container every period — so keep the script fast.

q: You run kubectl logs deploy/web and get: 'a container name must be specified for pod web-abc, choose one of: [app, sidecar]'. What happened and what is the fix?
options: The Deployment is broken — logs require single-container pods
Use kubectl logs --all-containers instead
The pod name must be used, not the Deployment name
