The pod has two containers, so kubectl can't guess — add -c: kubectl logs deploy/web -c app (or -c sidecar)
explain: kubectl logs needs -c <container> whenever a pod has more than one container — it refuses to guess. The deploy/web form works fine (it picks a pod), the missing piece is only the container name. On the exam, multi-container log tasks always hinge on -c; forgetting it costs a retry cycle.

q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs web-abc shows the CURRENT (just-started, still-booting) container's output, which reveals nothing. How do you see the logs from the container instance that actually crashed?
options: kubectl logs web-abc --all — it aggregates all instances
kubectl logs web-abc --previous — it shows the last terminated container instance's logs
Crashed container logs are lost; check the events instead
Wait for the next crash and run logs faster
explain: --previous (-p) is the CrashLoopBackOff essential: it fetches logs from the previous terminated instance — the one that holds the actual error — instead of the freshly restarted one. Pair it with -c for multi-container pods. The standard crash debug sequence: describe (exit code, events) → logs --previous (the error) → fix.

q: The task says: 'Inspect the running payment pod's filesystem and open connections WITHOUT restarting or disrupting it.' The image is distroless with no shell. What is the modern answer?
options: Copy the filesystem out with kubectl cp and inspect locally

kubectl debug with an ephemeral container (kubectl debug -it pod/payment --image=busybox --target=payment) — it attaches a troubleshooting container sharing the target's process namespace without touching the running container
Delete the pod and recreate it with a debug image
kubectl exec -it — it works on distroless images too
explain: kubectl debug --target launches an ephemeral container alongside (and sharing the process namespace of) the target container — full shell and tools, zero disruption to the running app. exec fails on distroless (no shell to exec), and recreating the pod destroys the state you're debugging. 'Troubleshoot without disrupting the pod' is the exam's cue for kubectl debug.

q: You run kubectl top pod and get 'error: Metrics API not available'. The pods are healthy. What does this mean?
options: The metrics-server isn't installed or isn't healthy in the cluster — kubectl top depends on the Metrics API, which metrics-server provides
kubectl top only works for nodes, not pods
The pods have no resource requests set, so there's nothing to report
You need -o wide for metrics output
explain: kubectl top is a Metrics API client — no metrics-server, no data. It's a cluster component, not something a developer installs on the CKAD (but you must recognize the error). Resource requests don't affect it, and top works for both pods and nodes when the API is present.

q: A pod was evicted and you need the timeline of what the cluster did and why. Which command gives the cluster-level event stream, newest last?
options: kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler
kubectl get pods -o wide — the AGE column is the timeline
kubectl describe node — it shows the eviction policy
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp (optionally -n <ns> or --field-selector) — events record scheduling, pulling, probing, eviction decisions with reasons and timestamps
explain: Events are the cluster's diary: Scheduled, Pulled, Started, Unhealthy (probe failures), Evicted — with reasons like 'The node was low on resource: memory.' Sorting by creationTimestamp gives the timeline; kubectl describe <pod> shows the same events scoped to one pod. Reading events before logs is the disciplined debug order: know WHAT the cluster did before asking the app WHY.

q: You apply a manifest using apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 for an Ingress and the API server rejects it as not found. The manifest worked two years ago. What happened?
options: extensions/v1beta1 was removed in modern Kubernetes — Ingress moved to networking.k8s.io/v1 long ago; check the current apiVersion in the docs (kubectl api-resources lists what's served) and update the manifest
Ingress was removed from Kubernetes entirely; use Gateway API only
The manifest needs kind: IngressV1 instead
The cluster lost the extensions API group in a network partition
explain: API deprecations are a tested CKAD topic: old beta versions (extensions/v1beta1 for Ingress/Deployments, etc.) are REMOVED in current releases, not just deprecated. The fix is the current apiVersion (networking.k8s.io/v1 for Ingress, apps/v1 for Deployments) with the current schema (note: networking/v1 made pathType required). kubectl api-resources shows exactly what your cluster serves.

q: A Helm chart from 2021 fails to install with 'unable to recognize "": no matches for kind "Deployment" in version "extensions/v1beta1"'. What is the underlying problem?
options: The chart's templates reference a removed API version — old charts hardcode extensions/v1beta1 (or apps/v1beta1); they must be updated to apps/v1 (and the values/schema adjusted)
Helm no longer supports Deployments
The cluster's Helm version is too new; downgrade Helm
The chart needs --api-versions flag on every install
explain: Same deprecation story through Helm: ancient charts template against dead API versions. The durable fix is updating the chart's templates to apps/v1 (checking for schema changes like the selector requirement). This is why 'check the chart's templates when install fails with no matches for kind' is a CKAD-level debugging reflex — the error names the exact dead version.

q: A pod is CrashLooping. Which investigation order wastes the LEAST time?
options: kubectl describe pod (exit code + events tell you HOW it died) → kubectl logs --previous (tells you WHY, from the crashed instance) → fix the cause — read the cluster's verdict before the app's story
kubectl exec into the pod and run the app by hand
Delete the pod immediately — a fresh pod usually fixes it
kubectl logs first, then guess at fixes and reapply until it works
explain: The disciplined order: describe gives you the exit code (137 = OOMKilled, 1 = app error) and the event trail (FailedMount, Unhealthy, BackOff); logs --previous gives you the crashed instance's actual error. Exit code first narrows everything: OOMKilled means memory, not code. Exec-ing into a CrashLooping pod races the restart loop, and deleting evidence before reading it is how you burn 20 exam minutes.

q: You run kubectl exec -it web-abc -- /bin/sh and land in the WRONG container (the logging sidecar, not the app). The pod has containers app and sidecar. How do you target the app container, and is there a way to make it the default?
options: kubectl exec -it web-abc -c app -- /bin/sh — -c selects the container; you can also set the kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container annotation on the pod to change the default
kubectl exec always picks alphabetically; rename the containers
Use --container=0 to pick the first defined container
exec cannot target a specific container; use kubectl debug
explain: -c <name> targets a specific container for exec, logs, and debug alike — without it kubectl picks the first container (or the annotated default). The kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container annotation sets the preferred default per pod. On multi-container exam tasks, -c is as reflexive as the namespace flag.

q: A pod's memory usage climbs steadily in kubectl top until it gets OOMKilled, then the cycle repeats after each restart. CPU is normal. What is the diagnosis, and what are the two possible resolutions?
options: The node is overcommitted — add more nodes

A memory leak in the application (usage grows unboundedly across restarts of the same workload pattern) — fix the leak in code, or as a stopgap raise the memory limit (and request) to extend the time between kills
The metrics-server is misreporting; ignore kubectl top
Normal behavior — Kubernetes restarts pods to clear memory; increase the liveness probe frequency
explain: Steadily climbing memory + periodic OOMKills = the leak signature: the app allocates and never frees, so every container instance marches toward the limit. The real fix is in the code; the operational band-aid is a bigger limit (keeping request ≤ limit). More nodes don't help — the pod would leak on any node. Recognizing the pattern from top + OOMKilled events is the observability skill the exam is actually testing.

q: Your team keeps 40 feature flags in a flags.env file (KEY=value per line). You need every flag as an environment variable in the app pods. What is the fastest correct way to build the ConfigMap, and how does the parser treat comments?
options: kubectl create configmap flags --from-env-file=flags.env — each line becomes its own key; blank lines are skipped and lines starting with # are treated as comments and ignored
kubectl create configmap flags --from-file=flags.env, then reference each flag with envFrom — --from-file stores the whole file under one key, so envFrom would inject a single variable
--from-env-file only works for Secrets, not ConfigMaps
There is no bulk import — write 40 env entries by hand
explain: --from-env-file parses KEY=value lines into individual keys — the bulk path for dotenv-style files. --from-file would store the entire file content under a single key named flags.env (right for mounting as a file, wrong for env vars). The #1 mix-up the exam plants is file→one key vs env-file→many keys; comments (#) and blank lines are ignored by the parser.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ConfigMap has a key named app.properties (with a dot). The app needs that value as the environment variable APP_PROPERTIES. Loading the ConfigMap with envFrom silently injects nothing for that key. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Dots are illegal in ConfigMap keys — recreate it as app_properties
envFrom handles dots fine; the app must be reading the wrong variable name

Dots are legal in ConfigMap keys but NOT in POSIX environment variable names, so envFrom silently skips the key — use an explicit env entry with name: APP_PROPERTIES and valueFrom.configMapKeyRef: {name: ..., key: app.properties} to rename it on injection
Switch to a Secret — Secrets allow dots in env var names
explain: The constraint is on env var names, not ConfigMap keys: dots are invalid in variable names, and envFrom skips such keys without error — a silent-drop trap. The explicit env + configMapKeyRef form maps any key to any legal variable name, which is the fix. Secrets have the identical constraint (the rule is about the variable name, not the source type), and dots are perfectly legal in ConfigMap keys.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You add an env: block directly under spec: in a Deployment's pod template, next to containers:. kubectl apply rejects the manifest. What is wrong?
options: env requires its ConfigMap to exist first — create the ConfigMap and the error clears
env is a container-level field — it must live under an individual container, not at the pod spec level; move it inside containers[0]
The Deployment needs spec.template.metadata.labels before env validates
env: must be written as envs: (plural) at the pod level
explain: The classic nesting trap: env, envFrom, ports, resources, and volumeMounts are all container-level fields. The pod spec level holds volumes, containers, securityContext, serviceAccountName, and the like. Putting env at pod level fails validation — move it under the specific container. The other options invent requirements that don't exist.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Each replica must include its own pod name in every log line for correlation, but the image is frozen — no code changes allowed. How do you inject the pod's name as an environment variable?
options: Hardcode the pod name in the Deployment manifest — every replica gets the same value anyway
Have the app query the API server at startup — the downward API cannot expose names
Set the variable from the container hostname — the hostname is always the pod IP
env: - name: POD_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}} — the downward API exposes pod fields as env vars with zero code changes
explain: The downward API's fieldRef exposes metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, status.podIP, and resource requests/limits as env vars (or files) — no code, no API calls, no RBAC. Replica pod names are generated (web-abc123-x), so hardcoding is impossible. The hostname IS the pod name by default, but the explicit env var is the reliable, exam-graded mechanism.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A monitoring agent in the pod must read the pod's labels from /etc/podinfo/labels as files, without granting the pod any RBAC access to the API. Which volume type does this?
options: A downwardAPI volume with items: [{path: "labels", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels}}] — it projects pod metadata as files, and needs no RBAC because the kubelet already holds the pod object
A ConfigMap volume with the labels copied in by hand at deploy time
An emptyDir — the kubelet writes pod labels there automatically
A Secret volume — pod labels are stored as Secrets
explain: The downwardAPI volume is the file-based sibling of fieldRef env vars: it projects metadata.name, labels, and annotations as files into the container. No RBAC is needed since the kubelet assembles the content locally. A hand-copied ConfigMap goes stale on every relabel; emptyDir and Secret volumes have nothing to do with pod metadata.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod needs ONE directory /etc/app-config containing: db.conf from ConfigMap db-cfg, tls.crt from Secret db-tls, and the pod's namespace from the downward API. Which volume type composes multiple sources into a single mount?
options: Three separate volumes mounted at three paths — one directory can never mix sources
An init container that copies from three separate mounts into an emptyDir

A projected volume with sources: [{configMap: {name: db-cfg}}, {secret: {name: db-tls}}, {downwardAPI: {...}}] — projected volumes merge configMap, secret, downwardAPI, and serviceAccountToken sources into one directory
A configMap volume — Secrets and downward API data can be embedded inside ConfigMaps
explain: projected is the union volume: one mount, multiple sources merged into a single directory. The init-container copy achieves the same result but is the manual reimplementation of what projected does natively — the exam wants the native type. You cannot nest a Secret inside a ConfigMap, and separate mounts defeat the 'one directory' requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod calls a cloud API that accepts Kubernetes service-account tokens, but requires tokens minted for audience 'storage.example.com' expiring after 10 minutes. The default mounted token is rejected. What do you configure?
options: automountServiceAccountToken: true plus a custom audience annotation on the pod — annotations can retarget the default token
A projected serviceAccountToken volume with audience: storage.example.com and expirationSeconds: 600 — projected tokens are audience-bound and short-lived, unlike the legacy auto-mounted token
Copy the default token and set its expiry with kubectl — token lifetime is client-controlled
Nothing — service-account tokens cannot carry audiences; use a cloud IAM key in a Secret instead
explain: Projected service-account tokens (projected → sources → serviceAccountToken) support audience and expirationSeconds — short-lived, audience-bound credentials, the modern pattern for workload-to-cloud auth. The legacy automounted token carries the cluster's default audience and long life, which is why the cloud API rejects it. Token expiry and audience are minted server-side; there is no kubectl edit for them.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A developer must debug the payments namespace: read pods, read pod logs, and create/delete pods — but must NOT touch Deployments or Secrets. Which RBAC construction grants exactly this?
options: A ClusterRole with verbs: ["*"] bound via a ClusterRoleBinding — simplest and covers the debugging needs
A RoleBinding alone referencing the developer — bindings imply the permissions they point at
The cluster-admin ClusterRole — debugging requires full access

A Role in namespace payments with rules on resources ["pods", "pods/log"] and verbs ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "delete"], bound to the developer with a RoleBinding — least privilege, namespace-scoped
explain: The least-privilege construction: Role (namespaced) + RoleBinding, with explicit resources — note pods/log is its own resource for log access — and explicit verbs. A ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding would grant it cluster-wide, the over-permissioning trap. A binding without a role references nothing, and cluster-admin for debugging violates every least-privilege principle the exam tests.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The cluster enforces Pod Security Standards. Your namespace must REJECT any pod that runs as root or is privileged. Which configuration does this?
options: Label the namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted — the built-in PodSecurity admission controller then rejects violating pods at creation time
Annotate each pod with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
Create a PodSecurityPolicy named restricted in the namespace
Set spec.securityLevel: restricted on the Namespace object
explain: PSS is enforced via namespace LABELS (enforce/audit/warn crossed with baseline/restricted), handled by the built-in PodSecurity admission controller — no custom resources needed. PodSecurityPolicy was removed in Kubernetes 1.25; the exam still dangles it as a trap for outdated study material. The labels go on the namespace, not the pod, and there is no spec.securityLevel field.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The hardening checklist says: 'the app must never gain more privileges than it starts with.' The container already runs as non-root, but the task still flags it. Which field completes the hardening, and what kernel mechanism does it use?
options: privileged: false — already the default, so there is nothing to do
capabilities: {drop: [ALL]} — dropping capabilities also blocks privilege escalation
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in the container securityContext — it sets the kernel's no_new_privs flag, so even a setuid-root binary inside the container cannot grant new privileges
runAsNonRoot: true — a non-root process cannot escalate by definition
explain: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false sets no_new_privs on the container's processes — the specific control for 'never gain more privileges.' privileged: false is indeed the default but doesn't set no_new_privs. Dropping capabilities is complementary hardening, not the escalation control. The dangerous misconception is the last option: a non-root process executing a setuid-root binary CAN become root without no_new_privs — exactly the escalation this field prevents.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Every new Deployment in namespace team-a pulls from the private registry, and developers keep forgetting imagePullSecrets in their pod specs. What is the durable one-time fix so no pod spec needs the field?
options: Put imagePullSecrets in the namespace annotations — the kubelet reads pull secrets from there

Create the docker-registry Secret once, then patch the namespace's default ServiceAccount: kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}' — every pod using that account inherits the pull secret automatically
Create the Secret in kube-system so it becomes global — Secrets are visible cluster-wide from there
There is no such fix — every pod spec must declare imagePullSecrets
explain: ServiceAccounts carry imagePullSecrets, and pods inherit their ServiceAccount's list automatically — patching default (or a custom account) fixes it once for the whole namespace. Namespace annotations do nothing for pull secrets. Secrets are namespace-scoped everywhere including kube-system — there is no 'global' namespace for them, the same scoping trap as mounting Secrets across namespaces.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A developer can still create pods, but creating a 4th ConfigMap fails: 'exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: configmaps=1, used: configmaps=3, limited: configmaps=3'. Pod creation is unaffected. What does this prove about the quota?
options: The quota is corrupt — quotas only track CPU and memory, never objects
ConfigMaps count against the pod quota — delete a pod to make room
The developer hit the namespace's default LimitRange, not a quota
ResourceQuotas can cap OBJECT COUNTS (count/configmaps: "3") independently of compute — this quota limits ConfigMap objects while leaving CPU/memory alone
explain: ResourceQuota tracks two families: compute (requests.cpu, limits.memory) AND object counts (count/configmaps, count/deployments.apps, pods, services, and more). This quota caps ConfigMaps at 3 while compute stays open — the fix is raising count/configmaps or deleting unused ConfigMaps. The first option states the exact misconception the error disproves; LimitRange sets per-container defaults/bounds, not namespace totals.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod requesting limits.memory: 4Gi is REJECTED at admission: 'maximum memory usage per container is 2Gi'. No ResourceQuota exists in the namespace. What enforced this, and where do you look?
options: A LimitRange with max: {memory: 2Gi} — LimitRange enforces per-container min/max bounds at admission, not just defaults; check with kubectl get limitrange
The node's allocatable memory — the scheduler rejected the pod
The container runtime's built-in default cap
A ResourceQuota — quotas also set per-container maximums
explain: LimitRange does two jobs: defaulting containers that omit resources, AND bounding them with min/max — violations are rejected at admission. The scheduler (which would leave the pod Pending, not reject it) and ResourceQuota (namespace aggregates, never per-container values) are the wrong layers. When a pod is REJECTED for size rather than left Pending, think LimitRange max.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The app needs every key from ConfigMap app-cfg AND every key from Secret db-creds as environment variables. Both define a key named DB_HOST. How do you load both sources without a collision?
options: envFrom accepts only one source — merge the ConfigMap and Secret into a single ConfigMap first

envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: app-cfg}}, {secretRef: {name: db-creds}, prefix: DB_}] — envFrom takes a list mixing both ref types, and prefix namespaces the Secret's keys so DB_HOST becomes DB_DB_HOST
List both refs with no prefix — on collision the Secret's value silently wins, which is fine
Run two containers, one per source — env vars can't be shared across sources
explain: envFrom is a list and each entry can independently be a configMapRef or secretRef, each with its own optional prefix — the cross-source version of the collision-avoidance pattern. Without the prefix, the later entry's DB_HOST silently overwrites the earlier one — a real production footgun the exam wants you to defuse. The list form exists precisely so sources can be mixed.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: An operator expects a Secret of type kubernetes.io/basic-auth, but yours is type Opaque with keys user and pass. The operator ignores it. What are the two problems?
options: Only the type is wrong — Opaque works as long as the keys are right
Only the key names are wrong — the type field is informational
Recreate it with kubectl create secret tls — the tls subcommand makes basic-auth Secrets

Both the type AND the key names: kubernetes.io/basic-auth requires exactly username and password keys — set type: kubernetes.io/basic-auth and rename the keys (stringData lets you write them in plain text)
explain: Typed Secrets are contracts: the type AND the key names both matter — tls demands tls.crt/tls.key, basic-auth demands username/password. Opaque imposes no key contract, which is why the operator ignores it. The fix is a manifest (or regenerate) with the right type and key names; stringData keeps it human-writable. There is no kubectl create subcommand for basic-auth — unlike tls and docker-registry, it must be written as YAML.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A Deployment references a ConfigMap that exists in prod but NOT in dev. In dev the pods fail to start. The app has built-in defaults and should start fine without the ConfigMap. Which field allows the pods to start when the source is missing?
options: Delete the env entry in the dev overlay — there is no optional mechanism
Set the ConfigMap immutable: false — missing ConfigMaps are then tolerated
valueFrom.configMapKeyRef.optional: true (also available on secretKeyRef and the envFrom ref forms) — the pod starts and the variable is simply left unset when the source is absent
Use envFrom instead of env — envFrom never fails on a missing ConfigMap
explain: optional: true tells the kubelet to tolerate a missing ConfigMap/Secret (or missing key) — the variable is left unset instead of blocking pod startup. It's the standard 'config exists in prod only' pattern. envFrom fails just as hard on a missing source without optional: true, and immutability has nothing to do with absence.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A database password rotates every 24 hours via an operator that updates the Secret. The app reads the password from an environment variable and fails auth after every rotation until someone restarts the pods. What is the durable fix?
options: Switch the app to read the password from a mounted Secret volume file — the kubelet refreshes projected Secret files in running containers (roughly every minute plus cache), so rotation is picked up without restarts; env vars are frozen at container start
Shorten the rotation interval so the resulting restarts happen on a schedule
Use configMapKeyRef instead of secretKeyRef — ConfigMap-backed env vars refresh live
Set the Secret immutable: true so it stops rotating
explain: The env-var freeze applies to Secrets exactly as it does to ConfigMaps: injected once at container start, never updated. Volume-mounted Secret (and ConfigMap) files ARE refreshed by the kubelet in live containers. For rotating credentials the app must read from the file (or watch it for changes) — not from env. Making the Secret immutable would break the rotation the security team requires.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Two containers in one pod — app as UID 1000, sidecar as UID 2000 — both need write access to a shared emptyDir. Files created by one are unreadable by the other. Which securityContext combination fixes group sharing without running as root?
options: privileged: true on both containers — privilege bypasses the permission problem

Pod-level fsGroup: 3000 plus runAsGroup: 3000 on both containers — fsGroup makes the kubelet chown mounted volumes to group 3000 (with the setgid bit so new files inherit it), and runAsGroup puts both containers' processes in that group
runAsUser: 0 on both containers — root bypasses all permission checks
Move to hostPath — emptyDir cannot be shared between different UIDs
explain: fsGroup is the volume-ownership control (kubelet chowns the volume to the group before containers start); runAsGroup puts each container's processes in that group. Together, UID 1000 and UID 2000 collaborate through group permissions — no root, no 777. The privileged/root options abandon the least-privilege posture, and emptyDir sharing across UIDs is routine with the right group setup.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A batch container writes gigabytes of temp files to its writable layer; on one node the disk fills and the kubelet evicts NEIGHBORING pods. Which resource constraint contains the disk hog?
options: An emptyDir sizeLimit — that caps one volume, not the container's writable layer and logs
Add disk capacity to the node — capacity planning, not a pod-level control
Raise the memory limit — disk usage counts against the memory limit

resources.requests/limits with ephemeral-storage (e.g., limits: {ephemeral-storage: 5Gi}) — the kubelet tracks the writable layer, logs, and emptyDir against it; requests reserve disk at scheduling time and breaching the limit evicts the pod
explain: ephemeral-storage is a first-class resource: requests reserve node disk for scheduling, limits trigger pod eviction when exceeded — covering the container writable layer, logs, and emptyDir together. sizeLimit only caps a single emptyDir, and memory limits don't see disk at all. This is the 'noisy neighbor on disk' control the exam expects developers to know.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: None of the 50 Deployments in namespace batch ever call the Kubernetes API, and editing every pod spec is impractical. How do you stop the service-account token from being mounted namespace-wide with a single change?
options: Delete the token path from the container images — the kubelet recreates it anyway
Set runAsNonRoot: true on the namespace — namespaces have no such field and it doesn't affect token mounting
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the default ServiceAccount — every pod using that account inherits the setting with zero pod-spec edits
Delete the default ServiceAccount — pods run fine without any identity
explain: automountServiceAccountToken is honored at both levels: the pod-spec form hardens one workload, the ServiceAccount-level form propagates to every pod using that account — the one-change hardening for a whole namespace. Deleting the default ServiceAccount breaks pod creation, and runAsNonRoot has nothing to do with token mounting.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A Dockerfile ends with ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"] and CMD ["--port=8080"]. The pod spec sets only args: ["--port=9090"]. What actually runs, and what is the general mapping rule?
options: /app/server --port=8080 — the Dockerfile always wins over the pod spec
--port=9090 runs as PID 1 with no entrypoint — args replaces both ENTRYPOINT and CMD
/app/server --port=9090 — pod spec command overrides Docker ENTRYPOINT and args overrides Docker CMD, each independently; setting only args keeps the image's ENTRYPOINT and replaces CMD
The pod fails validation — command and args cannot be combined with a Dockerfile CMD
explain: The mapping is command→ENTRYPOINT, args→CMD, and the pod spec wins on each independently. Setting only args keeps the image's ENTRYPOINT and swaps CMD — the standard 'same image, different flags per environment' pattern. The first option inverts the precedence; the second misunderstands args as replacing the entrypoint too.

q: A 3-node consensus cluster must start node-0 fully before node-1 begins (it bootstraps from node-0), and each node needs a stable network identity (db-0, db-1, db-2). Which workload provides both ordered startup and stable identity?
options: Three separate Deployments named db-0, db-1, db-2 — the manual way to get stable names

A StatefulSet fronted by a headless Service — StatefulSets create pods strictly in order (each ordinal only after the previous is Running and Ready) with stable names and stable DNS (db-0.db, db-1.db)
A Deployment with 3 replicas and a headless Service — Deployments start pods in parallel with random names
A DaemonSet — it runs one pod per node, in node order
explain: StatefulSet's contract: ordered creation (and ordered rolling updates), stable pod names, and stable per-pod DNS via the required headless Service (spec.serviceName). Deployments parallelize startup and randomize names — right for stateless, wrong for bootstrapping clusters. Separate Deployments are the manual reimplementation of what StatefulSet automates.

q: Each of 3 database replicas needs its OWN 10Gi persistent volume that stays bound to that replica across rescheduling. Hand-writing 3 PVCs won't scale to 30 replicas. What is the StatefulSet-native mechanism?
options: volumeClaimTemplates: [{metadata: {name: data}, spec: {accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce], resources: {requests: {storage: 10Gi}}}}] — the StatefulSet mints a dedicated PVC per pod (data-db-0, data-db-1, ...), each reattached to its own pod on reschedule
One shared PVC mounted by all replicas — PVCs are shareable by default
An emptyDir per pod — it survives rescheduling
A hostPath with the pod name in the path
explain: volumeClaimTemplates is the StatefulSet storage contract: one template, N per-pod PVCs with predictable names, sticky to their pod identity across rescheduling. A shared RWO PVC can't attach to multiple nodes and would corrupt a database; emptyDir dies with the pod. Per-replica durable storage is the core reason StatefulSets exist for databases.

q: You must roll a 5-replica StatefulSet to v2 but keep replicas 0-3 on v1 as the control group, updating only replica 4 first. Which updateStrategy setting expresses this partial rollout?
options: Pause the StatefulSet and delete pod db-4 by hand — the replacement comes up on v2
partition: 1 — the partition counts down from the highest ordinal, so 1 means only db-4 updates
StatefulSets cannot do partial rollouts — convert it to a Deployment
updateStrategy: {type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: {partition: 4}} — ordinals >= partition take the new template while lower ordinals stay; lowering the partition later rolls the rest
explain: partition is the ordinal cutoff: pods with ordinal >= partition update to the new template, lower ordinals stay put. partition: 4 on 5 replicas = only db-4 updates — the stateful canary. The exam tests the threshold direction: it is >= partition that moves, so partition: 1 would update db-1 through db-4, not just the last one.

q: Every node in the cluster — including nodes added next month — must run exactly one fluent-bit log collector. Which workload expresses this, and what happens when a node joins?
options: A Deployment with replicas set to the current node count — remember to update it whenever nodes join
A DaemonSet — the controller maintains one pod per matching node continuously; a new node automatically gets its pod, a removed node loses it
A static pod manifest copied to each node — the API server manages static pods as a workload
A CronJob that starts fluent-bit hourly on each node
explain: DaemonSet's contract is 'one pod per node,' maintained continuously — node joins and leaves are handled by the controller, which is why node-level agents (log collectors, monitoring daemons) are its textbook use. A Deployment can't track node membership; static pods are kubelet-managed and invisible to the API as a workload.

q: You try to change a Deployment's spec.selector.matchLabels from app: web to app: web-v2. The API server rejects the edit. Why, and what is the correct way to change the selector?
options: spec.selector is immutable after creation — the API rejects any change to it; the supported path is delete and recreate the Deployment (or use a new Deployment name for a blue/green cutover)
The new label doesn't exist on the pods yet — add it to the pod template first, then the selector change validates
Selectors can only be changed with kubectl edit, not kubectl apply
Change the Service's selector instead — Deployment selectors follow the Service
explain: The selector is the controller's identity anchor — changing it would orphan or adopt the wrong pods, so the API forbids it outright. Template labels must MATCH the selector, but the selector itself can never change. The supported path is recreate (accepting brief downtime) or a fresh Deployment for blue/green. The edit-vs-apply distinction is imaginary.

q: A data-import Job must NEVER run longer than 10 minutes — a stuck import once ran 6 hours burning budget. Which field enforces a global wall-clock timeout, and what happens at the deadline?
options: backoffLimit: 1 — that limits retry attempts, not runtime
ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600 — that cleans up 10 minutes AFTER the Job finishes
activeDeadlineSeconds on the pod template — it is a Job-level field, not a pod-template field
activeDeadlineSeconds: 600 on the Job spec — the controller terminates all pods and marks the Job Failed (reason DeadlineExceeded) when the deadline hits, even mid-retry
explain: activeDeadlineSeconds is the Job's wall-clock, measured from the first pod start: exceeding it kills the Job outright, regardless of retries remaining. It lives on the Job spec. backoffLimit counts attempts, not minutes; ttlSecondsAfterFinished is post-completion cleanup. The three Job time/count fields each answer a different question: how many tries (backoffLimit), how long total (activeDeadlineSeconds), how long to keep the corpse (ttlSecondsAfterFinished).

q: The nightly report CronJob must be paused for a two-week finance freeze — no runs, but the definition and its history must stay intact. What is the cleanest toggle?
options: Edit the schedule to a date in 2030 — the runs stop, technically
suspend: true on the CronJob spec — scheduled runs stop; flipping it back to false resumes; definition and history are untouched
Scale the CronJob to zero — CronJobs do not scale
Delete the CronJob and reapply it in two weeks — history is preserved in etcd
explain: suspend is the CronJob's pause button — declarative, reversible, and it keeps the run history for audit. Deleting loses history and risks manifest drift on reapply; editing the schedule is the hacky version of the same toggle. The exam wants the native field, not the workaround.

q: The 2 AM export CronJob was missed because the cluster was down 2:00-2:10. At 2:11 the controller starts the export anyway — but finance says a late run on the wrong data window is worse than no run. Which field prevents starting a schedule that is already too old?
options: startingDeadlineSeconds: 300 — if the scheduled time is more than 300s in the past when the controller notices, the run is counted as missed instead of started
activeDeadlineSeconds: 300 — that caps how long the export may run, not how late it may start
concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — that prevents overlapping runs, not late ones
Nothing — CronJobs never start missed schedules; the cluster clock must be wrong
explain: startingDeadlineSeconds is the 'too late to matter' cutoff: missed schedules older than the deadline are skipped rather than started late on recovery. The three CronJob time fields each answer a different question: when (schedule), how late is too late (startingDeadlineSeconds), how long may one run take (activeDeadlineSeconds). concurrencyPolicy governs overlap, not lateness.

q: The app drops in-flight requests on every rollout: SIGTERM arrives and the container exits instantly, but requests need 15 seconds to drain. Which lifecycle hook fixes this, and what must accompany it?
options: postStart with a sleep 15 — that delays startup, not shutdown
A longer liveness probe timeout — probes do not affect shutdown
preStop: {exec: {command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 15"]}} — it runs BEFORE SIGTERM, buying drain time; it must be paired with terminationGracePeriodSeconds >= 20 so the kubelet does not SIGKILL mid-drain
preStop alone is sufficient — the kubelet always waits for hooks to finish regardless of the grace period
explain: preStop executes before the TERM signal — the standard drain pattern is a sleep (or a /drain endpoint call) inside it. But the hook runs INSIDE the termination grace window: if terminationGracePeriodSeconds expires first, SIGKILL ends the drain. So the pair is hook + grace period sized to cover it. The last option states the trap: the grace period is a hard ceiling that hooks cannot extend.

q: A worker must flush its buffer to object storage on shutdown — the flush takes up to 60 seconds. With default settings, data is lost on every rollout. What do you set on the pod?
options: preStop: sleep 90 — the hook alone extends the shutdown window
activeDeadlineSeconds: 90 — that is a Job field, and it caps runtime rather than extending shutdown
Nothing — Kubernetes always waits for the app to exit cleanly on its own
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90 — extends the SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL window so the flush can complete; the app must actually trap SIGTERM and flush within it
explain: The grace period is the shutdown budget: SIGTERM, wait up to N seconds, then SIGKILL. The app has to USE it — Kubernetes cannot flush buffers for you, so the app must trap SIGTERM. A preStop hook cannot outlive the grace period, and the 'always waits' option states a comforting falsehood the exam loves to puncture.

q: Compliance requires production to ALWAYS run the exact bits that passed QA — tags like web:v2 can be overwritten upstream after QA signs off. What image reference makes the Deployment immune to tag mutation?
options: image: web:v2 with imagePullPolicy: Always — Always re-pulls, but still resolves the MUTABLE tag
image: web@sha256:<digest> — the digest pins exact image content; retagging upstream cannot change what this reference resolves to
image: web:v2.0.0-final-locked — longer, scarier tags cannot be overwritten
imagePullPolicy: Never — the node keeps whatever it first pulled
explain: Digests are content-addressed and immutable — web@sha256:abc... always resolves to the same bits, defeating the stale/mutated-tag trap at the reference level. imagePullPolicy: Always re-pulls but still follows the moving tag. When the requirement is 'exactly these bits,' the digest is the compliance-grade answer.

q: A pod needs (1) a database schema migration, then (2) a seed-data load — strictly in that order — before the app starts. How do you express the ordering?
options: List both as initContainers in order — init containers run SEQUENTIALLY in list order, each to completion before the next starts
List both as regular containers — containers start in parallel, so order is not guaranteed
One init container cannot run two steps — use two separate pods
Init container order is random — add sleep commands between them
explain: Init containers are the ordered gate: they execute strictly in list order, each must exit 0 before the next begins, and app containers never start until all succeed. Regular containers start in parallel. 'Migrate, then seed, then app' is the textbook multi-init example — and the reason init containers exist alongside the single 'wait for DB' use.

q: A cache sidecar writes to an emptyDir with no size limit; on one node the cache grew until the disk filled and the kubelet evicted NEIGHBORING pods. How do you contain the cache to its own pod?
options: Set resources.limits.memory on the sidecar — disk usage counts against the memory limit
Make the cache smaller in application code — Kubernetes cannot cap emptyDir
emptyDir: {sizeLimit: 1Gi} — the kubelet monitors the volume and evicts THIS pod if it exceeds the limit, protecting its neighbors
Switch to hostPath — it has automatic per-pod quotas
explain: sizeLimit gives an emptyDir a quota: exceeding it evicts the offending pod — the containment the scenario asks for, enforced by the kubelet's eviction manager against ephemeral storage. Memory limits don't see disk, and surrendering a platform control to application code is the non-answer. The evicted-this-pod-not-neighbors behavior is exactly the bulkhead you want.

q: A legacy app logs in a proprietary binary format, but the cluster's log pipeline only accepts JSON on stdout. Rebuilding the app image is not allowed. Which multi-container pattern solves this?
options: An init container that converts the logs — it exits before the app runs and cannot transform a live stream
An ambassador sidecar — that pattern proxies network connections, not log formats
Bigger resource limits — log formatting is not a CPU allocation problem
An adapter sidecar — a sidecar that reads the app's output via a shared volume and transforms it (binary to JSON on stdout), adapting the app to the platform's expectations
explain: The three sidecar patterns: sidecar (helper alongside), adapter (normalize/transform the app's output for the platform), ambassador (proxy outbound connections). Reformatting logs for the pipeline is the textbook adapter — it sits between the app's reality and the platform's contract. An init container can't touch a live log stream, and the ambassador pattern answers a networking question, not a data-format one.

q: An ML inference Deployment must land ONLY on nodes labeled accelerator: nvidia-t4. Which scheduling field expresses this simple node-label match?
options: tolerations — tolerations permit scheduling onto tainted nodes; they do not attract pods to labeled nodes
nodeName: nvidia-t4 — nodeName takes a node NAME, not a label, and pins the pod to one node with no failover
nodeSelector: {accelerator: nvidia-t4} — the pod schedules only on nodes carrying that label; the simplest node targeting
No field is needed — the scheduler detects GPU requests automatically
explain: nodeSelector is the exact-match node targeting: every listed label must be present on the node. nodeName pins to one specific node by name (brittle, no failover). Tolerations are the classic confusion — they allow scheduling onto tainted nodes but don't SELECT labeled ones. The scheduler never infers hardware placement without being told.

q: A Job's workers pull items from a shared Redis queue; the total item count isn't known up front. Workers should keep pulling until the queue is empty, then all exit and the Job completes. Which completions/parallelism shape is this?
options: completions: 10, parallelism: 3 — the fixed-count pattern; wrong when the total isn't known in advance

Leave completions unset with parallelism: 3 — the work-queue pattern: the controller runs 3 workers that pull from the queue and exit when it's empty; the Job completes once all pods have terminated with at least one success
completions: 3, parallelism: 3 — the Job completes after 3 pods succeed regardless of queue state
Jobs cannot share a queue — use a Deployment with a sleep loop
explain: The work-queue pattern: completions unset, parallelism = worker count. Workers coordinate through the external queue (each exits when it's empty), and the Job completes when all its pods have terminated with at least one success. The fixed-count pattern (completions: N) is for known work totals. This is the documented answer to 'process a queue of unknown length.'

q: You must record the team's Slack channel and the Jenkins build URL on every Deployment for the runbook — data operators read, but nothing should ever SELECT pods by it. Labels or annotations?
options: Labels — all operational metadata belongs in labels
Neither — put it in the container image tag where operators will see it
Annotations — non-identifying metadata (contacts, build URLs, descriptions) belongs in annotations; labels are for identification and selection, with strict syntax limits
A ConfigMap — operational metadata belongs in ConfigMaps, not on objects
explain: The labels-vs-annotations rule: labels identify and select (used by selectors, so they must be short, structured, DNS-safe); annotations carry arbitrary non-identifying metadata (URLs, contacts, timestamps, tool config). Build URLs and Slack channels are the textbook annotation examples. Stuffing URLs into labels breaks selector syntax and pollutes selection — the trap the first option sets.

q: The app must register itself with the service-discovery sidecar the moment it starts, before serving traffic. Code changes are frozen. Which hook does this, and what happens if the hook fails?
options: preStop — it runs at shutdown, far too late for registration
An init container — it runs before the app exists and cannot register a running app
postStart hooks run asynchronously and their failures are ignored — safe for best-effort tasks only
postStart: {exec: {command: ["/register.sh"]}} — it fires after container creation; if the hook fails, the container is killed and restarted per restartPolicy
explain: postStart fires after the container starts (concurrently with the entrypoint — ordering against the main process isn't guaranteed). Critically, a failing postStart KILLS the container — it is not best-effort, which is the dangerous misconception the third option states. For 'act on start without code changes' it's the native answer; init containers can't reach a running app.

q: A pod runs app + log sidecar with no per-container memory limits. The sidecar leaks memory, yet the kernel OOM-kills the APP container, not the sidecar. What is the fix, and why did the app die?
options: Set a memory limit on the sidecar container — without per-container limits the pod is one memory pool and the OOM killer scores by usage-vs-request (the app can outscore the actual leaker); a sidecar limit makes the leaker breach its OWN cap and get restarted alone
Raise the app's memory request — requests are scheduling guarantees, not kill protection
Move the sidecar to its own pod — sidecars cannot have resource limits
Nothing can be done — the OOM killer's choice is random
explain: Per-container limits are bulkheads: the container that breaches its own limit is the one restarted. Without them, the pod shares one cgroup budget and the kernel's OOM scoring (usage relative to request) can pick the app over the true leaker. The fix is always the same shape: limit the untrusted/noisy container so its failure is contained. Limits are per-container by design — the third option denies the actual API.

q: You rolled the web Deployment v3 -> v4 -> v5. v5 is broken — but v4 had a data-corruption bug, so you must return to v3 specifically, skipping v4. Which command does this?
options: kubectl rollout history deploy/web to list revisions, then kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=3 — jumps directly to v3's ReplicaSet instead of stepping back one
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web — that returns to v4, the immediately previous revision: the wrong target
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=latest-minus-2 — no such flag exists
Delete the Deployment and reapply the v3 manifest — works, but forfeits the rolling (zero-downtime) rollback
explain: rollout undo defaults to the previous revision; --to-revision jumps to any retained revision (subject to revisionHistoryLimit). history shows the revision-to-change mapping so you pick the right one. Deleting and reapplying works but causes downtime — the whole point of keeping ReplicaSet history is the zero-downtime rollback, which the last option throws away.

q: You are about to apply a hand-edited 400-line manifest to the production Deployment and want to see EXACTLY what will change before anything is touched. Which command previews the change without applying it?
options: kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f web.yaml — validates locally but prints no diff
kubectl diff -f web.yaml — computes the server-side three-way diff against the live object, prints it, applies nothing, and exits non-zero when differences exist
kubectl get deploy web -o yaml and eyeball it against the file — the manual, error-prone version
kubectl rollout history deploy/web — shows past changes, not pending ones
explain: kubectl diff is the pre-apply preview: it shows precisely what apply would change, changing nothing. --dry-run only validates. On the exam, 'show me what would change before I commit' is always diff — it's the careful-engineer answer that prevents the 400-line surprise, and in CI its non-zero exit on differences makes it a gate.

q: You need a Deployment manifest for web with 3 replicas as a starting file — no editor session, no cluster changes. Which one-liner generates it?
options: kubectl apply -f web.yaml --dry-run — requires the file to exist first; it cannot conjure one
kubectl run web --image=web:v2 --replicas=3 — modern kubectl run creates a bare pod only, and --replicas was removed from it
kubectl create deployment web --image=web:v2 --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml — renders the manifest to stdout/file without persisting anything
There is no generator — write the 40 lines from memory
explain: --dry-run=client -o yaml turns any create/expose/autoscale command into a manifest generator: correct apiVersion, selector, and template skeleton with zero cluster impact, ready to refine. The kubectl run option is the outdated-docs trap — run no longer makes Deployments. This generator is the fastest path to a valid starting file under exam time pressure.

q: Traffic spikes: the web Deployment must go from 3 to 8 replicas RIGHT NOW, without editing any files. Which command does this, and what is the gotcha with the manifest on disk?
options: Edit web.yaml and apply — the only supported path; there is no imperative scale
kubectl rollout restart deploy/web — restarts pods but does not change the count
Scaling is permanent and rewrites web.yaml automatically
kubectl scale deploy/web --replicas=8 — updates the live object immediately; but web.yaml on disk still says 3, so the next apply -f would revert the emergency scale (declarative drift)
explain: kubectl scale is the imperative fast path — instant, no file edit. The gotcha is declarative drift: the on-disk manifest still says replicas: 3, so a later apply -f silently reverts your emergency scale. The disciplined habit is scale now, then update the file (or re-apply with 8) so declared state matches reality. The exam loves this two-step.

q: The web Deployment swings between idle and 10x traffic daily. You need 2-10 replicas driven by CPU at 70% utilization. Which command creates this, and what prerequisite must the containers satisfy?
options: kubectl scale deploy/web --replicas=10 --auto — no such flag exists

kubectl autoscale deploy/web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70 — creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler; containers MUST set resources.requests.cpu, because utilization is computed as actual usage divided by request
The HPA works without requests — it computes utilization against limits
Set replicas: 10 permanently — simpler and equivalent
explain: HPA scales on utilization = usage / request — with no CPU request the denominator doesn't exist and the HPA cannot compute (it refuses to act). The requests requirement is the #1 HPA exam trap, tying autoscaling back to resource sizing. A permanent 10 replicas is the expensive non-answer; there is no --auto flag on scale.

q: An HPA targets 70% CPU with min 2, max 10. Load rises slowly; at 4 replicas the average utilization sits at 69%. What does the HPA do, and what mechanism prevents flapping?
options: It scales to 5 immediately — any upward movement triggers scale-up
It scales down to 2 — below target means over-provisioned
It reacts only to memory — CPU is ignored by the HPA
Nothing yet — 69% is below the 70% target (desired = ceil(4 x 69/70) = 4); and stabilization windows delay scale-down after spikes so brief dips don't yo-yo the replica count
explain: HPA acts on the target math: desiredReplicas = ceil(current x (currentUtil/targetUtil)) = ceil(4 x 69/70) = 4, so it holds. Anti-flap comes from the stabilization windows — notably the scale-down delay — so a brief dip after a spike doesn't immediately shed replicas. The exam wants the formula, not vibes: below target with the math rounding to current = hold.

q: You must upgrade the payments chart such that ANY failure automatically restores the previous release — no manual rollback step, no half-broken state left behind. Which Helm flag gives you this transactional upgrade?
options: helm upgrade --force payments ./chart — force recreates resources aggressively; it is the opposite of safe
helm rollback --auto — no such flag exists
Run helm upgrade, then helm rollback manually if you notice a failure — the manual version of what should be automatic
helm upgrade --atomic payments ./chart — on failure Helm automatically rolls back to the previous release (it implies --wait so Helm actually observes the outcome)
explain: --atomic makes the upgrade transactional: failure triggers automatic rollback to the prior revision, and the implied --wait means Helm watches long enough to judge success. It's the exam's 'all-or-nothing upgrade' answer. --force is the dangerous cousin — it bulldozes resources rather than protecting state. The manual rollback is what --atomic automates away.

q: Install the api chart as release api-v2 into the staging namespace, creating the namespace if it is missing. Which single command does this?
options: helm install api-v2 ./chart --namespace staging --create-namespace — the namespace flags the exam plants as the 'namespace not found' trap
kubectl create namespace is mandatory first — Helm cannot create namespaces
helm install api-v2 ./chart — installs into the current kubeconfig namespace (often default), not staging
helm install api-v2 ./chart --namespace staging — fails with 'namespace not found' when staging doesn't exist
explain: --create-namespace (with --namespace) is the one-command path: Helm creates the namespace, then installs into it. The bare --namespace form requires the namespace to already exist — the exact failure the last option describes. Installing without --namespace lands the release in whatever namespace kubectl points at, the classic wrong-namespace surprise.

q: After a messy upgrade you need (1) the EFFECTIVE values Helm used and (2) the actual manifests it applied. Which two commands give you inputs and outputs?
options: helm get values api-v2 (effective values: chart defaults + -f files + --set, merged) and helm get manifest api-v2 (the rendered Kubernetes YAML that was applied)
helm show values api-v2 — that shows the chart's DEFAULTS, not what this release used
kubectl get deploy -o yaml — shows live cluster state, not Helm's inputs or rendered output
helm history api-v2 — shows the revision list, not values or manifests
explain: get values = the merged inputs for THIS release; get manifest = the rendered output it applied. The show-vs-get confusion is the planted trap: show values reads the chart (defaults), get values reads the release (effective). When debugging 'why did it deploy THAT,' effective values plus rendered manifest is the diagnostic pair.

q: A helm upgrade failed halfway. helm list shows the release as failed, and a second upgrade errors about the release being in a bad state. What is the diagnosis and the recovery?
options: Delete the namespace and reinstall — the only way to clear a failed release
helm rollback api-v2 — rolls the FAILED release back to its last good revision, clearing the failed state; use helm history to pick the revision
helm upgrade --force — force does not clear failed release state
Wait ten minutes — failed releases self-heal automatically
explain: A failed upgrade leaves the release in failed/pending state; helm rollback returns it to the last deployed revision and clears the state — the standard recovery, and the failure-case application of release rollback. Deleting the namespace is the nuclear option that loses history; failed releases never self-heal. The exam tests whether you reach for rollback before rebuild.

q: The chart needs the ENTIRE contents of app.conf (multiline, special characters, no YAML structure) as values.configData. --set mangles the newlines. Which flag injects the file's raw content cleanly?
options: --set configData=$(cat app.conf) — shell interpolation mangles newlines and needs heroic escaping
-f app.conf — -f expects a VALUES YAML file, not raw config content
--set-file configData=./app.conf — reads the file's raw bytes into the value, preserving newlines and special characters
Paste the content into --set with \n escapes — brittle and error-prone
explain: --set-file is the file-content injector: raw bytes become the value, no shell mangling, no YAML parsing. --set passes through shell expansion and comma/quote parsing — the classic mangled-config trap. -f parses its file as values YAML, which a raw .conf isn't. For 'this whole file becomes one value,' --set-file is the native answer.

q: Staging and prod overlays deploy the SAME base, and every resource name must be prefixed per environment (web becomes staging-web) without editing the base. Which transformer does this, and what happens to internal references?
options: commonLabels — labels don't rename resources
Rename everything in the base by hand per environment — and chase every reference yourself
namePrefix only renames Deployments — Services keep their old names and break
namePrefix: staging- — prepends to every resource name, and Kustomize rewrites cross-references (Service selectors and the like) to match the new names automatically
explain: namePrefix (and nameSuffix) rename all resources in the overlay, and Kustomize's reference tracking updates the internal wiring so a Service's selector still finds its Deployment. That's what makes it safe — unlike hand-renaming, where every reference is yours to chase. The third option states the fear the transformer was built to eliminate.

q: Your prod overlay sets namespace: prod on all resources. Apply fails: 'namespaces "prod" not found'. Why doesn't the declaration create it?
options: The namespace: transformer only SETS the namespace field on resources — it never creates the namespace object; create it (kubectl create namespace prod) or add a Namespace resource to the kustomization
Apply with -f instead of -k — -f creates namespaces, -k doesn't
Kustomize cannot set namespaces — remove the field and set it per-manifest
Overlays can't target namespaces that don't exist yet — deploy the base first
explain: namespace: is a field-setter, not a provisioner — the #1 Kustomize 'but I declared it!' trap. The namespace must exist beforehand: imperative create, or a v1/Namespace entry in resources:. This mirrors the Helm --create-namespace lesson: declaring a target namespace never conjures it. The -f-vs--k distinction is about manifest building, not namespace provisioning.

q: You want the canary (v2) to receive ONLY requests carrying header X-Beta: true, with everything else staying on v1. Can a native Kubernetes Service express this routing?
options: Yes — add a header selector to the Service spec
Yes — sessionAffinity: ClientIP routes by request header
Yes — create two Services with the same ClusterIP and split by header
No — native Services route by label selector and distribute randomly; header/cookie-based routing needs an Ingress with canary annotations or a service mesh
explain: The native canary splits traffic by replica count only — Services have no Layer-7 awareness, no header selectors, and no shared-ClusterIP tricks. Header-based routing is Ingress-annotation or mesh territory. The exam tests this boundary deliberately: know what the built-in primitives CANNOT do, so you don't design an impossible task and burn the clock.

q: Blue (v1) and green (v2) Deployments run with labels app: web, version: blue|green. One Service fronts them. Which single field performs the cutover from blue to green?
options: The Deployments' version labels — change them and the Service follows automatically
The Service's spec.selector: change version: blue to version: green — endpoints swap atomically to the green pods; rollback is the reverse edit
The Service's clusterIP — traffic follows the virtual IP
Scale blue to 0 — that is the cutover mechanism
explain: The blue/green cutover IS the selector flip: one field, atomic endpoint swap, instant rollback by flipping back. Changing Deployment labels orphans pods from the Service — the Service selector is the steering wheel, not the labels. Scaling blue to zero works but destroys the instant-rollback property, which is the whole point of keeping both environments live.

q: A Deployment has replicas: 5, maxSurge: 30%, maxUnavailable: 30%. During the rollout, how many pods above desired may exist, and how many may be unavailable?
options: 2 extra, 2 unavailable — percentages round UP to whole pods
1.5 pods each way — Kubernetes allows fractional pods during rollouts
1 extra, 1 unavailable — percentages resolve against desired replicas and round DOWN to whole pods (30% of 5 = 1.5 -> 1)
Percentages are invalid for these fields — only integers are accepted
explain: Surge/unavailable percentages resolve against desired replicas and round DOWN: 30% of 5 = 1.5 -> 1 extra, 1 unavailable. This is why small replica counts with percentages behave nearly like integers — and why 25% of 3 rounds to 0 unavailable (a stricter guarantee than it looks). The fields accept both integers and percentage strings; the rounding rule is the tested detail.

q: Three engineers rolled the web Deployment this week. rollout history shows bare revisions with no record of who changed what. How do you attach a human-readable note to each future revision?
options: Edit the revision numbers by hand — revisions are controller-assigned and immutable
Keep a separate wiki — history cannot carry notes
kubectl annotate deploy/web kubernetes.io/change-cause="Bump to v2 for CVE fix" — the annotation is recorded per revision and shown by rollout history
kubectl apply --record — the supported modern flag that stamps every change
explain: The kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation is surfaced by rollout history — the audit trail for 'who changed what.' (--record, which once set it automatically, is deprecated/removed, so the manual annotate is the current practice — the last option names the outdated path as the trap.) Revisions are controller-assigned; you annotate the Deployment and the controller carries the annotation into the revision record.

q: In a bandwidth-constrained edge cluster, pulling the new 4GB image takes 12 minutes. Every rollout is marked Failed (ProgressDeadlineExceeded) even though the image eventually pulls fine. Which field fixes this?
options: progressDeadlineSeconds: 1200 (or higher) — the 600s default assumes no single step takes longer than 10 minutes without observable progress; slow pulls need a longer progress budget
backoffLimit — that is a Job field, not a Deployment field
activeDeadlineSeconds — that caps total pod lifetime; it acts in the wrong direction here
Shrink the image — good engineering, but the exam asks for the control that matches the deadline to the environment
explain: progressDeadlineSeconds is the 'no progress' tripwire — a 12-minute pull shows zero observable progress for 12 minutes, tripping the 10-minute default. Raising it matches the deadline to the environment's reality. backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds belong to Jobs; shrinking the image is virtuous but doesn't answer 'which field.'

q: Your CI pipeline runs kubectl rollout status after each deploy, but a stuck rollout hangs the pipeline forever. How do you bound the client-side wait so CI fails fast instead?
options: progressDeadlineSeconds — that marks the Deployment failed server-side but does not bound the CLI's watch
Run rollout status in the background and hope — the pipeline still hangs
kubectl rollout status deploy/web --timeout=5m — the command exits non-zero after the timeout instead of blocking indefinitely, so CI can fail the build and alert
Timeouts cannot be set — rollout status always waits forever by design
explain: --timeout bounds the client-side watch — essential in automation so a wedged rollout fails the pipeline instead of hanging the runner. progressDeadlineSeconds is the server-side tripwire; both matter, but only --timeout answers 'bound the CLI wait.' This CI-hardening detail is exactly the kind of operational sharpness the exam rewards.

q: Security review demands to see the EXACT manifests a chart will produce before it touches the cluster. Which command renders them fully locally with your values?
options: helm show values ./chart — shows the chart's defaults, not rendered manifests
helm template myapp ./chart -f prod-values.yaml --set image.tag=v2 — renders all templates locally to stdout; nothing is sent to the cluster
helm install --dry-run — also renders, but still talks to the cluster and can behave differently with lookup functions
kubectl apply --dry-run=client — needs the rendered YAML as input first
explain: helm template is the pure-local renderer — no cluster connection, the security-review path for 'show me exactly what this chart creates.' --dry-run is close but still contacts the API server (and fails without one). The exam distinction: template = local preview, dry-run = server-validated preview. For a review gate with no cluster side effects, template is the answer.

q: You must expose an Oracle database running OUTSIDE the cluster at 10.0.5.20:1521, so pods can reach it via the stable in-cluster DNS name oracle-db. Which construction does this?
options: A Service with no selector plus a hand-written Endpoints object named oracle-db listing 10.0.5.20:1521 — the Service gets a ClusterIP and DNS name, and kube-proxy routes to your manual endpoints
A normal Service with a label selector — selectors only match pods, never external IPs
An Ingress — Ingress routes HTTP, not raw TCP to an external database
An ExternalName Service with the IP address — ExternalName takes a DNS name, not a raw IP
explain: Selector-less Service + manual Endpoints is the 'external backend behind a Service abstraction' pattern: pods get stable DNS and a virtual IP, and the backing address can change without touching clients. Selectors match pods only, which is why the normal path fails here. ExternalName is the sibling pattern, but it requires a DNS NAME (CNAME) — not a raw IP.

q: The app must reach the managed database at db.prod.example.com (outside the cluster) via the in-cluster name postgres. Which Service type does this, and what does its DNS return?
options: A ClusterIP Service with clusterIP set to db.prod.example.com — ClusterIPs are IPs, not names
type: ExternalName with externalName: db.prod.example.com — DNS for postgres returns a CNAME to db.prod.example.com; no ClusterIP, no proxying, no selector
A NodePort Service — it exposes node ports, it doesn't alias external DNS
A headless Service — it returns pod IPs, which don't exist for an external host
explain: ExternalName is a pure DNS alias: no virtual IP, no kube-proxy rules — queries for postgres.<ns>.svc.cluster.local return CNAME db.prod.example.com. It's the complement to the manual-Endpoints pattern: ExternalName for external DNS names, manual Endpoints for external IPs. The other types all assume pod backends.

q: You run kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 — targeting the Service instead of a pod. Which backend actually serves your requests?
options: All backends round-robin — port-forward load-balances exactly like the Service
The Service's ClusterIP itself — port-forward proxies through kube-proxy's rules
One specific backing pod — port-forward picks a single pod behind the Service and pins to it for the command's lifetime; there is no load balancing
It fails — port-forward only accepts pod names, never Services
explain: kubectl port-forward targets ONE endpoint: given a Service it selects a single backing pod and forwards to it — no balancing, for the life of the command. If that pod dies, the forward breaks. It's a debugging shortcut, not a traffic path — which matters when your 'test through the Service' only ever exercises one replica.

q: Clients reach the app through a cloud LoadBalancer, and the app rate-limits by client IP — but it only ever sees NODE IPs, so one abusive client gets a whole node blocked. What is the fix?
options: sessionAffinity: ClientIP — that gives sticky routing, not source-IP preservation
Change the Service to ClusterIP — internal-only, and irrelevant to external source IP
Add more replicas — replica count doesn't change which IP the app observes
Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on the Service — traffic is only routed to pods on the node that received it, skipping the SNAT hop and preserving the real client source IP
explain: The default Cluster traffic policy SNATs external traffic through kube-proxy, masking client IPs; Local preserves the source IP by routing only to node-local pods (trade-off: load spreads only across nodes that have pods). This is THE answer whenever 'the app needs the real client IP' behind a LoadBalancer or NodePort. sessionAffinity is the classic confusion — it pins routing but preserves nothing.

q: Two game-server replicas listen on RANDOM ports chosen at startup. Clients must discover both the pod IPs AND their current ports via DNS. Which Service feature enables port discovery?
options: Name the Service ports (name: game) — Kubernetes publishes SRV records (_game._tcp.web.default.svc.cluster.local) carrying the port numbers alongside the A records
Rely on A records — they carry IPs only, never ports
Use a headless Service — it publishes pod IPs but no port information
Hardcode the ports — random ports cannot be discovered, so fix them
explain: Named ports generate SRV records: DNS answers with both the host and the port — the discovery mechanism for dynamic ports. A records alone carry only IPs. This is why the exam cares about port NAMES: they're not cosmetic, they drive SRV generation. Hardcoding defeats the dynamic-port design the scenario requires.

q: An Ingress has path: /api with pathType: Prefix. Which requests match: /api, /api/, /api/users, /apiversion?
options: All four — Prefix is a plain string prefix
/api, /api/, and /api/users — but NOT /apiversion: Prefix matches on PATH ELEMENTS, so /api matches itself and everything beneath it, but /apiversion is a different first element
Only the exact /api — that describes Exact, not Prefix
/api/ and below only — /api itself does not match its own prefix
explain: The official Prefix rule is element-wise: /api matches /api, /api/, /api/users — but NOT /apiversion. 'It's a string prefix' is the exact misconception the Ingress documentation warns against. This element rule is a favorite exam precision test because the wrong mental model (plain string matching) fails silently in production routing.

q: An Ingress routes shop.example.com and api.example.com. Requests to any OTHER host get the controller's generic 404 page, but the task requires them to reach a custom sorry Service. Which field catches requests that match no rule?
options: Another rule with host: "*" — wildcard hosts are not a thing in Ingress rules
A / Prefix rule with ImplementationSpecific matching — still scoped to its own host; unknown hosts fall through
spec.defaultBackend: {service: {name: sorry, port: {number: 80}}} — the Ingress-wide catch-all for requests matching no rule, including unknown hosts
A second Ingress with no hosts — multiple Ingresses merge unpredictably and won't reliably catch the fallthrough
explain: defaultBackend is the Ingress-wide catch-all: no rule matched (unknown host or unmatched path) goes to this Service. A / Prefix rule only covers paths under its own host — unknown hosts still fall through it. This is the 'graceful custom 404' mechanism straight from the Ingress spec, and the exam's answer to 'handle everything else.'

q: You set the deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx annotation, but the cluster's controller ignores the Ingress. spec.ingressClassName is empty. What is wrong?
options: The annotation value should be nginx-ingress, not nginx — the value isn't the problem
Annotations remain the only mechanism — the controller must be broken
IngressClass names are case-sensitive — capitalize it to Nginx
Modern controllers match spec.ingressClassName — the annotation is legacy and ignored by class-aware controllers; set ingressClassName: nginx
explain: The class moved from annotation to spec field in networking.k8s.io/v1: controllers watch IngressClass objects and match spec.ingressClassName. The old annotation is silently ignored by class-aware controllers — the manifest looks right but nothing acts on it. This is the 'Ingress exists, controller ignores it' variant of the missing-controller failure, and the exam loves the old-docs trap.

q: HTTPS to shop.example.com serves the site, but browsers show a certificate name warning. The Ingress tls section references Secret web-tls; its type (kubernetes.io/tls) and namespace are verified correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: tls.hosts lists api.example.com while the rule serves shop.example.com — the controller cannot match the cert to the requested host and falls back; tls.hosts must include the actually served host
Port 443 is missing from the Service's ports — TLS terminates at the controller, so backend Services stay on plain HTTP ports
The Ingress needs ingressClassName: nginx — TLS works on any controller that implements it
Browsers always warn on Kubernetes-terminated TLS — this is expected behavior
explain: The tls.hosts-to-rule-host binding: the controller selects the certificate by SNI/host match — a cert for api.example.com presented to shop.example.com clients triggers the name-mismatch warning. With type and namespace already verified, the host binding is the remaining link. The port-443 option is the persistent misconception: TLS terminates at the Ingress controller, never at the backend Service.

q: One Ingress must route shop.example.com to svc-shop and api.example.com to svc-api — both over HTTPS, each with its own certificate. What is the correct structure?
options: Two Ingress resources — a single Ingress cannot carry two hosts

Two rules with different host: values and their own backend Services, plus a tls: LIST with one entry per host (each with its hosts: and secretName:) — Ingress fans out by host and path in one resource
Path-based routing with the hosts ignored — hosts are the fan-out key here, not paths
One tls entry with a single secretName covering both — spec.tls is a list, not a singleton
explain: Ingress rules fan out by host AND path within a single resource, and spec.tls is a list — each entry maps hosts to its Secret. Two Ingresses would work but the exam asks for the single-resource shape; the singleton-tls option misreads the list as singular. This is the standard multi-tenant TLS fan-out, tested as a YAML-assembly task.

q: You must apply a default-deny-ingress policy to EVERY pod in namespace lockdown — including pods created next month. Which selector matches all current and future pods, and what completes the deny?
options: List every pod name in the selector — future pods won't be covered
Omit podSelector — it is a required field
podSelector: {} with policyTypes: [Ingress] and empty ingress rules — the empty selector matches all pods in the policy's namespace; claiming Ingress with no allow rules denies all ingress
A namespaceSelector — that selects namespaces in from/to peers, not the policy's target pods
explain: podSelector: {} means 'all pods in this policy's namespace' — the namespace-wide default-deny shape, future-proof by construction. Empty ingress rules plus Ingress in policyTypes = deny all ingress (default deny is just an empty allow list). The namespaceSelector option confuses peer matching (sources) with target selection — a different axis entirely.
