q: API pods expose metrics on a port NAMED metrics — the number changes per build. The NetworkPolicy must allow the monitor to reach the metrics port without hardcoding a number that rots. How?
options: Hardcode the current number and update the policy every build — the toil the question asks you to avoid
ports: [{port: metrics}] — the port field accepts a NAMED port, resolved against the target pods' container port names, so it tracks the port across builds
ports: [{port: 9090}] and hope the number never changes — hope is not a policy
Use an ipBlock for the monitor — unrelated to expressing the port
explain: The port field is an IntOrString: give the container port's NAME and the policy follows it even as the number changes — the same 'names over numbers' principle behind DNS SRV records. Hardcoding the number is the toil trap that breaks on the next build. Named ports in policies are the durable, exam-grade answer.

q: Lock down namespace api with ONE policy: default-deny ALL ingress and egress, then allow ONLY ingress from frontend pods on 8080, egress to kube-dns on 53, and egress to the payments API at 203.0.113.50/32 on 443. Which shape expresses this?
options: podSelector: {app: api}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress], ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {app: frontend}, namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: frontend}}}], ports: [{port: 8080}]}], egress: [{to: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}, namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: kube-system}}}], ports: [{port: 53, protocol: UDP}, {port: 53, protocol: TCP}]}, {to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 203.0.113.50/32}}], ports: [{port: 443}]}]
Two separate policies — ingress and egress cannot be mixed in one policy
policyTypes: [Ingress] only — that leaves egress wide open, violating the requirement
Allow 0.0.0.0/0 egress — simpler but violates 'ONLY these destinations'
explain: One policy CAN claim both directions — policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] with both rule sets; everything unlisted is denied. The egress side composes both peer types: namespace+pod selectors for kube-dns (note DNS needs BOTH UDP and TCP 53 — the classic half-open DNS trap) and ipBlock for the external API. The 'can't mix' option invents a limitation; the open-egress options fail the stated requirement.

q: Sticky sessions via sessionAffinity: ClientIP work, but users get rebalanced to different pods after about 3 hours even mid-session. Which field tunes this, and what is the default?
options: The 3-hour timeout is fixed — stickiness cannot be tuned
The liveness probe's timeoutSeconds — probes don't govern affinity
Recreate the Service hourly — the pin resets on Service updates, not on a timer
sessionAffinityConfig: {clientIP: {timeoutSeconds: 3600}} — the stickiness TTL, defaulting to 10800s (3h); raising it extends the pin
explain: ClientIP affinity entries expire after timeoutSeconds (default 10800 = 3h) — the 'mysterious 3-hour rebalance' has a name and a knob, nested under sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP and only meaningful with sessionAffinity: ClientIP. The other options invent immutability or blame unrelated fields; the exam wants the exact field path.

q: A Service of type LoadBalancer stays <pending> forever on your on-prem cluster, while the same manifest gets an IP in seconds on a cloud cluster. What is missing on-prem?
options: Cloud provider credentials in kubeconfig — the cluster, not your client config, provisions the LB
An Ingress — LoadBalancer Services don't require one
A load-balancer implementation (e.g., MetalLB) — the type only REQUESTS an external LB; something must provision it, and bare metal runs nothing for it by default, so it pends
Change the type to NodePort — that's a workaround, not the diagnosis
explain: LoadBalancer is a request, not a mechanism — cloud providers satisfy it via their controller; bare metal needs an implementation like MetalLB (or manually assigned IPs). <pending> with no errors is the tell: nobody is listening for the request. NodePort is a valid workaround but the exam asks for the diagnosis: the type needs an implementer.

q: Create a ClusterIP Service named web exposing Deployment web on port 80, forwarding to container port 8080 — without writing YAML. Which command does this?
options: kubectl run web --image=web:v2 --expose --port=80 — modern kubectl run makes a bare pod, and --expose was removed; it creates no Service
kubectl create service nodeport web --tcp=80:8080 — that creates a NodePort Service, not ClusterIP
Services can only be created from YAML — there is no imperative path
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080 — generates the Service from the Deployment's selector; the type defaults to ClusterIP
explain: kubectl expose is the workload-to-Service generator, inheriting the selector from its target. --port is the Service port, --target-port the container port — the imperative form of the port/targetPort mapping. The kubectl run option is the outdated-docs trap (--expose is gone); the nodeport variant answers a different question than asked.

q: A Cassandra cluster uses a headless Service for peer discovery, but new pods can't find peers that are still STARTING (not yet Ready). Which Service field publishes not-ready pods in DNS?
options: publishNotReadyAddresses: true — headless Service DNS then includes all backing pods regardless of readiness, so peers discover each other during bootstrap
sessionAffinity: ClientIP — stickiness has nothing to do with DNS publication
Weaken the readiness probe so pods become Ready earlier — that corrupts the readiness signal
Switch to a ClusterIP Service — it load-balances; it doesn't publish individual pod IPs at all
explain: Even headless DNS lists only Ready pods by default — fatal for quorum systems where peers must find each other BEFORE anyone is ready. publishNotReadyAddresses: true publishes every backing pod's A record. It's the standard Cassandra/Kafka/ZooKeeper-on-Kubernetes setting, and 'peers can't bootstrap' is the exam's cue for it.

q: An Ingress backend specifies port: {name: http}, but the controller reports the port not found. The Service manifest has port: 80 with no name. What is wrong?
options: Ingress backends only accept port numbers — names are invalid there
The Service's port entry needs name: http — a backend port NAME resolves against the Service's port NAMES, not its numbers; add the name or reference port: {number: 80}
Rename the Service itself to http — Service names don't resolve ports
The name must match the CONTAINER's port name — it resolves against the Service's port name
explain: port: {name:} in an Ingress backend looks up the Service's port entry BY NAME — an unnamed port 80 never matches 'http'. Either name the Service port or use port: {number: 80}. The near-miss is the container-port option: it's the Service port name that matters here (naming consistently across Service and container is good hygiene, but the lookup is against the Service).

q: Two NetworkPolicies both select app: db. Policy A allows ingress from app: web on 5432. Policy B allows ingress from app: monitor on 9090. After applying both, can web reach 5432 AND monitor reach 9090?
options: No — the second policy overwrites the first; only one policy may select a pod
No — only the alphabetically-first policy takes effect
Yes — NetworkPolicies are ADDITIVE: the effective ruleset is the union of every policy selecting the pod; there are no deny rules, only allow lists
Only if the policies are merged into one — the API rejects overlapping selectors
explain: The additive model is the keystone: every policy selecting a pod contributes its allow rules; isolation = 'selected by at least one policy,' allowed = 'matched by at least one rule.' There is no rule priority, no overwrite, no deny — 'default deny' is simply an empty allow list. The other options import firewall rule-ordering mental models that don't apply to NetworkPolicy.

q: You write a peer as from: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 10.0.0.0/8}, podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}] and the API server rejects the policy. Why?
options: The CIDR is too broad — /8 ranges are rejected by validation
ipBlock only works in egress rules — it works in both directions
The field should be ipBlocks (plural) — no such field exists
ipBlock cannot be combined with podSelector/namespaceSelector in the SAME from/to entry — they are mutually exclusive peer types; split them into two separate entries (the union is additive)
explain: The API validation rule, stated plainly: one peer entry takes EITHER ipBlock OR selectors, never both — the exam's favorite 'why was my policy rejected' syntax trap. The fix is two entries in the from/to list, whose union is additive. There is no CIDR-size restriction; the constraint is purely the peer-type exclusivity.

q: The /healthz endpoint requires an Authorization: Bearer <token> header; without it returns 401. The readiness probe keeps failing with 401s. How do you pass the header from the probe?
options: httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080, httpHeaders: [{name: Authorization, value: "Bearer <token>"}]} — probes support custom headers natively
Probes cannot send headers — expose a second, unauthenticated health endpoint
Put the token in the URL query string — works, but leaks the token into access logs
Switch to a tcpSocket probe — it performs the HTTP handshake including headers
explain: httpGet.httpHeaders is the native answer — name/value pairs sent with every probe request. The query-string workaround leaks secrets into logs and event strings; tcpSocket only opens a TCP connection (no HTTP at all). Note the token lives in the pod spec — fine for a health-check token, not for real credentials.

q: The app serves its health endpoint over TLS at https://:8443/healthz with a self-signed certificate. The httpGet probe fails the TLS handshake. Which field makes the probe speak TLS?
options: Change the probe port to 443 — the port number doesn't select TLS; the scheme does
httpGet: {scheme: HTTPS, port: 8443, path: /healthz} — scheme defaults to HTTP; HTTPS switches the probe to TLS (the kubelet does not verify the serving cert for probes)
Probes cannot do TLS — use an exec probe with curl -k instead
httpGet follows redirects, so probing the HTTP port is enough — the kubelet does not switch schemes on redirect
explain: scheme: HTTPS is the TLS switch for probes — and the kubelet skips certificate verification for probes, so self-signed certs don't break them. The port-443 option confuses addressing with protocol: TLS is negotiated by scheme, not by using 443. The exec-with-curl workaround is what you do when you don't know the field exists.

q: The SLO requires a deadlocked container to be restarted within 30 seconds of the deadlock. The liveness probe uses periodSeconds: 10. What failureThreshold meets the SLO, and what is the worst-case detection time?
options: failureThreshold: 30 — that yields ~300s detection, ten times the budget
successThreshold: 3 — rejected by the API on liveness probes (must be 1), and it governs marking healthy, not detecting failure
failureThreshold: 3 — worst-case detection is approximately failureThreshold x periodSeconds = 3 x 10s = 30s, exactly the budget
initialDelaySeconds: 30 — that only delays the FIRST probe; it doesn't bound steady-state detection at all
explain: Worst-case failure detection is approximately failureThreshold x periodSeconds — the formula that turns probe tuning into SLO math. 3 x 10s = 30s meets the budget exactly (in production you'd add margin rather than ride the edge). successThreshold is the validation trap from the probe API rules, and initialDelay only affects startup, never steady-state detection.

q: The liveness probe calls /ready, which checks the database. During a 30-second DB failover, EVERY app pod restarts simultaneously — turning a blip into a full outage. What is the design error, and the fix?
options: Increase the liveness timeout — a longer blip still causes the same mass restart
Remove all probes — flying blind is worse than the current failure mode
The DB failover is the real problem — the probes are correctly configured

Liveness must test the APP itself (is this container deadlocked?), not its dependencies — move the DB check to the readiness probe: DB down means pods go unready (traffic stops) but containers survive; liveness stays a local self-check
explain: The cardinal probe-design rule: liveness = 'is THIS container dead' (restart helps); readiness = 'should this pod get traffic' (includes dependencies). Probing dependencies from liveness converts external blips into mass restarts — the cascading-failure pattern. Failing readiness merely removes endpoints; the pods ride out the blip and recover with zero restarts.

q: You need the last 200 lines from the app container, each prefixed with its timestamp, without streaming. Which command does this?
options: kubectl logs deploy/web -c app --tail=200 --timestamps — tail bounds the output to 200 lines, timestamps prefixes each with RFC3339 time; without -f it exits
kubectl logs deploy/web -c app -f — follows forever; the opposite of a bounded dump
kubectl logs deploy/web --tail=200 — still needs -c on a multi-container pod
kubectl logs deploy/web -c app --since=200 — --since takes a duration (e.g., 5m), not a line count
explain: The log-flag trio: --tail=N (last N lines), --timestamps (prefix times), -f/--follow (stream). The --since option is the unit trap: it's time-bounded (--since=5m), while --tail is line-bounded. 'Last N lines with timestamps' is exactly this flag pair — and -c remains mandatory on multi-container pods.

q: An error is sporadic across 12 web pods. You need to grep the app container's logs from ALL of them at once, with each line tagged by pod. Which command?
options: Loop over kubectl get pods and call logs per pod — the manual version of what the selector flag does
kubectl logs deploy/web -c app — the deploy/ shorthand picks a single pod, not the fleet
-l doesn't work with kubectl logs — selector flags are get-only
kubectl logs -l app=web -c app — fans out across every matching pod, multiplexing the stream with each line prefixed by its pod name
explain: kubectl logs -l <selector> is the 'grep the fleet' command: every matching pod's logs, multiplexed, pod-name-prefixed. The deploy/ shorthand picks ONE pod — the trap for anyone assuming it aggregates. -c is still required for multi-container pods; the selector composes with the container flag rather than replacing it.

q: You're investigating yesterday's eviction, but kubectl get events shows nothing older than an hour. Where did yesterday's events go?
options: Events are permanent — you must be querying the wrong namespace
kubectl get events only shows warnings — add --all to see historical ones
Events expire — etcd retains them about 1 hour by default (tunable cluster-side); yesterday's timeline is gone unless an external log aggregator captured it
No event means no eviction happened — the pod must have been deleted, not evicted
explain: Events are ephemeral by design (default ~1h TTL in etcd) — they're a live troubleshooting stream, not an audit log. The lesson: read events DURING the incident for the timeline, and rely on cluster logging/monitoring for post-mortems. There is no --all resurrection flag; once the TTL passes, the events are simply gone.

q: Pods on node-1 can't reach the cluster DNS IP, but the kubelet is healthy. You suspect the node's iptables and have no SSH access. How do you get a shell ON the node?
options: kubectl exec into a pod on the node — that stays in the pod's network namespace; host iptables are invisible there
kubectl debug pod/... — that debugs pods, not nodes
Nodes can't be inspected without SSH — escalate to the cluster admin
kubectl debug node/node-1 -it --image=busybox — creates a privileged debug pod bound to that node with host namespaces; chroot /host to inspect the node's filesystem and iptables
explain: kubectl debug node/... is the node-shell escape hatch: a privileged pod scheduled onto the node with host PID/network namespaces, chroot /host for the node's filesystem. Exec into a workload pod never leaves the pod's namespaces, so host-level state stays invisible. This is the 'suspect the node, not the pod' tool — the escalation step when pod-level debugging exonerates the workload.

q: You attached an ephemeral debug container to a production pod. When you're done, can you remove just the debug container?
options: No — ephemeralContainers are append-only for the pod's lifetime: they can't be removed, restarted, or image-swapped while the pod lives; the debug container stays until the pod is recreated
Yes — kubectl delete ephemeralcontainer/<name> removes it cleanly
Yes — edit the pod spec and delete the ephemeralContainers entry
It removes itself when you detach — detach only closes your session
explain: The ephemeral-container contract: once added, no removal, no updates, no restarts — the API forbids mutating them, and pod specs are largely immutable anyway. Detaching just ends your session. Operationally they're cheap and safe to leave idle, but you can't tidy them away without recreating the pod — plan debug sessions accordingly.

q: Which command lists the api pods' memory usage sorted highest-first, so you can spot the top consumers?
options: kubectl top pod --sort-by=cpu -l app=api — sorts by CPU, not memory
kubectl get pods -l app=api --sort-by=.status.startTime — sorts by age, not usage
top can't filter by label — it can; -l works fine
kubectl top pod -l app=api --sort-by=memory — sorts the metrics table by memory, descending
explain: kubectl top accepts --sort-by=cpu|memory plus label selectors — the 'who's eating the node' one-liner (metrics-server required). The label-denial option invents a limitation; top is a proper Metrics API client, not just a pretty printer. Sorting by the right resource is the difference between finding the leak and admiring the table.

q: The app wrote /tmp/dump.hprof (a binary heap dump) inside pod web-abc, and the pod may be evicted soon. Which command copies it to your machine intact?
options: kubectl logs web-abc — logs are stdout/stderr, not arbitrary files
kubectl exec -it web-abc -c app -- cat /tmp/dump.hprof > dump.hprof — works for text but terminal encoding mangles binary files
kubectl cp web-abc:/tmp/dump.hprof ./dump.hprof -c app — the file shuttle: pod:/path to ./local (reverse direction uploads); -c selects the container
kubectl cp only uploads local-to-pod — it works in both directions
explain: kubectl cp is the byte-preserving file shuttle: pod:/path → ./local downloads, ./local → pod:/path uploads, -c picks the container on multi-container pods. The exec-and-redirect workaround corrupts binary content through terminal encoding. For 'get that file out before the pod dies,' cp is the exam's answer — logs are for streams, cp is for files.

q: Every rollout burns the FULL 30-second grace period even though the app could exit in 2 seconds — deploys crawl. The container runs a shell script as PID 1 with no trap. What is happening?
options: Increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds — that makes shutdown slower, not faster
Add a preStop hook — preStop doesn't fix ignored SIGTERM handling
This is normal — all pods take the full grace period to terminate

PID 1 ignores signals with default dispositions unless it installs handlers — the shell script never traps SIGTERM, so the kubelet waits out the whole grace period then SIGKILLs; fix by trapping SIGTERM or exec'ing the app so IT is PID 1
explain: The PID-1 signal trap: PID 1 doesn't get default signal behavior — a shell script as PID 1 without a trap silently ignores SIGTERM, and every rollout burns the full 30s. The fix is signal handling in the app or the exec form so the real app is PID 1. Longer grace periods worsen it; 'this is normal' normalizes a real, fixable bug.

q: Node maintenance must never leave fewer than 2 of the 3 web replicas available, but drains keep taking down 2 at once. Which object enforces the availability floor during voluntary disruption?
options: A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 2 (or maxUnavailable: 1) selecting app: web — kubectl drain respects PDBs and will block rather than evict pods that would violate the budget
replicas: 3 — replica count doesn't constrain voluntary disruption
A NetworkPolicy — it governs traffic, not eviction
Cordon the node first — cordon only stops NEW scheduling; it protects nothing during a drain
explain: PDBs guard VOLUNTARY disruption (drains, upgrades): minAvailable/maxUnavailable makes drain wait or block instead of violating the floor. They can't stop involuntary failures — a kernel panic takes what it takes — which is the voluntary/involuntary line the exam draws. Cordon is the classic confusion: it marks unschedulable but evicts nothing and protects nothing.

q: You must OS-patch node-2: stop new pods from scheduling there AND gracefully move existing pods elsewhere. Which single command does both?
options: kubectl cordon node-2 — only marks the node unschedulable; existing pods stay put

kubectl drain node-2 --ignore-daemonsets — cordons the node AND evicts its pods gracefully (honoring grace periods and PDBs); the flag skips DaemonSet pods, which are per-node by design and can't move
kubectl delete node node-2 — removes the object; pods go down without graceful eviction
kubectl uncordon node-2 — the exact opposite of what's needed
explain: drain = cordon + evict: it marks the node unschedulable, then gracefully evicts pods (SIGTERM, grace periods, PDBs honored). cordon alone is half the job — the classic 'I cordoned, why are pods still there' confusion. The DaemonSet flag matters because per-node pods can't relocate, so drain would otherwise block on them forever.

q: Patching on node-2 is done. How do you return the node to scheduling service?
options: kubectl drain node-2 again — that keeps it drained
Delete the node and let it rejoin — unnecessary surgery for a flag flip
kubectl uncordon node-2 — clears the unschedulable mark; the scheduler can place pods there again
Wait ten minutes — drained nodes auto-return on a timer
explain: uncordon reverses the scheduling block from cordon/drain — the close-out step of the maintenance dance (drain → work → uncordon). There is no auto-return; a drained node stays unschedulable until uncordoned, which is the entire explanation for the 'patched but still empty' mystery.

q: The app writes request logs to /var/log/app/requests.log (a file), and kubectl logs shows nothing useful. Why, and what are the two idiomatic fixes?
options: Increase --tail — tail can't show what was never captured
Mount the log file via a ConfigMap — unrelated to log capture
kubectl logs --file — no such flag exists
kubectl logs only returns the container's stdout/stderr — file logs bypass it entirely; fix by logging to stdout (the container-native way) or adding a sidecar that tails the file to its own stdout
explain: The container-logging contract: the kubelet captures stdout/stderr; anything written to files is invisible to kubectl logs. The two fixes are the platform's answers — stdout-first (preferred), or the tail-sidecar adapter that bridges file logs to stdout. This is why 'log to stdout' is container gospel, and the exam tests whether you know exactly where the boundary lies.

q: The app exposes gRPC health checking on port 9090 and no HTTP endpoint. Which probe type checks its health natively, without protocol translation hacks?
options: grpc: {port: 9090, service: myservice} — the native gRPC probe, speaking the gRPC health protocol directly (service name optional)
httpGet on port 9090 — gRPC is not HTTP/1.x REST; httpGet fails against it
tcpSocket on port 9090 — only proves the port accepts connections, not that the service is healthy
An exec probe running grpcurl — works, but reinvents the first-class probe type
explain: The grpc probe type speaks the gRPC health-checking protocol natively, with an optional service name for the health service. tcpSocket is the shallow version — port open does not equal healthy. The exec/grpcurl workaround functions but the exam wants the first-class field, completing the probe-type taxonomy: httpGet, tcpSocket, exec, grpc.

q: App boot time varies from 30 to 90 seconds. The readinessProbe uses initialDelaySeconds: 120 — safe, but after every routine restart the pod sits trafficless for the full 120s even when boot took 35s. What is the more efficient construct?
options: Lower initialDelaySeconds to 30 — risks failing readiness during slow boots

A startupProbe with failureThreshold x periodSeconds covering 120s — it ENDS as soon as the app is actually up (35s boot -> traffic at ~35s), then hands off to readiness; initialDelaySeconds always waits the full fixed delay
initialDelaySeconds is the only boot control — accept the wasted 85 seconds
Remove the readiness probe — then traffic hits a cold app
explain: The adaptivity difference: initialDelay is a fixed blind wait paid on EVERY start; a startupProbe exits early on success — fast boots get traffic fast, slow boots still get their full budget. This is the 'stop paying the worst-case tax on every restart' optimization, and the exam's preferred answer for variable boot times.

q: A pod sits Pending; describe shows '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.' There are no quota errors. What does this mean, and what are the two remedies?
options: The cluster is out of pod slots — that's a 'too many pods' message, not this one
The image can't be pulled — that surfaces as ImagePullBackOff, a different pod phase
The pod's CPU request exceeds free allocatable CPU on every node — the scheduler cannot place it; remedies: lower the request to fit available capacity, or add capacity (larger or additional nodes)
Delete the pod — Pending pods can never schedule once they've failed placement
explain: 'Insufficient cpu' is the scheduler's capacity verdict: existing requests plus this pod's request exceed each node's allocatable CPU. It's a REQUESTS (scheduling) problem, not a limits/throttling (runtime) problem. The two outs are smaller requests or more capacity — and the exam distinguishes this from quota rejections (admission-time failures) and image failures (different phases and events).

q: Your manifest uses a beta API version and you want the API SERVER to fully validate it — admission, quotas, unknown fields — without persisting anything. Which dry-run mode does this, and how does it differ from the other mode?
options: kubectl apply --dry-run=client — validates only against the local schema, with no server knowledge
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f web.yaml — the object goes through full API-server validation (admission chain, quotas, dropped fields) but is not persisted; client mode only checks local schema
There is only one dry-run mode — there are two, client and server
Apply it and delete on failure — the reckless path that the question asks you to avoid
explain: The two dry-run modes: client = local schema check only (catches typos, misses admission/quota/dead APIs); server = full API-server validation without persistence (catches 'rejected by LimitRange/quota/unknown apiVersion'). For 'will the cluster ACCEPT this,' server is the answer — it's the validate-before-apply discipline, and kubectl diff uses server dry-run under the hood.

q: You run kubectl create configmap app-conf --from-file=./conf/ where ./conf/ holds app.yaml, db.yaml, and a nested subdirectory certs/tls.crt. Which keys does the ConfigMap get?
options: One key per FILE in the top directory — app.yaml and db.yaml, each named by its basename; the nested certs/ subdirectory is skipped because --from-file does not recurse
A single key named conf holding the whole directory as one blob
Keys app, db, and certs/tls.crt — subdirectories are recursed with path-style key names
--from-file only accepts a single file, never a directory
explain: --from-file on a directory creates one key per file, keyed by basename — and it never descends into subdirectories. The single-key option describes --from-file=<one file> (key = filename), while --from-env-file is the KEY=value parser. For nested trees, flatten them or create the ConfigMap from a manifest.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container sets env: - name: DB_HOST value: db.internal, then - name: DB_URL value: "postgres://$(DB_HOST):5432/app", then - name: PRICE value: "$$(5)". How does the kubelet expand these at container start?
options: No expansion happens — $(...) is passed through literally and the app must expand it
$(DB_HOST) expands to db.internal at container start, and $$(5) collapses to a literal $(5) — doubled dollars are the escape for a literal dollar sign
$(DB_HOST) expands only if DB_HOST is defined BEFORE DB_URL in the list — later definitions are invisible to earlier entries
Expansion happens live on every read, so changing DB_HOST later would update DB_URL too
explain: The kubelet expands $(VAR) references once at container start; unresolved references are left unchanged, and $$ is the escape hatch for a literal $. Definition order in the env list doesn't matter, and like all env vars the values are frozen at start — there is no live re-expansion.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You want the container to see its OWN CPU request in millicores as the env var CPU_REQUEST_M. Which valueFrom form does this?
options: fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu} — fieldRef cannot reach resource values
No env mechanism exposes requests — the app must query the API server
resourceFieldRef: {containerName: app, resource: requests.cpu, divisor: 1m} — resourceFieldRef exposes a container's own requests/limits as env vars, and divisor: 1m renders CPU in millicores
A downwardAPI volume is the only way — resourceFieldRef doesn't exist
explain: resourceFieldRef is the resource sibling of fieldRef: containerName picks which container, resource names requests.cpu/limits.memory, and divisor controls units (1m = millicores, 1Mi = mebibytes). fieldRef handles metadata (name, namespace, podIP); resourceFieldRef handles the container's own resource fields.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You must hand-write the imagePullSecret for the private registry as YAML. Which type and key does the kubelet require for it to actually be used on pulls?
options: type: Opaque with keys username and password — the kubelet reads those directly
type: kubernetes.io/basic-auth with a .dockercfg key — basic-auth is the registry type
Any type works as long as the Secret is named regcred — the kubelet sniffs the content
type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson with a single key .dockerconfigjson holding the JSON auth blob — exactly what kubectl create secret docker-registry generates
explain: Pull secrets are typed: the kubelet only honors kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (key .dockerconfigjson). Opaque or basic-auth Secrets are silently ignored for image pulls — the same 'type is a contract' lesson as TLS and basic-auth Secrets. When in doubt, generate with kubectl create secret docker-registry and read back the YAML.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: One debugging pod needs its service-account token, but every other pod in the namespace must not mount one. The default ServiceAccount already has automountServiceAccountToken: false. How do you grant the token to just the one pod?
options: Set automountServiceAccountToken: true in that pod's spec — the pod-level field overrides the ServiceAccount-level setting for that pod alone
Impossible — the ServiceAccount setting is absolute for all pods using it
Create a second ServiceAccount with automount true — no pod-level field exists
Set it in the container's securityContext — that's where token mounting is controlled
explain: The field exists at both levels and the pod spec wins for that pod: SA-level false plus pod-level true mounts the token on exactly one workload. The inverse (SA true, pod false) hardens one workload. securityContext has no token-mounting field — that's the nesting distractor.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The regcred pull secret exists in namespace team-a. A pod in team-b references imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}] and fails with ImagePullBackOff. The credentials are valid. Why?
options: Pull secrets are cluster-scoped — team-b can't see it, so use a ClusterSecret (which doesn't exist)
Secrets are namespace-scoped — team-b cannot reference team-a's Secret; create an equivalent regcred in team-b (or sync it with tooling)
imagePullSecrets must reference the Secret by UID, not by name
Cross-namespace pull secrets require the Secret type to be Opaque
explain: No cross-namespace Secret references exist anywhere — not in volumes, env, or imagePullSecrets. The fix is duplicating the Secret per namespace (kubectl get secret --export is gone; get -o yaml and reapply, or use a sync tool). The name resolving fine in team-a is what makes this a namespace-scoping trap rather than a credential problem.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The task says: 'Drop all capabilities from the app container, then add only NET_BIND_SERVICE.' You put the capabilities block under the pod's securityContext and the API server rejects the manifest. Why?
options: Capabilities can't be dropped at all — they're kernel-granted and immutable
The syntax is capabilities: {drop: ALL} at pod level — you just wrote it wrong
capabilities is a CONTAINER-level field — it lives in the securityContext under the individual container; the pod-level securityContext has no capabilities field, so move the block into the container
Only cluster admins can set capabilities — developers can't
explain: The nesting trap again: pod-level securityContext holds runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, supplementalGroups, and sysctls; capabilities add/drop live per container. The API rejection is the tell — an unknown field at pod level fails validation. Move it under the container and it validates.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Two containers run as different UIDs but both need read access to a shared volume whose files are group-owned by GID 3000. You don't want the kubelet to chown the volume (no fsGroup). Which field gives both containers group-3000 membership?
options: runAsUser: 3000 — that changes the UID, not group membership
fsGroup is the only mechanism — accept the chown
privileged: true — bypasses group checks entirely but abandons hardening
supplementalGroups: [3000] at the pod level — every container's process gains group 3000 in its supplementary groups, so group-readable files open without chowning the volume
explain: supplementalGroups adds group memberships to all containers' processes; fsGroup makes the kubelet chown the volume to the group. Use supplementalGroups when the volume's existing group ownership must be preserved (shared or pre-provisioned storage), fsGroup when the kubelet may own the volume's ownership.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A critical alerting pod must be scheduled even if it means evicting less important batch pods. Which construction expresses this?
options: A PriorityClass (e.g., value: 1000) referenced via priorityClassName, with preemptionPolicy: Preempt (the default) — when the pod can't schedule, the scheduler evicts lower-priority pods to make room
Set resources.requests very high — big requests reserve space but never evict anyone
nodeSelector onto the biggest node — placement doesn't evict
Priority only affects scheduling order, never eviction — preemption doesn't exist
explain: PriorityClass + preemption is the eviction mechanism: higher value preempts lower when capacity is short. preemptionPolicy: Never would opt out. Resource requests only reserve — they never displace running pods, which is the misconception the second option states.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The security team requires the payments pods to run under the gVisor sandbox runtime. The cluster has a RuntimeClass named gvisor installed. How do you select it?
options: Annotate the pod runtimeclass: gvisor — annotations don't select runtimes
Set runtimeClassName: gvisor in the pod spec — the kubelet hands the pod to that RuntimeClass's handler
Set the container image to gvisor/payments — runtimes aren't images
Runtimes are per-node, so cordon all non-gVisor nodes instead
explain: runtimeClassName is the pod-level selector; the RuntimeClass object maps the name to a handler (runsc for gVisor, kata for Kata Containers). It's how you mix sandboxed and standard workloads on the same cluster without node partitioning.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A network-monitoring pod must sniff the node's physical interface. You set hostNetwork: true. Which consequences must you accept?
options: None — it only adds a capability; pod networking is unchanged
The pod gets two IPs — one host, one pod — and can use both freely
The pod shares the host's network namespace: its IP IS the node's IP, ports it binds must not collide with host daemons, and the default dnsPolicy shifts (ClusterFirstWithHostNet)
hostNetwork pods can't use Services — all Service DNS breaks
explain: hostNetwork removes the pod network namespace entirely: no pod IP, real port-conflict risk with host processes, and DNS policy adjusts. Services still work — the pod dials them like any host process would. It's the right tool for node-level networking agents, with sharp edges.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Pods must resolve names against the corporate DNS at 10.0.0.2 with search domain corp.example.com, ignoring cluster DNS entirely. Which pod spec does this?
options: dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst and hope — ClusterFirst always prepends cluster DNS
hostAliases — that only appends /etc/hosts lines, it doesn't set a resolver
dnsPolicy: Default — that inherits the NODE's resolv.conf, not your custom servers
dnsPolicy: None with dnsConfig: {nameservers: ["10.0.0.2"], searches: ["corp.example.com"]} — None discards all defaults so dnsConfig fully defines resolv.conf
explain: dnsConfig is only fully honored with dnsPolicy: None; other policies merge or override parts of it. This is the 'corporate resolver, no cluster DNS' shape — and the reason None exists as a policy.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The app must resolve db.internal to 10.0.0.5, but you can't touch cluster DNS or the image. Which pod field adds this static entry?
options: hostAliases: [{ip: "10.0.0.5", hostnames: ["db.internal"]}] — the kubelet appends these lines to the pod's /etc/hosts
An annotation like hosts: db.internal=10.0.0.5 — annotations don't edit /etc/hosts
dnsConfig searches — search domains don't map names to IPs
Edit /etc/hosts with kubectl exec — the kubelet manages that file and rewrites it
explain: hostAliases is the declarative /etc/hosts mechanism — no CoreDNS changes, no image rebuild. Exec edits to /etc/hosts get clobbered because the kubelet owns the file.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container dies with exit 137 and no useful stdout. You want its FINAL log lines surfaced in kubectl describe pod without changing the app. Which setting does this?
options: terminationMessagePath: /var/log/app.log — the path must be written by the app itself; pointing it at an arbitrary log file does nothing
terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError — on non-zero exit the kubelet uses the container's last log lines as the termination message, shown in describe
restartPolicy: Never — that only stops restarts, it surfaces nothing
Nothing — describe never shows container output
explain: The default File policy reads /dev/termination-log (which the app must write); FallbackToLogsOnError falls back to the tail of stdout/stderr when the app wrote nothing. For crash-debugging without code changes, it's the one-line fix — the message then appears under Last State in describe.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The team quota must cap total persistent storage claims at 100Gi across the namespace, regardless of CPU/memory. Which ResourceQuota entry does this?
options: limits.memory: 100Gi — a memory quota doesn't count disk
count/persistentvolumeclaims: "100" — that caps the NUMBER of PVCs, not their size
requests.storage: "100Gi" — the quota tracks the sum of all PVC storage requests against this ceiling
Quotas can't track storage — use a LimitRange
explain: requests.storage is the quota resource for PVC capacity; count/* caps object counts. LimitRange bounds individual claims (min/max/defaults), but only ResourceQuota caps the namespace total — the two controls answer different questions.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You must store a binary Java keystore (non-UTF8 bytes) in a ConfigMap via YAML. The data: field rejects it. Which field accepts raw binary?
options: stringData — still requires valid UTF-8
data with base64 content — ConfigMap data is never base64-encoded
Store it in a Secret instead — ConfigMaps can't hold binary, period
binaryData: {keystore.jks: <base64>} — binaryData takes base64-encoded bytes for non-UTF8 content; data is UTF-8 strings only
explain: binaryData exists precisely for non-UTF8 payloads (keystores, protobuf blobs); values are base64 in the manifest, matching Secret data conventions. stringData is the plaintext convenience for data, not a binary path.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Every pod gets dozens of <SVC>_SERVICE_HOST env vars the app never uses, cluttering its environment dump. How do you stop the injection for one Deployment's pods?
options: enableServiceLinks: false in the pod spec — disables the automatic Service host/port env var injection for those pods
Delete the Services — the app still needs them for DNS discovery
Service env injection is mandatory — it can't be disabled
Set dnsPolicy: None — DNS policy doesn't control env vars
explain: enableServiceLinks defaults to true (the Docker-legacy link vars); false keeps DNS-based discovery while dropping the env clutter. It's per-pod-spec, so one Deployment opts out without affecting the namespace.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: With a headless Service named web, you need each pod's hostname to be its FULL DNS name (web-0.web.default.svc.cluster.local) instead of just web-0. Which field does this?
options: hostname: web-0.web.default... — hostname must be a short name, not a dotted FQDN
setHostnameAsFQDN: true — the kubelet sets the hostname to the pod's FQDN (it needs the headless Service backing it)
subdomain: web — subdomain affects DNS records, not the hostname value
Hostnames can't be FQDNs in Kubernetes
explain: setHostnameAsFQDN flips the hostname to the FQDN form; the headless Service + subdomain provide the DNS side. Apps that validate their own FQDN (Kerberos, some databases) need exactly this.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You write a Deployment whose pod template sets restartPolicy: OnFailure. The API server rejects the Deployment. Why?
options: OnFailure is misspelled — the valid values are Always, OnFailure, Never, and you spelled it right
Deployments default restartPolicy for you — you must omit it
Controllers that manage replicas (Deployments, DaemonSets, StatefulSets) require restartPolicy: Always — OnFailure/Never are only valid on bare Pods and Jobs
restartPolicy belongs on the container, not the pod template
explain: Replica controllers assume self-healing: a pod that stays dead contradicts the controller's contract, so only Always validates. OnFailure/ Never belong to run-to-completion semantics — bare Pods and Jobs. The field lives at the pod spec level, which is correctly placed here.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A data-loader pod (not a Job) must be killed if it ever runs longer than 30 minutes, whatever it's doing. Which pod-spec field enforces this?
options: activeDeadlineSeconds on a Job spec — there is no Job here
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1800 — that's the shutdown window AFTER SIGTERM, not a runtime cap
A livenessProbe with timeoutSeconds: 1800 — probe timeouts don't cap pod lifetime
activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800 on the POD spec — the kubelet terminates the pod with reason DeadlineExceeded once it has been active that long; it applies to any pod, not just Jobs
explain: activeDeadlineSeconds exists at both levels: on the Job it bounds the whole Job, on the pod spec it bounds that pod's lifetime from first start. The grace period only governs how long SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL takes once termination begins.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The app pod must land on the SAME node as the cache pod (labeled app: cache) to use local Unix sockets. Which affinity rule expresses 'schedule me where cache pods run'?
options: podAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution, labelSelector {app: cache}, topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname — requires a node already running a cache pod
podAntiAffinity with the same selector — that spreads AWAY from cache pods, the opposite
nodeAffinity on label app=cache — nodeAffinity matches NODE labels, never pod labels
A toleration for app=cache — tolerations permit tainted nodes; they don't attract pods to other pods
explain: podAffinity = co-location by pod labels; topologyKey sets the granularity (hostname = same node, zone = same zone). Anti-affinity is the mirror image, nodeAffinity matches node labels, and tolerations answer a taint question — the three classic confusions.

q: The 6 web replicas must spread across availability zones so a zone failure can't take them all — but scheduling must never block on it. Which is the soft form?
options: podAffinity required — affinity attracts, and required would force co-location

podAntiAffinity with preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, weight: 100 — the scheduler prefers spreading replicas across zones but still schedules if it can't
nodeSelector zone: a — pins everything to ONE zone
Anti-affinity only supports required, not preferred
explain: preferred + weight = best-effort spread; required = hard constraint that can leave pods Pending. topologyKey: zone spreads per zone (hostname would spread per node). The soft form is the production default for HA spreading.

q: Pods must land only on nodes with disktype=ssd OR disktype=nvme. nodeSelector can't express OR. Which field can?
options: Two nodeSelectors — a pod spec takes one, and its entries are ANDed
nodeName with both node names — nodeName takes a single node

nodeAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution and nodeSelectorTerms matchExpressions [{key: disktype, operator: In, values: [ssd, nvme]}] — the expressive form with In/NotIn/Exists operators
A taint on the HDD nodes — taints repel, but don't select among the remaining nodes
explain: nodeAffinity adds set operators nodeSelector lacks; In gives the OR across values, and multiple nodeSelectorTerms are ORed. Taints answer 'keep off,' not 'pick among' — different axis.

q: GPU nodes are tainted dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule. Your ML pods must tolerate this taint. Which toleration matches?
options: No toleration needed — pods schedule onto tainted nodes by default
tolerations: [{key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: cpu, effect: NoSchedule}] — the value doesn't match the taint's gpu value
nodeSelector: {dedicated: gpu} — taints aren't labels; selecting doesn't grant toleration
tolerations: [{key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule}] — key, value, and effect all match the taint, so the pod schedules there
explain: A toleration must match the taint's key, value (unless operator: Exists), and effect. nodeSelector matches labels — a different object entirely — and no toleration means NoSchedule blocks the pod. This key+value+effect triple is the exam's taint question.

q: You want at most ONE replica more in any zone than in any other zone (maxSkew: 1), but scheduling must never block on it. Which constraint?
options: topologySpreadConstraints: [{maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway, labelSelector: {app: web}}] — caps zone imbalance, best-effort
whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule — that's the hard form; it can leave pods Pending
podAntiAffinity required per zone — cruder; it forbids ANY co-location rather than capping skew
maxSkew counts nodes, not pods — so it can't express pod imbalance
explain: topologySpreadConstraints = fine-grained spread (maxSkew caps the imbalance) vs anti-affinity's all-or-nothing. ScheduleAnyway is the soft form; DoNotSchedule is the hard gate. The labelSelector says which pods count toward the skew.

q: A log-shipper must start BEFORE the app container and keep running alongside it for the pod's life. Native sidecars (Kubernetes 1.29+) express this how?
options: A regular container listed first — containers start in parallel; list order is not a startup guarantee
An initContainer with restartPolicy: Always — restartable init containers start before app containers (in order) and then keep running as sidecars
A plain init container — it exits before the app starts, so it can't ship live logs
A postStart hook — hooks can't run a long-lived process
explain: restartPolicy: Always on an init container = native sidecar: ordered startup like an init container, long-lived like a regular container. Plain init containers must exit before app containers start — right for setup, wrong for a live log shipper.

q: The CronJob must fire at 9 AM America/New_York time, including DST shifts. The cluster runs on UTC. Which field handles this?
options: Prefix the schedule with TZ=America/New_York — cron syntax has no TZ prefix
Run a sidecar that converts timezones — the schedule field is not UTC-only anymore
spec.timeZone: "America/New_York" — the controller interprets the cron schedule in that IANA timezone
CronJobs always use the controller manager's local timezone — unconfigurable
explain: spec.timeZone decouples the schedule from the controller's timezone (UTC by default); the controller handles DST transitions. Without it, 9 AM means 9 AM UTC — the classic off-by-hours scheduling bug.

q: The export CronJob takes 10 minutes but runs every 5. Overlapping runs corrupt the file; skipping a run is worse than replacing it. Which concurrencyPolicy, and what does it do?
options: Forbid — skips the new run while one is active; that's skipping, not replacing
Allow — the default; runs overlap, which corrupts the file
suspend: true — stops ALL runs, not just overlaps
Replace — the controller deletes the currently running Job and starts a fresh one, so only the newest run ever executes
explain: Allow overlaps, Forbid skips, Replace restarts — 'latest wins.' Replace is the answer when a stale run's output is worthless and only the newest data matters.

q: Finished Jobs pile up — you want each Job object auto-deleted 1 hour after it completes, success or failure. Which field?
options: ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 on the Job spec — the controller deletes the finished Job after the TTL elapses
successfulJobsHistoryLimit — that's CronJob history pruning, not standalone Jobs
backoffLimit: 0 — that controls retries, not cleanup
activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600 — that caps runtime before finishing, not cleanup after
explain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished = post-completion garbage collection for Jobs. History limits belong to CronJobs; backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds govern the run itself, not the corpse.

q: A Job needs 5 workers, each handling shard N (0-4), with the shard index available inside the container. Which Job shape gives each pod its index?
options: completions: 5, parallelism: 5 — pods are identical; nothing tells a pod which shard it owns
completionMode: Indexed with completions: 5 — each pod automatically gets JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX (0-4) as an env var
Five separate Jobs named shard-0 through shard-4 — the manual reimplementation
Parse the pod name suffix — pod names carry random suffixes, not the index
explain: Indexed completion mode = built-in shard identity via the JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX env var (also as hostname subdomain). The default NonIndexed mode has no per-pod identity — that's the work-queue pattern instead.

q: A Job is misconfigured and spawning expensive pods. You need to freeze it NOW without deleting its definition or history. Which field?
options: Delete the Job — that loses the definition and history
Scale it to zero — Jobs don't scale
spec.suspend: true — the Job controller stops creating pods; flip it back to false to resume
backoffLimit: 0 — that only stops retries after failures
explain: suspend exists on Jobs too, not just CronJobs — the pause button for runaway work. The Job object, its completed pods, and its counters all survive; only new pod creation stops.

q: The fluent-bit DaemonSet update takes down too many collectors at once. How do you limit the rolling update to one node at a time?
options: DaemonSets update all pods simultaneously — it's unconfigurable
partition: 1 — that's a StatefulSet field
maxSurge: 1 — DaemonSet RollingUpdate has no maxSurge
updateStrategy: {type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: {maxUnavailable: 1}} — at most one DaemonSet pod is unavailable during the update
explain: DaemonSet RollingUpdate supports only maxUnavailable — no surge, because one-pod-per-node is the invariant (surging would put two on a node). maxUnavailable: 1 = one node at a time.

q: A 10-replica StatefulSet of independent workers (no ordering needs) starts painfully slowly — each pod waits for the previous to be Ready. Which field parallelizes startup?
options: podManagementPolicy: Parallel — pods launch in parallel instead of strict ordinal order
updateStrategy: RollingUpdate — that governs updates, not initial creation
parallelism: 10 — that's a Job field
OrderedReady is the only policy — StatefulSets can't parallelize
explain: OrderedReady (default) = strict ordinal startup for bootstrapping clusters; Parallel = burst for independent workers. Keep OrderedReady when order matters (databases), switch to Parallel when it doesn't.

q: You want full manual control over the StatefulSet rollout: the new template applies ONLY to pods you delete by hand. Which updateStrategy?
options: partition: 0 — with RollingUpdate that rolls EVERYTHING automatically
updateStrategy: {type: OnDelete} — the controller takes no rollout action; pods you delete come back on the new template
Suspend the StatefulSet — StatefulSets have no suspend field
Delete the StatefulSet — that destroys the pods and their sticky identity
explain: OnDelete = manual rolling: you drive the rollout pod by pod, useful for sensitive stateful upgrades. partition is the automatic canary knob — partition: 0 means everything updates on its own.

q: You apply a StatefulSet without spec.serviceName and the API server rejects it. Why is the Service name mandatory?
options: It isn't — serviceName is optional and defaults to the StatefulSet's name
The Service must merely exist first — creation order is the issue, not the field
The StatefulSet controller needs the headless Service's name to build each pod's stable DNS identity (pod-0.service...); without serviceName the identity has no domain
It's only required when volumeClaimTemplates are used
explain: serviceName is required validation: it must name the (headless) Service that gives the pods their network identity. The stable name + stable DNS contract is the whole point of a StatefulSet — no serviceName, no identity.

q: You add a readinessProbe to an init container and the API server rejects the pod. What's the rule?
options: Init containers can't have any probes — they can have liveness and startup probes
The probe port is wrong — any valid port passes validation; that's not the rejection
Probes must be named on init containers — probes are never named
Init containers do not support readinessProbes — readiness gates traffic to app containers; init containers run to completion before any traffic exists, so the field is rejected
explain: Init containers support liveness and startup probes but not readiness — there's nothing to route to while the pod is still initializing. The API rejection is the tell that this is a schema rule, not a runtime preference.

q: args: ["echo", "$GREETING"] prints the literal string $GREETING instead of the variable's value. Why, and what's the fix?
options: args run without a shell, so $GREETING is never expanded — wrap it: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo $GREETING"]
Env vars can't be referenced in args at all — use envFrom instead
The variable must be exported first — Kubernetes doesn't export env vars to the process
Use $(GREETING) — that's the expansion syntax in args
explain: The exec form (command/args arrays) runs with no shell: $VAR is literal text. $(VAR) IS expanded by the kubelet in args, but shell-style $VAR needs a real shell — hence the ["/bin/sh", "-c", "..."] wrapper. This is the #1 'my variable didn't expand' gotcha.

q: The nightly CronJob's logic needs a one-off manual run RIGHT NOW, without waiting for the schedule. Which command creates it from the CronJob's template?
options: kubectl run manual --image=... — rebuilds the pod spec by hand, duplicating the template and inviting drift
kubectl create job manual-run --from=cronjob/nightly — stamps a Job from the CronJob's jobTemplate
Copy the CronJob YAML and change kind to Job — the schemas differ (schedule wrapper, jobTemplate nesting)
Set suspend: false — it's already unsuspended; that doesn't trigger an immediate run
explain: --from=cronjob/<name> is the one-off trigger: same template the schedule uses, no YAML surgery. Hand-copying invites schema mistakes (the CronJob wraps the Job spec in jobTemplate).

q: A node is tainted maintenance=true:NoExecute. A running pod has NO toleration for it. What happens to the pod?
options: Nothing — NoExecute only blocks NEW pods, like NoSchedule
The pod keeps running forever — taints never evict
The pod is evicted — NoExecute evicts running pods lacking a matching toleration (tolerationSeconds can delay it)
The pod is evicted only after a fixed 300-second delay
explain: NoSchedule = block new pods; NoExecute = block new AND evict existing ones without a matching toleration. tolerationSeconds makes the eviction delayed rather than immediate. This is the effect the exam pairs with 'drain this node for maintenance.'

q: You'd LIKE the frontend pods on SSD nodes, but they must still schedule elsewhere if no SSD node has capacity. Which is the soft form?
options: nodeSelector — a hard requirement; pods go Pending with no SSD capacity
nodeAffinity requiredDuringScheduling — also a hard gate
A taint on non-SSD nodes — repels, which is the opposite direction
nodeAffinity with preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution and a weight — a soft preference the scheduler honors when possible, never blocking
explain: preferred + weight = best-effort ('like SSD, accept anything'); required = hard gate. Soft preferences never leave pods Pending — the scheduler just scores SSD nodes higher.

q: Two tools both manage the same Deployment and keep overwriting each other's fields. Which apply mode tracks field ownership and reports conflicts instead of silently stomping?
options: kubectl apply --server-side -f web.yaml — the API server tracks which manager owns each field, and conflicts surface explicitly instead of last-writer-wins
kubectl apply (client-side) — last-writer-wins with no ownership record
kubectl create --force — create never updates an existing object
Field ownership is automatic in all modes — there's nothing to opt into
explain: Server-side apply = ownership tracking per field per manager; two managers touching the same field get a conflict instead of a silent overwrite. Client-side apply is last-writer-wins. The exam's answer to multi-writer fights (GitOps + kubectl both editing one Deployment).

q: You must change a Deployment's selector (normally immutable). Which command deletes and recreates the object to push the change through?
options: kubectl apply -f — the API rejects immutable field changes
kubectl replace --force -f web.yaml — deletes and recreates the object, allowing immutable fields to change (with brief downtime)
kubectl edit — the API still validates immutability on save
kubectl patch — patches can't touch immutable fields either
explain: --force = delete + recreate; the escape hatch for immutable fields like selectors. It costs a brief outage (pods are recreated), which is why the normal path is 'selectors never change' — reach for this only deliberately.

q: Before installing a chart you wrote, you want a static check for template errors and bad values — no cluster contact. Which command?
options: helm install --dry-run — needs a cluster and renders server-side
helm status — only works on installed releases
helm lint ./chart — validates the chart's templates and values locally, no cluster needed
kubectl apply --dry-run=client — needs rendered YAML as input first
explain: lint = chart hygiene (template syntax, values schema, chart metadata); template = render; install --dry-run = server-validated preview. Lint first, render second, dry-run third — the pre-install chain.

q: helm install must not return until the Deployment's pods are actually ready, and must fail if that takes over 10 minutes. Which flags?
options: No flags — install returns once objects are created, which is enough for CI
helm install --wait alone — waits indefinitely with no bound; a wedged rollout hangs CI
--timeout alone — without --wait nothing is waited on, so the timeout does nothing
helm install api-v2 ./chart --wait --timeout 10m — --wait blocks until resources are ready; --timeout bounds the wait
explain: --wait without --timeout can hang forever; --timeout without --wait waits for nothing. The pair is the bounded readiness gate — exactly what CI pipelines need instead of a blind sleep.

q: You uninstall a release but must keep its revision history for the audit trail. Which flag?
options: helm uninstall api-v2 --keep-history — removes the resources but retains the release record
Plain helm uninstall — it purges the release record by default
helm rollback — that reverts to a prior revision, it doesn't uninstall
History can't be kept — uninstall always purges everything
explain: Default uninstall wipes the release record; --keep-history preserves it (the release shows as 'uninstalled' in helm list -a). Auditors get their trail; the cluster gets its cleanup.

q: After an upgrade, you need the release's current status, revision number, and the chart's notes in one view. Which single command?
options: helm list — inventory only: name, namespace, revision, status — no notes
helm status api-v2 — release status, revision, and the rendered NOTES.txt in one view
helm get manifest — the rendered resources, not status or notes
kubectl get deploy — cluster state, not release metadata
explain: status = the release health dashboard (status, revision, notes with next steps). list = inventory across releases; get manifest = what was applied. When someone asks 'did the upgrade work and what do I do now,' status is the answer.

q: You pass --set adminPassword=00742 and the app receives 742 (a number), breaking auth. How do you force the value to stay the string "00742"?
options: --set adminPassword="00742" — shell quotes don't survive Helm's type coercion
Quote it in values.yaml — the task needs a CLI fix
--set-string adminPassword=00742 — set-string disables type coercion and keeps the value a string
--set-json adminPassword=00742 — for JSON blobs, not scalar coercion
explain: --set coerces numerics and booleans (00742 → 742, "true" → true); --set-string preserves strings. The leading-zero password and the literal string "true" are the classic casualties — the exam's type-coercion trap.

q: The chart's Chart.yaml declares a postgres subchart dependency, but charts/ is empty and install fails. What populates it?
options: helm repo add — registers the repo; it doesn't fetch subcharts
helm install --with-dependencies — no such flag
Copy the subchart by hand — the manual version of the command
helm dependency update ./chart — downloads declared dependencies into charts/
explain: dependency update (or dependency build from a lock file) vendors subcharts into charts/. repo add only registers the source. An empty charts/ with declared dependencies is the tell — the vendoring step was skipped.

q: A failed helm install leaves stray resources behind. Which flag automatically cleans up after a failed install?
options: helm upgrade --install api-v2 ./chart --cleanup-on-fail — on failure, uninstalls the resources the failed release created
--atomic — rolls back upgrades, but a fresh install has no previous release to roll back to
--force — recreates resources; it doesn't clean up
Failed installs clean up after themselves — they don't
explain: --cleanup-on-fail = uninstall-on-failure for installs; --atomic = rollback-on-failure for upgrades. Pair them (upgrade --install --atomic --cleanup-on-fail) and both directions are covered.

q: You need redis chart version 17.x specifically, not the latest 20.x. How do you discover which versions the repo offers?
options: helm install bitnami/redis --version 17 — guessing the version string and hoping
helm search repo bitnami/redis --versions — lists all published chart versions
helm repo list — lists repos, not chart versions
helm show values — shows the latest chart's defaults, not its version catalog
explain: search repo --versions = the version catalog; then --version 17.x pins it. Chart versions and app versions are different fields (check both) — pinning the chart is what makes installs reproducible.

q: Every resource in the staging overlay must carry the annotation cost-center: staging for chargeback. Which kustomization field?
options: commonLabels — labels, not annotations
namePrefix — renames, doesn't annotate
commonAnnotations: {cost-center: staging} — merged into every resource's metadata.annotations
patches — overkill for a uniform annotation
explain: commonAnnotations/commonLabels = uniform metadata injection across the whole overlay. patches are for surgical per-resource edits — the wrong tool for 'stamp everything.'

q: In the prod overlay you must raise the web Deployment's memory limit without editing the base. Which Kustomize mechanism targets just that field?
options: Edit the base — forbidden by the task
namePrefix — renames only
A second base — bases compose; they don't patch fields
patches with a target {kind: Deployment, name: web} and a strategic-merge or JSON-6902 patch — applied to the matched resource only
explain: patches = surgical overlay edits: target selects kind/name (and optionally namespace), the patch body edits fields. It's the Kustomize answer to 'change one field in one resource without forking the base.'

q: The staging overlay needs 2 replicas and prod needs 6, from a base with 3. Which kustomization stanza sets this per overlay?
options: replicas: [{name: web, count: 6}] — sets the replica count on the named workload
commonLabels — doesn't touch replica counts
A patch to spec.replicas — works, but the dedicated transformer is cleaner
Two bases with different counts — duplicates the whole Deployment
explain: replicas: is the purpose-built transformer for per-environment counts — declarative, no patch syntax needed. Patches can do it, but the transformer expresses intent directly.

q: configMapGenerator appends a content hash to names (app-config-7d9f...), which triggers rolling updates on config change. You need a STABLE name because an external system references it. Which setting?
options: Delete the hash by hand after apply — it regenerates on the next apply
generatorOptions: {disableNameSuffixHash: true} — keeps the plain name; you lose the automatic rolling on content change and must roll pods yourself
Use --from-literal — literals get hashed too
Hashes can't be disabled — redesign the external reference
explain: disableNameSuffixHash trades the auto-roll for a stable name. With it set, changing the ConfigMap no longer renames it — so nothing triggers a rollout, and you must bounce pods (rollout restart) yourself. Know which behavior you're giving up.

q: You want to see the fully rendered staging overlay WITHOUT applying it. Which command?
options: kubectl apply -k overlays/staging --dry-run=client — validates but doesn't print the built manifests
kubectl diff -k — needs a cluster for the server-side diff
kubectl kustomize overlays/staging — builds and prints the manifests locally, the Kustomize analog of helm template
kubectl get -k — no such command
explain: kubectl kustomize = local render; diff = cluster comparison; --dry-run = validation. For 'show me exactly what this overlay produces,' render locally first.

q: Pods must not receive traffic until an external warmup controller marks them ready via a custom condition. Which pod spec field gates readiness on it?
options: readinessProbe — probes are kubelet-executed checks, not external conditions
A stronger livenessProbe — liveness restarts containers; it doesn't gate traffic
An annotation — annotations don't affect readiness
readinessGates: [{conditionType: "example.com/warmed-up"}] — the pod stays unready until that condition is True, letting external controllers gate traffic
explain: readinessGates extend readiness beyond probes to custom conditions the kubelet doesn't evaluate itself — the controller sets the condition, the kubelet honors it. Probes answer 'is the app up'; gates answer 'is the platform ready for it.'

q: kubectl autoscale only exposes --cpu-percent. You need the Deployment to scale on MEMORY utilization at 80%. How?
options: Write the HPA manifest directly with metrics: [{type: Resource, resource: {name: memory, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80}}}] — the API supports memory; only the kubectl shorthand is CPU-only
--cpu-percent=80 with a comment saying memory — the CPU flag can't target memory
The HPA can't scale on memory — CPU only, by design
Use the VPA — it resizes containers, it doesn't change replica counts
explain: autoscaling/v2 HPAs support memory (and custom) metrics; the imperative kubectl autoscale generator just doesn't expose them. When the CLI shorthand can't express it, write the manifest — the exam tests whether you know the API goes further than the generator.

q: rollout history shows 4 revisions. You need to see the actual pod template of revision 2 to find when an env var changed. Which command?
options: kubectl get deploy web -o yaml — shows the CURRENT template only
kubectl rollout history deploy/web --revision=2 — prints that revision's pod template and change-cause
helm history — that's Helm releases, not Deployment revisions
Revision templates aren't retained — only the numbers are
explain: --revision drills into one retained ReplicaSet's template (kept per revisionHistoryLimit). history without the flag lists revisions; with it, you get the actual manifest that ran — the forensics view.

q: Two operators might scale the Deployment concurrently. You want the scale to apply ONLY if replicas are currently 3. Which flag gives this optimistic concurrency?
options: No flag — kubectl scale always wins blindly
--timeout — bounds the wait; it doesn't check current state
kubectl scale deploy/web --replicas=8 --current-replicas=3 — the scale is rejected unless the live replica count is 3
Edit web.yaml — files don't do concurrency checks
explain: --current-replicas = compare-and-swap for scaling: the precondition guards against racing scalers (or a stale runbook). Without it, the last writer wins silently.

q: The chart has 30 templates; you want to review ONLY the rendered Deployment before installing. Which command?
options: helm template ./chart — renders everything; you grep through 30 documents
helm lint — checks the chart; it doesn't render
helm show values — defaults, not manifests
helm template myapp ./chart --show-only templates/deployment.yaml — renders just that template file
explain: --show-only filters template output to named files — the focused-review path for big charts. Combine with -f/--set to review the Deployment exactly as your values would render it.

q: The container port is NAMED http (currently 8080). The Service should forward port 80 to it without hardcoding the number. Which targetPort form?
options: targetPort: http — the name resolves against the container's port names, tracking the number if it ever changes
targetPort: 8080 — works today but hardcodes the number the task wants to avoid
Target ports can't be names — only numbers are valid
name: http on the Service port — that names the SERVICE port, not the target
explain: targetPort accepts a name or a number; the name resolves against the pod's container port names. Name the container port once, reference it everywhere — the same 'names over numbers' principle as named ports in NetworkPolicies and SRV records.

q: Security policy forbids the default 30000-32767 NodePort range. Where is the range actually configured?
options: In the Service manifest — nodePort must fall inside the range, but the range itself isn't defined there
The kube-apiserver flag --service-node-port-range — the range is cluster configuration, not per-Service
kubectl expose --port-range — no such flag exists
The range is compiled in and can't be changed
explain: The range is API-server config (--service-node-port-range); Services only pick within it. A nodePort outside the configured range is rejected at admission — the error that sends people hunting in the Service YAML for a setting that lives on the control plane.

q: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, the cloud load balancer needs a per-node health-check endpoint. Which Service field controls the node port used for it?
options: nodePort — that's the traffic port, not the health-check port
Health checks always use port 80 — not configurable
healthCheckNodePort — auto-allocated when Local is set; set it explicitly to pin the health-check port
externalTrafficPolicy has no health-check concept — the LB guesses
explain: Local mode serves /healthz on healthCheckNodePort on every node; the cloud LB probes it to learn which nodes actually have local pods. Auto-allocation is the norm; pin it when firewall rules need a known port.

q: The Ingress must strip the /api prefix before proxying to the backend (the backend expects /users, not /api/users). With the NGINX controller, which annotation does this?
options: pathType: Prefix — routing only, no rewriting
A second Service — Services don't rewrite paths
Rewrite it in the app — the task wants it at the edge
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2 with path /api(/|$)(.*) — captures the remainder and proxies it without the prefix
explain: rewrite-target is the NGINX path-surgery annotation; native Ingress has no rewrite concept — path rules only SELECT the backend. The capture-group pattern (/api(/|$)(.*) → /$2) is the standard prefix-strip.

q: You need regex path matching (/api/v[0-9]+/.*) on the NGINX Ingress controller. Which combination enables it?
options: pathType: ImplementationSpecific with nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex: "true" — ImplementationSpecific delegates matching semantics to the controller
pathType: Prefix with the regex — Prefix is element-wise matching, not regex
pathType: Exact with the regex — Exact is literal matching
No Ingress controller supports regex paths
explain: ImplementationSpecific = 'the controller decides what this means'; NGINX then honors use-regex. Prefix and Exact have fixed spec semantics that no annotation can override — putting a regex there matches it literally.

q: Which single command creates the correct TLS Secret for an Ingress from certificate files?
options: kubectl create secret generic web-tls --from-file=tls.crt=cert.pem --from-file=tls.key=key.pem — generic type lacks the TLS contract; controllers expect kubernetes.io/tls
kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem — sets type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt/tls.key keys
kubectl create configmap web-tls — certificates don't belong in ConfigMaps
TLS Secrets must be hand-written YAML — no generator exists
explain: The tls subcommand builds the typed Secret (type kubernetes.io/tls, keys tls.crt/tls.key) that the Ingress TLS machinery looks for. A generic Secret with the same files is ignored — the type-is-a-contract rule again.

q: Your NetworkPolicy declares ingress rules but omits policyTypes entirely. What does the API server do?
options: Rejects it — policyTypes is a required field
Defaults to Ingress only and leaves egress wide open
Infers policyTypes from the rules present: ingress rules imply Ingress; adding egress rules later would add Egress too
Defaults to denying both directions — an accidental default-deny
explain: Omitted policyTypes are inferred from which rule blocks exist — ingress rules → Ingress, egress rules → Egress, both → both. Explicit is better (inference surprises people when they add a second direction later), but the inference is the documented behavior.

q: The api pods must allow egress ONLY to the db pods in the SAME namespace. The policy lives in that namespace. How do you express the peer?
options: podSelector plus namespaceSelector — namespaceSelector would also match other namespaces carrying the label
An ipBlock with the pod CIDR — coarse and fragile
Egress rules can't select pods — peers are ingress-only
egress: [{to: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: db}}}], ports: [{port: 5432}]}] — a bare podSelector in the policy's own namespace matches only that namespace's pods
explain: A bare podSelector = same-namespace pods; add namespaceSelector only to reach across namespaces. The third option invents a direction asymmetry that doesn't exist — to/from peers work in both directions.

q: You must allow egress to 0.0.0.0/0 EXCEPT the internal 10.0.0.0/8 range. Which peer expresses 'everywhere but 10/8'?
options: to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: "0.0.0.0/0", except: ["10.0.0.0/8"]}}] — except carves exclusions out of the CIDR
Two ipBlock entries — the union is additive, so two entries can't subtract
except without a cidr — except only modifies a cidr entry
0.0.0.0/0 alone — that includes 10/8, violating the requirement
explain: except = subtraction within one peer entry — the only way to express 'all but' since policy unions are purely additive. except entries must be within the parent CIDR.

q: DNS for db.data fails from the api pods. You need a quick throwaway pod to run nslookup. Which command?
options: kubectl exec into an api pod — it may be distroless with no nslookup
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup db.data.svc.cluster.local — an ephemeral debug pod, removed on exit
nslookup from your laptop — that tests YOUR resolver, not the cluster's
kubectl logs on CoreDNS — logs don't run queries
explain: run --rm -it = disposable debugging; -- separates kubectl flags from the container command. Using the FQDN avoids ndots:5 search-domain surprises, and the pod vanishes on exit — no cleanup.

q: kubectl get endpoints web shows the endpoints, but you've heard Endpoints are legacy. What's the modern object, and how do you list it for the Service?
