options: Endpoints are the only object — nothing replaced them
EndpointSlices are internal — users can't list them
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web — EndpointSlices are the scalable successor, labeled by their Service
Services now store endpoints inline — check the Service YAML
explain: EndpointSlices replaced Endpoints for scalability (the controller mirrors them); each carries the kubernetes.io/service-name label. Endpoints still exist, but slices are what modern clusters actually use — and what the exam now expects.

q: The headless Service web fronts a StatefulSet in namespace default. What is the FULL DNS name of the first pod?
options: web-0 — the short name only, unqualified
web.default.svc.cluster.local — that's the SERVICE name, not the pod
web-0.default.pod.cluster.local — pods don't get a .pod subdomain
web-0.web.default.svc.cluster.local — podName.serviceName.namespace.svc.cluster.local
explain: Headless Services mint per-pod A records as <pod>.<service>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local — the stable identity peers dial during bootstrap (with publishNotReadyAddresses when they must find each other before Ready).

q: The on-prem firewall team will only allow traffic to a FIXED cluster IP 203.0.113.50 for the app Service. Which Service field requests that IP?
options: spec.externalIPs: ["203.0.113.50"] — kube-proxy serves the Service on that IP on every node (your network must actually route the IP to the nodes)
clusterIP: 203.0.113.50 — clusterIPs come from the service CIDR, not public ranges
loadBalancerIP — only for LoadBalancer-type Services with a cloud provider
externalName — that's a DNS alias, not an IP
explain: externalIPs = 'also serve the Service here'; the cluster doesn't provision the address — your network must route it to the nodes. It's the on-prem answer to 'give this Service a known ingress IP' without a cloud LB.

q: The LoadBalancer Service must accept traffic ONLY from the office range 203.0.113.0/24. Which field restricts the cloud LB's source IPs?
options: A NetworkPolicy — it filters pod traffic, not the cloud LB's front door
loadBalancerSourceRanges: ["203.0.113.0/24"] — the cloud provider configures the LB firewall from this
externalTrafficPolicy: Local — preserves source IP but filters nothing
The Service port — ports don't filter sources
explain: loadBalancerSourceRanges = LB-level firewall (cloud-enforced); NetworkPolicy = pod-level filtering. Defense in depth uses both — but only the source ranges touch the LB itself.

q: Internal clients need the REAL client pod IP preserved for audit, but the traffic never leaves the cluster. externalTrafficPolicy only affects external traffic. What's the internal equivalent?
options: Nothing — internal traffic always SNATs; accept it
sessionAffinity: ClientIP — pins routing; it preserves nothing
internalTrafficPolicy: Local — ClusterIP traffic routes only to node-local pods, skipping the SNAT hop and preserving the source pod IP
A headless Service — bypasses the virtual IP but doesn't preserve source through kube-proxy
explain: internalTrafficPolicy mirrors external's Local/Cluster choice for in-cluster traffic: Local preserves the source pod IP at the cost of node-local-only routing. The audit requirement ('which pod called me') is the cue.

q: You create a NodePort Service without specifying nodePort. What happens?
options: The API rejects it — nodePort is required
It defaults to port 80 — privileged ports are never auto-assigned
It silently becomes ClusterIP — the type doesn't downgrade
The API server auto-allocates a free port from --service-node-port-range — omit nodePort when you don't care about the exact number
explain: nodePort is optional; allocation is automatic from the configured range. Specify it only when the port must be stable or known (firewall rules, documentation) — otherwise let the API server pick.

q: One certificate covers *.example.com and must terminate TLS for shop.example.com and api.example.com on a single Ingress. How do you reference it?
options: tls: [{hosts: ["shop.example.com", "api.example.com"], secretName: web-wildcard}] — list the served hosts; the wildcard cert matches both
hosts: ["*.example.com"] — tls.hosts takes concrete hostnames, not patterns
One tls entry per host with the same secret — works but redundant; a single entry listing both hosts is cleaner
Wildcard certs don't work with Ingress — you need one cert per host
explain: tls.hosts lists the concrete hosts served; matching those against the cert's SANs (including wildcards) is the controller's job. One entry, both hosts, one wildcard Secret — the standard multi-host TLS fan-out.

q: The API server rejects your Service: port name "HTTPS-Web-Frontend" is invalid. What's the naming rule?
options: Port names must be uppercase — it's lowercase that's required
Port names must be valid IANA service names: lowercase alphanumerics and '-', max 15 characters — rename it to https-web
Port names can't contain dashes — they can
Port names are unlimited — the rejection is a bug
explain: IANA_SVC_NAME: lowercase, digits, dashes, 15 characters max. The length cap is the surprise — long descriptive names get rejected, which is why short names (http, https, metrics, grpc) are the convention.

q: kubectl port-forward works on your laptop, but a teammate can't reach it from their machine. Why, and what's the flag to share it?
options: port-forward is broken for remote use — expose a Service instead
Their firewall is blocking it — the listener never bound remotely
It binds 127.0.0.1 by default — add --address 0.0.0.0 to listen on all interfaces
port-forward always requires --address — it has a safe default
explain: Localhost binding is the safety default; --address 0.0.0.0 opens it deliberately. It's still a debugging tool, not a sharing mechanism — for real sharing, use a Service.

q: You create a Service of type LoadBalancer. Besides the external LB IP, what cluster networking does it ALSO get?
options: Nothing — LoadBalancer replaces ClusterIP entirely
Only a NodePort — ClusterIP is skipped for external Services
Only a ClusterIP — NodePorts are a separate type
Both a ClusterIP AND a NodePort — LoadBalancer builds on NodePort builds on ClusterIP; internal clients use the ClusterIP while the cloud LB targets the NodePorts
explain: The types layer: ClusterIP ⊂ NodePort ⊂ LoadBalancer. The layering explains health checks (LB → nodePort), internal access (ClusterIP), and why a 'pending' LB still has a working ClusterIP.

q: You need logs since exactly 09:00 UTC today — not 'the last hour' relative to now. Which flag expresses an absolute start time?
options: --since-time=2026-10-18T09:00:00Z — an absolute RFC3339 timestamp; --since takes only relative durations like 2h
--since=2026-10-18T09:00:00Z — --since takes durations, not timestamps
--tail with a timestamp — tail counts lines, not time
Logs can't be time-bounded — only line-bounded
explain: --since-time = absolute (RFC3339); --since = relative (5m, 2h). The unit trap again: reaching for --since with a timestamp silently misbehaves — the exam loves the since/since-time pair.

q: describe pod shows 'Warning BackOff Back-off restarting failed container' repeating. The container never stays up. What's the reading, and the next command?
options: The image can't be pulled — that's ImagePullBackOff, a different event
CrashLoopBackOff: the container starts then exits non-zero, and the kubelet backs off between restarts — run kubectl logs <pod> --previous -c app to see the crashed instance's output
The node is out of CPU — that surfaces as FailedScheduling, not BackOff
BackOff means the scheduler gave up — delete the pod
explain: 'Back-off restarting failed container' = the crash loop: start, exit non-zero, exponential backoff. --previous fetches the dead container's logs (current logs show the just-started instance). ImagePullBackOff is the lookalike with a different cause.

q: You need to list only pods that are NOT Running, cluster-wide. Which command filters server-side?
options: kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running — works, but filters client-side after fetching everything
Field selectors don't support != — they do
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector status.phase!=Running — server-side filtering on the phase field
Field selectors only work on labels — that's -l/--selector
explain: --field-selector = server-side field filtering (=, ==, !=); -l = label selector. status.phase is the filterable field for 'not Running.' Server-side filtering is cheaper and the exam's expected form.

q: You want the app and track labels as separate COLUMNS in the pod list. Which flag?
options: --show-labels — dumps all labels into one LABELS column
-o wide — adds node/IP columns, not label columns
-l app — that's a filter, not a column
kubectl get pods -L app,track — one column per named label
explain: -L = label columns (one per name); --show-labels = single blob column. -l filters rows, -L adds columns — the case-sensitive pair the exam confuses deliberately.

q: Before running a deploy script as the CI service account, you want to verify it can create deployments in prod — without attempting it. Which command checks?
options: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --namespace=prod — evaluates the RBAC rules for the current identity (or --as another one)
kubectl get deployments — read access doesn't imply create access
Just run the apply and see — the question asks for a pre-check
auth can-i only works for cluster-admins — anyone can check their own access
explain: auth can-i = dry-run authorization check against RBAC. Pair with --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer to vet another identity's permissions — the pre-flight check before a deploy script runs.

q: You're writing a manifest and can't remember the exact fields under pod.spec.containers[].resources. Which command documents them with types, offline?
options: kubectl api-versions — lists API versions, not fields
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources — recursive field documentation with types and descriptions
kubectl get --help — CLI help, not API schema
Only the website documents fields — explain mirrors it from the cluster's own schema
explain: kubectl explain = offline schema browser served from the API's OpenAPI; add --recursive for full depth. It's the fastest way to check a field path or nesting level under exam time pressure.

q: You want the events for ONE pod (web-abc) without the namespace-wide noise. Which command?
options: kubectl get events | grep web-abc — client-side, and grep misses involvedObject subtleties
kubectl describe pod web-abc — shows events but mixed into the full pod detail
kubectl events --for pod/web-abc — the dedicated event viewer filtered to that object
Events can't be filtered by object — only by namespace
explain: kubectl events with --for = scoped event stream for one object (pods, nodes, deployments). describe mixes events with spec/status; get events is namespace-wide. For 'what happened to THIS pod,' --for is the direct path.

q: The pod has app, sidecar, and proxy containers. You need recent logs from ALL of them in one command. Which flag?
options: -c app — one container only
kubectl logs deploy/web — the deploy/ shorthand still needs -c on multi-container pods
--prefix — prefixes lines with pod/container names; it doesn't select containers
kubectl logs pod/web-abc --all-containers=true — streams every container's logs
explain: --all-containers = the whole pod's log output in one stream; it composes with -l for fleet-wide multi-container logs. -c picks one; --prefix only labels the lines.

q: You need destructive diagnostics (strace, package installs) against a COPY of the production pod, WITHOUT touching the live one. Which kubectl debug form?
options: kubectl debug -it web-abc --copy-to=web-debug --container=debugger --image=busybox — clones the pod spec into web-debug and attaches your debug container there; the original is untouched
kubectl debug -it web-abc — attaches an ephemeral container to the LIVE pod
kubectl exec — can't install packages on a distroless image
Copy the YAML by hand — the manual version of --copy-to
explain: --copy-to = sandboxed clone for disruptive debugging; plain debug = ephemeral container in the live pod (safe for inspection, not for experiments). The copy shares the original's spec — volumes, env, and all.

q: Your ephemeral debug container must see the app container's processes (ps across containers). Which debug flag shares the process namespace?
options: It shares by default — it doesn't; each container keeps its own PID namespace
kubectl debug -it web-abc --image=busybox --share-processes --container=debugger — the debug copy runs all containers in one PID namespace
Set shareProcessNamespace on the live pod — the field exists, but running pod specs are immutable
ps always sees all containers — it only sees its own PID namespace
explain: --share-processes on the debug copy enables cross-container ps; on the live pod you'd need the pod-spec field shareProcessNamespace, which can't be added to a running pod. Debug copies exist precisely to bypass that immutability.

q: describe node node-2 shows Conditions: DiskPressure=True, MemoryPressure=False, and pods are being evicted from node-2. What's the reading?
options: The scheduler is broken — pressure conditions are kubelet-reported, not scheduler state
MemoryPressure=False means the node is fine — DiskPressure alone triggers evictions
The kubelet's eviction manager is reclaiming DISK — DiskPressure=True means disk is exhausted; check image layers, container writable layers, logs, and emptyDir usage on that node
Conditions are informational — the kubelet never acts on them
explain: The kubelet acts on pressure signals: DiskPressure evictions target disk hogs (images, logs, emptyDir, writable layers). MemoryPressure=False doesn't cancel a disk eviction — each pressure is independent. describe node Conditions is the first place to look when evictions cluster on one node.

q: kubectl drain node-2 hangs: 'cannot delete Pods with local storage'. The pods use emptyDir. How do you proceed?
options: Delete the node object — loses the graceful path entirely
drain --force — overrides other blockers, but local storage needs its own explicit flag
Manually delete each pod — the manual version of the flag below
kubectl drain node-2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data — acknowledges the emptyDir data loss and evicts
explain: Drain protects local data by default (emptyDir/hostPath don't survive); --delete-emptydir-data = informed consent to lose it. --force handles different blockers (unreplicated pods). The flag name states exactly what you're sacrificing.

q: Before kernel patching, you want the scheduler to avoid node-3 — but the monitoring DaemonSet (which tolerates everything) must still be schedulable there. Which command repels selectively?
options: kubectl taint nodes node-3 maintenance=true:NoSchedule — new pods without the toleration won't schedule there; tolerant ones (the monitoring DaemonSet) still can
kubectl cordon node-3 — blocks ALL new pods indiscriminately, including monitoring
kubectl label nodes node-3 maintenance=true — labels alone repel nothing
Delete the node object — overkill for a scheduling preference
explain: Taints = selective repelling via tolerations; cordon = blanket unschedulable. When some workloads must stay schedulable during maintenance, taint (with tolerations on the exceptions), then drain.

q: You need to move pod web-abc into the canary slice: change its track label from stable to canary. Which command?
options: kubectl label pods web-abc track=canary — rejected: the label already exists with another value
kubectl label pods web-abc track=canary --overwrite — overwrites the existing label value
Labels are immutable — delete and recreate the pod
kubectl annotate — annotations aren't labels; selectors won't see them
explain: label without --overwrite fails on existing keys — the safety default against accidental relabeling. --overwrite = intentional change. (Note: relabeling a running pod can detach it from its Service — know what selects that label first.)

q: metrics-server is down and you need raw node CPU numbers NOW for a capacity decision. Which command hits the API directly, bypassing metrics-server?
options: kubectl top node — needs metrics-server
SSH to each node — you have no SSH access
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/node-2/proxy/stats/summary — the kubelet's stats summary via the API proxy; no metrics-server required
Raw API access isn't possible — kubectl always needs metrics-server
explain: --raw = direct API calls; the kubelet /stats/summary endpoint is the metrics-server-independent source (it's what metrics-server scrapes). When the metrics pipeline is down, go to the source.

q: Pods are slow cluster-wide and you suspect one hot node. Which command ranks nodes by live CPU/memory usage?
options: kubectl describe nodes | grep -i cpu — shows capacity/allocatable, not live usage
kubectl top pod -A — pod-level; doesn't rank nodes
Read the scheduler logs — not a usage ranking
kubectl top node --sort-by=cpu — live usage per node, sorted descending
explain: top node = node-level live metrics with --sort-by=cpu|memory; top pod = pod-level. describe shows allocatable capacity — a different question. (metrics-server required for both.)

q: The web pods could be in ANY namespace. Which command finds them all cluster-wide?
options: kubectl get pods -A -l app=web — -A/--all-namespaces widens the search to every namespace
kubectl get pods -l app=web — current namespace only
Namespaces can't be searched together — check each one
-A lists namespaces — it modifies the get scope, it doesn't list namespaces
explain: -A widens get (and describe, logs -l, delete) across namespaces; it composes with selectors. The default namespace-scoped behavior is the trap when resources are spread around.

q: One pod of the web Deployment is wedged in a weird half-broken state (not crashlooping — just serving errors) while its 19 siblings are fine. What's the fastest targeted fix?
options: kubectl delete pod web-abc — the ReplicaSet immediately creates a fresh replacement; only the bad pod is disrupted
kubectl rollout restart deploy/web — restarts all 20 pods; overkill for one wedged pod
Delete the Deployment — destroys all pods and the rollout history
Wait for the liveness probe — it's not failing, so nothing will happen
explain: Controllers self-heal single-pod deletes — the fastest minimal-blast-radius bounce for one wedged pod. rollout restart is the tool when ALL pods need cycling (config change); deleting the Deployment is never the fix for one bad pod.

q: A pod has been stuck Terminating for 20 minutes (its preStop hangs and the node is gone). What's the last-resort removal, and its risk?
options: Wait longer — the kubelet will eventually give up; not when the node is gone
kubectl drain the node — the node is already gone
kubectl delete pod web-abc --grace-period=0 --force — bypasses graceful shutdown; risks leaked resources (volumes, IPs) if the kubelet is actually still alive
--force alone — it needs --grace-period=0 to take effect
explain: Force delete = the API removes the object without kubelet confirmation. Use it only when the node/kubelet is truly dead — otherwise you get zombie processes holding volumes and IPs. --force without --grace-period=0 is silently ignored.

q: Your CI script must wait until the new pod is Ready (up to 2 minutes) before running smoke tests. Which command blocks until the condition holds?
options: sleep 120 — a blind wait: wastes time on fast starts, races on slow ones
kubectl rollout status — watches workload rollouts, not individual pods
A loop over kubectl get — the manual version of the built-in below
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web-abc --timeout=120s — blocks until Ready or the timeout, exiting non-zero on timeout
explain: kubectl wait = the condition gate for scripts: --for=condition=Ready|Completed or --for=delete, with --timeout bounding it. It replaces sleep-loops with an event-driven wait that fails the build properly on timeout.

q: You need one ConfigMap holding LOG_LEVEL=debug as a literal plus the entire contents of ./conf/ as files. Which single command builds it?
options: kubectl create configmap app --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug --from-file=./conf/ — --from-literal and --from-file compose freely in one command; each literal becomes one key and each file becomes a key named for the file
--from-literal and --from-file are mutually exclusive; build two ConfigMaps and merge them with kubectl merge
kubectl create configmap app --from-env-file=./conf/ --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug — --from-env-file reads a directory
Imperative creation can't mix sources; hand-write the YAML
explain: The create flags are additive: stack as many --from-literal, --from-file, and --from-env-file flags as you need in one invocation. There is no kubectl merge command, and --from-env-file parses a single KEY=value file, not a directory.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Compliance requires credential rotation with instant rollback: the new DB password must go live via a rolling update, and the old Secret must remain usable until every pod has moved. Which pattern satisfies this?
options: Edit the Secret's data in place, then kubectl rollout restart — simple, but the old value is unrecoverable

Create db-creds-v2 with the new password, update the Deployment to reference db-creds-v2, and roll — old pods keep working against db-creds until replaced, and the old Secret is your instant rollback target
Delete db-creds first so pods are forced onto the new Secret immediately
Secrets can't be rotated without downtime; schedule a maintenance window
explain: Versioned Secret names turn rotation into a normal rolling update: the reference change creates a new ReplicaSet, old pods keep their already-injected old values until replaced, and rollback is just flipping the reference back. In-place edits give you no previous version to return to, and deleting first guarantees an outage.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The frozen JVM image needs its cgroup memory limit to size its heap at startup, exposed as a FILE the entrypoint script can read. How do you project the container's memory limit into a file?
options: Query the metrics server from the entrypoint script — it knows every container's limits
resourceFieldRef only works for CPU requests, not memory limits

A downwardAPI volume with items: [{path: "mem-limit", resourceFieldRef: {containerName: app, resource: limits.memory}}] — the kubelet writes the limit into the file; the script reads it to compute -Xmx with zero code or RBAC changes
Hardcode -Xmx in a wrapper script baked into a new image — the image is frozen, so this is impossible
explain: resourceFieldRef works in both env vars AND downwardAPI volume items, for requests and limits of CPU and memory. The volume form is the answer when the consumer needs a file (JVM heap sizing is the classic case). The metrics server reports usage, not configured limits, and the frozen image rules out rebuilds.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You try to change a RoleBinding's roleRef from view to edit with kubectl apply and the API server rejects it. What is the rule, and the fix?
options: RoleBindings can't reference ClusterRoles — create a Role instead
kubectl apply can't update RBAC; use kubectl edit and it will succeed
roleRef is namespace-scoped; switch to a ClusterRoleBinding
roleRef is immutable after creation — delete and recreate the RoleBinding pointing at the new role; subjects can be updated in place, but the role reference cannot
explain: The API forbids changing roleRef on an existing binding — least-privilege grants can't be silently escalated by editing. Delete and recreate the binding (or render the new one with --dry-run=client -o yaml and replace). Updating the subjects list in place is fine; only the roleRef is frozen.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A Role grants get and list on pods in namespace payments, but kubectl logs is still rejected with Forbidden. What is missing?
options: pods/log is a separate API subresource — the Role must also grant get on pods/log; read access to pods never implies log access
Log access requires cluster-admin; namespace Roles can never grant it
The developer also needs get on events — logs are served from events
kubectl logs needs list on pods/log, not get
explain: kubectl logs calls the pods/log subresource, and RBAC treats subresources as distinct resources: verbs on pods don't cover pods/log (same story for pods/exec and pods/portforward). Add resources: ["pods/log"] with verbs: ["get"] to the Role. The verb for reading logs is get.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The platform team wants baseline violations LOGGED but not blocked, while restricted stays enforced. Which namespace configuration expresses this?
options: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline plus pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted — warn only notifies, it doesn't log

pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: baseline (violations are recorded in the audit log but pods are still admitted) alongside pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted — enforce, audit, and warn are independent modes, and enforce-version pins which standard version applies
Pod Security Standards can only enforce; there is no warn-only mode
Set both labels to audit — that enforces and logs
explain: The three modes are independent per namespace: enforce blocks, audit records violations in the audit log without blocking, warn returns a warning to the client. Combining audit: baseline with enforce: restricted gives exactly 'log baseline, block restricted'. The version pin (enforce-version: latest or v1.x) stops behavior from shifting under you on upgrade.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The pod sets seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}, but the debug container in the same pod needs full syscall access. How do you exempt just that container?
options: Remove the pod-level profile — every container loses confinement
seccompProfile is pod-level only; per-container exemption is impossible
Set seccompProfile: {type: Unconfined} on the debug container's securityContext — container-level settings override pod-level for the same field, so the app stays confined
Add privileged: true to the debug container — that disables seccomp
explain: seccompProfile is valid at both levels with the standard override rule: container-level wins. Unconfined on the debug container lifts only its filter while the app keeps RuntimeDefault. privileged: true is a far broader hammer and would fail the hardening review this task is clearly under.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A node provides the custom AppArmor profile k8s-nginx. How do you confine ONLY the web container of a pod with it?
options: securityContext.appArmorProfile at the pod level — that confines every container
An annotation on the Deployment — AppArmor is per-pod, not per-Deployment
apparmor: k8s-nginx as a container spec field — no such field exists

The per-container annotation container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/web: localhost/k8s-nginx — the annotation is keyed by container name, so siblings are unaffected; runtime/default would select the runtime's default profile
explain: AppArmor confinement is applied via a container-name-keyed annotation (localhost/<profile> for node-loaded profiles, runtime/default for the runtime default). Pod-level securityContext can't express per-container AppArmor, and there is no apparmor field on the container spec in the annotation-based mechanism.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You add securityContext.sysctls: [{name: "kernel.msgmax", value: "65536"}] to a pod and it's rejected, while net.ipv4.ip_unforward is accepted. Why?
options: kernel.msgmax is an unsafe sysctl — the API rejects it unless the kubelet was started with --allowed-unsafe-sysctls; namespaced safe sysctls like net.ipv4.ip_unforward are allowed by default
sysctls belong in the container securityContext, not the pod's
sysctl values must be integers, not strings — YAML typing issue
Any sysctl requires privileged: true
explain: Sysctls are split into safe (namespaced, allowed by default, e.g. net.ipv4.ip_unforward) and unsafe (node-affecting, e.g. kernel.msgmax), which the kubelet rejects unless explicitly allow-listed at startup. sysctls live in the pod-level securityContext, values are strings, and no privileged flag is involved.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Files the app creates must be group-owned by GID 3000 so the backup sidecar (running as a different UID) can read them by group. runAsUser: 1000 is set. Which field sets the primary group?
options: fsGroup: 3000 — that only chowns mounted volumes, not new files
runAsGroup: 3000 in the pod's securityContext — sets the primary GID of every container process, complementing runAsUser; new files get group 3000
supplementalGroups: [3000] — that adds a supplementary group, not the primary one
capabilities: {add: [CHOWN]} — capabilities don't set group ownership
explain: runAsGroup sets the primary GID for all container processes (new files inherit it as their group). supplementalGroups adds extra group memberships without changing the primary group, and fsGroup only affects volume ownership at mount time. The three fields answer three different questions — the exam mixes them deliberately.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: With readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, the app still needs a writable /tmp — and the data must never touch disk. Which volume fits?
options: hostPath at /tmp — node disk, shared and unportable
A PersistentVolumeClaim — durable disk storage, overkill for scratch
emptyDir: {medium: Memory} mounted at /tmp — tmpfs backed by RAM: writable despite the read-only root filesystem, never touches disk, and counts against the container's memory limit
A ConfigMap mounted at /tmp — read-only by design
explain: medium: Memory turns the emptyDir into a tmpfs — RAM-backed scratch space that stays writable under readOnlyRootFilesystem. The catch the exam may probe: tmpfs counts against the container's memory limit, so size it (sizeLimit) or risk OOMKills. hostPath and PVCs both hit disk.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The app terminates TLS itself (no Ingress) and needs /etc/tls/tls.crt and /etc/tls/tls.key. The certificate lives in a kubernetes.io/tls Secret. How do you deliver the files?
options: envFrom the Secret — that injects variables, not files
Bake the certificate into the image — leaks secrets into image layers
Secrets can only be consumed by Ingress TLS; apps can't mount them
Mount the Secret as a volume at /etc/tls — each key becomes a file, so tls.crt and tls.key appear with exactly the names the app expects
explain: A kubernetes.io/tls Secret is still a Secret: mounting it as a volume projects tls.crt and tls.key as files, which is exactly what an app-side TLS terminator needs. The tls type only matters to Ingress controllers; volume mounting works for any Secret type.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The mounted Secret's key files are world-readable (0644) and the auditor flags it. How do you lock them down?
options: Set defaultMode: 0400 on the secret volume (or mode per item) — projected Secret files default to 0644; the mode is controlled on the volume spec, and the leading zero marks it octal
Run an init container that chmods the files — the kubelet resets modes on sync
Set readOnly: true on the volume — that doesn't change permission bits
File modes are fixed on projected volumes and can't be changed
explain: defaultMode (volume-wide) and per-item mode control the permission bits of projected Secret/ConfigMap files — 0400 gives owner-read-only. An init-container chmod fights the kubelet's periodic sync, and readOnly only blocks writes. Watch the YAML: 0400 is octal; 400 without the leading zero is decimal and means something else.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ResourceQuota with scopes: [NotBestEffort] caps memory at 4Gi, but BestEffort pods keep being created past it. Is the quota broken?
options: Yes — quotas always count every pod in the namespace

No — scopes: [NotBestEffort] makes the quota count only pods that set CPU/memory requests or limits; BestEffort pods (no requests, no limits) are invisible to it. That scoping is the designed semantics
Scopes only work when a LimitRange is also present
BestEffort pods are exempt from all quotas by default, scoped or not
explain: Quota scopes filter WHICH pods count: NotBestEffort matches pods with requests/limits set, BestEffort matches pods without any, and PriorityClass/Terminating add more filters. An unscoped quota counts everything; a scoped one deliberately ignores the rest. Check the scope before declaring the quota broken.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A LimitRange sets maxLimitRequestRatio: {cpu: "4"}. A container requesting 250m CPU with a 2-core limit is rejected. Why?
options: Limits can never exceed requests — set them equal
The ratio counts memory too; the memory ratio failed
limit/request = 2000m/250m = 8, exceeding the max ratio of 4 — the LimitRange caps how far the limit may exceed the request; drop the limit to at most 1000m (4 x 250m) or raise the request
Ratios only apply to memory, not CPU
explain: maxLimitRequestRatio bounds burstiness: limit ÷ request must stay under the ratio per resource. 2000m/250m = 8 > 4, so admission rejects it. Either raise the request (better scheduling signal anyway) or lower the limit to 4x the request.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Node memory pressure forces the kubelet to evict pods. Which pod is evicted LAST?
options: A BestEffort pod with no requests or limits — evicted first, not last
A Burstable pod currently using 10x its request — Burstable pods are evicted before Guaranteed ones
Any pod with a liveness probe — probes don't affect eviction order
A Guaranteed pod — every container has requests == limits for CPU and memory; the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable, and Guaranteed last
explain: QoS class drives eviction order under node pressure: BestEffort (no requests/limits) dies first, Burstable (some requests/limits) next, Guaranteed (requests == limits on every container for both CPU and memory) last. Setting requests == limits is the strongest protection a pod can buy against noisy neighbors.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Every audit log line must include which ServiceAccount the pod runs as, but the image is frozen — no code changes. How?
options: env: [{name: SA_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.serviceAccountName}}}] — the downward API exposes the pod's ServiceAccount name with no code or RBAC changes
Read /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace — that's the namespace, not the ServiceAccount name
Have the app call kubectl auth can-i — that's a permission check, not an identity source
The ServiceAccount name isn't visible inside the pod
explain: fieldRef exposes a fixed menu of pod fields — metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.podIP, and more — as env vars or files. No API calls, no RBAC, no code changes. The serviceaccount directory gives you token/ca.crt/namespace, but not the account's name.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod lists two imagePullSecrets: reg-old (expired credentials) followed by reg-new (valid). The image pull succeeds. Why didn't the bad secret break it?
options: Kubernetes merges both secrets and the valid credentials win
The kubelet tries each imagePullSecret in order until one authenticates — reg-old fails, reg-new succeeds; order only decides which is tried first
Only the last secret in the list is ever used
Expired registry credentials are refreshed automatically
explain: imagePullSecrets is a try-in-order list, not a merged credential set: the kubelet attempts each secret's credentials against the registry until one works. A dead first entry costs one failed attempt, not a failed pull. Keep the working secret in the list and clean up the dead one when convenient.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: CI rebuilds a ConfigMap from ./conf/ on every run, but kubectl create configmap fails on the second run with AlreadyExists. What is the idempotent one-liner?
options: kubectl replace -f conf/ — replace needs a manifest file, not a directory
kubectl delete then create in the pipeline — leaves a window with no ConfigMap at all

kubectl create configmap app --from-file=./conf/ --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - — renders the object client-side, then applies declaratively: creates on first run, updates on every later run
kubectl create --force — no such flag exists
explain: The --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - idiom turns any imperative create into an idempotent upsert — the standard CI pattern for generated ConfigMaps and Secrets. Delete-then-create risks a gap where pods see nothing, and there is no --force on create.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ConfigMap has keys 2fa-enabled and LOG_LEVEL. Loaded via envFrom, LOG_LEVEL appears but 2fa-enabled is silently missing. Why?
options: ConfigMap keys can't contain hyphens — they can; hyphens are legal in keys
envFrom only loads uppercase keys — it loads any valid name
The key needs a prefix: to be injected — prefix only renames, it doesn't fix validity

Environment variable names must match [-._a-zA-Z][-._a-zA-Z0-9]* — a leading digit is illegal, so envFrom silently skips the key (same silent-drop as dots in key names); map it explicitly with env + configMapKeyRef to a legal name
explain: The constraint is on the variable name, not the ConfigMap key: names can't start with a digit (or contain dots), and envFrom drops offending keys without an error. The explicit env entry with configMapKeyRef renames any key to any legal variable name — the universal fix for both the digit and dot variants of this trap.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Dockerfile: ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"] CMD ["--port=8080"]. The pod spec sets only command: ["/app/server"]. What actually runs?
options: /app/server with NO arguments — command replaces ENTRYPOINT, and the Dockerfile CMD is discarded when command is set without args; to keep the flag you must repeat it in args: ["--port=8080"]
/app/server --port=8080 — CMD survives any command override
The pod fails validation — command requires args to be set
--port=8080 becomes the entrypoint and /app/server becomes its argument
explain: The mapping is strict: command overrides ENTRYPOINT, args overrides CMD — and each override fully replaces its counterpart. Setting command without args wipes out the CMD silently. The exam's trap is assuming CMD is sticky; it isn't. When in doubt, set both fields explicitly.

q: The app reads ./config.yaml relative to its working directory and expects to run in /app, but the image's WORKDIR is /. Without rebuilding the image, how do you fix the working directory?
options: args: ["cd /app"] — args are passed to the entrypoint, not executed as shell
Set workingDir: /app on the container — it overrides the image's WORKDIR, equivalent to cd-ing before the entrypoint runs
A postStart hook running cd /app — the hook runs in a separate process; it can't change the main container's cwd
Mount an emptyDir at /app — that changes the filesystem, not the working directory
explain: workingDir sets the container process's current working directory, overriding whatever WORKDIR the image baked in. It's the one-field fix for 'app expects to run from /app'. A postStart cd affects only the hook's own shell, and volume mounts don't move the cwd.

q: A StatefulSet named db with a volumeClaimTemplates entry named data and 3 replicas is created. What PVCs exist, and what happens to them when db-1 is rescheduled?
options: One shared PVC named data-db used by all three pods — StatefulSets don't share claim templates that way
PVCs named data-0, data-1, data-2, deleted together with their pods

data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2 — one per ordinal, named <claim-template>-<sts-name>-<ordinal>; they survive pod rescheduling AND pod deletion, staying bound to their ordinal so the data follows the identity
PVCs are created lazily the first time each pod writes data
explain: volumeClaimTemplates stamps out one PVC per replica with the predictable <template>-<sts>-<ordinal> name, and the PVC lifecycle is decoupled from the pod: rescheduling or deleting db-1 leaves data-db-1 intact, and the replacement db-1 reattaches it. That's the whole point of stable storage for stateful workloads.

q: Scaling the StatefulSet from 5 replicas to 3 must ALSO delete the PVCs of ordinals 3 and 4 to free the storage. Which setting does this?
options: Nothing — PVCs are always deleted on scale-down
Set cascade: false on the scale operation — that controls pod deletion, not PVCs
Delete the PVCs by hand before scaling — manual and race-prone

persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy: {whenScaled: Delete} — governs PVC lifecycle on scale-down (whenDeleted covers StatefulSet deletion); the default Retain keeps them, which is the safe but storage-hungry behavior
explain: By default StatefulSet PVCs are retained on scale-down (data safety first). persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy lets you opt into Delete for the whenScaled and whenDeleted cases independently. The exam trap is assuming scale-down cleans up storage — it doesn't, unless you say so.

q: Compliance wants the last 5 successful AND the last 5 failed report Jobs kept for audit, with older ones cleaned up automatically. Which fields?
options: successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 5 and failedJobsHistoryLimit: 5 on the CronJob — they bound how many finished Jobs are retained; anything older is garbage-collected
ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 5 — that's a seconds-based deletion timer, not a count
backoffLimit: 5 — that caps retries, not history
History limits apply to pods, not Job objects
explain: The two history limits are the audit-friendly retention knobs: keep N successes and N failures as objects for inspection, and the CronJob controller prunes the rest. ttlSecondsAfterFinished is the alternative time-based cleanup — use counts when auditors want 'the last 5', TTLs when you want 'gone after an hour'.

q: Each nightly export run must never exceed 10 minutes, but the CronJob's schedule itself must keep firing nightly. Where does the timeout go?
options: activeDeadlineSeconds on the CronJob spec — that field doesn't exist at the CronJob level
activeDeadlineSeconds: 600 inside the jobTemplate's Job spec — it bounds each spawned Job's wall-clock run; the CronJob schedule is unaffected and keeps firing
startingDeadlineSeconds: 600 — that bounds how late a MISSED schedule may still start, not how long a run may take
backoffLimit: 600 — that caps retry attempts, not runtime
explain: Timeouts compose by level: the CronJob owns the schedule, each Job it spawns owns its own run. activeDeadlineSeconds in the jobTemplate kills a runaway export at 10 minutes while tomorrow's 2 AM run still fires. startingDeadlineSeconds answers a different question — 'how stale may a missed run be before we skip it'.

q: A pod's app containers request 1 CPU total; its init container requests 4 CPU. The pod stays Pending on nodes with 2 CPUs free. Why?
options: Init containers don't count toward scheduling — they do, via the max rule below
The scheduler sums everything: 1 + 4 = 5 CPU — it doesn't sum; it takes the max

Scheduling uses max(sum of app container requests, largest init container request) = max(1, 4) = 4 CPU — init containers run before the app starts, so the node must fit the biggest init container; shrink the init's request
Pending means the init image can't be pulled — check describe for the real reason, but the math here is the cause
explain: The scheduler's init-container rule: effective request = max(total app requests, each init request). Init containers run sequentially before app containers, so the node must accommodate the largest one. A bloated init request (debug images, migrations) is a classic mystery-Pending cause — describe shows Insufficient cpu with no quota errors.

q: You attach an ephemeral debug container with a livenessProbe to a running pod and the API server rejects it. Why?
options: Ephemeral containers can't use custom images — they can, any image works
The target pod must be restarted before attaching — ephemeral containers attach to running pods, no restart needed
Probes are allowed on ephemeral containers; the YAML indentation was wrong
Ephemeral containers don't support probes, ports, or lifecycle hooks — they're short-lived debugging aids; drop the probe and attach again
explain: The ephemeral container spec is deliberately restricted: no probes, no ports, no lifecycle, no startup ordering. They're for 'get a shell with the right tools next to the app', not for running services. kubectl debug rejects probe fields at validation — read the error, drop the probe.

q: A postStart hook registers the pod with the discovery service, but traffic sometimes arrives BEFORE registration completes. Why can't postStart guarantee ordering?
options: postStart runs asynchronously alongside the container's entrypoint — the container is marked Running and added to endpoints without waiting for the hook; only a FAILING hook blocks, by killing and restarting the container
postStart runs before the entrypoint starts — it runs after
Hooks only execute on the very first container start — they run on every start
postStart is deprecated in favor of prestart — no such field exists
explain: postStart is fire-and-forget from the kubelet's perspective: it doesn't gate Running status or endpoint publication. Relying on it for 'register before serving' is racy by design. If ordering truly matters, do the registration in an init container or make the app itself register before listening.

q: The app needs /etc/app/config.yaml rendered from a template at startup. The image is frozen and ConfigMaps can't template. Which pattern works?
options: A sidecar that rewrites the file in a loop — overkill and racy at startup
An init container that renders the template into a shared emptyDir mounted at /etc/app in the app container — init containers complete before the app starts, so the file is guaranteed ready
Have the app write to the ConfigMap volume — ConfigMap volumes are read-only
Mount the template with subPath and let the app render it — the app can't render; the image is frozen
explain: The init-container-prepares-shared-volume pattern is the answer whenever the app needs computed files it can't produce itself: init renders, app consumes, the emptyDir is the handoff. It composes with the frozen-image constraint because all the logic lives in the init container's image.

q: Nodes carry dedicated=<team>:NoSchedule taints with a different value per team. Your platform pod must tolerate ALL of them regardless of value. Which toleration?
options: key: dedicated, value: "", effect: NoSchedule — Equal (the default operator) requires an exact value match, so empty matches nothing here
Write one toleration per team value — works but rots every time a team is added
tolerations: [{key: dedicated, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}] — Exists matches any value for the key; it's the wildcard form of tolerations
Tolerations can't wildcard values; use nodeAffinity instead — affinity doesn't bypass taints
explain: operator: Exists matches a taint by key alone, ignoring value — the wildcard for taints whose values vary. The default operator Equal demands key+value(+effect) all match. Don't confuse tolerations with affinity: affinity attracts, tolerations merely permit.

q: You taint archive nodes workload=archive:PreferNoSchedule. Pods without tolerations still sometimes land there. Is the taint broken?
options: Yes — any taint repels all untolerating pods unconditionally
No, but the pods landing there is a bug — file it
PreferNoSchedule is not a valid effect; the taint was ignored
No — PreferNoSchedule is a soft preference: the scheduler avoids those nodes when possible but still schedules there if nothing else fits; NoSchedule is the hard repel
explain: The three effects form a hardness ladder: PreferNoSchedule (try to avoid), NoSchedule (never schedule new pods without toleration), NoExecute (also evict running pods without toleration). 'Sometimes lands there' is PreferNoSchedule working as designed under capacity pressure.

q: The fluent-bit DaemonSet must be upgraded one node at a time BY HAND during a maintenance window — no automatic rolling. Which updateStrategy?
options: updateStrategy: {type: OnDelete} — the new template applies only to pods you delete manually, giving full per-node manual control
RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 — still automatic, just gentler
Delete and recreate the DaemonSet for each node — destroys the update history
suspend: true on the DaemonSet — no such field exists
explain: OnDelete freezes the rollout: DaemonSet pods keep the old template until you delete them, and the controller recreates each with the new template. It's the manual-gate upgrade strategy — pair it with cordon/drain per node for a controlled fleet upgrade.

q: You scale a StatefulSet from 5 replicas to 3. Which pods terminate, and what happens to their PVCs?
options: db-0 and db-1 — the lowest ordinals go first
db-4 then db-3 — scale-down removes the HIGHEST ordinals first (reverse of ordered scale-up); their PVCs are retained by default, so scaling back to 5 reattaches the same data
Two random pods — StatefulSet ordering is only for startup
All pods restart with new ordinals — ordinals are stable
explain: StatefulSet scaling is ordinal-ordered in both directions: up from 0, down from the top. PVC retention on scale-down is the default (persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled: Retain), so the data waits for the ordinal to return — delete the PVCs explicitly if you truly want the storage back.

q: You're building a throwaway interactive debug pod and need a real terminal — arrow keys and Ctrl-C must work. Which container fields?
options: interactive: true — no such field exists
tty: true alone — without stdin there's nothing to type into
stdin: true and tty: true — together they attach stdin and allocate a TTY; it's exactly what kubectl run -it sets
command: ["/bin/sh"] alone — gives you a shell with no terminal attached
explain: stdin: true wires the container's stdin to your client and tty: true allocates a pseudo-terminal — you need both for interactive use. kubectl run -it is shorthand for exactly this pair. Without tty, Ctrl-C and line editing misbehave.

q: A container sets env: [{name: GREETING, value: "hello $(UNDEFINED_SUFFIX)"}]. UNDEFINED_SUFFIX is defined nowhere. What does the app see?
options: The pod fails to start — undefined variable references are rejected at admission
The literal string hello $(UNDEFINED_SUFFIX) — that's what $$(...) produces
The value of UNDEFINED_SUFFIX from the node's environment — kubelet never reads node env for this
hello  (with a trailing space) — references to undefined variables expand to the empty string; only the $$(VAR) escape produces a literal dollar
explain: Variable expansion is lenient: $(DEFINED) substitutes, $(UNDEFINED) becomes empty, $$(VAR) escapes to literal $(VAR). The exam loves the three-way distinction — expansion, empty-on-missing, and escape. A missing variable never blocks pod creation.

q: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30. preStop runs sleep 20, then the app needs 15s to drain after SIGTERM. Does it drain cleanly?
options: No — preStop runs first and consumes 20s of the 30s grace; SIGTERM fires at 20s leaving only 10s, so SIGKILL cuts the 15s drain short. Raise the grace to cover preStop time PLUS drain time (40s+)
Yes — the grace period restarts fresh after preStop completes
Yes — preStop and SIGTERM run in parallel, so the app gets the full 30s
The grace period only applies to preStop; SIGTERM waits indefinitely
explain: Shutdown is strictly sequential inside ONE grace budget: preStop hook → SIGTERM → grace expires → SIGKILL. Budget the whole sequence: hook duration + drain duration + margin. The classic exam math is exactly this — a 20s hook plus a 15s drain needs more than 30s.

q: Nodes have the image pre-loaded and you must guarantee the registry is NEVER contacted. Which imagePullPolicy, and what is its failure mode?
options: IfNotPresent — it still contacts the registry when the image is absent
imagePullPolicy: Never — the kubelet uses only local images; if the image is missing the container fails with ErrImageNeverPull instead of pulling
Always with a pull secret — Always contacts the registry by definition
Never is not a valid policy — it is, alongside Always and IfNotPresent
explain: Never is the air-gap policy: purely local images, zero registry traffic. Its failure mode is honest — ErrImageNeverPull tells you the preload missed a node. IfNotPresent is the usual default for tagged images, but it WILL pull when the cache misses.

q: A Job sets completions: 3, parallelism: 10. How many pods ever run?
options: 10 — parallelism wins over completions
13 — completions plus parallelism
3 — completions caps the TOTAL work; parallelism only caps how many run CONCURRENTLY, so at most 3 pods ever exist and the Job completes after 3 successes
The Job is rejected — parallelism can't exceed completions
explain: completions is the finish line (how many must succeed), parallelism is the width (how many at once). Width beyond the finish line is harmless but meaningless — 3 pods, then done. The exam inverts it to check you know which field is the total and which is the concurrency cap.

q: You need a one-off debug pod that runs a command and exits WITHOUT being restarted, then cleans itself up. Which imperative command?
options: kubectl create deployment debug --image=busybox — Deployments restart exited containers forever
kubectl run debug --image=busybox — the default restart policy restarts the container on exit
Only a hand-written Job manifest can do one-off runs
kubectl run debug --restart=Never --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh — restartPolicy Never makes it a genuine one-off, and --rm deletes the pod when it exits
explain: kubectl run --restart=Never produces a pod that runs to completion like a Job's pod, without any controller resurrecting it. --rm cleans up on exit so failed experiments don't litter the namespace. It's the fastest one-off-debug shape on the exam.

q: You must change LOG_LEVEL on the running web Deployment without editing YAML. Which command does it, and do the pods roll?
options: kubectl set env deploy/web LOG_LEVEL=debug — it patches the pod template, which triggers a rolling update automatically so every pod picks up the new value
kubectl set env only annotates the Deployment object; pods keep the old value until you restart them
kubectl set env doesn't exist for environment variables — only for images
It patches the pods in place with no restart — env changes apply live
explain: kubectl set env is the imperative env-var updater: it rewrites the pod template, and any pod-template change drives a rollout. There's no in-place env update in Kubernetes — new values always mean new pods. It's the fastest exam answer for 'change an env var right now'.

q: Deployment: replicas 3, maxUnavailable: 25%, maxSurge: 25%. During the rollout, how many pods may be UNAVAILABLE?
options: 1 — 25% of 3 rounds up
0 — maxUnavailable percentages round DOWN (25% of 3 = 0.75 -> 0), so every old pod stays until its replacement is ready; note maxSurge rounds the opposite way
3 — the whole replica set may go down
Percentages under 100% are rejected by validation
explain: The rounding rules are asymmetric by design: maxUnavailable rounds DOWN (favoring availability), maxSurge rounds UP (favoring progress). 25% of 3 gives 0 unavailable and 1 surge pod. The exam tests this exact asymmetry — memorize: unavailable down, surge up.

q: Same Deployment (replicas 3, maxSurge: 25%). How many EXTRA pods may exist above desired during the rollout?
options: 0 — surge percentages round down, like maxUnavailable
3 — surge allows doubling
1 — maxSurge percentages round UP (0.75 -> 1), so one extra pod is allowed; the asymmetry (surge up, unavailable down) biases rollouts toward availability
Surge is ignored below 5 replicas
explain: maxSurge rounds UP: 25% of 3 is 0.75, which becomes 1 surge pod. Combined with maxUnavailable rounding down to 0, a 3-replica rollout with 25%/25% briefly runs 4 pods and never drops below 3. Small replica counts make the rounding dominate — that's the exam's favorite arithmetic.

q: Before installing the redis chart you want to see every configurable value and its default. Which command?
options: helm get values redis — that reads an already-installed release, which doesn't exist yet
helm template --dry-run — renders manifests, doesn't document the value surface
Read every template by hand — slow and error-prone
helm show values bitnami/redis — prints the chart's values.yaml with defaults and comments; the discovery command to run before any --set
explain: helm show values (and helm show chart/readme) is how you learn a chart's interface without reading all its templates. Guessing value names for --set is the classic Helm exam failure — discover first, then set. helm get values is for inspecting live releases, not charts.

q: You installed with --set image.tag=v1. Months later you run helm upgrade -f prod.yaml, which never mentions image.tag — yet the new pods still run v1, not the chart default. Why?
options: helm upgrade carries forward the release's previously supplied values — the old --set image.tag=v1 is stored with the release and reused; add --reset-values to start clean from chart defaults plus only the new inputs
prod.yaml implicitly resets every value it doesn't mention
--set flags expire 30 days after install
The chart's default tag must be v1 — check values.yaml
explain: Helm values are sticky: each upgrade reuses the last release's user-supplied values unless --reset-values drops them. Old --set flags haunting later upgrades is the standard 'why won't my value change' mystery. When an upgrade surprises you, helm get values is the first place to look.

q: Every resource in the overlay must carry team: payments — INCLUDING pod selectors and their template labels — without editing the base. Which kustomization field?
options: metadata.labels hand-edited per resource — exactly what we're avoiding, and it breaks selector matching
commonLabels: {team: payments} — Kustomize adds it to metadata.labels AND rewrites selectors and pod template labels to stay consistent, which hand-editing would break
commonAnnotations: {team: payments} — annotations aren't selectors and don't affect matching
A JSON patch per resource — works but verbose for a global label
explain: commonLabels is the label transformer that understands selectors: it adds the label everywhere AND updates every selector/template pair so they keep matching. Adding a label to pod templates by hand without updating the selector orphans the pods — the exact breakage commonLabels exists to prevent.

q: You rotate the TLS certificate monthly and want pods to roll automatically on each rotation — the same hash-triggered rollout configMapGenerator gives you. Which generator gives Secrets the same behavior?
options: configMapGenerator with binary data — wrong object type for a TLS secret
Hand-edit the Secret in place — pods never roll on in-place Secret edits
secretGenerator — it appends a content hash to the Secret name and rewrites references in the Deployment, so each rotation produces a new name and therefore a rolling update
Secrets can never trigger rollouts; always restart by hand
explain: secretGenerator mirrors configMapGenerator: content-hashed names (app-tls-8f2k…) mean any content change renames the object, the Deployment reference updates, and the pods roll. In-place Secret edits never trigger rollouts — the hash-suffix indirection is what makes rotation automatic.

q: You deleted the old metrics Deployment from your manifests and ran kubectl apply -f ., but it still runs in the cluster. What is the declarative fix?
options: The API server caches deletions for an hour — wait
kubectl delete -f old.yaml — works once, but isn't declarative going forward
apply -f . only reads files in the current directory, not subdirectories
kubectl apply only creates and updates — it never deletes orphans; re-apply with --prune -l app=web so labeled resources missing from your files are garbage-collected
explain: apply is create/update-only by design; deletions need --prune with a label selector scoping what's safe to remove. Without the selector guard, prune could eat resources other tools manage — always scope it. This is the standard GitOps gotcha: removing a file doesn't remove the cluster object.

q: The web Deployment's app container needs its memory limit raised to 1Gi — no YAML editing allowed. Which command?
options: kubectl set resources deploy/web -c app --limits=memory=1Gi — patches the container's resources and rolls the Deployment
kubectl top deploy/web and adjust the output — top is read-only observability
Only kubectl edit can change resources — set resources exists precisely for this
kubectl scale deploy/web --limits=memory=1Gi — scale changes replica counts, not resources
explain: kubectl set resources is the imperative counterpart to editing the resources block: -c selects the container, --limits/--requests set the values, and the pod-template change rolls the Deployment. Forgetting -c on a multi-container pod is the usual mistake — the command then doesn't know which container you mean.

q: You must inject every key of ConfigMap app-cfg as environment variables prefixed with APP_ into the web Deployment — imperatively, no YAML. Which command?
options: kubectl set env deploy/web --from=configmap/app-cfg — imports the keys but with no prefix
kubectl set env deploy/web --from=configmap/app-cfg --prefix=APP_ — imports all keys with the prefix applied, and rolls the pods to pick them up
envFrom can only be declared in YAML manifests
--prefix only works with secret sources, not ConfigMaps
explain: set env --from imports a whole ConfigMap or Secret as env vars, and --prefix namespaces them — the imperative twin of the envFrom+prefix manifest pattern. Like every pod-template change, it triggers a rollout automatically.

q: Product wants EXACTLY 10% of traffic on v2 (canary) and 90% on v1. Can a native Kubernetes Service do weighted splitting?
options: Yes — Services have a weight field per endpoint
Yes — enable sessionAffinity: ClientIP and set the ratio

No — a native Service spreads traffic roughly evenly across ready endpoints; precise percentages need an Ingress controller or service mesh. The native approximation is replica ratios (1 canary : 9 stable ~= 10%)
Yes — create two Services and split DNS 10/90
explain: kube-proxy load-balances uniformly; there's no weight knob on a Service. Replica-count ratios give you coarse traffic shaping (and it's how the classic canary works), but 'exactly 10%' needs header/weight-aware routing from an Ingress controller or mesh. The exam checks that you don't promise the native Service something it can't do.

q: The stateful api must autoscale on CPU just like the stateless web Deployment. Does HPA support StatefulSets?
options: No — HPA only targets Deployments
No — StatefulSets can't change replica counts
Only with a custom metrics adapter — not for plain CPU
Yes — HPA targets anything with a scale subresource; set scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: StatefulSet, name: api} (kubectl autoscale sts/api works too)
explain: The HPA doesn't care about workload kind — it talks to the scale subresource, which Deployments, StatefulSets, ReplicaSets, and ReplicationControllers all expose. kubectl autoscale accepts sts/ and rs/ prefixes the same way it accepts deploy/.

q: A rollout is stuck in ImagePullBackOff on a bad tag. You need to freeze it mid-flight while you investigate, then continue after fixing the image. Which sequence?
options: kubectl rollout pause deploy/web — freezes the rollout in place; fix with kubectl set image, then kubectl rollout resume to continue
kubectl rollout undo immediately — abandons the new ReplicaSet you may want to inspect
Delete the stuck ReplicaSet — the Deployment will recreate it and retry
Pause only works before a rollout starts, not mid-flight — it works any time
explain: rollout pause isn't just for planned multi-change updates — it also freezes a broken in-flight rollout so it stops churning while you diagnose. Fix the image (set image), then resume; the rollout continues from where it paused instead of restarting.

q: Chart.yaml has version: 2.5.0 and appVersion: 1.18.3. A teammate bumps version to 2.5.1 for a config-only change. Which statement is correct?
options: appVersion must always equal version — they're independent
version is the CHART's own version (bump it on any chart change); appVersion is the version of the application the chart deploys — bumping the chart version doesn't redeploy or change the app
version is the Kubernetes API version the chart targets
Bumping version automatically rolls the app's pods
explain: version versions the packaging (templates, defaults, helpers); appVersion versions the payload. A config-only chart change bumps version while appVersion stays put — and Helm only rolls pods when the rendered manifests actually change. Confusing the two is the standard Chart.yaml exam trap.

q: The staging overlay must combine the app base AND a shared monitoring base (dashboards, alerts) without copying files. How?
options: Kustomize allows only one base per overlay
Copy the monitoring manifests into the overlay — duplication rots
List both under bases: (or resources:) in the overlay's kustomization.yaml — Kustomize merges multiple bases and your patches and transformers apply across the union
Overlays can't reference sibling directories — they can, via relative paths
explain: An overlay can compose any number of bases — shared platform bases plus the app base is the intended pattern. Transformers like namePrefix, commonLabels, and patches then apply to the merged set, which is how one overlay brands shared resources as its own.

q: kubectl autoscale deploy/web --min=2 --cpu-percent=70 fails validation. What is missing?
options: --min must be 1 — any min is legal
cpu-percent requires the metrics server error to be fixed first — that's a runtime error, not a validation failure
autoscale can't target Deployments — it can
--max is required — the HPA needs an upper bound; e.g. --max=10 --min=2 --cpu-percent=70
explain: --max is the one mandatory autoscale flag: an autoscaler without a ceiling is a runaway risk, so the API demands it. --min defaults to 1 if omitted. The exam's trap is treating --min as the required one.

q: After kubectl set image on the db StatefulSet, how do you watch the rolling update run to completion?
options: kubectl rollout status sts/db — rollout status works for Deployments, StatefulSets, and DaemonSets, blocking until the update completes or fails
rollout status is Deployment-only — it covers all three rolling workloads
Poll kubectl get pods in a loop — the manual version of the built-in
StatefulSets don't report rollout progress — they do, via their status fields
explain: rollout status is workload-agnostic across the three: it watches the controller's status until updatedReplicas == replicas (and analogous conditions) or the progress deadline hits. After any set image on a StatefulSet or DaemonSet, it's the same one-command watch as for Deployments.

q: An HPA (min 2, max 10, target 70%) manages web. During a sale you kubectl scale deploy/web --replicas=8; an hour later it's back at 3 and the sale suffers. What happened?
options: The scale command failed silently — it succeeded, then was reverted

The HPA owns the replica count — it continuously reconciles toward its target, so your manual scale was reverted when utilization allowed fewer replicas. To hold 8, raise the HPA's minReplicas or pause the HPA
Manual scaling requires --current-replicas to stick — that flag is for optimistic concurrency, not persistence
HPAs only scale up, never down — they do both within min/max
explain: Two writers, one field: the HPA's control loop will always drag replicas back to what its math says. Manual kubectl scale on an HPA-managed workload is a temporary suggestion at best. Either change the HPA's bounds or disable it for the event window — don't fight the controller.

q: A Deployment uses strategy: {type: Recreate} with rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}. During the update all pods go down at once. Why didn't maxUnavailable: 0 protect it?
options: maxUnavailable: 0 is invalid — it's the strictest valid setting
The scheduler ignored the setting — the strategy did

Recreate kills ALL old pods before creating new ones by design — the rollingUpdate parameters only apply to the RollingUpdate strategy and are silently ignored with Recreate; zero-downtime and Recreate are mutually exclusive
You needed maxSurge: 0 instead — surge is also ignored under Recreate
explain: Recreate is 'stop the world, then start': every old pod terminates before any new pod is created, so downtime is inherent and the rollingUpdate stanza is dead config. If the task says zero-downtime, Recreate is disqualified no matter what the surge/unavailable fields say.

q: Traffic spikes 10x in 30 seconds; the HPA jumps 2 -> 10 replicas instantly and the cold backends collapse. How do you rate-limit scale-UP specifically?
options: Lower the CPU target — that scales MORE aggressively, not less
Set stabilizationWindowSeconds — that delays scale-DOWN flapping, not scale-up speed
Reduce maxReplicas — that caps the ceiling but the jump to the ceiling is still instant
behavior: {scaleUp: {policies: [{type: Pods, value: 2, periodSeconds: 60}]}} — caps scale-up velocity (2 pods/min here) while leaving scale-down behavior alone
explain: HPA behavior policies pace scaling per direction: scaleUp.policies throttles how fast replicas are added per period, independent of scaleDown. stabilizationWindowSeconds is the anti-flap delay (mostly for scale-down); policies are the speed limit. Cold-start-sensitive backends want a gentle scale-up policy.

q: From a pod, curl payments.example.com takes 5+ seconds to START, then transfers instantly. External DNS is healthy. What is the likely cause?
options: ndots: 5 (the default) — names with fewer than 5 dots are tried against every search domain first (payments.example.com.default.svc.cluster.local, ...), each attempt timing out before the real lookup; fix with a trailing dot (payments.example.com.) or ndots: 1 in dnsConfig
CoreDNS is down — then nothing would resolve at all
The Service has no endpoints — then the transfer would fail, not stall at start
An MTU black hole — that breaks transfers, not name resolution
explain: The default ndots:5 means any short name goes through the full search-domain expansion before the real query — each bogus suffix costs a timeout against cluster DNS. The trailing dot makes a name fully-qualified (skipping search), and dnsConfig ndots tunes the threshold. Slow-start-but-fast-transfer is the signature symptom.

q: A legacy monitoring pod must resolve names using the NODE's DNS (corporate resolvers), bypassing cluster DNS entirely. Which dnsPolicy?
options: ClusterFirst — that's cluster DNS with upstream fallback, the default
dnsPolicy: Default — the pod inherits the node's /etc/resolv.conf resolvers and ignores cluster DNS entirely
None without a dnsConfig — None REQUIRES an explicit dnsConfig
HostFirst — no such policy exists
explain: Default means 'behave like a plain host process': the pod gets the node's DNS and no cluster search domains or cluster DNS. It's the escape hatch for workloads that must use corporate DNS. (None + dnsConfig is the fully-custom variant; ClusterFirst is the normal cluster-DNS behavior.)

q: You create Service oracle-db with no selector, plus an Endpoints object named oracle-db-ips holding the database IP. Pods can't connect via oracle-db. What is wrong?
options: Services without selectors can't have endpoints — they can, via manually created Endpoints
The Endpoints object needs its own selector — Endpoints are address lists, they don't select
The Endpoints object MUST share the Service's name (oracle-db) — kube-proxy only wires identically-named Endpoints to a selector-less Service
External IPs require type: LoadBalancer — manual Endpoints work with plain ClusterIP
explain: For selector-less Services the name IS the link: the Endpoints object must be named exactly like the Service, or kube-proxy never associates them. With a selector, the Endpoints controller fills the (same-named) object automatically; without one, you're the controller — and the naming contract is on you.

q: On-prem with no cloud load-balancer controller, the firewall team will send traffic to 203.0.113.50 and expects the cluster to serve the app there. Which Service field?
options: clusterIP: 203.0.113.50 — clusterIPs must come from the service CIDR, not arbitrary public IPs
nodePort: 443 — outside the valid NodePort range and the wrong mechanism
type: LoadBalancer — stays <pending> forever with no cloud controller
spec.externalIPs: [203.0.113.50] — kube-proxy routes that IP to the Service on every node; you then route the IP to a node at the network layer
explain: externalIPs is the on-prem 'bring your own IP' mechanism: kube-proxy installs the routing for that IP on all nodes, and your network routes the IP to any node. The Service itself stays ClusterIP — no cloud controller needed. It's the classic answer when MetalLB isn't available and the firewall team owns the IP.

q: Two Ingresses both claim host shop.example.com with path / but point at different backends. What happens?
options: Undefined behavior — the Ingress spec defines no merge order; controllers typically serve one (often last-applied wins) or surface a conflict; never rely on it, keep host+path unique per Ingress
Traffic splits 50/50 between the backends
The API server rejects the second Ingress — it accepts both
Both backends receive every request
explain: Duplicate host+path across Ingresses is a configuration conflict the API won't catch — the controller decides, and different controllers decide differently. The safe rule: one owner per host+path. When routing mysteriously goes to the 'wrong' backend, duplicate Ingress claims are high on the suspect list.

q: The Ingress must route ONLY /healthz (exactly) to the monitor Service — /healthz/detailed must NOT match. Which pathType?
options: Prefix — /healthz with Prefix also matches /healthz/detailed and /healthz-anything
pathType: Exact with path: /healthz — matches only that exact path; Prefix would swallow everything beneath it
ImplementationSpecific — controller-defined matching, not exactness
Exact is not a valid pathType — it is, alongside Prefix and ImplementationSpecific
explain: Exact means element-for-element equality on the path (trailing slash aside); Prefix means the path plus anything under it. Health-check-style single endpoints want Exact; API trees want Prefix. Mixing them up is how /healthz/detailed ends up on the wrong Service.

q: The team wants HTTP header-based routing and distinct route kinds per protocol, and finds Ingress annotations messy. Which Kubernetes-native successor should they evaluate?
options: Write a custom Ingress controller — reinventing the wheel
NodePort Services per route — no L7 routing at all
The Gateway API (Gateway, HTTPRoute, etc.) — the Ingress successor with expressive, role-separated routing; Ingress stays supported, but new routing features land in Gateway API
CoreDNS rewrite rules — DNS doesn't route HTTP
explain: The Gateway API is the official next generation of Kubernetes routing: typed routes (HTTPRoute, TLSRoute, TCPRoute), header/method matching, and separated roles (infra vs app teams). CKAD-level awareness: know it exists, what problem it solves, and that Ingress isn't going away — you're not expected to write Gateway manifests.

q: A NetworkPolicy declares policyTypes: [Ingress] and also contains an egress: [...] rule. Pods can still reach destinations the egress rule should block. Why?
options: Egress rules must live in a separate policy object — one policy can hold both
The to: peer selector must be wrong — the structural issue is bigger than the peer
Egress is allow-all by default and can't be restricted — it can, with a proper policy
Egress rules are IGNORED unless policyTypes includes Egress — policyTypes declares which directions the policy governs; rules for an undeclared direction never take effect
explain: policyTypes is the master switch: list Ingress, Egress, or both, and only rules for listed directions are enforced. An egress rule under policyTypes: [Ingress] is dead config — the API won't even warn you. When an egress rule 'does nothing', check policyTypes first.

q: The egress rule must allow DNS to kube-dns in kube-system, selected by namespace NAME (its labels may vary). How do you match the namespace?
options: namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}} — every namespace automatically carries this label with its name; combine with podSelector: {} to reach all kube-dns pods in it
podSelector: {matchLabels: {name: kube-system}} — podSelector only matches pods in the POLICY's own namespace
ipBlock with the DNS ClusterIP — brittle; the IP can change
A namespaceName field on the peer — no such field exists
explain: kubernetes.io/metadata.name is the automatic 'this namespace's name as a label' — the reliable way to select a namespace by name when you can't trust its other labels. podSelector never crosses namespace boundaries; that's namespaceSelector's job. This exact pattern (DNS egress to kube-system) is the most common real-world use.

q: The policy must allow ingress on TCP ports 30000-32767 (the NodePort range) from the office. How do you express the range without listing 2768 ports?
options: List every port — 2768 entries of YAML pain
ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 30000, endPort: 32767}] — endPort defines an inclusive range starting at port; both must be set and endPort must be >= port
port: "30000-32767" as a string — not valid syntax
Omit ports entirely — that allows ALL ports, far too broad
explain: endPort is the range operator for policy ports: port is the start, endPort the inclusive end. Both fields required, endPort >= port. It's the only sane way to allow a NodePort-sized range — and the exam's way of checking you know policies have range support.

q: The egress policy allows TCP 53 to kube-dns. DNS mostly works, but large responses intermittently fail. What is missing?
options: DNS never uses TCP — it does, for large/truncated responses
Allow port 5353 instead — that's mDNS, unrelated
