UDP 53 as well — DNS normally uses UDP but falls back to TCP for large responses; allowing only TCP breaks the common case in reverse... and allowing only one protocol flakes. Allow both UDP and TCP on 53
DNS requires port 443 — that's HTTPS
explain: DNS is a two-protocol protocol: UDP for normal queries, TCP when responses exceed UDP size limits (truncation bit set). A policy allowing only one of them produces 'mostly works, sometimes doesn't' — the most confusing failure signature. Always allow both on 53 for DNS.

q: A NetworkPolicy selects app: api with policyTypes: [Egress] and NO egress rules. What happens to the api pods' outbound traffic?
options: Nothing — empty rules mean allow-all
Only DNS is blocked — everything is blocked
Egress is unaffected; the policy is a no-op — declaring the direction is what activates the deny
ALL egress is denied — an empty rule list for a DECLARED direction is a default-deny for that direction. Contrast: a policyTypes: [Ingress]-only policy leaves egress completely untouched
explain: This is the default-deny idiom: declare the direction, provide zero rules, and everything in that direction is denied. The critical contrast the exam probes: policyTypes gates per direction, so an ingress-only policy never affects egress. Forgetting DNS egress in a default-deny-egress policy is the #1 self-inflicted outage.

q: The task: 'allow egress ONLY to payments.example.com (an external SaaS), deny everything else.' Can a NetworkPolicy match the hostname?
options: No — NetworkPolicy peers are IPs/CIDRs, pod selectors, and namespace selectors; there is no DNS-name peer. Resolve the SaaS to CIDRs and use ipBlock (accepting the brittleness), or use a service mesh / egress gateway for true FQDN filtering
Yes — to: [{dnsName: payments.example.com}] — no such peer exists
Yes — route it through an Ingress — Ingress is for inbound
Yes — pair it with an ExternalName Service — ExternalName doesn't create a policy peer
explain: NetworkPolicies operate at L3/L4 — they can't see DNS names, only IPs. SaaS CIDRs change, which is why ipBlock answers are brittle and FQDN egress is genuinely a mesh/gateway feature. The exam plants dnsName-shaped distractors; the correct answer is knowing the boundary of what policies can express.

q: An Ingress in namespace shop routes to Service api in namespace billing. It never serves traffic. Why?
options: Cross-namespace routing requires a Gateway API — Ingress simply forbids it
Ingress backends must be Services in the SAME namespace as the Ingress — cross-namespace service references are not honored; create the Ingress in billing or mirror the routing there
Services can't be referenced by name, only by IP — they can
You need an ExternalName Service — that's for external targets, not this
explain: Ingress is namespace-scoped in its backends: every backend.service must live in the Ingress's own namespace. The manifest applies cleanly and then silently does nothing — no error, just no route. When an Ingress 'never works' and the controller is healthy, check the backend's namespace first.

q: A NodePort Service (nodePort 31080) has its only pod on node-1. Can clients reach the app via node-2's IP on port 31080?
options: No — only the node actually running the pod serves the NodePort
Only via the ClusterIP — the ClusterIP is separate from NodePort access
Yes — kube-proxy opens the NodePort on EVERY node and routes to the pod wherever it runs (an extra network hop unless externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps it on-node)
Only if the pod uses hostNetwork — unrelated
explain: NodePort is cluster-wide: every node's IP:nodePort reaches the Service, with kube-proxy forwarding to the pod's node. That any-node reachability is why NodePort works behind external load balancers without pod placement awareness — and why externalTrafficPolicy: Local exists, to cut the extra hop (at the cost of uneven distribution).

q: One Ingress rule must catch every path NOT matched by more specific rules and send it to the sorry Service. Which path does it?
options: path: /* — that's regex syntax, only meaningful with ImplementationSpecific on some controllers
Omit the paths list — invalid; a rule needs paths or a defaultBackend
pathType: Exact with path: / — matches only the bare /
path: / with pathType: Prefix — Prefix / matches every path by segment; longest-match wins, so specific rules still take precedence and / catches the rest
explain: Prefix / is the catch-all: every path starts with /. Ingress controllers use longest-prefix-match, so /api rules win over / and only truly unmatched traffic falls through. Pair it with defaultBackend if you want unmatched HOSTS caught too.

q: An ingress rule lists from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}] with NO ports specified. Which traffic from web pods is allowed?
options: All ports — omitting ports in a rule allows every port from those peers; add ports: [{port: 5432}] to narrow it
No ports — an empty ports list blocks everything
Only port 80 — there is no default port
The policy is invalid without ports — it's valid
explain: In NetworkPolicy rules, an omitted ports field means 'all ports' — the rule filters only on the peer selectors. Least-privilege policies always name their ports. The exam's version of this trap: a rule that looks restrictive (specific peer) but is wide open on ports.

q: The task: 'DENY traffic from app: evil, allow everything else to reach db.' How do you write the deny?
options: An ingress rule with action: deny — no such action exists
You can't — NetworkPolicies are allow-lists ONLY, with no deny rules; invert the design: default-deny ingress on db, then add allow rules for the legitimate peers
Use ipBlock except with the evil pods' IPs — pod IPs are ephemeral; except is for CIDRs
Put an egress policy on the evil pods — wrong direction for protecting db
explain: There is no deny primitive in NetworkPolicy — only allow rules, and anything not explicitly allowed (once a policy selects the pod) is denied. 'Deny X, allow everything else' must be rewritten as 'deny everything, allow everyone except X' via enumerated allow rules. Thinking in allow-lists is the core NetworkPolicy mindset shift.

q: The app needs end-to-end TLS — the Ingress must NOT terminate, just pass TCP 443 through to the pods. Can a standard Ingress do this?
options: Yes — Ingress never terminates TLS by itself
Set tls: null on the rule — that just disables TLS config

No — Ingress is HTTP(S) reverse-proxying and terminates TLS by design; passthrough needs a controller-specific annotation (e.g. nginx ssl-passthrough), a raw TCP Service, or the Gateway API's TLSRoute
Use a headless Service — headless affects DNS, not TLS
explain: Standard Ingress semantics are terminate-and-proxy: the controller holds the certificate. True TCP passthrough (SNI-routed, pods terminate) is outside the Ingress spec — it's a controller extension or a Gateway API TLSRoute. The exam checks you don't assume Ingress can do everything a mesh can.

q: You need a quick local port-forward to the web app without looking up a pod name first. Which works?
options: Only pods are valid port-forward targets
You must resolve the pod IP yourself before forwarding
port-forward deploy/web forwards to ALL pods at once — it picks one
kubectl port-forward deploy/web 8080:80 — port-forward accepts pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets, Jobs, and Services, selecting one ready pod behind them
explain: port-forward isn't pod-only: give it a deploy/, rs/, svc/, or job/ and it resolves to a single ready pod for you. For Services it picks one backing pod (don't expect load balancing — it's one TCP stream to one pod). It's the fastest 'reach the app now' path when you don't care which replica answers.

q: startupProbe: {periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 30}. The app boots in 6 minutes under load and gets restarted at the 5-minute mark. What happened, and the fix?
options: The startup window is failureThreshold x periodSeconds = 300s; the app exceeded it and was killed — raise failureThreshold (e.g. 40 -> 400s) so slow boots survive
Increase initialDelaySeconds — that delays the FIRST probe but doesn't extend the window
Decrease periodSeconds — that SHORTENS the window (same threshold, faster checks)
startupProbes can't allow more than 5 minutes — they can; the window is just arithmetic
explain: The startup probe's grace window is pure multiplication: failureThreshold × periodSeconds. 30 × 10s = 300s, so a 6-minute boot gets killed at 5. Tune the threshold (not the delay) to cover your slowest realistic boot — that's the entire purpose of the startup probe.

q: successThreshold: 3 on a readinessProbe is accepted, but the same value on a livenessProbe is rejected. Why the difference?
options: Both should accept it — the rejection is a bug

readiness successThreshold > 1 is legal — the pod needs N consecutive successes to become Ready (a flap guard); liveness successThreshold must be 1, because a live container shouldn't need multiple successes to avoid being killed
liveness uses failureThreshold for the same purpose — different field, different semantics
successThreshold only works with exec probes
explain: The asymmetry is deliberate: readiness gates traffic, so demanding 3 consecutive successes before advertising Ready is a legitimate anti-flap measure; liveness gates restarts, and requiring repeated successes to STAY alive makes no sense — hence the API forces it to 1. The exam loves this exact contrast.

q: The httpGet probe uses the default timeoutSeconds: 1. The healthy app answers in 2.5s under load, and pods flap between Ready and NotReady. Why?
options: The app is unhealthy — 2.5s responses are slow but not failed
periodSeconds is too high — that spaces checks out, it doesn't fail them
The probe times out before the app answers — a timeout counts as a probe FAILURE; raise timeoutSeconds (keeping it below periodSeconds) to match the app's real response time
Timeouts are warnings, not failures — they are failures
explain: timeoutSeconds defaults to just 1s, and an exceeded timeout fails the probe exactly like a bad status code. Under load, healthy-but-slow apps flap. The fix is sizing the timeout to reality — always keep timeoutSeconds < periodSeconds, or the next check fires before the last one can finish.

q: A Redis cache exposes no HTTP endpoint. Which probe type checks that it's accepting connections?
options: httpGet on / — there's no HTTP server to answer it
exec running redis-cli — the image doesn't ship redis-cli
grpc — Redis doesn't speak gRPC
tcpSocket: {port: 6379} — opens a TCP connection; success means the port accepts. It's the probe for non-HTTP services
explain: tcpSocket is the protocol-agnostic probe: if the three-way handshake completes, the check passes. It can't verify application logic (use exec with a real client for that), but 'is the port accepting connections' is exactly the right granularity for caches, queues, and databases without HTTP health endpoints.

q: The container exposes its health endpoint on a NAMED port metrics (the number changes per build). The probe must track the name, not the number. How?
options: httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: metrics} — probes accept a port NAME, resolved against the container's ports list, decoupling the probe from renumbering
Probes require numeric ports — they accept names too
Reference the Service's port name — probes resolve against the CONTAINER's ports, not the Service's
Hardcode the number and update it every build — toil the named port eliminates
explain: Port names aren't just for Services: httpGet/tcpSocket probes resolve a named port against the container's own ports[]. A renumbered build keeps working because the name is stable. It's the same decoupling principle as named targetPorts — names for humans, numbers for machines.

q: kubectl logs works fine, but your forensics agent needs to read container logs directly from the node's filesystem. Where does the kubelet store them?
options: /etc/kubernetes/logs — no such directory
/var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod-name>_<uid>/<container>/ — the kubelet's log directory, which kubectl logs serves through the API; /var/log/containers holds symlinks pointing into it
Inside etcd alongside the pod objects — etcd stores specs, not log streams
/var/log/syslog on the node — that's the node's own syslog
explain: The kubelet writes container stdout/stderr as JSON-ish log files under /var/log/pods/.../<container>/, and /var/log/containers/*.log are symlinks there for human convenience. kubectl logs is just the API reading those files. Knowing the real path matters for node-level agents, disk-pressure forensics, and log-rotation tuning.

q: kubectl get events shows ONE Warning row with COUNT 47 instead of 47 rows. Where did the other 46 go?
options: Lost — events after the first are dropped
Paginated away — raise --limit
Nowhere — the API server aggregates identical events, incrementing count and refreshing lastTimestamp; it's compression, not loss. Sort by lastTimestamp to see what's flapping RIGHT NOW
Removed by etcd compaction — compaction doesn't target live event counts
explain: Event aggregation collapses repeats into count + first/last timestamps, which is why a CrashLoop shows one row with a climbing count instead of a flood. For triage, --sort-by=.lastTimestamp surfaces what's actively failing; the count tells you how long it's been failing.

q: kubectl top pod shows the web pod at 900Mi, but is the hog the app container or the sidecar? Which flag breaks it down?
options: top can't break down containers — it can
kubectl top pod --sort-by=memory — that sorts PODS, not containers
kubectl describe pod — shows limits and requests, not live usage
kubectl top pod --containers — per-container CPU/memory rows; the fastest way to blame the app vs the sidecar
explain: --containers switches top from pod-level to container-level rows — essential when a pod has app + sidecar + proxy and you need to know WHO is eating the memory. Pair it with per-container limits (so the hog gets OOMKilled instead of its neighbor) once you've found the culprit.

q: A pod has a 2-minute init container; the app container's livenessProbe sets initialDelaySeconds: 30. When does the first probe fire?
options: 30s after the APP container starts — initialDelaySeconds counts from container start, not pod creation; the 2-minute init phase doesn't consume any of it
30s after pod creation — the probe would fire mid-init and kill the pod; it doesn't work that way
30s after the init container finishes, measured from pod creation — the clock starts at app-container start
Probes are disabled when init containers are present — they're just delayed
explain: initialDelaySeconds is per-container, measured from that container's start. Long init phases don't eat into it — which is exactly why init containers plus modest delays compose safely. The exam's trap is treating the delay as pod-age; it's container-age.

q: A CrashLooping pod restarts slower and slower — 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s — then holds at 5 minutes between attempts. Is this tunable?
options: It's broken — restarts should be immediate and constant
This is the kubelet's exponential back-off (10s, 20s, 40s... capped at 300s) — deliberate, to avoid hot-looping a broken container; fix the crash, not the timer, which isn't per-pod configurable
Set backoffLimit: 0 on the pod — that's a Job field
Change restartPolicy to OnFailure — same back-off applies
explain: CrashLoopBackOff's growing delay is the kubelet protecting the node from a tight crash loop: 10s doubling each time, capped at 5 minutes. It resets after 10 clean minutes. You can't tune it per pod — and shouldn't want to; the fix is always the underlying crash, visible via kubectl logs -p.

q: A container runs an interactive migration script; you need to see its prompts AND type answers into the RUNNING process. exec gives you a new shell, not the script's stdin. Which command?
options: kubectl logs -f — read-only, no input
kubectl debug — attaches a NEW container, not the running process
kubectl attach -it <pod> -c app — attaches your terminal to the RUNNING container's stdin/stdout; what you type goes to the process's terminal
SSH to the node and use docker attach — nodes don't expose that path
explain: attach vs exec is the key distinction: exec starts a NEW process in the container, attach wires you to the EXISTING PID 1's stdio. For interactive scripts already running (migrations, installers), attach is the only way to converse with them. Detach with the standard escape sequence without killing the process.

q: kubectl exec web-abc -- rm -rf /tmp/cache — what does the -- do, and what breaks without it?
options: It's optional decoration — try omitting it with flags in the command
It selects the container — that's -c
Commands can't start with rm — they can
It separates kubectl's flags from the command — without it, flags inside your command (like -rf) are parsed as kubectl flags and rejected; everything after -- is passed through verbatim
explain: The double dash is the Unix 'end of options' convention: kubectl stops flag-parsing there. Without it, rm -rf looks like kubectl flags -r and -f, and the command fails confusingly. Any exec/debug command containing dashes needs the -- — it's muscle memory worth building.

q: A PDB sets maxUnavailable: 1 on the 3-replica web app. A node CRASHES, taking 2 pods with it. Does the PDB prevent the second loss?
options: No — PDBs constrain only VOLUNTARY disruptions (drains, deletes, upgrades); involuntary failures like node crashes bypass them entirely. For voluntary ops, maxUnavailable: 1 keeps at least 2 of 3 available
Yes — PDBs block all pod loss regardless of cause
maxUnavailable is invalid; only minAvailable works — both are valid, they're duals
PDBs only apply to DaemonSets — they apply to any scalable workload
explain: A PodDisruptionBudget is a budget for disruptions YOU cause — the eviction API checks it before draining. Kernel panics, kubelet deaths, and network partitions don't ask permission. Design for both: PDBs for maintenance, plus enough replicas (and anti-affinity) to survive the involuntary kind.

q: kubectl drain node-2 refuses: 'cannot delete DaemonSet-managed pods'. The DaemonSet pods should stay until the node actually goes down. How do you proceed?
options: --force — that's for pods with local storage, a different error
--ignore-daemonsets — DaemonSet pods are controller-owned and would be instantly recreated, so drain requires you to explicitly opt into skipping them; they terminate when the node itself shuts down
Delete the DaemonSet first — destroys fleet-wide coverage for one node's maintenance
Drain can never proceed with DaemonSets present — it can, with the flag
explain: Drain is conservative by default: it won't touch DaemonSet pods (deleting them is pointless — the controller recreates them immediately) without explicit consent. --ignore-daemonsets is that consent. The DaemonSet pods ride the node down naturally at shutdown; everything else gets evicted gracefully first.

q: Before patching node-3 you must stop NEW pods from landing there — reversibly, in one command — WITHOUT evicting anything already running. Which command?
options: kubectl drain node-3 — evicts everything; too much for 'repel only'
kubectl taint nodes node-3 maintenance=true:NoSchedule — works, but heavier than needed
kubectl cordon node-3 — marks the node Unschedulable so the scheduler avoids it; running pods are untouched; kubectl uncordon reverses it in one command
Delete the node object — destructive and unnecessary
explain: cordon vs drain is the key choice: cordon repels only NEW scheduling (reversible with uncordon), drain = cordon PLUS eviction of everything moveable. When the task says 'keep what's running, stop new arrivals', cordon is the one-command answer.

q: The app logs multi-line Java stack traces; the aggregator splits EVERY line into a separate event, shredding the traces. What is the fix?
options: Log to a file instead of stdout — kubectl logs and most collectors only tail stdout/stderr
Raise --tail on the log queries — that returns more lines, still split
kubectl logs reassembles multi-line entries automatically — it doesn't

Emit single-line JSON per event — the runtime treats each newline-terminated line as one log record, so multi-line output is inherently split; keep each event (stack trace included) on one logical line
explain: Container log plumbing is line-oriented: one newline = one record, end of story. Multi-line stack traces get shredded by design, not by bug. The durable fix is single-line structured logging (JSON per event) — then every aggregator keeps each event atomic and your traces stay searchable.

q: kubectl top pod shows the app at 250m CPU and 128Mi memory. What do the units mean?
options: 250 millicpu (a quarter of a core) and 128 mebibytes — top reports CPU in millicores and memory in binary Mi, the same units requests and limits use
250 megabytes of CPU time and 128 millibytes of RAM — scrambled units
Percentages of node capacity — top shows absolute values
2.5 cores and 128 gigabytes — off by orders of magnitude
explain: top speaks the same language as your manifests: CPU in millicpu (1000m = 1 core), memory in Mi/Gi. Reading 250m as '250 megabytes' is the classic unit mix-up — and it matters, because those are the numbers you size your requests and limits from.

q: The app's readinessProbe starts failing (slow DB). The pod stays Running, is NOT restarted, but stops receiving traffic. Where did the traffic go, and how do you confirm?
options: The kubelet killed it silently — it's still Running; nothing was killed

Failing readiness removes the pod's IP from the Service endpoints — no traffic, no restart (restarting is liveness's job). Confirm with kubectl get endpoints web: the pod IP disappears while the pod lives
The Service was deleted — check get svc before theorizing
Readiness failures restart the pod — that's liveness; readiness only gates traffic
explain: Readiness is the traffic gate, liveness is the restart gate — the most-tested probe distinction on the exam. A failing readiness probe yanks the pod from endpoints (and EndpointSlices) while the container keeps running; recovery is automatic when the probe succeeds again. kubectl get endpoints is the ground truth for 'who gets traffic'.

q: Your script deletes 50 pods and must NOT block on each graceful termination. Which flag, and what does it actually change?
options: --grace-period=0 — that's forceful deletion, a different (riskier) thing
--timeout=0 — not a delete flag
--wait=false — kubectl returns as soon as the DELETE is accepted; termination still proceeds server-side with the normal grace period. It changes client blocking, not pod shutdown semantics
Deletes are always synchronous; script around it with & — --wait=false exists for exactly this
explain: --wait=false only affects the client: the API still honors terminationGracePeriodSeconds and preStop hooks server-side. Don't confuse it with --grace-period=0 --force, which actually bypasses graceful shutdown. For bulk deletes in scripts, --wait=false is the polite fast path.

q: While the startupProbe is still running (hasn't yet succeeded), what happens to the liveness and readiness probes?
options: They run in parallel with it — then slow boots would be killed by liveness
They're permanently disabled once a startupProbe is defined — they're deferred, not disabled
Only liveness is paused; readiness runs — both are held

Both are held off until the startupProbe succeeds — that's the design: startup owns the boot window, then hands off to liveness/readiness. If startup never succeeds, the container is killed per its own failureThreshold
explain: The startup probe is a gate, not a peer: while it runs, liveness and readiness are suspended, so a slow boot can't be misread as a deadlock. Once it succeeds, the other probes take over for the container's life. That's why the trio composes: startup for 'are we up yet', liveness for 'are we stuck', readiness for 'should we get traffic'.

q: The DB password Secret must never change in place — rotation happens by creating db-pass-v2 and rolling the Deployment, and any in-place edit of db-pass must be rejected by the API server. Which field enforces this, and what is the operational trade-off?
options: immutable: true on the Secret — the API server rejects any update to its data; rotation means creating a new Secret and rolling the pods to reference it
readOnly: true on the Secret — locks the Secret against edits
type: Opaque — Opaque Secrets cannot be modified after creation
An annotation like secrets.example.com/immutable: "true" — the API server enforces immutability annotations
explain: immutable: true is the real enforcement — once set, the API server rejects every update to the Secret's data, which is exactly the compliance posture described. The trade-off is operational: rotation can no longer be an in-place edit, so you create db-pass-v2 and roll the workload to reference it (which is also the safer pattern). There is no readOnly field on Secrets; type: Opaque is just the default type and says nothing about mutability; annotations are advisory metadata the API server never enforces.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The default ServiceAccount in team-a lists imagePullSecrets: [{name: reg-old}]. A pod in team-a sets its own imagePullSecrets: [{name: reg-new}]. The registry behind reg-old was decommissioned yesterday. Will this pod's image pulls succeed?
options: No — pod-level imagePullSecrets replace the ServiceAccount's list, and merging never happens
Yes — the two lists are merged (union) and the kubelet tries each credential in turn until one authenticates
No — ServiceAccount imagePullSecrets always win and the pod-level entry is ignored
No — the first failed credential aborts the pull, so the dead reg-old entry poisons every attempt
explain: The kubelet unions the pod's imagePullSecrets with the ServiceAccount's — they merge, neither replaces the other — and tries each credential in turn until one works, so the dead reg-old entry is simply skipped. That is why attaching a fallback pull secret to the ServiceAccount is safe: it never overrides what the pod declares. Options A and C invent a precedence rule that doesn't exist, and D misstates the retry behavior — one bad credential does not poison the list.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: PriorityClass "standard" already exists with globalDefault: true. You apply PriorityClass "critical" also with globalDefault: true. What happens?
options: Both are accepted; pods without an explicit priorityClassName get the higher value
The newer one silently wins and "standard" loses its default status
The API server rejects it — at most one PriorityClass in the cluster may set globalDefault: true
Pods get the average of the two values
explain: globalDefault is a cluster-singleton: the API server rejects a second PriorityClass claiming it, because unscheduled pods need exactly one default. The fix is to set globalDefault: false (or remove it) on one of them. There is no merging, averaging, or silent override — the validation exists precisely to keep the default unambiguous.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The alerting pods use PriorityClass "monitor" (value 1000000). They must NEVER evict lower-priority pods to get scheduled — staying Pending through a capacity crunch is preferable to knocking anything else over. Which field expresses this?
options: preemptionPolicy: Always — the default, which evicts lower-priority pods
Lower the value below the batch jobs so there is nothing to preempt
A PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable: 0
preemptionPolicy: Never on the PriorityClass — the pods never trigger preemption and simply wait for capacity
explain: preemptionPolicy: Never disables the preemption behavior of a PriorityClass: the pod can still schedule on free capacity and still outranks others for ordering, but it will never evict a lower-priority pod. Always is the default evicting behavior, lowering the value just reshuffles who gets evicted, and a PDB constrains voluntary evictions (drains) — it does not stop priority preemption.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You mount a projected service-account token with expirationSeconds: 600 and audience: "storage.example.com". The delivered token is valid for a full hour, not ten minutes. Why?
options: The kubelet enforces a minimum token lifetime of 3600 seconds and clamps smaller requests up to one hour
The audience claim overrides expirationSeconds
expirationSeconds must be a multiple of 3600
Projected tokens cannot expire in under 24 hours
explain: Bound service-account tokens have a floor: the kubelet will not mint one valid for less than an hour, so expirationSeconds: 600 is silently raised to 3600. The audience only scopes who the token is for — it doesn't touch lifetime — and there is no multiple-of-3600 rule or 24-hour minimum. If the external API truly needs 10-minute tokens, that constraint has to be enforced on its side, not the token's.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: ConfigMap app-cfg holds key db.conf, but the app expects the file at /etc/app/database.conf. You want the whole ConfigMap mounted at /etc/app with just that one file renamed. Which volume configuration does this?
options: subPath: database.conf on the volumeMount — renames the mounted file
volumes: [{configMap: {name: app-cfg, items: [{key: db.conf, path: database.conf}]}}] — items maps individual keys to custom file paths
Rename the key to database.conf in the ConfigMap
An env var pointing at the new filename
explain: The items list is the rename mechanism for ConfigMap (and Secret) volumes: each entry maps a key to the filename it appears as under the mount path, while unlisted keys keep their names. subPath mounts a single file and doesn't compose with a whole-directory mount the way items does. Renaming the key changes the source of truth for every consumer, and an env var can't rename a file.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container sets env: [{name: DB_PASSWORD, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-creds, key: password}}}], but the db-creds Secret only contains the key "passwd". What happens to the pod?
options: It starts with DB_PASSWORD set to an empty string
The kubelet falls back to the closest key name, passwd
The pod fails with CreateContainerConfigError — every referenced key must exist unless optional: true is set
The API server auto-creates the missing key
explain: secretKeyRef (and configMapKeyRef) resolve strictly: a missing name or key blocks container creation with CreateContainerConfigError, which is the fast diagnosis for 'pod won't start after a Secret change'. Setting optional: true is what yields the empty-string behavior of option A — useful for feature-flagged secrets. The kubelet never fuzzy-matches key names and the API server never invents keys.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A debug sidecar must see host PIDs in /proc (to correlate app threads with node-level ps output), but the pod may not be privileged and may not use hostPID. Which per-container setting unmasks /proc?
options: privileged: true — the only way to see host processes
hostPID: true on the pod
capabilities: {add: [SYS_PTRACE]}
securityContext: {procMount: Unmasked} on the debug container
explain: procMount: Unmasked removes the default /proc mask (which hides host PIDs and sensitive paths) for that container only — no privilege escalation, no shared PID namespace. privileged and hostPID are both heavier hammers the task forbids, and SYS_PTRACE governs ptrace-style debugging, not /proc visibility.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You set hostPID: true on a node-debug pod. Which statement about the resulting pod is correct?
options: It sees all node processes via /proc but keeps its own network namespace unless hostNetwork is also set — the host* flags are independent
hostPID implies hostNetwork and hostIPC automatically
hostPID requires privileged: true to take effect
hostPID only works on control-plane nodes
explain: The host* flags are orthogonal: hostPID shares the node's PID namespace (/proc shows every process), while networking, IPC, and filesystem stay namespaced unless their own flags are set. Nothing about hostPID implies the others, it needs no privileged flag, and it works on any node — which is exactly why it's a sharp tool to scope carefully.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod sets dnsPolicy: None with dnsConfig listing 4 nameservers and 8 search domains. What does the API server do?
options: Accepts it and the kubelet silently drops the extras
Rejects it — dnsConfig allows at most 3 nameservers and 6 search domains
Accepts it; kubelet truncates to the allowed maximums
Rejects it — dnsPolicy: None requires hostNetwork: true
explain: dnsConfig is validated, not truncated: more than 3 nameservers or more than 6 search domains is a rejection, matching resolv.conf limits. dnsPolicy: None simply means 'use only my dnsConfig' and pairs with any network mode. The exam plants this wherever custom DNS appears — count your entries before applying.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A LimitRange declares type: PersistentVolumeClaim with min: {storage: 1Gi} and max: {storage: 100Gi}. A user creates a 500Mi PVC. What happens?
options: It is created — LimitRange only constrains containers
It is defaulted up to 1Gi
It is rejected — below the min storage for PVCs in this namespace
It is created but stays Pending until resized
explain: LimitRange isn't container-only: the PersistentVolumeClaim type enforces min/max storage at admission, so the 500Mi claim is rejected outright. Unlike containers, PVC limits have no defaulting — there is no default/defaultRequest injection for claims — and Pending is a binding state, not an admission outcome.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A namespace is labeled pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted and pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline. You apply a pod that runs as root (violates restricted, passes baseline). What happens?
options: The pod is rejected
The pod is created with no output
The pod is created only after interactive confirmation
The pod is created and kubectl prints a warning — warn mode never blocks, it only reports
explain: The three PSS modes are independent: enforce blocks, audit logs, warn prints — and warn never rejects anything. Here baseline enforcement passes (running as root is allowed at baseline), while the restricted warning fires purely as advice. The trap is assuming any 'restricted' label means rejection; only enforce: restricted would block this pod.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Every start of a pod mounting a 2 TB volume takes 20 minutes while the kubelet recursively chowns the whole volume to fsGroup — even though the volume's group ownership is already correct from the previous run. Which setting skips the redundant chown?
options: fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch — the kubelet only chowns when the volume root's ownership is wrong
runAsGroup: 3000 — sets the group without chowning
supplementalGroups: [3000] — bypasses the chown
readOnly: true on the volumeMount
explain: OnRootMismatch changes the fsGroup behavior from 'chown everything every time' (the default Always) to 'chown only if the volume root's ownership doesn't match', which turns a 20-minute recursive chown of an already-correct 2 TB volume into a no-op. runAsGroup and supplementalGroups set identity, they don't control the chown pass, and a read-only mount would break the app's writes.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. Its health script calls `su postgres -c "pg_isready"` and now fails. Why?
options: su requires privileged: true
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false sets the no_new_privs bit, so setuid binaries like su and sudo can never gain privileges
It conflicts with runAsNonRoot: true
The seccomp profile blocks su
explain: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false sets no_new_privs on the container's processes: even setuid-root binaries (su, sudo) execute without gaining privilege, so any in-container privilege juggling breaks. It's not about the privileged flag or seccomp — it's the kernel refusing the setuid transition. The fix is to run the check as the right user directly rather than su-ing.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A shared volume's files are group-owned by GID 3000 and GID 4000, and the app (UID 1000) needs group-read through both. runAsGroup sets a single primary group. How does the pod get both GIDs?
options: Run two containers, one per GID
Set fsGroup twice in the securityContext
supplementalGroups: [3000, 4000] — the container's processes join both groups
Add the CAP_FOWNER capability
explain: supplementalGroups is the multi-group mechanism: the container's processes become members of every listed group, so group-permission checks pass for files owned by either GID. runAsGroup and fsGroup each take exactly one value, splitting containers doesn't change group membership, and CAP_FOWNER bypasses permission checks rather than granting group membership.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your CI system runs outside the cluster and needs a Bearer token for ServiceAccount "deployer" valid for 24 hours. Which command mints it without hand-editing Secret objects?
options: kubectl get secret deployer-token -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d
kubectl create secret generic deployer-token --from-literal=token=...
Copy the projected token out of a running pod
kubectl create token deployer --duration=24h
explain: kubectl create token mints a bound, audience-scoped token for a ServiceAccount on demand with a chosen duration — the supported path since auto-generated SA Secrets were removed in 1.24. Option A relies on the legacy auto-created secret that no longer exists; B hand-rolls an inert Secret the API server won't honor as a token; C yields a short-lived pod-bound token tied to that pod's audience.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You must attach the existing pull secret "regcred" to the default ServiceAccount in team-a, imperatively, so future pods inherit it. Which command does this?
options: kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n team-a -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "regcred"}]}'
kubectl set imagepullsecret default regcred -n team-a
kubectl annotate serviceaccount default imagepullsecret=regcred -n team-a
kubectl create serviceaccount default --image-pull-secret=regcred -n team-a
explain: ServiceAccounts are patched like any object: a strategic merge patch adding the imagePullSecrets list entry is the imperative path, and every future pod using that SA inherits it. There is no kubectl set imagepullsecret command, annotations don't attach pull secrets, and create would fail since the SA already exists.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You are hand-writing a Secret of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson in YAML. Under data:, which key must hold the base64-encoded Docker config JSON for the kubelet to use it on pulls?
options: .dockerconfig
.dockerconfigjson
docker-config-json
auths
explain: The kubelet looks for exactly one key: .dockerconfigjson (note the leading dot), whose value is the base64 of a standard Docker config.json. auths is a field INSIDE that JSON, not the Secret key, and the other names are invented. This is why kubectl create secret docker-registry exists — it gets the type and key name right in one shot.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The entrypoint script needs the container's memory LIMIT in mebibytes as the env var MEM_LIMIT_MI. Which valueFrom form produces it?
options: fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.annotations['mem-limit']}
resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.memory} — it already reports mebibytes
resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.memory, divisor: 1Mi}
A downwardAPI volume — env vars can't carry resource values
explain: resourceFieldRef exposes requests/limits as env vars, but the raw value is in bytes; divisor: 1Mi scales it to mebibytes (use 1m for millicores on CPU). fieldRef only covers pod metadata, not resources, and the downwardAPI volume is the file-based alternative — env vars carry resource values just fine.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Compliance sets automountServiceAccountToken: false on the default ServiceAccount, so no pod gets the legacy token mount. One pod must call a cloud API that requires a token minted for audience "storage.example.com" expiring after 1 hour — without re-enabling the default mount. How?
options: Set automountServiceAccountToken: true on that pod
Copy a token from a pod in another namespace
Mount the kubelet's token via hostPath
Add a projected volume with serviceAccountToken: {audience: "storage.example.com", expirationSeconds: 3600, path: token} — an explicit opt-in that doesn't touch the default mount
explain: Projected service-account tokens are independent of automountServiceAccountToken: you can project a purpose-built token (custom audience, bounded lifetime) into exactly the pods that need it while the default mount stays off everywhere. Re-enabling automount on the pod (A) brings back the broad legacy token the policy forbids; B and C are insecure fabrications — tokens are audience- and pod-bound.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A Job's pods exit 3 on transient network flakes (safe to retry) but exit 1 on invalid input (must fail fast, not burn retries). backoffLimit retries both indiscriminately. Which Job field lets exit code 3 not count against the retry budget while exit code 1 still fails the Job?
options: podFailurePolicy: {rules: [{action: Ignore, onExitCodes: {operator: In, values: [3]}}]} — ignored failures don't count toward backoffLimit
activeDeadlineSeconds — bounds total Job time instead
backoffLimitPerIndex — limits retries per shard
restartPolicy: Never — moves retries to new pods
explain: podFailurePolicy classifies failures: action Ignore on exit code 3 means those pod failures are disregarded for backoffLimit accounting, while exit 1 follows the default counting path toward Job failure. activeDeadlineSeconds bounds wall-clock time rather than classifying failures, backoffLimitPerIndex is about indexed shards, and restartPolicy only controls where the retry happens.

q: Nodes are tainted maintenance=true:NoExecute during a 10-minute window. Pods tolerating the taint should finish in-flight work for up to 5 minutes, then be evicted. Which toleration expresses this?
options: A toleration with no tolerationSeconds — evicted immediately when the taint appears
tolerationSeconds: 300 on the matching toleration — the pod tolerates the taint for 5 minutes, then is evicted
Effect: NoSchedule — prevents eviction entirely
A PreferNoSchedule taint instead — the scheduler avoids but never evicts
explain: tolerationSeconds starts a countdown when a NoExecute taint lands: the pod keeps running for that many seconds, then is evicted — exactly the graceful-drain window described. Omitting tolerationSeconds tolerates forever (immediate eviction is what happens with NO toleration at all). NoSchedule never evicts existing pods, and PreferNoSchedule is only a soft scheduling hint.

q: You set pod.spec.nodeName: node-3 directly on a pod while the scheduler is down for maintenance. What happens?
options: The pod stays Pending until the scheduler returns
nodeName is only a soft hint the scheduler may ignore
The kubelet rejects the pod — nodeName requires scheduler approval
The pod binds to node-3 with no scheduling involved; if node-3 is later deleted the pod sits Pending forever
explain: nodeName bypasses the scheduler entirely — the pod is statically assigned, which is why it works during scheduler downtime. The cost is the loss of every scheduler guarantee: no resource checks, no affinity, and if the node vanishes the pod has no path to another node. It is a hard binding, not a hint.

q: A pod sets schedulerName: custom-scheduler, but no such scheduler is running in the cluster. What is the pod's fate?
options: The default scheduler picks it up after a grace period
The API server rejects the pod at admission
It schedules normally after a 10-minute timeout
It stays Pending indefinitely — only the named scheduler will ever process it
explain: schedulerName is a strict claim: the pod is invisible to every scheduler except the named one, and nothing times out or falls back — Pending forever until custom-scheduler appears. The API server accepts the pod happily; the failure mode is silent starvation, which is why a typo in schedulerName is such a classic 'why is my pod Pending' trap.

q: The app must advertise its own pod IP to a service registry at startup. The image is frozen and the pod gets no RBAC access to the API. Which env entry gives the app its pod IP?
options: valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.podIP}}
valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.hostIP}}
valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
Hardcode the IP in the Deployment — pod IPs are stable
explain: The downward API's fieldRef exposes status.podIP with no code changes and no RBAC — the kubelet already knows it. status.hostIP is the NODE's IP (the classic mix-up), metadata.name is the pod name, and pod IPs are emphatically not stable across rescheduling, so hardcoding rots on the first rollout.

q: A nodeAffinity rule uses matchExpressions: [{key: disktype, operator: Gt, values: ["ssd"]}]. What happens on apply?
options: It is accepted and matches nodes alphabetically greater than "ssd"
It is rejected — Gt and Lt only work on integer values, and "ssd" is not one
It is accepted but matches nothing
Gt coerces the label value to a number automatically
explain: Gt/Lt are numeric-only operators: the API server validates that values parse as integers, so a string label value is a rejection, not a silent no-match. For string labels the operators are In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist. The exam loves this because Gt reads naturally until you remember the type constraint.

q: Six web replicas must NEVER share an availability zone — a hard requirement. If only two zones have capacity, the remaining replicas must stay Pending rather than double up. Which affinity expresses this?
options: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution podAntiAffinity on the zone key
topologySpreadConstraints with whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution podAntiAffinity with topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
nodeSelector on the zone label
explain: requiredDuringScheduling is the hard form: the scheduler will leave pods Pending before violating it, which is exactly the stated requirement. preferredDuringScheduling is best-effort (it would double up), ScheduleAnyway is the soft topology-spread variant, and nodeSelector pins to one zone rather than spreading across them.

q: RuntimeClass "kata" declares overhead: {podFixed: {cpu: "250m", memory: "128Mi"}}. A pod using kata requests 500m CPU and 512Mi memory. What does the scheduler account for this pod?
options: 500m / 512Mi — overhead is informational only
250m / 128Mi — overhead replaces the requests
750m / 640Mi — requests plus overhead
250m / 384Mi — overhead minus requests
explain: Pod overhead is additive: the scheduler reserves requests + overhead (750m/640Mi here) because the sandbox runtime genuinely consumes those resources outside the containers. Forgetting overhead is how kata/gVisor pods get scheduled onto nodes that can't actually fit them — the requests alone understate the footprint.

q: Each run of the nightly-export CronJob must have its Job object auto-deleted one hour after finishing, success or failure. Where does ttlSecondsAfterFinished belong?
options: spec.jobTemplate.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished — on the Job template inside the CronJob
spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished — directly on the CronJob
successfulJobsHistoryLimit / failedJobsHistoryLimit — they already do time-based cleanup
spec.template.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished — on the pod template
explain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished is a Job-spec field, so in a CronJob it lives under spec.jobTemplate.spec — there is no CronJob-level ttl field and the pod template is the wrong level. The history-limit fields keep the last N Jobs by count, not by age; ttl is the time-based reaper. Misplacing it is a silent no-op, which is the trap.

q: You write a CronJob whose jobTemplate pod spec omits restartPolicy entirely (defaulting to Always). What happens on apply?
options: It is accepted and runs normally
It is rejected — the jobTemplate pod's restartPolicy must be OnFailure or Never
It is accepted but the Jobs loop forever
The CronJob controller silently rewrites it to OnFailure
explain: Job pods may never use Always — the controller needs a terminal pod phase to judge completion, so the API server rejects Always in any Job template, CronJob's included. This mirrors the classic standalone-Job error; the fix is restartPolicy: OnFailure (retry in place) or Never (fresh pod per attempt).

q: A container's preStop hook runs an exec that exits 1 (the notify script failed). What happens to the container's termination?
options: Termination is blocked until the hook succeeds
The pod is stuck in Terminating forever
The hook failure is logged as a Warning event and termination proceeds — SIGTERM is still sent and the grace period still applies
The container is restarted instead of terminated
explain: preStop is best-effort: a failing hook is recorded in events but never vetoes termination — the SIGTERM still goes out on schedule and the grace-period countdown is unaffected. That is why preStop must be idempotent and fast: it can delay termination only by running long, never by failing.

q: A one-shot manifest pod runs a database migration that exits 3 (failure). Compare restartPolicy: Never versus OnFailure for this pod.
options: Both retry the migration until it succeeds
Never creates a replacement pod; OnFailure retries in place
The pod phases are identical either way
Never: the pod goes Failed with no retry; OnFailure: the kubelet restarts the container in the SAME pod with backoff
explain: restartPolicy governs the kubelet's in-place behavior: Never means the failed container stays dead and the pod phase becomes Failed; OnFailure means the kubelet restarts that container in the same pod (same IP, same volumes) with exponential backoff. New pods only come from a controller (like a Job with restartPolicy: Never) — the kubelet itself never creates them.

q: Job A uses restartPolicy: OnFailure; Job B uses restartPolicy: Never. A container in each Job's pod exits 1. Where does each Job's retry happen?
options: Job A: the kubelet restarts the container in the SAME pod; Job B: the Job controller creates a brand NEW pod
Both create new pods
Both restart the container in the same pod
Neither retries — Jobs only run once
explain: This is the same kubelet-vs-controller split one level up: OnFailure retries in place (same pod, same volumes — good for resume-from-disk), Never lets the pod die Failed and the Job controller schedules a fresh pod (good for clean-slate retries). backoffLimit counts both kinds of retries, which is why the distinction matters for retry budgets.

q: A container declares ports: [{containerPort: 8080}] but no Service exists. Curling the pod IP on 8080 works. What did the containerPort declaration actually accomplish?
options: It published 8080 on the node
Nothing functional — containerPort is purely informational; reachability comes from the app listening, not the declaration
It created an implicit ClusterIP Service
It registered the port in cluster DNS
explain: containerPort is documentation the runtime mostly ignores: the port is reachable because the process listens, with or without the declaration. Services never read containerPort (they use their own targetPort), and nothing is published on the node — that's hostPort. The declaration still matters for humans and tooling, just not for traffic.

q: Two pods in the same Deployment both set hostPort: 8080 and land on the same node. What happens to the second pod?
options: Both run fine; kube-proxy load-balances the node port
The second pod's hostPort is silently remapped
It can't bind — the port is already in use on that node, so the container fails and the pod can't become Ready there
The scheduler auto-assigns it a free nodePort
explain: hostPort binds a real port on the node's network namespace, so two pods claiming the same one collide: the second gets address-in-use and never becomes Ready on that node. This is why hostPort is an anti-pattern for replicated workloads — it breaks scheduling density — and why the exam contrasts it with containerPort (informational) and nodePort (Service-managed).

q: Each replica must mount its ConfigMap key app.conf as /etc/app/$(POD_NAME).conf, where POD_NAME is a downward-API env var. Using subPath: "$(POD_NAME).conf" produces a literal file named $(POD_NAME).conf. Which field expands the variable?
options: subPath with $$ escaping — $$POD_NAME
Templating in mountPath
The items path field
subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME).conf — subPathExpr expands env vars, subPath does not
explain: subPathExpr is the expanding twin of subPath: it runs env-var expansion on the value, so $(POD_NAME) resolves per-pod, while plain subPath is always literal. The $$ escape is for env-value expansion (to produce a literal $), not volume paths, and items maps keys to static paths. This is the standard pattern for per-replica config file names.

q: A pod uses image: web@sha256:9f86d08... with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent. The registry later publishes new code under the tag web:v2. The pod restarts. What runs?
options: The exact bytes of digest 9f86d08 — a digest pins content immutably, so the tag moving changes nothing for this pod
The new web:v2 code, because IfNotPresent re-resolves tags
The pull fails — digests require imagePullPolicy: Always
Whatever web:v2 pointed to when the node last pulled
explain: A digest is a content address: sha256:9f86d08… names exact bytes, and no tag mutation upstream can change what it resolves to — that immutability is the whole point of digest pinning for compliance. IfNotPresent only skips the pull when those bytes are cached; it never re-resolves anything. The tag web:v2 is irrelevant to a pod that references a digest.

q: A container runs command: ["sh", "-c", "/app/server"] as PID 1. Every rollout burns the full termination grace period. Changing it to ["sh", "-c", "exec /app/server"] fixes the shutdown. Why?
options: exec makes the server start faster
exec replaces the shell process so the server becomes PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly — a shell PID 1 doesn't forward signals to its children
It changes the image's entrypoint
It implicitly adds a preStop hook
explain: The shell-as-PID-1 trap: sh doesn't forward SIGTERM to its child, so the server never sees the signal and the kubelet waits out the full grace period before SIGKILL. exec swaps the shell for the server in the same process slot, making the server PID 1 — signals land directly and shutdown is prompt. This is the same root cause as the shell-script shutdown questions, fixed at the command level.

q: A pod has a restartable init container (restartPolicy: Always, native sidecar) requesting 1 CPU, plus app containers requesting 2 CPU total. What CPU does the scheduler reserve for the pod?
options: 2 CPU — the max of init vs app sums, inits never add
1 CPU — only the largest single container counts
3 CPU — restartable init containers run for the pod's lifetime, so their requests are added to the app containers' sum
2 CPU — init containers are ignored entirely
explain: Native sidecars changed the scheduling math: a restartable init container is effectively a long-lived container, so its requests are ADDED to the app containers' sum (1 + 2 = 3) instead of participating in the old max(init, sum-of-apps) rule. Regular init containers still use the max rule since they exit. Undersizing here is how sidecar pods get scheduled onto nodes that can't fit them.

q: Your monitoring DaemonSet creates pods on every worker, but none appear on the control-plane nodes, which carry the taint node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule. What is missing?
options: hostNetwork: true on the DaemonSet pods
A nodeSelector for the control-plane nodes
A higher priorityClass
A matching toleration — DaemonSets don't automatically tolerate the control-plane taint
explain: DaemonSets get no free pass on taints: the control-plane NoSchedule taint blocks their pods like any other workload until you add the matching toleration. hostNetwork is unrelated to scheduling, a nodeSelector would narrow placement further, and priority doesn't override taints. If the monitoring must run on control-plane nodes, the toleration is the missing piece.

q: You create an HPA targeting the nightly-export CronJob to scale it on queue depth. What happens?
options: It can't work — CronJobs expose no scale subresource; HPA supports Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, and ReplicationController
It scales the Job's parallelism for the next run
It works via the CronJob's status subresource
It scales how often the schedule fires
explain: HPA only speaks the scale subresource, which CronJobs (and DaemonSets, and bare Jobs) don't implement — the HPA will sit UnableToScale. The supported targets are Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, and ReplicationController. Queue-driven CronJob scaling needs an external scaler (like KEDA), not a native HPA.

q: Traffic spikes then drops; the HPA flaps 10→3→8→4 replicas every minute, thrashing the backends. Which behavior field damps scale-DOWN specifically?
options: behavior.scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds — it covers both directions
behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds — it delays scale-down decisions over a window
Lowering the CPU target
Raising minReplicas
explain: The behavior stanza splits by direction: scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds holds the replica count at its recent maximum for the window, so a momentary dip doesn't immediately kill pods. scaleUp has its own independent window; changing the target or minReplicas shifts the setpoint rather than damping the oscillation. The exam tests whether you know the two directions are tuned separately.

q: An HPA targets CPU 70% and memory 80%. Current load suggests 4 replicas by CPU but 7 by memory. How many replicas does the HPA set?
options: 4 — CPU is the primary metric
6 — the average, rounded up
7 — with multiple metrics the HPA takes the maximum recommendation
2 — the minimum that satisfies both
explain: Multi-metric HPAs compute a desired replica count per metric and take the MAX — the rationale being that satisfying the hungriest metric satisfies them all. There is no primary metric and no averaging. The trap answers assume CPU wins or the values blend; the controller is deliberately pessimistic.

q: Right after helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami, helm install myapp bitnami/redis fails with 'chart "redis" not found'. What is the fix?
options: Add --version to the install
Run helm upgrade instead
Remove and re-add the repo
helm repo update — the local chart index is empty until it is refreshed
explain: helm repo add only registers the URL; the local index cache starts empty, so no chart names resolve until helm repo update downloads the index. Re-adding the repo doesn't populate the cache either. This is the single most common Helm 'it worked in the tutorial' failure, and the fix is one command.

q: Chart.yaml lists dependencies and Chart.lock exists with pinned versions. Which command populates charts/ with exactly the locked versions?
options: helm dependency build — installs precisely what Chart.lock pins
helm dependency update — re-resolves to the newest matching versions and rewrites Chart.lock
helm repo update — refreshes the index only
helm install --deps — there is no such flag
explain: build honors the lockfile (reproducible installs — what CI should run); update re-resolves semver ranges, pulls the newest matches, and rewrites Chart.lock. Mixing them up is how 'works on my machine' chart builds happen: a developer runs update, commits nothing, and CI builds different dependency versions.

q: Release api is at revision 5 (broken); revision 4 was good. Roll back to revision 4 and don't return until the workloads are actually ready. Which command?
options: helm undo api 4
helm rollback api 4 --wait
helm rollback api — without a revision it already targets the previous one
helm uninstall api && helm install api ./chart
explain: helm rollback takes an explicit revision (4 here) and --wait blocks until the rolled-back workloads report ready — both requirements in one command. A bare rollback does target the previous revision, but without --wait it returns while pods are still churning. There is no helm undo, and uninstall/reinstall loses revision history and causes downtime.

q: kubectl apply --server-side fails: 'Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "helm" ... field is managed by helm'. You intentionally want kubectl to take ownership of the field. Which flag does this?
options: --overwrite — takes ownership on the next apply
--force — recreates the object
--force-conflicts — applies anyway and transfers field ownership to your manager
Rename your field manager to "helm"
explain: Server-side apply tracks field ownership per manager; a conflict means Helm owns the field and your apply is refused. --force-conflicts is the deliberate override: it applies your value and transfers ownership to your field manager. --overwrite is the client-side-apply equivalent and does nothing for SSA conflicts; --force is kubectl replace's recreate flag; impersonating Helm's manager name is a hack that corrupts ownership tracking.

q: A kustomization's configMapGenerator builds app-config from literals, and a second fragment must ADD more keys to the same ConfigMap without replacing the first set. Which generator behavior merges them?
options: behavior: create — the default, which errors on duplicates
behavior: replace — drops the other fragment's keys
behavior: append — merges literal lists
behavior: merge — combines entries from multiple generators into one ConfigMap
explain: behavior: merge is the additive mode: multiple configMapGenerator (or secretGenerator) entries with the same name combine their keys instead of conflicting. create (the default) fails when two generators claim the same name, and replace lets the last one win, dropping the other's keys. There is no append behavior — that's the distractor for people guessing from the name.

q: The staging overlay must pin the web image to an immutable digest, not a mutable tag. Which kustomize images entry does this?
options: images: [{name: web, digest: sha256:9f86d08...}]
images: [{name: web, newTag: sha256:9f86d08...}] — digests go in newTag
images: [{name: web, newName: web, digest: sha256:9f86d08...}] — digest requires newName
Kustomize only handles tags; digests must be patched by hand
explain: The images stanza has a dedicated digest field precisely for pinning; newTag is tag-only and stuffing a digest there produces a broken reference. No newName is required alongside digest. This is the declarative equivalent of the digest-pinning pattern — the overlay guarantees staging runs exact bits regardless of tag movement.

q: Every resource in the canary overlay must end with -canary (web becomes web-canary, db becomes db-canary) without editing the base. Which kustomization field does this?
options: namePrefix: canary- — prepends instead of appending
nameSuffix: -canary
commonLabels: {track: canary} — labels don't rename resources
A patches entry per resource
explain: nameSuffix appends to every resource name in the build — the mirror of namePrefix, and like the prefix it also updates name references (Service selectors, etc.) so the renamed set stays consistent. commonLabels only labels; per-resource patches would work but are verbose busywork compared to the one-line field.

q: Before applying the staging overlay, you want to see exactly what would change, computed server-side with admission applied. Which command does this?
options: kubectl apply --dry-run=client -k overlays/staging
kubectl kustomize overlays/staging — renders locally with no server comparison
kubectl diff -k overlays/staging
helm template ./chart -f staging.yaml
explain: kubectl diff -k renders the kustomization and diffs it against the live cluster state server-side, showing the exact add/modify/delete set before anything is touched. --dry-run=client never talks to the server (no admission, no current-state comparison), kubectl kustomize only renders YAML, and helm template is the wrong tool for a kustomize overlay.

q: Team policy: charts are distributed via the OCI registry, no chartmuseum. Which sequence packages and publishes ./chart version 1.0.0?
options: helm repo add oci https://registry.example.com && helm push
helm package ./chart — packaging alone doesn't publish
docker push registry.example.com/charts/mychart:1.0.0
helm package ./chart && helm push ./mychart-1.0.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts
explain: OCI-native chart flow: helm package produces the .tgz, helm push with an oci:// URL uploads it — no helm repo add involved (that's for classic HTTP chart repos). docker push speaks the wrong artifact protocol for Helm's expectations. The exam contrasts this with the classic repo flow whenever registry questions appear.

q: Two overlays both need the same 'add network policy' fragment, but the fragment is not a standalone deployable app — just a reusable piece. Which kustomize construct is designed for this?
options: components — reusable fragments composed into kustomizations, not built alone
bases — full deployable apps
resources — lists files directly
patches — a different mechanism for targeted edits
explain: components are kustomize's fragment mechanism: they can't be built standalone (kustomize build on a component fails) and exist to be mixed into multiple kustomizations. bases are complete deployable units, resources just lists inputs, and patches edit existing resources rather than contributing new ones. When the same snippet is needed in N overlays, component, not copy-paste.

q: Your kustomization uses labels: [{pairs: {team: payments}}]. The label lands on metadata, but the Deployment's pod template labels and selector are unchanged. How do you extend the label into selectors and template labels too?
options: Switch to per-resource patches — the labels field can't do this
labels: [{pairs: {team: payments}, includeSelectors: true}]
Labels can never touch selectors; edit the base
Add a second labels entry with includeTemplate: true
explain: The newer labels field defaults to metadata-only; includeSelectors: true extends it into selectors and pod-template labels (the older commonLabels field includes selectors by default). There is no includeTemplate field, and editing the base defeats the overlay pattern. The trap is assuming 'labels' behaves like commonLabels — it doesn't, deliberately.

q: In the prod overlay only, remove the debug sidecar (second container) from the web Deployment. Which patch does this cleanly?
options: A strategic merge patch with $patch: delete on containers
The images stanza — it only rewrites image fields
patchesJson6902: [{target: {kind: Deployment, name: web}, patch: [{op: remove, path: /spec/template/spec/containers/1}]}]
nameSuffix — it renames, it doesn't remove
explain: JSON 6902 patches address list elements by index, so op: remove on /spec/template/spec/containers/1 surgically drops the sidecar in the overlay without touching the base. Strategic merge is awkward for removing a list element by position, and the other stanzas do unrelated jobs. Index-based removal is brittle if container order changes — worth a comment in the overlay, but it's the correct mechanism.

q: Release api was installed with --set replicaCount=5 for a load test. The test is over, and helm upgrade -f prod.yaml should return to the chart's default replica count — but the old --set replicaCount=5 keeps surviving every upgrade. Which flag discards the previous --set overrides?
options: --reuse-values — that names the current behavior, which keeps the override
--set replicaCount="" — sets an empty value, not the chart default
Uninstall first, then install fresh
--reset-values — discards previous --set/--set-file values so the upgrade uses only the chart defaults plus -f files
explain: Helm upgrade reuses the previous release's computed values by default, so the old --set replicaCount=5 survives upgrades that never mention it — --reset-values drops those overrides and rebuilds values from the chart defaults plus your -f files. --reuse-values names the default behavior explicitly; setting an empty value doesn't restore the default; reinstall loses history and causes downtime.

q: For the audit you need EVERY value Helm computed for release api — chart defaults plus all overrides — not just what you supplied. Which command shows the full computed set?
options: helm get values api --all — includes chart defaults alongside user-supplied values
helm get values api — user-supplied values only
helm show values ./chart — the chart's defaults, not this release's computed set
helm get manifest api — manifests, not values
explain: --all expands helm get values beyond the user-supplied subset to the fully computed values (defaults merged with overrides) — the auditable 'what did Helm actually use'. Without --all you see only what was passed via -f/--set; helm show values shows the chart's pristine defaults with no release context; get manifest shows rendered YAML, not the values behind it.

q: The canary Deployment carries labels app: web, track: canary. QA needs a stable endpoint hitting ONLY canary pods for direct testing, while the main Service keeps serving all pods. Which Service does this?
options: selector: {app: web} — reaches both stable and canary pods
A second Service with selector: {app: web, track: canary}
A headless Service — it still selects by labels the same way
Impossible — one Deployment can only back one Service
explain: Services select purely by label matching, and nothing limits a Deployment's pods to one Service: a second Service selecting {app: web, track: canary} gives QA a canary-only endpoint while the main Service (selector {app: web}) continues splitting across everything. Headless changes DNS behavior, not selection, and the 'one Service per Deployment' limit doesn't exist.

q: kubectl rollout restart deploy/web triggers a rolling update without any manifest change. What did the command actually change?
options: The image tag — it bumps to the latest
The replica count — it scales up then down
It sets the kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation on the pod template — a template change the Deployment rolls on
Nothing — it deletes the pods directly and the ReplicaSet recreates them
explain: rollout restart works by mutating the pod template's annotations (kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt: <timestamp>); any template change triggers a rolling update, so this is the declarative-safe way to bounce pods. It doesn't touch the image or replica count, and it doesn't delete pods directly — the standard rolling-update machinery (surge/unavailable) applies.

q: You deleted the old metrics Deployment from your kustomize manifests. On the next apply, declaratively remove it (and any other orphans) from the cluster, scoped to labels app=web. Which command?
options: kubectl apply -k . — apply never deletes orphans
kubectl delete deployment metrics-old — manual, not declarative
kubectl apply -k . --prune — prune requires --all and a selector to scope it
kubectl apply -k . --prune --all -l app=web
explain: Pruning needs all three: --prune to enable deletion of orphans, --all to consider all namespaced types, and -l to scope which objects are candidates — without the selector, prune refuses to run (a safety catch against wiping the namespace). Plain apply only creates/updates, and manual deletes aren't declarative or repeatable.

q: Security policy forbids exposing NodePorts: the cloud LoadBalancer Service must not allocate node ports at all. Which field disables the automatic NodePort allocation?
options: allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
externalTrafficPolicy: Local — changes routing, not allocation
healthCheckNodePort: 0 — only affects the health-check port
type: ClusterIP — but then there is no load balancer
explain: LoadBalancer Services allocate NodePorts by default (kube-proxy still needs a node-level entry); allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false skips that allocation for locked-down environments. externalTrafficPolicy changes source-IP/routing behavior, healthCheckNodePort only tunes the LB health check, and ClusterIP drops the LB entirely — none of them control port allocation.

q: The on-prem cluster runs MetalLB alongside a second load-balancer controller. The app Service must be provisioned specifically by MetalLB. How do you select the implementation?
options: An annotation — controller selection is annotation-only
spec.loadBalancerClass: metallb (matching the controller's advertised class)
type: NodePort — bypasses LB controllers entirely
externalIPs — a different mechanism for fixed IPs
explain: loadBalancerClass is the portable selector: the Service is claimed only by the controller advertising that class, so coexisting implementations don't fight over it. Annotations are controller-specific extras, not the selection mechanism; NodePort and externalIPs sidestep the LB controller rather than choosing one.

q: An Ingress routes shop.example.com and api.example.com. Requests that match NO host rule (direct-IP hits, unknown hosts) must reach the sorry Service instead of the controller's default 404. Which Ingress section handles unmatched traffic?
options: A rule with host: "*" — wildcard hosts aren't valid in rules
An annotation — there's no standard annotation for this
spec.defaultBackend — serves traffic that matches no rule
A second Ingress — merging across Ingresses for the same traffic is undefined
explain: spec.defaultBackend is the Ingress-level catch-all: anything not matching a rule (no host match, no path match) goes there. host: "*" isn't valid rule syntax (a rule with no host matches all hosts, which is different from a fallback), and splitting the fallback into a second Ingress leaves the merge behavior controller-dependent.

q: With the NGINX Ingress controller, 10% of traffic must go to the canary Service and 90% to the main Service, configured via two Ingress objects. Which annotations go on the canary Ingress?
options: canary-weight on the MAIN Ingress — the weight belongs on the canary
Path-based splitting — that's for paths, not percentages
Header-based canary annotations — a different canary mode than weight
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true" and nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
explain: The NGINX canary annotations mark the alternate Ingress (canary: "true") and its share (canary-weight: "10" = 10%); the main Ingress carries no canary annotations. Putting the weight on the main Ingress or using header-mode annotations answers a different question, and path splitting can't express percentages.

q: The NGINX Ingress must pin clients to backends with a cookie (the Service's sessionAffinity isn't visible at L7 through the Ingress). Which annotation enables cookie-based sticky sessions?
options: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: "cookie"
sessionAffinity: ClientIP — that's a Service field, not an Ingress one
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/upstream-hash-by — consistent hashing, a different mechanism
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect — forces HTTPS, unrelated
explain: The affinity: "cookie" annotation makes NGINX insert its own sticky cookie, independent of the backend Service's sessionAffinity (which operates at the kube-proxy layer the Ingress bypasses). upstream-hash-by hashes on a request attribute instead of setting a cookie, and sessionAffinity isn't a valid Ingress field at all.

q: The NGINX Ingress serves both HTTP and HTTPS; every plain-HTTP request must be redirected to HTTPS with a 308. Which annotation does this?
options: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl — not the real annotation name
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
tls: {redirect: true} — no such Ingress field
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol — selects the backend protocol, unrelated
explain: ssl-redirect: "true" is the NGINX annotation that 308-redirects HTTP to HTTPS (it defaults on when TLS is configured, but the explicit annotation is the exam answer). force-ssl isn't a real annotation name, there's no tls.redirect field, and backend-protocol governs how NGINX talks to the pods, not client redirects.

q: A pod sets hostNetwork: true and suddenly can't resolve cluster Service names — it's using the node's resolv.conf. Which dnsPolicy restores cluster DNS while keeping host networking?
options: ClusterFirst — with hostNetwork the pod keeps node DNS behavior
Default — inherits the node's DNS only, which is the current broken state
ClusterFirstWithHostNet — cluster DNS for host-networked pods
None with a hand-written dnsConfig — works but is unnecessary manual labor
explain: ClusterFirstWithHostNet exists for exactly this case: host-networked pods that still need kube-dns for cluster names. Plain ClusterFirst on a hostNetwork pod behaves like Default (node DNS), so the names stay broken; None + dnsConfig would work but hand-maintains what the dedicated policy does automatically.

q: A Service port 8080 serves HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c); the service mesh needs the protocol declared on the port to route correctly. Which Service port field declares it?
options: name: h2c — the name is a label, not a protocol declaration
An annotation — not the structured field
targetPort: h2c — targets a container port, doesn't declare protocol
appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c
explain: appProtocol is the structured protocol declaration on a Service port (kubernetes.io/h2c, kubernetes.io/ws, or plain http); meshes and Gateway implementations read it to pick ALPN/framing. The port name is freeform and carries no protocol semantics, targetPort only selects the backend, and annotations are the unstructured fallback.

q: A NetworkPolicy declares egress: [{ports: [{port: 443, protocol: TCP}]}] with NO "to" peer. What does this rule allow?
options: TCP 443 to ALL destinations — an omitted peer means all peers
Nothing — a rule without "to" matches no traffic
Only DNS — port 443 is unrelated to DNS
It's invalid — "to" is required whenever ports is set
explain: In a NetworkPolicy rule, omitted fields are wildcards: no "to" means all destinations, no "ports" would mean all ports — so this rule allows 443 everywhere. The common misread is that the rule does nothing or is invalid; it's valid and broad, which is why pairing ports with an explicit "to" is the tight version.
