q: An Ingress in namespace shop references the TLS Secret web-tls, which exists (correct type, correct keys) but only in namespace default. HTTPS serves the controller's fake certificate. Why?
options: Wrong Secret type — assume kubernetes.io/tls is correct
The TLS Secret must live in the SAME namespace as the Ingress
Missing ingressClassName — that affects routing, not certificates
TLS hosts mismatch — assume hosts match the rules
explain: Ingresses can only reference Secrets in their own namespace — cross-namespace Secret references are not permitted, so the controller falls back to its default fake cert. The type and keys can be perfect and it still fails. The fix is to create the TLS Secret in shop (external-secrets or a replication mechanism in real setups).

q: Using the Gateway API, 90% of traffic must go to Service v1 and 10% to Service v2 — true weighted splitting, natively. Which construct expresses this?
options: Two Services — Services don't weight between each other
An Ingress canary annotation — NGINX-specific, not native
An HTTPRoute with backendRefs weighted 90 and 10
sessionAffinity — stickiness, not weighting
explain: HTTPRoute backendRefs carry per-backend weights natively — the Gateway data plane splits 90/10 with no annotations or extra controllers. This is the answer to 'can native Kubernetes do weighted splitting' that plain Services can't give (their selection is label-based, unweighted). Ingress canary annotations are controller-specific; sessionAffinity is orthogonal stickiness.

q: End-to-end TLS is required: the edge must NOT terminate TLS, just pass TCP 443 through to the pods with SNI-based routing. Which Gateway API route type does this?
options: A standard Ingress — it terminates or can't passthrough
HTTPRoute — Layer 7, terminates TLS
TCPRoute without hostname — passes TCP but can't route by SNI
TLSRoute with SNI hostname matching — passthrough with per-hostname routing
explain: TLSRoute is the Gateway API's passthrough primitive: it routes on the SNI hostname without terminating, so pods see the original TLS session end-to-end. Standard Ingress can't express passthrough (the classic exam 'can it?' — no), HTTPRoute is L7-terminating, and a bare TCPRoute passes bytes with no hostname awareness.

q: An HTTPRoute in namespace shop lists a backend Service api in namespace billing. It never serves traffic and the route shows as not permitted. What is missing?
options: A ReferenceGrant in billing permitting the route to reference that Service
A cross-namespace Ingress — Ingresses can't do this either
A ServiceExport — that's multi-cluster, not multi-namespace
A cluster-scoped HTTPRoute — routes are namespaced by design
explain: Gateway API is secure by default across namespaces: a route may only reference backends in another namespace when that namespace grants permission via a ReferenceGrant. This is the designed answer to the old Ingress cross-namespace limitation — explicit grant, not ambient access. ServiceExport belongs to multi-cluster Services; there is no cluster-scoped route to reach for.

q: A NodePort Service with externalTrafficPolicy: Local has pods only on node-1. Clients hitting node-2:31080 get connection refused. Why?
options: kube-proxy is broken on node-2
With Local policy, nodes without local endpoints drop (refuse) the traffic instead of forwarding it cluster-wide
The nodePort isn't allocated on node-2 — it is, allocation is cluster-wide
The firewall blocks node-2 — the refusal is from kube-proxy's Local semantics
explain: externalTrafficPolicy: Local trades forwarding for source-IP preservation: only nodes with local ready endpoints serve the traffic; the rest refuse it rather than proxying. That's the documented cost of Local — with the default Cluster policy, node-2 would have forwarded to node-1 (at the price of SNAT hiding the client IP). The nodePort exists on every node; the refusal is policy, not a missing port.

q: The app needs the port number of the Service port NAMED grpc via DNS — the number changes per build, so it can't be hardcoded. Which DNS record type provides named-port lookup?
options: A records — IPs only, no ports
CNAME — aliases names, carries no ports
SRV records, e.g. _grpc._tcp.web.default.svc.cluster.local
TXT records — arbitrary text, not the port mechanism
explain: Kubernetes publishes SRV records for named Service ports (_<port-name>._<proto>.<svc>...), which is the DNS-native way to discover a changing port number. A records give only IPs, CNAME only aliases, and TXT is unstructured. If the port weren't named, there'd be no SRV record at all — the name is what creates it.

q: A Service uses the default externalTrafficPolicy. The app's access logs show every client IP as a node IP. Why, and which setting preserves the real client IP?
options: A logging bug — the IPs are correct
kube-proxy is misconfigured — reinstall it
A NetworkPolicy is rewriting addresses — policies don't NAT
The default Cluster policy SNATs external traffic through kube-proxy; externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves the source IP
explain: Cluster (the default) routes external traffic through kube-proxy with source NAT, so backends see node IPs — the price of cluster-wide forwarding. Local skips the extra hop and preserves the client IP, at the cost of dropping traffic on nodes without local endpoints (the previous question's scenario). NetworkPolicies filter; they never NAT.

q: You create a second NodePort Service requesting nodePort: 31080, already taken by another Service. What happens?
options: The API server rejects it — the nodePort is already allocated
Both Services share the port
The second Service gets silently remapped to a free port
The second Service stays Pending until the port frees up
explain: nodePorts are cluster-wide singletons: the API server validates uniqueness and rejects the duplicate outright. There's no sharing, no silent remap, and no Pending state for Services — the conflict surfaces at admission, which is why explicit nodePorts need coordination (or just let the API allocate).

q: You scale web to 5 replicas. For about 30 seconds, existing pods can't resolve the new pods' DNS names; then resolution starts working with no intervention. What explains the delay?
options: kube-proxy sync — that affects traffic, not DNS
CoreDNS caching — responses are cached (30s default TTL), so new records appear after the cache expires
Endpoints delay — Endpoints update within seconds, not 30
ndots misconfiguration — that slows external names, not new pod records
explain: CoreDNS caches both positive and negative responses with a 30-second default TTL, so freshly created DNS records (and freshly deleted ones) take up to ~30s to become visible to pods that already queried. Endpoints for traffic update in seconds — DNS lags behind by design. The exam uses this to separate 'traffic works but DNS doesn't yet' from real misconfigurations.

q: An HTTPRoute must match ONLY /healthz exactly (not /healthz/detailed) and everything under /api/ by prefix. Which match types express this?
options: Prefix for both — /healthz as Prefix also matches /healthz/detailed
Exact for both — /api/ as Exact wouldn't match /api/users
Exact for /healthz, Prefix for /api/
RegularExpression for both — overkill and harder to read
explain: HTTPRoute path matches are typed: Exact matches only the literal path, Prefix matches the path and everything beneath it — the same semantics as Ingress pathTypes Exact/Prefix. Using Prefix for /healthz would swallow /healthz/detailed; Exact for /api/ would miss /api/users. Regex works but is the blunt instrument when the typed matches say it precisely.

q: A ClusterIP Service manifest includes nodePort: 31080 in its port entry. What happens on apply?
options: It's accepted and the port is allocated on every node
It's silently ignored
The Service is converted to type NodePort
It's rejected — nodePort may only be set on NodePort or LoadBalancer Services
explain: The API server validates the pairing: nodePort is only legal on NodePort and LoadBalancer types (LoadBalancer allocates NodePorts by default). On a ClusterIP Service it's a validation error, not a silent ignore or a type conversion. The trap is assuming the field is harmless metadata — the API treats it as a contract about the Service type.

q: Your CI script deletes pod web-abc and must block until the pod is fully GONE (up to 2 minutes) before recreating it. Which command waits for the deletion?
options: kubectl wait --for=delete pod/web-abc --timeout=120s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web-abc — waits for readiness, the opposite
sleep 120 — waits blindly without checking
kubectl get pod web-abc -w — watches but doesn't exit on deletion the way wait does
explain: kubectl wait --for=delete blocks until the object disappears (or the timeout hits) — the precise primitive for delete-then-recreate sequencing. --for=condition=Ready waits for the pod to become ready, sleep doesn't observe anything, and get -w streams events rather than resolving on the deletion condition.

q: kubectl debug node/node-1 -it --image=busybox gives you a shell, but you see the container's filesystem, not the node's. How do you inspect the node's actual root filesystem?
options: Add a hostPath volume — debug node already mounts the host for you
chroot /host — the debug container mounts the node's root at /host
nsenter — that's for entering namespaces, not the filesystem view here
Recreate with --privileged — privilege doesn't change which root you see
explain: kubectl debug node mounts the node's root filesystem at /host inside the debug container; chroot /host pivots your shell into it so tools and paths resolve against the node. No extra volumes or flags are needed — the mount is the feature. nsenter enters namespaces of processes, and privileged only widens capabilities, neither re-roots your shell.

q: You want to test whether image web:v2 fixes the crash — WITHOUT touching the live web-abc pod. Which kubectl debug invocation creates a testable copy running v2?
options: kubectl set image pod/web-abc app=web:v2 — mutates the live pod
An ephemeral debug container — it runs its own image but doesn't change the app container
kubectl debug web-abc --copy-to=web-test --set-image=app=web:v2
kubectl run web-test --image=web:v2 — a fresh pod, not a copy of the live one's spec
explain: --copy-to duplicates the pod's full spec (env, volumes, probes) under a new name, and --set-image swaps the app container to v2 in the copy only — the live pod is untouched. set image mutates live workloads, ephemeral containers don't replace the app container, and kubectl run starts from scratch without the live pod's configuration.

q: Before handing the CI pipeline its kubeconfig, verify what ServiceAccount ci/deployer can do — checked AS that identity, not as yourself. Which command?
options: kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n prod — checks YOUR permissions
kubectl auth can-i ... --as=deployer — needs the full serviceaccount username
kubectl describe serviceaccount deployer -n ci — shows metadata, not permissions
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer
explain: --as impersonates the full service-account username system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name> for the authorization check, so you see exactly what CI will be allowed. Without --as you test yourself; the bare short name isn't a valid username; describe shows the SA object, never its effective RBAC.

q: kubectl describe node shows Capacity: cpu 8, but Allocatable: cpu 7400m. Why the gap, and which number governs scheduling?
options: The kubelet reserves CPU for system/kube daemons and eviction thresholds (system-reserved, kube-reserved); the scheduler fits pods against Allocatable
Metrics-server lag — the numbers come from node config, not metrics
Taints reduce allocatable — taints don't change the numbers
Capacity governs scheduling; Allocatable is informational
explain: Allocatable = Capacity minus kube-reserved, system-reserved, and eviction thresholds — the slice actually offered to pods — and the scheduler accounts requests against Allocatable, not Capacity. The gap is normal and configured, not a metrics artifact; taints affect eligibility, not the arithmetic.

q: One-liner: print each web pod's name alongside its first container's restart count. Which output flag does this?
options: -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}' — phase only, no restart counts
-o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}{"\n"}{end}'
-o jsonpath='{.spec.restartPolicy}' — the policy, not the count
custom-columns can't read containerStatuses — it can, it's just more verbose
explain: restartCount lives at .status.containerStatuses[].restartCount; the range construct iterates pods and prints name plus count per line. Phase and restartPolicy are different fields entirely, and custom-columns could do it — jsonpath is simply the terser exam one-liner. The [0] indexes the first container; adjust for multi-container pods.

q: The gRPC health probe must check the specific service "payments.Billing", not just the server. Which probe field names the service?
options: An httpGet path — gRPC probes don't use HTTP
tcpSocket — verifies the port accepts connections, knows no service names
grpc: {port: 9090, service: payments.Billing}
An exec running grpcurl — works but isn't the native probe
explain: The native grpc probe takes an optional service field naming the service to health-check per the gRPC health protocol; omit it and it checks the server overall. tcpSocket can't name a service, httpGet is the wrong protocol, and exec/grpcurl is the hand-rolled fallback the native probe exists to replace.

q: The pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30s for fast voluntary deletes, but liveness-triggered restarts must allow the 60s preStop flush to complete. Which probe-level field overrides the grace period for probe-initiated kills?
options: timeoutSeconds — bounds a single probe attempt, not termination
periodSeconds — probe frequency, unrelated
failureThreshold — how many failures trigger the kill, not the grace
terminationGracePeriodSeconds on the probe — overrides the pod-level grace for that probe's restarts
explain: Probes accept their own terminationGracePeriodSeconds (1.25+): when THAT probe kills the container, its value wins over the pod-level setting — decoupling crash-restart grace from voluntary-delete grace. timeoutSeconds, periodSeconds, and failureThreshold all tune detection, not the kill that follows.

q: A PodDisruptionBudget sets maxUnavailable: 0 for the 3-replica critical app. You run kubectl drain node-1. What happens?
options: The drain hangs on those pods — zero voluntary evictions are allowed; remove or relax the PDB first
The drain proceeds — PDBs don't apply to drains
One pod is evicted anyway — the PDB is advisory
The node is cordoned but the drain is skipped silently
explain: maxUnavailable: 0 means NO voluntary disruption is permitted, and drain's evictions are voluntary — so drain blocks (until its timeout) rather than violate the budget. PDBs absolutely apply to drains; that's their main job. The escape hatches are deleting the PDB, raising maxUnavailable, or accepting that this workload can't be drained gracefully.

q: A new pod first shows ErrImagePull, then minutes later ImagePullBackOff. What is the distinction between the two?
options: They're different errors with different causes
ErrImagePull is the immediate pull failure; after repeated failures the kubelet backs off and reports ImagePullBackOff
ImagePullBackOff means the registry is down; ErrImagePull means the tag is wrong
ErrImagePull is fatal — the pod will never retry
explain: Same root cause, different phase: ErrImagePull is each fresh failure, ImagePullBackOff is the kubelet's exponential-backoff state between retries. The progression tells you the failure is persistent (bad tag, bad creds, registry down) rather than transient. Neither is fatal on its own — the kubelet keeps retrying with growing delays.

q: The export Job finished and you need its logs without looking up which pod ran it. Which command selects the Job's pods directly?
options: kubectl logs deploy/export — that's a Deployment, not this Job
kubectl logs cronjob/export — logs doesn't accept CronJob as a source
kubectl logs job/export
kubectl describe job export — shows status, not logs
explain: kubectl logs accepts Job (and Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, ReplicaSet) as a log source, selecting the underlying pods via the job-name label — no pod-name lookup needed. CronJob isn't a valid logs source (its Jobs are), and describe shows object status, never container output.

q: The 2 AM CronJob has no Job for last night. What's the fastest check of whether the controller even attempted the schedule?
options: Describe a pod — there is no pod to describe
Read the controller-manager logs — heavy and usually unnecessary
Scan all events — noisy compared to the status field
kubectl get cronjob export -o jsonpath='{.status.lastScheduleTime}'
explain: status.lastScheduleTime is the controller's own record of its last attempt — empty or stale means the schedule never fired (missed window, suspend, or controller issue). It's the first check before digging into events or component logs, which are the second line, not the first.

q: The HPA shows <unknown> for CPU and isn't scaling. kubectl describe hpa reports 'failed to get cpu utilization: missing request for cpu'. What is wrong?
options: The target pods declare no CPU requests — utilization needs a request denominator
metrics-server is down — that produces a different error about the metrics API
The HPA target is misconfigured — the target is fine, the pods are
minReplicas is unset — that doesn't cause <unknown>
explain: CPU utilization = usage ÷ request; with no request on the pods there's no denominator, so the HPA can't compute a percentage and reports <unknown>. The fix is adding CPU requests to the pod template. A dead metrics-server fails differently ('unable to get metrics'), and minReplicas is unrelated to metric collection.

q: kubectl describe node, 'Allocated resources': requests cpu 6500m (87%), limits cpu 12 (160%). A new pod requesting 1 CPU stays Pending. Why, if the node 'has capacity'?
options: The limits block scheduling — the scheduler ignores limits
Scheduling accounts requests against Allocatable: 87% + 1000m exceeds it; limits are irrelevant to the fit check
The percentages are miscalculated — they're correct
The node always needs more nodes at 87% — no, it needs the request to fit
explain: The scheduler's fit check is sum-of-requests vs Allocatable — limits play no role (they're enforcement, not placement). At 87% of 7400m allocatable, another 1000m doesn't fit, hence Pending. Limits can exceed capacity freely (160% here) because they're ceilings, not reservations — the classic requests-vs-limits scheduling confusion.

q: Cluster-wide, you want ONLY Warning events to triage problems fast, without the Normal noise. Which command filters server-side?
options: kubectl get events -A — returns Normal too
kubectl get pods -A — wrong resource
kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning
kubectl logs -A — logs aren't events
explain: --field-selector type=Warning filters at the API server, so only Warning events cross the wire — the fast triage view. Unfiltered get events drowns you in Normal informational events; pods and logs are different data entirely. (Note: field selectors support only == and != on a small set of fields — type is one of them.)

q: A livenessProbe sets failureThreshold: 1 with periodSeconds: 10. What is the effect?
options: Same as the default — the default is 3, not 1
The probe is disabled — 1 is valid, not disabling
It waits 10s longer — periodSeconds is the interval, unchanged in meaning
A SINGLE failed check restarts the container — hair-trigger; the default 3 tolerates transient blips
explain: failureThreshold is consecutive failures before action: 1 means any single failed probe kills the container, with no tolerance for a momentary stall. The default 3 exists precisely to absorb transient blips. Setting 1 is occasionally justified for fast-fail workloads, but it's a deliberate hair-trigger, not a tuning no-op.

q: A readinessProbe sets successThreshold: 3 with periodSeconds: 5. A recovered pod needs how long, minimum, before it receives traffic again?
options: 15 seconds — 3 CONSECUTIVE successes at 5s intervals
5 seconds — one interval is enough
Immediately — the first success re-adds it
It's rejected — that's only true for liveness probes
explain: successThreshold on readiness means N consecutive successes before the pod is marked Ready: 3 × 5s = 15s minimum after recovery. Unlike liveness (which rejects successThreshold > 1), readiness accepts it — the trade-off is slower traffic restoration for stronger 'really healthy' confidence. The exam pairs this with the liveness rejection rule to test that you know which probe allows it.

q: Compare kubectl delete pod web-abc --now with kubectl delete pod web-abc --force --grace-period=0.
options: Identical — both force-delete immediately
--now sets grace-period 0 but still deletes gracefully (SIGTERM is sent); --force bypasses graceful deletion entirely and risks orphaned resources
--now is the forceful one — backwards
--force is graceful — backwards
explain: --now is shorthand for --grace-period=0: the SIGTERM still goes out, just with no wait before SIGKILL. --force skips the graceful path at the API level — the object is ripped out of etcd, which can orphan dependents and confuse controllers. --now is aggressive but clean; --force is the last resort for pods stuck on dead nodes.

q: You need the crashed container's LAST exit code as a one-liner, without kubectl describe. Which jsonpath reads it?
options: {.status.phase} — pod phase, not the exit code
{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount} — the count, not the code
{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.exitCode}
{.status.podIP} — the IP, unrelated
explain: lastState.terminated holds the previous run's termination record, including exitCode and reason (OOMKilled, Error) — the scriptable equivalent of reading 'Last State' in describe output. phase is too coarse, restartCount counts without explaining, and podIP is networking. For multi-container pods, index or range over containerStatuses.

q: kubectl describe pod shows 'QoS Class: Burstable'. Under node memory pressure, what does this tell you about eviction order?
options: It's never evicted — that's Guaranteed, and even Guaranteed can go last, not never
It's evicted first — BestEffort goes first
Its memory is guaranteed — Burstable has no such guarantee
It's evicted after BestEffort pods but before Guaranteed ones
explain: QoS eviction order under node pressure: BestEffort first, then Burstable (starting with the ones exceeding their requests most), then Guaranteed last. Burstable — requests set but not equal to limits — sits in the middle: safer than BestEffort, less safe than Guaranteed. The class derives from the requests/limits relationship, which is why describe shows it.

q: You put defaultMode: 0400 under the secret: source of a projected volume and kubectl apply rejects the manifest with an unknown-field error. Where does defaultMode belong?
options: On the projected volume itself (volumes[].projected.defaultMode) — per-source defaultMode is not a field; override individual files with items[].mode when one file needs to differ
Under each source — the API just needs the value quoted as "0400"
In the pod's securityContext as fsGroup — fsGroup controls ownership, not permission bits
defaultMode is only valid on Secret volumes, never on projected volumes
explain: VolumeProjection types (SecretProjection, ConfigMapProjection, etc.) have no defaultMode field, so strict decoding rejects it. ProjectedVolumeSource.defaultMode sets the default for every source, and items[].mode overrides per file. Quoting never creates a missing field, and fsGroup governs ownership, not mode bits.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The compliance scan flags that the app container can read /proc/kcore (a window into host memory). The pod must keep its other /proc views intact. Which securityContext entry hides just that path?
options: capabilities.drop: [SYS_RAWIO] — capabilities restrict syscalls, they don't mask filesystem paths
maskedPaths: ["/proc/kcore"] in the pod's securityContext — the kubelet masks the listed paths while leaving the rest of /proc visible
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — that only affects the container's root filesystem, not /proc
hostPID: false — the pod doesn't use hostPID, and this wouldn't mask anything anyway
explain: maskedPaths is the surgical tool: the kubelet masks exactly the listed paths inside the container's mount namespace. Capabilities gate syscalls rather than hiding files, readOnlyRootFilesystem doesn't touch /proc, and hostPID is about the PID namespace, not /proc visibility.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The nodes enforce SELinux. Pods must run their processes with the label system_u:system_r:container_t:s0. Where is this expressed?
options: An annotation on the Deployment — SELinux labels are not annotation-driven
capabilities.add: [MAC_ADMIN] — Linux capabilities are a different mechanism from MAC labels
securityContext.seLinuxOptions: {user: system_u, role: system_r, type: container_t, level: s0} at pod or container level — the kubelet applies the SELinux context to the container processes
runAsUser: 0 — SELinux identity is independent of the UID
explain: seLinuxOptions sets the SELinux user/role/type/level for container processes, which is what SELinux-enforcing nodes check. Annotations don't configure it, capabilities are the DAC/capability axis rather than MAC labels, and the UID is a separate identity dimension.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod sets resources.requests: {hugepages-2Mi: 512Mi} and resources.limits: {hugepages-2Mi: 1Gi}. The API server rejects it. Why?
options: Hugepage quantities must be whole pages — 512Mi is a valid quantity, so that is not the problem
Nodes need a feature gate for hugepages — hugepages are GA and need no gate
Hugepage requests must EXCEED limits — the rule is the opposite
Hugepages don't support overcommit, so requests must equal limits — if you set only limits, requests default to the same value
explain: Per the Kubernetes docs, huge page requests must equal the limits (setting only limits auto-defaults requests to match). Unlike CPU/memory, hugepages can't be overcommitted, so the API enforces equality. The other options invent gates, direction, or quantity rules that don't exist.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container sets env: [{name: PRICE_MSG, value: "cost: $$5"}]. What does the application actually see?
options: cost: $5 — $$ is the escape for a literal dollar sign; only the $(VAR) form triggers expansion
cost: with an empty value — undefined variables expand to empty, but $$5 is not a variable reference at all
The pod fails to create — a bare $ is legal; only $(VAR) is special
cost: $$5 — the escape for a literal dollar is $$, which collapses to a single $
explain: Variable expansion only fires on $(NAME) references; $$ collapses to one $. So $$5 renders as $5 with no lookup attempted. Option D describes the mechanism but states the wrong result — the collapse is the whole point.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The node ships a custom seccomp profile at the kubelet's seccomp directory as profiles/audit.json. The pod must run under it. Which snippet is correct?
options: seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} — that selects the container runtime's builtin default, not the custom file
seccompProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: profiles/audit.json} — Localhost selects a node-local file, with the path relative to the kubelet's seccomp root
The annotation seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod: profiles/audit.json — the annotation mechanism is deprecated in favor of the field
securityContext.seccomp: profiles/audit.json — no such field exists
explain: type: Localhost plus localhostProfile points at a profile file on the node (path relative to <kubelet-root>/seccomp). RuntimeDefault is the runtime's own default profile, the beta annotation is the legacy path, and there is no bare seccomp string field.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You set runtimeClassName: gvisor on a pod, but no RuntimeClass named gvisor exists in the cluster. What happens?
options: The pod runs with the default runtime — an unknown runtimeClassName is never silently ignored
The API server rejects the pod at admission — admission doesn't validate RuntimeClass existence
The pod is admitted and scheduled, but never starts — the kubelet can't map the name to a runtime handler, so the pod sits Pending with handler errors
The scheduler refuses to schedule it — the scheduler doesn't validate runtime handlers
explain: Nothing admission-side or scheduler-side checks that the RuntimeClass exists; the failure surfaces at the kubelet, which reports no matching runtime handler and never creates containers. The pod is admitted and scheduled but stuck Pending — the classic 'forgot to install the RuntimeClass' symptom.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: CI must create the registry pull secret imperatively from shell variables — no YAML files allowed. Which command does it?
options: kubectl create secret generic regcred --from-literal=.dockerconfigjson=... — hand-building the JSON under the generic type is error-prone; use the purpose-built subcommand
kubectl create configmap regcred --from-env-file — a ConfigMap is the wrong kind entirely
docker login on each node — node-local docker config never reaches the kubelet's image pulls
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=REG --docker-username=U --docker-password=P — assembles the kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret with the correct type and key
explain: kubectl create secret docker-registry exists exactly for this: it builds the .dockerconfigjson payload with type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson. The generic form requires you to hand-craft that JSON, a ConfigMap can't serve as an imagePullSecret, and docker login only affects the local Docker client.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The namespace must never hold more than 20 Secrets — a runaway operator once created hundreds. Which ResourceQuota entry enforces an object count?
options: count/secrets: "20" (shorthand secrets: "20") — quotas support object-count resources, and the 21st Secret creation is rejected
requests.storage: 20Gi — that caps PVC storage, not object counts
limits.memory: 20Gi — compute quotas don't count objects
ResourceQuotas can't count Secrets — they can; object counts are first-class quota resources
explain: ResourceQuota resource names include count/<resource> forms (pods, services, secrets, configmaps, persistentvolumeclaims...), so the 21st Secret is rejected at admission. Storage and compute quotas measure different dimensions, and object-count quotas are fully supported.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A LimitRange sets min: {cpu: 250m} for containers. A developer applies a pod whose container requests 100m CPU. What happens?
options: The request is silently raised to 250m — LimitRange never mutates requests up to min; it rejects
The pod is rejected — LimitRange min/max are admission-time bounds, and violating containers fail creation
It schedules fine — min applies to requests too, so it is enforced
The LimitRange only warns — enforcement is the default; warnings need PSS-style modes, not LimitRange
explain: LimitRange enforces min/max at admission: below-min or above-max containers are rejected outright. It only mutates via default/defaultRequest, never by clamping to min. There is no warn-only mode for LimitRange.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The deployer ServiceAccount must be able to read ONLY the Secret db-creds — not every Secret in the namespace. Which Role rule expresses this?
options: resources: [secrets], verbs: [get] — that grants read on ALL Secrets, the overbroad version
resources: [secrets/db-creds], verbs: [get] — there is no slash syntax; the field is resourceNames
resources: ["secrets"], resourceNames: ["db-creds"], verbs: ["get"] — resourceNames scopes the rule to the named object
Only a ClusterRole can do this — namespaced Roles govern Secrets in their namespace just fine
explain: resourceNames whitelists specific object names within the listed resources — the standard least-privilege pattern. Option A is the trap (all Secrets), B invents slash syntax, and namespaced Roles are exactly the right scope here.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The pod sets automountServiceAccountToken: false, but one container still needs a short-lived, audience-bound token for a cloud API. Which approach works?
options: Nothing works — disabling automount disables all token delivery, which is false
Set automountServiceAccountToken: true on the ServiceAccount — that re-enables the broad legacy mount the policy forbids
Mount the node's token via hostPath — insecure and the node has no such token to share
Add a projected serviceAccountToken volume — projection is independent of the automount flag, delivering a purpose-built token without the default mount
explain: Projected tokens are explicit opt-in and unaffected by automountServiceAccountToken: you get a short-lived, audience-bound credential exactly where needed while the legacy default mount stays off. Re-enabling automount would restore the broad token the policy bans.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The namespace enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard and your pod is rejected: containers must drop ALL capabilities. Which fix satisfies it?
options: securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] on each container — restricted requires dropping all, then adding back only what the app needs
Drop capabilities at the pod level — capabilities is a container-level field; pod-level placement is rejected
Set privileged: true — the exact opposite of what restricted allows
Capabilities are a seccomp concern — they are separate mechanisms; seccomp filters syscalls, capabilities gate privileges
explain: The restricted standard mandates dropping ALL capabilities (alongside runAsNonRoot, seccomp, and no privilege escalation). Capabilities live under each container's securityContext — the pod-level placement is the Q207 trap — and privileged: true could never pass restricted.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The node provides the AppArmor profile k8s-nginx. What is the modern, non-annotation way to confine the web container with it?
options: The beta annotation container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/web: localhost/k8s-nginx — deprecated in favor of the field
securityContext.appArmorProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: k8s-nginx} — the GA field that replaces the annotation
seccompProfile — that selects a seccomp profile, not an AppArmor profile
runtimeClassName — that selects the container runtime, not the MAC profile
explain: appArmorProfile is the field form of AppArmor confinement (type Localhost + the on-node profile name); the per-container beta annotation is deprecated. Seccomp and RuntimeClass are different isolation axes entirely.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod sets imagePullPolicy: Never, but the image was never pulled to this node. What status do you see?
options: ImagePullBackOff — that implies pull attempts happened; Never means no pull is ever attempted
The pod runs anyway — Never doesn't conjure a local image
ErrImageNeverPull — the kubelet refuses to contact the registry and the image is absent locally
Pending forever with no events — the kubelet always records the reason in events
explain: Never restricts the kubelet to images already on the node; when absent you get ErrImageNeverPull, distinct from ImagePullBackOff (which follows failed pull attempts). The policy is about pre-loaded/air-gapped nodes, and it fails loudly rather than hanging silently.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Every pod carries the label team: payments, and the frozen image needs its own team label as the env var TEAM. Which valueFrom form does it?
options: configMapKeyRef — labels live on the pod object, not in a ConfigMap
fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name} — that's the pod name, not a label value
secretKeyRef — labels are not Secrets
fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels['team']} — the downward API exposes individual labels (and annotations) as env vars
explain: The downward API's fieldRef supports metadata.labels['key'] and metadata.annotations['key'], projecting pod metadata without RBAC or code changes. ConfigMap/Secret refs read those objects, not pod metadata, and metadata.name is a different field.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A monitoring sidecar needs the host's FULL /proc — the default masking hides /proc/kcore and /proc/sched_debug, which it must read. Which setting lifts the masking?
options: securityContext.procMount: Unmasked — removes the default /proc masking for that container
privileged: true — far broader than needed; procMount is the targeted knob
hostPID: true — shares the PID namespace, but /proc stays masked without procMount
capabilities.add: [SYS_PTRACE] — enables tracing, doesn't unmask /proc files
explain: procMount: Unmasked is precisely the /proc masking control (default is a masked /proc). hostPID changes PID visibility but the mask remains; privileged and SYS_PTRACE are heavier or orthogonal tools.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container's env entry sets both value: "x" and valueFrom: {configMapKeyRef: {...}}. What does the API server do with the manifest?
options: value wins and valueFrom is ignored — there is no silent precedence
Rejects the manifest — an env var may specify value or valueFrom, never both
valueFrom wins as the more specific source — no precedence rule exists
Merges them with value as the default — no merge behavior exists
explain: The API validates that exactly one of value/valueFrom is set — specifying both is a validation error, not a precedence question. This is the classic copy-paste trap when converting a literal to a reference.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create a ConfigMap with the key "app/config.yaml" and the API server rejects it. Why?
options: Slashes are fine in keys — they aren't; the key charset is restricted
Keys can't contain dots — they can (dotted keys are common)
ConfigMap data keys must match [-._a-zA-Z0-9]+ — slashes are rejected; control the file path with items: [{key: ..., path: "app/config.yaml"}] on the volume instead
Keys are limited to 32 characters — no such limit applies here
explain: ConfigMap (and Secret) data keys are restricted to alphanumeric characters plus -._ — slashes are invalid. The file layout is controlled separately via items[].path on the volume or projected source, so the key stays simple while the path nests.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A LimitRange sets defaultRequest: {memory: 256Mi}. Afterwards, pods created WITHOUT any requests start failing ResourceQuota with 'exceeded quota'. What is going on?
options: The LimitRange is broken — defaults legitimately count against quota
The quota counts limits instead of requests — quotas track requests and limits as separate resources
Pods without requests are BestEffort and exempt from quota — no workload is exempt
LimitRange is mutating admission: it injects the 256Mi request before quota evaluation, so the defaulted requests consume quota
explain: Mutating admission (LimitRange defaults) runs before validating admission (ResourceQuota), so injected requests count against the quota — the classic 'sudden quota failures after adding a LimitRange' surprise. The fix is raising the quota or scoping the defaults, not blaming the quota.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: An emptyDir volume sets sizeLimit: 1Gi. The app's cache grows to 2Gi. What does the kubelet do?
options: Evicts the pod — breaching an emptyDir sizeLimit is a kubelet eviction trigger
Deletes only the excess files — the kubelet never prunes application data selectively
Throttles the writes — storage has no throttle mechanism
Nothing — sizeLimit is advisory documentation
explain: sizeLimit is enforced: when the emptyDir exceeds it, the kubelet evicts the pod (the same local-storage pressure path as ephemeral-storage limits). It doesn't delete files or throttle — the whole pod goes, which is why sizeLimit is the containment tool for runaway caches.

q: Cache pods run in namespace cache-infra, but the app pods that must colocate with them run in namespace app. Your podAffinity term's labelSelector matches app: cache, yet nothing colocates. What's missing?
options: Pod affinity can't cross namespaces — it can, but you must say so explicitly
namespaces: ["cache-infra"] (or a namespaceSelector) on the affinity term — selectors default to the pod's own namespace
Use nodeAffinity instead — that constrains nodes, not pod colocation
Put both workloads in one namespace — unnecessary; the namespaces field exists for this
explain: Affinity terms are namespace-scoped by default; the namespaces list (or namespaceSelector) extends pod selection across namespaces. Without it, the selector looks for app: cache pods in namespace app, finds none, and the rule silently never matches.

q: A node goes NotReady. Its pods aren't evicted immediately — they hang around for about 5 minutes first. Where does the 5-minute delay come from?
options: The kubelet waits for the node to recover — the delay is taint-eviction timing, not kubelet patience
terminationGracePeriodSeconds defaults to 300 — the default grace period is 30s
Pods carry automatic tolerations for node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable with tolerationSeconds: 300 — taint-based eviction fires when the toleration expires
The scheduler re-evaluates every 5 minutes — scheduling cadence is unrelated to eviction
explain: Kubernetes adds default 300-second tolerations for the not-ready and unreachable NoExecute taints, so pods tolerate a brief node outage and are only evicted after ~5 minutes of continuous NotReady. It's toleration expiry — not grace periods or scheduler timing — that sets the delay.

q: An indexed Job (completions: 50) has one poison shard that always fails, and its retries keep burning the Job-wide backoffLimit while 49 healthy shards suffer. Which field gives each index its own retry budget?
options: backoffLimit: 1 — still Job-wide; one bad shard still poisons the whole Job
activeDeadlineSeconds — bounds total time, not per-index retries
podFailurePolicy — matches on exit codes across the Job, not per-index counts
backoffLimitPerIndex — a per-index failure budget for indexed Jobs; the poison index fails out without killing its siblings
explain: backoffLimitPerIndex (indexed completion mode) lets each index fail independently up to its own budget, so one bad shard doesn't consume the shared backoffLimit. podFailurePolicy handles exit-code rules globally, and activeDeadlineSeconds is a time bound, not a retry bound.

q: A pod declares initContainers: [proxy (restartPolicy: Always — native sidecar), migrate (regular init)]. proxy starts successfully, then crashes twice while migrate is running. What happens to migrate and the pod?
options: migrate proceeds and the pod continues — once a restartable init container has started successfully, subsequent init containers start; proxy restarts under its own Always policy without blocking the chain
migrate waits for proxy to stabilize — startup gating ends at successful start, not at stability
The pod fails — a crashed sidecar doesn't fail the pod; it restarts
migrate is skipped — the init chain never aborts over a sidecar restart
explain: Per the sidecar KEP, subsequent init containers start after the sidecar's successful start (startupProbe), not its exit — so a later crash just triggers the sidecar's own restart. Only a sidecar that never starts successfully blocks what follows. The init chain is gated on start, not on continued health.

q: You want web pods spread across zones keyed by their own app label, without hardcoding any label value in the constraint itself. Which topologySpreadConstraints field does this?
options: labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}} — that hardcodes the value you want to avoid
matchLabelKeys: ["app"] — the constraint uses the incoming pod's own app label value as the match key
podAffinity — that's attraction toward pods, not spreading
nodeSelector — pins nodes, can't express spreading
explain: matchLabelKeys computes the spreading criteria from the pod being scheduled — each pod spreads against others sharing its own label values, no hardcoded selector needed. labelSelector pins explicit values, and affinity/nodeSelector are different scheduling tools.

q: A pod sets activeDeadlineSeconds: 600. Its init container hangs downloading a dataset for 11 minutes. What happens?
options: Nothing — the deadline only counts app-container runtime, which is false
The init container is killed but the pod continues — the deadline terminates the whole pod
The entire pod is terminated with reason DeadlineExceeded — the deadline spans the full pod lifetime, including init containers
Init containers are exempt from the deadline — they aren't
explain: activeDeadlineSeconds is measured from pod start across all phases, init included. Exceeding it kills the whole pod with reason DeadlineExceeded — a long init phase burns the same budget as the main workload.

q: You add an ephemeralContainers entry to a pod manifest and run kubectl apply. What happens?
options: It works like a regular container — ephemeral containers have a completely separate lifecycle
The pod restarts with the debug container — pods never restart to gain containers
It's silently dropped — the API rejects the field rather than dropping it
The API server rejects it — ephemeralContainers can't be set at creation or via spec updates; use kubectl debug, which targets the ephemeralcontainers subresource
explain: The field is immutable via the main pod resource — it can't be specified when creating a pod nor modified by updating the spec. Additions go through the ephemeralcontainers subresource, which is what kubectl debug drives. kubectl apply/edit of the pod spec can never add one.

q: Each StatefulSet replica needs its ordinal (0, 1, 2...) as the env var SHARD_ID, but the downward API exposes no ordinal field. What's the standard workaround?
options: Parse it from the hostname — StatefulSet pod names end in the ordinal (web-0, web-1), so deriving SHARD_ID from metadata.name/hostname is the canonical trick
fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.ordinal} — no such fieldPath exists
An annotation on the StatefulSet — annotations are shared, not per-ordinal
It's impossible; use a Deployment — the stable identity is exactly what makes this solvable
explain: StatefulSets give each pod a stable ordinal-suffixed hostname; shell-parsing the trailing -N (or a small entrypoint script) is the standard way to expose it. The downward API genuinely has no ordinal field, and annotations can't carry per-pod values.

q: Six web replicas must NEVER share a node — a hard requirement, not a preference. Which affinity expresses it?
options: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution podAntiAffinity — preferred is soft and may be violated
requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution podAntiAffinity with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname and a labelSelector matching app: web — at most one matching pod per node
nodeAffinity — constrains which nodes, not pod colocation
topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1 — spreading is best-effort unless combined with DoNotSchedule; anti-affinity is the direct hard tool
explain: Required pod anti-affinity on the hostname topology domain means no two matching pods may share a node — a hard scheduling constraint. Preferred is violable, nodeAffinity doesn't model pod-to-pod rules, and topology spread is the softer cousin.

q: A CronJob sets timeZone: "Mars/Olympus_Mons". It never fires and creates no Jobs. What's wrong?
options: CronJobs don't support timeZone — they do; the value is the problem
The schedule expression is wrong — the timezone fails before the schedule matters
The timezone name is invalid — the controller can't parse it, so no schedule ever fires; use a valid IANA name like America/New_York
timeZone needs a feature gate — it's been stable without one
explain: An unparseable timeZone breaks the CronJob controller's scheduling for that object — it logs the error and never fires. Valid IANA timezone names (with DST handling) are required; the cron expression is never even evaluated.

q: You set suspend: true on a Job that currently has 3 active pods. What happens to those pods?
options: They run to completion — suspend tears them down immediately
They're paused in place — pods can't be paused; they're deleted
Nothing until the Job finishes — suspend acts immediately on active pods
The active pods are deleted; setting suspend: false later recreates them and the Job continues from its completion count
explain: Suspending a Job deletes its active pods at once; the Job object (and its completed count) persists, so resuming recreates pods and continues. It's the 'freeze the burn rate NOW' switch — not a pause, and not deferred.

q: You add replicas: 3 to a DaemonSet manifest and kubectl apply fails. Why?
options: DaemonSets have no replicas field — one pod per matching node is the entire cardinality model; unknown fields are rejected
replicas must be 1 — there is no replicas field at all, valid or otherwise
Use kubectl scale instead — DaemonSets scale by node matching, not by count
The API server will default it — unknown fields are rejected, never defaulted
explain: A DaemonSet's pod count derives from node selection, not a replica number — spec.replicas simply doesn't exist on the type. Scaling a DaemonSet means changing its nodeSelector/affinity/tolerations, not a count.

q: Container A in a pod defines env FOO=bar. Container B in the SAME pod sets args: ["$(FOO)"]. What does container B receive?
options: bar — expansion doesn't work pod-wide
The literal string $(FOO) — $(VAR) expansion is scoped to each container's own env list
An empty string — that's for undefined vars within the same container, not cross-container references
The pod is rejected — cross-references aren't forbidden, they're just not resolved
explain: Variable expansion only sees the same container's env entries (plus the standard service env vars). To share, both containers must define it — via envFrom, a shared ConfigMap, or the downward API — because there is no pod-level env inheritance.

q: A StatefulSet rollout went bad. Does kubectl rollout undo sts/db work?
options: No — undo is Deployment-only, which is false
Only with --to-revision — plain undo works too, targeting the previous revision
Yes — the rollout family (history, status, undo, pause, restart, resume) supports Deployments, DaemonSets, and StatefulSets
Only for DaemonSets — StatefulSets are equally supported
explain: kubectl rollout operates on all three rolling-update workloads: deployments, daemonsets, and statefulsets. StatefulSet revisions work like Deployment revisions, so undo/pause/history all apply — Jobs and bare pods are the types it can't touch.

q: You set updateStrategy: {type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 1}} on a DaemonSet and the API server rejects it. Why?
options: maxUnavailable: 1 is invalid — it's perfectly valid on a DaemonSet
DaemonSets can't rolling-update — RollingUpdate is their standard strategy
Only percentages are allowed — integers are fine
DaemonSet rollingUpdate supports only maxUnavailable — maxSurge isn't a field there, unlike on Deployments
explain: DaemonSet update strategy is deliberately simpler: surge makes no sense when cardinality is node-derived, so only maxUnavailable exists. Copying a Deployment's rollingUpdate block verbatim is the trap.

q: You try to change a Job's spec.selector.matchLabels and the API server rejects the edit. Why?
options: Selectors are immutable after creation — the same rule as Deployments; delete and recreate the Job to change them
Jobs don't have selectors — they do (auto-generated unless manualSelector: true)
Only the controller may edit selectors — nobody can; they're frozen for everyone
The error is transient — immutability rejections are permanent for that object
explain: Workload selectors are immutable once set — the API server rejects any change, so the path is delete + recreate (or kubectl replace --force). The rule is identical for Deployments, Jobs, and StatefulSets.

q: You nest imagePullSecrets under a container spec and kubectl apply fails. What's wrong?
options: Pull secrets require a ServiceAccount — they can also be declared at pod level without one
imagePullSecrets is a pod-spec field — the kubelet merges pod-level and ServiceAccount secrets; containers can't declare their own
Secrets must be mounted as volumes — pull secrets are referenced by name, never mounted
The secret name is misspelled — the error is structural placement, not the name
explain: imagePullSecrets lives at spec.imagePullSecrets (pod level) and unions with the ServiceAccount's list. There's no per-container variant — the field simply doesn't exist under containers, so strict decoding rejects it.

q: Which schedule value runs a CronJob once a day at midnight?
options: "daily" — not a valid cron expression
"0 0 * *" — that's only four fields; cron needs five
"@daily" — cron presets (@yearly, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @hourly) are valid schedule values
"24:00" — not a thing in cron
explain: Standard cron implementations (and Kubernetes) accept the @-presets; @daily equals 0 0 * * *. The exam loves the four-field trap — cron always needs five fields.

q: You need a CronJob created imperatively — no YAML file. Which command does it?
options: kubectl run --schedule — run has no schedule flag
kubectl create job --cron — no such flag exists
kubectl expose --schedule — expose creates Services
kubectl create cronjob NAME --image=img --schedule="0 2 * * *" — the imperative generator, with -- command args appended after --
explain: kubectl create cronjob is the purpose-built generator (--image and --schedule are required; the container command follows --). The other commands lack any scheduling flags — run/expose/create job do different jobs.

q: A Deployment sets revisionHistoryLimit: 0. After a bad rollout, kubectl rollout undo fails with 'no rollout history found'. Why?
options: Zero means keep no old ReplicaSets — with no retained revisions there is nothing to roll back to; raise the limit to keep history
undo needs --to-revision — plain undo works fine when history exists
The limit only affects ConfigMaps — it governs retained ReplicaSets
0 means unlimited — 0 means keep none
explain: revisionHistoryLimit caps how many old ReplicaSets are retained; 0 discards history immediately, so undo has no target. The default 10 keeps the rollback ladder. This is the deliberate-config cousin of the missing-history case — the limit, not the tooling, ate the history.

q: The single-replica web Deployment must roll out with zero downtime: the old pod keeps serving until the new one is Ready. Which strategy settings give that, and what's the peak pod count?
options: maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 — the old pod dies before the replacement is Ready: brief downtime
maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 — the surge pod is created first (peak 2 pods) and the old pod terminates only after the new one passes readiness
type: Recreate — kills everything first by design; the opposite of zero downtime
maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 0 — deadlocks the rollout: it can neither create nor terminate
explain: Integer surge/unavailable (not percentages) is how you shape single-replica rollouts: maxSurge: 1 allows the extra pod, maxUnavailable: 0 keeps the old one until the new one is Ready. Recreate and maxUnavailable: 1 both introduce downtime; 0/0 can't progress.

q: An operator once ran helm upgrade --set logLevel=debug for troubleshooting. Every upgrade since keeps debug, even though nobody passes --set anymore and values.yaml says info. How do you permanently return to the chart default?
options: helm upgrade -f prod.yaml — previously-set values persist in the release; the file alone won't clear them
helm upgrade --reuse-values — that explicitly keeps the stored values
helm upgrade --reset-values — resets to chart defaults, discarding values from previous --set/--set-file flags
Edit values.yaml to say info — the release's stored values override chart defaults on upgrade
explain: Helm stores prior --set values in the release and reuses them on every upgrade — the sticky-values trap. --reset-values clears them back to chart defaults (values in -f files you pass now still apply). Editing values.yaml can't beat the stored release values.

q: helm history api shows older revisions marked SUPERSEDED and one marked FAILED. What do those statuses mean?
options: SUPERSEDED means deleted — superseded revisions are retained, just not current
FAILED means the chart is broken — it means that specific revision's install/upgrade operation failed
Only DEPLOYED matters — the history is the audit trail; every status informs
SUPERSEDED = replaced by a later revision; FAILED = that revision's operation failed; the live state is whatever the latest revision reports
explain: helm history is the revision ledger: each successful upgrade supersedes the last, and failed operations stay visible for diagnosis and rollback targeting. Reading the statuses tells you exactly which revision is live and which ones are safe rollback targets.

q: Your kustomization uses patchesStrategicMerge, and a teammate says it's deprecated. What is the current field?
options: patches: — the unified field accepting strategic-merge, JSON merge, and JSON 6902 patches
strategicPatches: — no such field exists
overlays: — that's the concept, not a kustomization field
It isn't deprecated — it is deprecated (still functional, but deprecated)
explain: patchesStrategicMerge (and patchesJson6902) are deprecated in favor of the single patches field, which takes inline patch: | blocks or path: references and auto-detects the patch style. Old keys still work but shouldn't be written in new code.

q: The overlay needs the image tag injected into an annotation value, but kustomize vars are deprecated. What replaces them?
options: Edit the base directly — that defeats the entire overlay purpose
replacements: — the transformer that substitutes field values (e.g., copying an image tag into an annotation) without vars
configMapGenerator — generates ConfigMaps; it doesn't rewrite arbitrary fields
Keep using vars — deprecated means stop writing new ones
explain: The replacements transformer is the vars successor: it sources a value from one field (like an image tag) and writes it into targets (like annotations). configMapGenerator solves a different problem, and editing the base breaks every other overlay.

q: kubectl apply -f . --prune fails, demanding a label selector. Why is the selector required?
options: Prune is server-side only — it works client-side too; the selector is about scoping
The flag is --prune-all — the scoping flags are -l/--selector (or --all)
Prune needs -l/--selector (or --all) to bound the inventory query — without a scope it can't know which cluster objects it owns and may delete
Prune doesn't work with directories — it does; the selector is the missing piece
explain: --prune deletes previously-applied objects absent from the current input, so kubectl needs a bounded inventory query to compare against. The label selector (or --all) defines that boundary — without it, prune can't distinguish 'should be deleted' from 'not mine to touch'.

q: You want the HPA to scale web to zero overnight. You set minReplicas: 0 and the API server rejects it. What's the rule?
options: minReplicas: 0 is valid — it isn't; the floor is 1
Use maxReplicas: 0 — that would cap the workload at zero permanently
Schedule a CronJob to scale — workable, but the real answer is the API rule
HPA minReplicas must be >= 1 — the HPA cannot scale to zero; true scale-to-zero needs KEDA (ScaledObject) or scheduled kubectl scale
explain: The HPA's floor is one replica by API validation — scale-to-zero is outside its design. Teams needing idle-to-zero use KEDA or cron-driven kubectl scale. Setting minReplicas: 0 is rejected, not silently clamped.

q: Traffic can double instantly, and you want the HPA allowed to at most double the replica count per minute. Which behavior stanza expresses that cap?
options: behavior: {scaleUp: {policies: [{type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 60}]}} — at most +100% of current replicas per 60s window
behavior: {scaleUp: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60}} — stabilization damps flapping; it doesn't cap the rate
behavior: {scaleUp: {selectPolicy: Max}} — selectPolicy chooses among policies, it doesn't define one
targetCPUUtilizationPercentage — that's the metric target, not a velocity bound
explain: behavior.scaleUp.policies bound scaling velocity: Percent 100 per 60s means at most doubling per minute. stabilizationWindowSeconds smooths oscillation (the Q442 topic), selectPolicy picks between multiple policies, and the utilization target is what triggers scaling, not how fast it may move.

q: Deployment web has containers app and sidecar. Update BOTH images in a single imperative command, with no YAML editing.
options: kubectl set image deploy/web web:v2 — web is the Deployment name, not a container name, and it only sets one image
kubectl set image deploy/web app=web:v2 sidecar=proxy:v3 — container=image pairs per container, one command, one resulting rollout
Two separate kubectl set image calls — works, but triggers two rollouts instead of one
kubectl edit — that's editor-driven, not imperative
explain: kubectl set image takes multiple CONTAINER=IMAGE pairs in one invocation, producing a single pod-template change and therefore one rollout. The names are container names from the pod spec — using the Deployment name as the container name is the classic mistake.

q: You want Helm to render the chart AND validate it against the cluster (admission webhooks, API schemas) without installing anything. Which flag?
options: helm template — client-side render only; never contacts the API server
helm lint — static chart checks; no cluster involved
helm install --dry-run=server (or upgrade --dry-run=server) — renders and submits to the API server for validation, persisting nothing
--dry-run=client — render only, no server validation
explain: dry-run=server exercises real admission (validating webhooks, quotas, API validation) without creating anything — the pre-install safety net. template and dry-run=client only render locally, and lint checks chart hygiene, not cluster acceptance.

q: kubectl apply --server-side fails: 'Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "helm"'. You intend to take field ownership away from Helm. Which flag does it?
options: Drop --server-side — sidesteps the conflict instead of resolving ownership
--validate=false — unrelated to field management
Delete the Helm release — destructive overkill for an ownership transfer
--force-conflicts — server-side apply transfers the contested fields to your manager despite the conflict
explain: --force-conflicts is the ownership-transfer switch: it reassigns the contested fields from helm to your field manager. The conflict error is SSA doing its job (two managers, one field); force-conflicts is the deliberate override, not an accident to work around.

q: Batch workers must scale UP fast on queue depth but must NEVER scale down automatically — a human scales them down after review. Which HPA behavior expresses this?
options: behavior: {scaleDown: {selectPolicy: Disabled}} — disables scale-down decisions entirely while leaving scale-up active
behavior: {scaleDown: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0}} — that makes scale-down MORE aggressive
minReplicas equal to maxReplicas — that also kills scale-up
The HPA can't do asymmetric directions — selectPolicy: Disabled exists exactly for this
explain: selectPolicy: Disabled turns off a scaling direction wholesale; Max/Min choose among defined policies. It's the asymmetric counterpart to stabilization damping (Q442) — one controls whether scaling happens, the other how fast.

q: You create an HPA in namespace team-a with scaleTargetRef: {name: web}. The web Deployment lives in team-b. What happens?
options: It works — HPAs are cluster-scoped, which is false; they're namespaced
It fails — the HPA and its scaleTargetRef must be in the same namespace; create the HPA in team-b
Cross-namespace works with a qualified name — scaleTargetRef has no namespace field
It silently targets a same-named Deployment in team-a — it errors instead of guessing
explain: HPA is a namespaced resource and scaleTargetRef carries only apiVersion/kind/name — no namespace. The target must live in the HPA's namespace, mirroring the Ingress cross-namespace rule (Q374): same-namespace references only.

q: The staging overlay must reuse a base that lives in a GitHub repo, without vendoring a copy into your repo. Which resources entry does that?
options: Copy the base files in — that's vendoring, exactly what you want to avoid
bases: [./shared] — local paths only
resources: ["github.com/org/repo//base?ref=v1.2.0"] — kustomize fetches remote git bases; the double slash selects the subdir and ?ref pins the version
Use Helm instead — different tool, and the ask is kustomize-native
explain: Kustomize supports remote git bases natively with the github.com/org/repo//path?ref= syntax — no cloning or vendoring needed, and ?ref pins reproducibility. Local bases (Q355's topic) are the alternative when the code lives in the same repo.

q: Write the autoscaling/v2 HPA metric for 'average memory utilization 80%'. Which snippet is correct?
options: targetMemoryUtilizationPercentage: 80 — that's the deprecated autoscaling/v1 field style
metrics: [{type: Resource, resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80}}}] — that's CPU, not memory
An annotation on the Deployment — metrics live in the HPA spec, not annotations
metrics: [{type: Resource, resource: {name: memory, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80}}}] — the v2 metrics-list form with a resource target
explain: autoscaling/v2 expresses metrics as a list; memory uses type: Resource with name: memory and an averageUtilization target. The flat targetMemoryUtilizationPercentage field is the v1 shorthand, and annotations play no role in metric definitions.

q: You must change a Service's clusterIP. kubectl apply fails: the field is immutable. What's the way through?
options: kubectl replace --force (or delete + recreate) — immutable core fields require recreation; --force performs delete+create in one command
kubectl patch — patches can't change immutable fields either
Edit the Endpoints object — a different object; the Service's clusterIP is what's fixed
clusterIP is mutable — it is assigned-once and immutable
explain: clusterIP is set at creation and immutable after — the only path is recreating the Service, and replace --force does the delete+create atomically from the client's view. Patching around immutability never works; the field must be reborn.

q: The prod overlay must drop the debug volumeMount from the web container (leaving the volume itself defined), without touching the base. Which patch does it?
options: A strategic-merge patch setting the volumeMount to null — list entries merge by name and null doesn't reliably delete them
patches: [{target: {kind: Deployment, name: web}, patch: "- op: remove\n  path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/volumeMounts/0"}] — JSON 6902 removal addressed by list index
Delete the volume from volumes: — that removes the volume, not the mount, and breaks the other containers using it
Edit the base manifests — that would drop the mount from every overlay
explain: JSON Patch op: remove with the volumeMount's list index surgically deletes the mount entry. Strategic merge can't address 'the first volumeMount' by position, deleting the volume is a different (breaking) change, and base edits leak across overlays.

q: After EVERY helm upgrade, a cache-flush Job must run exactly once. How do you wire that into the chart?
options: A CronJob — runs on a schedule, not on upgrades
helm test — only runs when invoked manually
Annotate the Job manifest with "helm.sh/hook": post-upgrade (plus hook-weight and hook-delete-policy as needed) — Helm executes it after each successful upgrade
A container postStart hook — that's pod lifecycle, not release lifecycle
explain: Helm hooks (pre/post-install, pre/post-upgrade, pre/post-delete, test) run Jobs at release lifecycle points; post-upgrade fires after every upgrade. hook-delete-policy controls cleanup (e.g., hook-succeeded), and hook-weight orders multiple hooks. CronJobs and container hooks operate on entirely different triggers.

q: You run kubectl scale deploy/web --replicas=8, then check rollout history — no new revision was recorded. Why?
options: A bug — scale is supposed to record, which is false
History needs --record — that flag is long removed; revisions come from pod-template changes
Scale targets a different resource — it edits the same Deployment
Revisions track pod-template changes only — scaling edits spec.replicas, not the template, so no new ReplicaSet or revision is created
explain: Rollout history is ReplicaSet lineage, and new ReplicaSets are born only from pod-template changes. Replica count lives outside the template, so scaling (manual or HPA) never bumps the revision — which is also why the HPA can fight your manual scale (Q358) without touching history.

q: A Service sets internalTrafficPolicy: Local. A client pod on node-2 calls it, but the only ready endpoints are on node-1. What happens?
options: The call fails — with Local, kube-proxy on node-2 sees zero node-local endpoints and drops the traffic, even though node-1 has healthy pods
It routes to node-1 — that's the default Cluster behavior
kube-proxy forwards it with SNAT — Local never forwards off-node
The Service loses its ClusterIP — the ClusterIP is still allocated; only endpoint selection changes
explain: internalTrafficPolicy: Local restricts kube-proxy to node-local endpoints; on a node with none, the Service behaves as if it had zero endpoints and traffic is dropped. It's the documented tradeoff: lower latency and no cross-node hops, at the cost of failed calls where no local pod exists.

q: On a single-stack IPv4 cluster, you apply a Service with ipFamilies: [IPv6]. What happens?
options: It's accepted and gets an IPv6 ClusterIP — the cluster can't allocate an address family it doesn't run
It's rejected — ipFamilies must be satisfiable by the cluster's configured families; a single-stack IPv4 cluster can't serve IPv6
It's silently converted to IPv4 — the API never silently rewrites your intent
It works if the pods are dual-stack — Service families are a cluster-level capability, not per-pod
explain: ipFamilies/ipFamilyPolicy are validated against the cluster's actual IP family configuration — dual-stack must be enabled cluster-wide. A single-stack cluster rejects unsatisfiable families rather than guessing.

q: An Ingress sets both the deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx annotation and spec.ingressClassName: haproxy. Which controller picks it up?
options: The annotation — annotations are legacy and lose to the field
Neither — conflicting configuration is not rejected; precedence resolves it
spec.ingressClassName — the field takes precedence over the annotation when both are set
Both controllers process it — that would double-serve; precedence prevents it
explain: Documented precedence: spec.ingressClassName wins over the ingress.class annotation when both are present. The annotation is the legacy path (the Q168 topic); the field is authoritative.

q: A Gateway defines listeners web-http (port 80) and web-https (port 443). An HTTPRoute must attach ONLY to the web-https listener. How?
options: Create two Gateways — unnecessary; one Gateway can host many listeners
Match on hostname — hostname is per-route matching, not listener selection
An annotation — Gateway API binding is structural, not annotation-driven
parentRefs: [{name: gw, sectionName: web-https}] — sectionName targets the named listener within the Gateway
explain: parentRefs bind a route to Gateways, and sectionName narrows the attachment to a specific listener (by its name or port). Without it the route attaches to every compatible listener — the usual source of 'why is my HTTPS route answering on port 80' surprises.

q: gRPC traffic needs method-level routing: payments.Billing/Charge goes to svc-v2, everything else to svc-v1. Ingress annotations are getting messy. Which Gateway API route kind does this natively?
options: GRPCRoute — matches on service and method names natively (matches: [{method: {service: payments.Billing, method: Charge}}])
HTTPRoute — has no gRPC method awareness
TCPRoute — L4 only; can't see methods
TLSRoute — SNI-based; can't see methods
explain: GRPCRoute is the method-aware route kind: it matches the gRPC service/method tuple directly. HTTPRoute matches paths/headers (wrong layer for method routing), and TCP/TLS routes only see L4/L5 fields. This is the Q367 'annotations are messy' answer for gRPC.

q: You apply an Ingress whose tls.secretName references Secret web-tls, which doesn't exist yet. The apply succeeds. What serves HTTPS traffic?
options: Nothing — the Ingress would be rejected, but it isn't; admission doesn't validate Secret existence
The controller serves its default/fake certificate and logs a warning until the real Secret appears
HTTP works but the HTTPS port never opens — the port opens with the default certificate
The Secret is auto-created — the API server never invents Secrets
explain: Ingress admission doesn't check that the TLS Secret exists; controllers fall back to their default certificate and warn. Creating web-tls later is picked up without re-applying the Ingress — the failure mode is a cert warning, not an outage.

q: Via the Gateway API, every request through the api HTTPRoute must carry the header x-tenant: acme (added when absent). Which route filter does this?
options: An Ingress-style annotation — Gateway API does header mutation structurally, not via annotations
URLRewrite — rewrites path/host, not headers
filters: [{type: RequestHeaderModifier, requestHeaderModifier: {add: [{name: x-tenant, value: acme}]}}] — the native header-mutation filter
ResponseHeaderModifier — that mutates the response path, not the request
explain: RequestHeaderModifier (add/set/remove) is the Gateway API's header filter — the structured replacement for the NGINX annotation soup. URLRewrite handles path/host; ResponseHeaderModifier is the mirror-image response filter.

q: An HTTPRoute must match ONLY requests carrying ?preview=true, regardless of path. Which match expresses that?
options: A path match — paths can't see query strings
A header match — query parameters aren't headers
It's impossible — HTTPRoute supports query matching natively
matches: [{queryParams: [{name: preview, value: "true", type: Exact}]}] — native query-parameter matching
explain: HTTPRouteMatch includes queryParams alongside path, headers, and method — each with Exact/RegularExpression types. Teams coming from Ingress (which can't match query strings) often assume it's impossible; the Gateway API models it explicitly.

q: Your kubectl port-forward deploy/web 8080:80 session dies right in the middle of a rollout, while the app itself stays reachable. What happened, and what's the fix?
options: The forward follows one specific pod — when the rollout replaced that pod, the session ended; just re-run the port-forward to attach to a new pod
The Service broke — the app stays reachable, so the Service is fine
Port-forward can't target Deployments — it can; it auto-selects a pod
The local port expired — ports don't expire; pod replacement killed the session
explain: port-forward to a workload type pins a single auto-selected pod; the session is tied to that pod's lifetime, not the Deployment's. Rollouts replace the pod and the forward drops — re-running re-attaches. For stability across rollouts, forward to the Service instead.

q: A NetworkPolicy peer reads from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {team: frontend}}, podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}]. Which pods does this peer match?
options: All team=frontend pods PLUS all app=web pods everywhere (OR) — selectors in one peer are ANDed, not ORed
Only pods that are BOTH in a team=frontend namespace AND labeled app=web — namespaceSelector and podSelector intersect within a single peer
Nothing — combining them is legal and meaningful
All pods in team=frontend namespaces — the podSelector is not ignored
explain: Within a single from/to entry, namespaceSelector and podSelector are ANDed (set intersection). OR semantics come from listing multiple peers. Misreading this as OR is how overly-broad allow rules get written.

q: The cluster was built with --cluster-domain=cluster.corp. What is the full DNS name of Service db in namespace data?
options: db.data.svc.cluster.local — that's the default domain, not this cluster's
db.data.cluster.corp — missing the svc segment
db.data.svc.cluster.corp — the flag replaces cluster.local everywhere: DNS names, search paths, and generated names
Cluster domains can't be changed — they can at cluster build time via the kubelet/API server flag
explain: --cluster-domain re-roots all Service DNS (db.data.svc.cluster.corp), search domains, and related generated names. Anything hardcoded to svc.cluster.local breaks on such clusters — the exam's default-domain questions (Q70, Q272) all assume the default.

q: On-prem with no cloud load balancer, the firewall team NATs 203.0.113.50 to the cluster and you must serve Service web on that exact IP. Which field does it?
options: loadBalancerIP — that's for cloud-provider LBs (and deprecated)
nodePort — exposes every node, not one fixed IP
hostNetwork on the pods — pod-level networking, wrong layer for a Service IP
spec.externalIPs: ["203.0.113.50"] — kube-proxy routes that IP to the Service on every node
explain: externalIPs are cluster-external IPs that kube-proxy will serve the Service on across all nodes — the on-prem fixed-IP mechanism without a cloud LB or MetalLB. loadBalancerIP is the cloud-LB analogue; nodePort can't pin a single IP.

q: Service web sets targetPort: http, but the pods' containerPorts are actually named web (8080). Endpoints exist for the Service. What do clients experience?
options: Connection refused/timeouts — endpoints list pod IPs, but kube-proxy can't resolve the port name, so traffic blackholes
