It works — names are not just hints; they must resolve
No endpoints are created — endpoint creation doesn't validate port names
The Service is rejected — named targetPorts aren't validated at admission
explain: Named targetPorts resolve against the pod spec at proxy time; a name mismatch means healthy-looking endpoints with dead backends. The Service is admitted and endpoints populate — the failure is silent until traffic flows, which is why the port names must match exactly.

q: One Ingress defines path /api with pathType Prefix routing to svc-a, and path /api with pathType Exact routing to svc-b. A request to exactly /api goes where?
options: Whichever rule is listed first — rule order doesn't decide; match specificity does
svc-b — Exact outranks Prefix regardless of rule order
svc-a — Prefix is not preferred over Exact
It's load-balanced — no; one rule wins deterministically
explain: Ingress path precedence is Exact first, then longest Prefix match — order in the manifest is irrelevant. /api/users would still hit the Prefix rule (no Exact match), which is why the two pathTypes compose the way they do.

q: A NetworkPolicy selects pods with app: db, but the actual database pods are labeled app: postgres. What is the policy's effect?
options: Default deny for the DB — a policy only affects pods it selects
The DB pods are isolated — nothing selects them, so they aren't
No effect at all — the policy matches zero pods, so all traffic remains allowed (no policy = default allow)
The API server rejects it — selectors aren't validated against live pods
explain: NetworkPolicies only apply to pods matching their podSelector; a selector matching nothing is a silent no-op, and with no applicable policy the namespace stays default-allow. Label drift between policy and pods is a classic 'policy isn't working' root cause.

q: A pod runs with hostNetwork: true. A default-deny-ingress NetworkPolicy selects it by label. Is the pod's traffic filtered?
options: Yes — policies apply to all pods, which is false for hostNetwork
Yes, but only egress — neither direction is enforced
Only if the CNI supports hostNetwork policies — hostNetwork bypasses the pod-network enforcement point entirely
No — NetworkPolicies don't apply to hostNetwork pods; they share the node's network stack outside policy enforcement
explain: NetworkPolicy enforcement happens at the pod network interface; hostNetwork pods use the node's stack directly, so policies can't select or filter them. Hardening hostNetwork pods means node-level firewalling, not NetworkPolicy.

q: A custom TCP protocol (not HTTP, not gRPC, not TLS) needs Gateway API routing by port. Which route kind fits?
options: TCPRoute — L4 port-based routing for arbitrary TCP traffic
HTTPRoute — requires HTTP semantics
GRPCRoute — requires gRPC
Ingress — HTTP(S) only, and not Gateway API at all
explain: TCPRoute is the raw-TCP route kind (TLSRoute adds SNI matching on top). When the protocol isn't HTTP/gRPC, L4 routing by listener port is the Gateway API answer — the complement to the Q565 method-routing question.

q: File uploads larger than ~1MB through the NGINX Ingress fail with 413, though the app handles large files fine. Which annotation fixes it?
options: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target — rewrites paths; unrelated to body size
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "50m" — raises the client_max_body_size the controller enforces (default 1m)
Increase the Service port — ports have nothing to do with body limits
Set it on the Deployment — it's an Ingress annotation, evaluated by the controller
explain: The NGINX Ingress controller caps request bodies at 1m by default; proxy-body-size overrides it per-Ingress. The 413 comes from the controller, not the app — raising the app's own limits won't help.

q: You create a Service of type LoadBalancer with nodePort: 31080 preset in its port entry. What happens?
options: It's rejected — presetting nodePort on a LoadBalancer Service is allowed
It's ignored and a random port is allocated — the preset is honored when free and in range
It's accepted — LoadBalancer Services also allocate NodePorts, and presetting works exactly like on a NodePort Service
It only works on cloud clusters — NodePort allocation is generic, on-prem included
explain: A LoadBalancer Service is ClusterIP + NodePort + external LB (the Q280 layering); the NodePort portion follows normal NodePort rules, including honoring a preset when free and in the configured range. A taken port is rejected just like the Q477 case.

q: An Ingress rule sets host: "*.example.com". Which requests match it?
options: Only the literal *.example.com — the wildcard matches subdomains
The bare apex example.com — a wildcard matches one DNS label, not the apex
Nothing — wildcards need no annotation; they're native
shop.example.com and api.example.com (any single-level subdomain) — but not the bare apex example.com
explain: Wildcard hosts match exactly one DNS label: shop.example.com yes, deep.shop.example.com no, and the apex example.com needs its own rule. It's the hostname analogue of Prefix path matching — broad but bounded.

q: A probe uses exec: {command: ["[[", "-f", "/tmp/healthy", "]]"]}. It always fails even though the file exists. Why?
options: exec probes run the binary directly with no shell — [[ is a shell builtin; wrap it as ["sh", "-c", "[[ -f /tmp/healthy ]]"]
Probes can't read /tmp — they can; the issue is the missing shell
exec probes need a shell: field — no such field exists
The file needs world-execute permission — it's a command-form problem, not permissions
explain: exec probes call execve directly — no shell, no builtins, no globbing. [[, &&, and pipes all need an explicit sh -c wrapper. The file existing is irrelevant when the 'binary' [[ can't even be found.

q: You need the namespace's events oldest-first to reconstruct an incident timeline. Which command orders them?
options: kubectl get events — default output order isn't chronological
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp — sorts by the event's timestamp
kubectl logs — that's container logs, not events
kubectl describe — shows only a trailing subset of events
explain: --sort-by works on any field path; .lastTimestamp orders the event stream chronologically for timeline reconstruction. Plain get events sorts by nothing useful, and describe truncates the history.

q: One misbehaving workload keeps spawning processes until its node starts evicting pods — yet CPU, memory, and disk pressure all read False. Which node Condition explains the evictions?
options: MemoryPressure — memory reads False in this scenario
DiskPressure — disk reads False too
PIDPressure — the node is exhausting process IDs; the kubelet evicts pods to reclaim PIDs, which is the fork-bomb containment
Ready=False — that's the node status, not the pressure signal
explain: PIDPressure fires on PID exhaustion, and the kubelet evicts pods to relieve it — the same pressure-evict family as DiskPressure and MemoryPressure. It completes the trio from the DiskPressure question.

q: A drain is blocked by a strict PDB (maxUnavailable: 0), but the node has a hardware fault and must go down NOW. Which flag forces the drain through?
options: --force — that changes pod deletion grace semantics, not PDB enforcement
Delete the PDB first — works but slower and discards the availability guard
--ignore-daemonsets — unrelated to PDB blocking
kubectl drain --disable-eviction — bypasses the eviction API with direct deletes, ignoring PDBs; last resort only
explain: --disable-eviction switches drain from eviction-API calls (which PDBs gate) to direct DELETEs (which they don't). It's the emergency escape hatch for dying hardware — and precisely why PDBs are a guardrail, not a guarantee.

q: Your manifest uses a beta API version and you want to confirm the API server actually serves that resource version before applying. Which command checks?
options: kubectl api-resources — lists resource kinds with their served API group/versions
kubectl version — shows client/server versions, not served resources
kubectl explain — documents fields of an already-known type
Just apply it and see — the question asks for a pre-check
explain: kubectl api-resources shows every kind the server offers and in which versions — the discovery pre-check before writing version-sensitive manifests. version and explain answer different questions, and blind applying is what the pre-check avoids.

q: Before handing CI its kubeconfig, you want the FULL permission inventory of ServiceAccount ci/deployer — not one verb at a time. Which command produces it?
options: kubectl auth can-i --all — no such flag exists
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer — enumerates every allowed verb/resource for that identity
kubectl get clusterroles — shows role definitions, not effective access
You can't check another identity — --as exists exactly for this
explain: --list dumps the complete allowed set instead of one yes/no, and --as vets another identity's permissions without its credentials. It's the pre-flight audit before a deploy script runs — the bulk form of the Q285 single-verb check.

q: The task requires a pod whose containers are never restarted after they exit. Your manifest is rejected: restartPolicy: Never sits inside containers[0]. What did you get wrong?
options: Never is not a valid policy — it is valid, just at the wrong level
Each container needs its own policy — no container-level restartPolicy exists
restartPolicy belongs at spec.restartPolicy (pod level) — it governs every container in the pod uniformly; there is no per-container restart behavior to configure
Only Jobs support Never — pods support Never directly
explain: restartPolicy is a pod-spec field (Always/OnFailure/Never) applying to all containers uniformly. Nesting it under a container is an unknown-field rejection — the same structural rule behind the Deployment/OnFailure rejection.

q: A PDB with minAvailable: 3 guards three web pods. You run kubectl delete pod web-0. Does the PDB block the deletion?
options: Yes — PDBs block all pod deletions, which is false
Yes, with a 429 Too Many Requests — that's the eviction API's denial, not delete's
Only with --force — plain delete also bypasses; --force isn't the distinction
No — kubectl delete pod issues a direct DELETE, not an eviction API call, so PDBs (which gate only the eviction subresource) don't apply; the Deployment recreates the pod
explain: PDBs are enforced solely on the eviction subresource — used by drain, the cluster autoscaler, and API-initiated evictions. kubectl delete pod takes the direct DELETE path and bypasses PDB checks entirely, which is why 'drain, don't delete' is the maintenance mantra.

q: Maintenance is over. Remove the taint maintenance=true:NoSchedule from node-1. Which command does it?
options: kubectl taint nodes node-1 maintenance=true:NoSchedule- — the trailing dash removes the taint
kubectl untaint — no such command exists
kubectl label node-1 maintenance- — labels and taints are different objects
kubectl cordon node-1 — cordon marks unschedulable; it doesn't remove taints
explain: The trailing - is the taint-removal syntax (key=value:effect- deletes that exact taint). There is no untaint subcommand; labels are unrelated, and cordon/uncordon manage the unschedulable flag, not taints.

q: After a disk-full incident, kubectl describe node shows a taint node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure:NoSchedule that nobody added manually. Where did it come from?
options: The scheduler added it — the kubelet manages node-problem taints
The kubelet applies it automatically when DiskPressure turns True — and removes it when pressure clears; pods without a matching toleration stop scheduling there
A controller added it — it's kubelet-driven, not controller-driven
Someone must have added it by hand — node-problem taints are automatic
explain: The kubelet auto-taints the node for disk, memory, and PID pressure (plus unreachable/not-ready), removing the taint when the condition clears. It's the scheduling half of the Q291 DiskPressure story: the Condition drives eviction, the taint steers new pods away.

q: A pod sets equal CPU/memory requests and limits on its app container, yet kubectl describe shows QoS class Burstable, not Guaranteed. The pod also has an init container with no resources set. Why?
options: Init containers don't count toward QoS — they do
Only memory matters for QoS — both CPU and memory are evaluated
Guaranteed requires EVERY container, including init containers, to set equal non-zero CPU and memory requests and limits
QoS assignment is random — it's fully deterministic from the spec
explain: Guaranteed demands equal requests==limits for CPU and memory on every application AND init container (ephemeral containers are excluded). One resource-less init container downgrades the whole pod to Burstable — the quiet QoS killer in pods with setup init containers.

q: You must delete the export Job but KEEP its finished pods for log forensics. Which flag does that?
options: Delete the pods first — backwards; they'd be gone
--grace-period=0 — that speeds deletion, it doesn't orphan dependents
Jobs can't be deleted without their pods — they can, with the right cascade policy
kubectl delete job export --cascade=orphan — deletes the Job and orphans its dependents, so the pods stay
explain: --cascade=orphan removes the ownerReferences instead of cascading the deletion, leaving finished pods behind for forensics. The default foreground/background cascading would garbage-collect the pods with the Job.

q: You want a live-updating pod list in one terminal while a rollout progresses. Which flag streams updates?
options: kubectl get pods -w — watch streams add/update/delete events for the list
kubectl top pods — a metrics snapshot, not a stream
A while-true loop with sleep — works, but -w is the built-in flag
kubectl describe --watch — describe doesn't watch
explain: -w/--watch turns any get into a streaming watch — the standard way to observe rollouts, scaling, and pod churn live without polling.

q: A pod runs app plus a metrics sidecar. The sidecar's livenessProbe starts failing. What gets restarted?
options: The whole pod — probes are per-container, not per-pod
Only the sidecar container — each container's probes govern that container alone
Nothing — sidecars absolutely can have probes
The Deployment rolls to a new pod — no; the kubelet restarts the container in place
explain: Probes are scoped to their container: a failing sidecar probe restarts just the sidecar, leaving the app untouched. Pod-level restart only happens if the pod's restartPolicy forces broader action — probe failures themselves are always container-local.

q: kubectl cp web-abc:/tmp/dump.hprof ./dump.hprof fails with 'tar: command not found'. What's the cause?
options: kubectl cp is broken — it works, but it needs tar inside the container
The pod's filesystem is read-only — the error names the missing tar binary
kubectl cp streams through tar in the target container — minimal/distroless images without tar can't serve copies
A permissions issue — it's the missing binary, not permissions
explain: kubectl cp works by executing tar inside the container to stream the archive; images without tar (distroless, scratch-based) can't serve copies. Workarounds: attach an ephemeral debug container with tar, or copy from a sidecar that has it.

q: You want to watch Warning events stream in live during a deploy. Which command does it?
options: kubectl get events --follow — --follow is a logs flag, not events
Poll get events in a loop — -w streams natively
kubectl describe -w — describe has no watch mode
kubectl get events -w (optionally --field-selector type=Warning) — watch streams new events as they're recorded
explain: -w works on get for any resource, including events — new events stream in as the deploy progresses. Pair with the type=Warning field selector (the Q495 filter) to cut the Normal noise.

q: You run kubectl rollout status job/export to watch the export Job. What happens?
options: It errors — rollout only supports Deployments, DaemonSets, and StatefulSets; Jobs have no rollout concept
It watches the Job's pods — Jobs are observed via get/wait/logs, not rollout
It shows CronJob status — wrong resource entirely
Jobs support pause/resume — they don't; that's a rollout-family feature
explain: kubectl rollout is scoped to the three rolling-update workloads (deployments, daemonsets, statefulsets). Jobs are one-shot controllers — watch them with kubectl wait --for=condition=complete, get, and logs (the Q491/Q300 patterns).

q: A namespace has been stuck in Terminating for an hour. What typically blocks it, and how do you inspect?
options: The scheduler is stuck — check .metadata.finalizers and remaining resources instead
Finalizers on the namespace or on resources inside it — inspect .metadata.finalizers and .status.conditions; a stuck resource (often with a foregroundDeletion finalizer) blocks completion
Delete it with --force — namespaces don't honor --force usefully; fix the blocker
An hour is normal — it isn't; something is wedged
explain: Namespace termination waits for every resource to be deleted and every finalizer to clear; a wedged finalizer (custom controllers, foregroundDeletion) stalls it indefinitely. Inspect finalizers first, resolve or (carefully) remove the blocker — never blind-force it.

q: A readinessProbe sets periodSeconds: 5 and failureThreshold: 3. The backing DB slows and the probe starts failing. How long until the pod stops receiving traffic?
options: Immediately — it takes 3 consecutive failures first
5 seconds — one period isn't enough
About 15 seconds — failureThreshold x periodSeconds of consecutive failures before the pod is marked Unready and removed from Endpoints
It keeps serving — that's liveness behavior; readiness gates traffic
explain: Readiness failure math: failureThreshold consecutive failures × periodSeconds ≈ 15s before the kubelet marks the pod Unready and the endpoints controller drops it. Readiness removes traffic without restarting — the liveness/readiness split from Q86 in quantitative form.

q: A pod was deleted overnight. kubectl get events shows the deletion but not WHO deleted it. Where is the actor recorded?
options: In the event message — events deliberately don't carry user identity
kubectl describe — same event data, no actor
The kubelet logs — the decision was made API-side
The API server audit log — events record what happened; user identity (who/what/when) lives in audit logs
explain: Events are operational signals without requester identity by design; attributing an action to a user or ServiceAccount requires the API server audit log. When 'who did this' matters, events are the wrong tool — audit is the record.

q: A container's env list reads: - name: DB_URL, value: "postgres://$(DB_HOST):5432/app", then - name: DB_HOST, value: "db.internal". The pod starts fine, but the app tries to connect to the literal host "$(DB_HOST)". What happened?
options: The $(VAR) syntax only works in args, not in env values
Order matters in the env list: a variable is only considered defined if it appears EARLIER in the list, so the forward reference to DB_HOST is left unchanged as a literal string
The reference resolves to an empty string when the target is defined later
The API server rejects forward references, so the pod should never have started
explain: Kubernetes expands $(VAR) top-down: only variables defined earlier in the env list are visible, and an unresolvable reference is left unchanged (not emptied), which is why the app saw the literal $(DB_HOST). The fix is to list DB_HOST before DB_URL. Option A is wrong — $(VAR) expansion works in env, command, and args. C misstates the fallback (unchanged, not empty), and D is wrong because bad references never block container startup.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A namespace enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard. You apply a pod with runAsNonRoot: true and image nginx (which defaults to root with no USER directive). Admission accepts it, but the pod sits in CreateContainerConfigError: "container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root". Why did admission pass if the pod cannot run?
options: Pod Security admission is advisory only and never blocks anything
The imagePullSecrets are missing, so the kubelet cannot inspect the image

PSS admission checks the pod SPEC (runAsNonRoot: true satisfies the policy), while the kubelet checks the IMAGE's actual user at container start — two different layers, and the image fails the second one
The seccomp profile is missing, which overrides the runAsNonRoot check
explain: Admission and the kubelet enforce different things: the restricted policy only requires the spec to declare runAsNonRoot, so the pod is admitted; the kubelet then inspects the image config, finds UID 0, and refuses to start the container. The fix is runAsUser on a non-zero UID or a non-root image. A is wrong (enforce mode does block), B is unrelated to the user check, and D invents an interaction that doesn't exist.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ResourceQuota sets hard: {pods: "2"} with scopes: [Terminating]. The team creates five ordinary long-running pods and all are admitted. Why didn't the quota stop them at two?
options: The Terminating scope only counts pods with activeDeadlineSeconds set — ordinary pods never match the scope, so the quota doesn't see them
ResourceQuota scopes are advisory and never block admission
The quota only counts pods in Failed phase
Scopes require a matching LimitRange to take effect
explain: The Terminating scope matches only pods whose spec.activeDeadlineSeconds is set (pods with a bounded lifetime, typically Jobs); plain Deployments and bare pods don't match, so they're invisible to this quota. B is wrong — quotas do block admission when matched. C invents a phase rule, and D invents a dependency between the two objects.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A quota sets hard: {pods: "3"} with scopeSelector: {matchExpressions: [{scopeName: PriorityClass, operator: In, values: [high]}]}. Three high-priority pods and ten normal pods run fine, but a fourth high-priority pod is rejected while more normal pods are still admitted. What does this prove?
options: PriorityClass values are capped at 3 per namespace
Normal pods bypass all quotas
The quota controller is stuck and needs a resync
Only pods with priorityClassName: high count against this quota — the scopeSelector narrows quota accounting to the matching scope, so normal pods are invisible to it
explain: scopeSelector with the PriorityClass scopeName makes the quota count only pods carrying that PriorityClass; the three high-priority pods exhaust it while normal pods never enter the accounting. A invents a cap, B is false (normal pods count against unscoped quotas), and C blames the controller for correct behavior.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A LimitRange of type Container sets default: {memory: 512Mi} and defaultRequest: {memory: 128Mi}. A developer applies a container with no resources section at all. What does the container get?
options: requests.memory: 512Mi and limits.memory: 512Mi — default wins for both
requests.memory: 128Mi and limits.memory: 512Mi — defaultRequest supplies the request, default supplies the limit
requests.memory: 128Mi and limits.memory: 128Mi — the smaller value is used for both
The pod is rejected — with a LimitRange present, resources must be set explicitly
explain: defaultRequest injects requests and default injects limits, independently per container — the container lands with request 128Mi / limit 512Mi. A and C conflate the two fields, and D is wrong: the whole point of a LimitRange is to supply values so bare containers are admitted.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A frozen monitoring image must register each pod with an external system using the NODE's IP address (not the pod IP), with no code changes and no RBAC access to the API. Which env entry does this?
options: env: [{name: NODE_IP, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.hostIP}}}] — the downward API exposes the node IP
env: [{name: NODE_IP, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.podIP}}}]
env: [{name: NODE_IP, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.nodeName}}}]
env: [{name: NODE_IP, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.namespace}}}]
explain: status.hostIP is the node's IP as the cluster sees it, exposed via fieldRef with no RBAC needed. B gives the pod's own IP, C gives the node's name (not an IP), and D gives the namespace — none of which is the node's address.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod needs projected service-account tokens for TWO audiences: "vault" and "storage.example.com". You write a single serviceAccountToken source with audience: "vault,storage.example.com". What is wrong?
options: Nothing — comma-separated audiences are minted as two tokens
The kubelet only uses the first audience and ignores the rest
audience is a single string, so the token is minted for one literal audience "vault,storage.example.com" that neither backend accepts — you need two serviceAccountToken sources with different paths
The API server rejects the manifest — audience must be a list
explain: The projected token's audience field is singular: whatever string you put there becomes the token's aud claim verbatim, so the comma-joined value matches nothing. The fix is two sources in the projected volume, each with its own path and audience. A and B invent multi-audience parsing that doesn't exist, and D is wrong — the API accepts any string.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The payments Deployment reads an optional audit endpoint: env AUDIT_SINK from secretKeyRef {name: audit-cfg, key: endpoint, optional: true}. The same manifest deploys to dev (no audit-cfg Secret exists) and prod (the Secret exists). How does the pod behave in each environment?
options: Blocked in dev until someone creates the Secret; normal in prod
CrashLoops in dev while resolving the reference
AUDIT_SINK is set to an empty string in dev
Dev pods start with AUDIT_SINK unset; prod pods get the value — optional: true tolerates the missing Secret instead of blocking startup
explain: optional: true makes the kubelet skip missing sources: the variable is omitted (not set-empty) and the pod starts. A and B describe the default non-optional behavior, and C is the classic trap — the var is unset, which apps can distinguish from an empty string.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Two containers run as UID 1000 and UID 2000 and both must write to a shared volume whose files are owned root:root. Which securityContext approach actually fixes the writes?
options: fsGroup: 3000 at the pod level — the kubelet chowns the volume's files to group 3000 at mount time, so both containers can write via group permissions
supplementalGroups: [3000] — it chowns the volume exactly like fsGroup
runAsGroup: 3000 — it changes the volume's group ownership on mount
Fixing the file ownership in the Dockerfile
explain: Only fsGroup changes volume ownership at mount: the kubelet recursively chowns the volume to the fsGroup, giving both UIDs group-write access. supplementalGroups merely adds the group to the processes' membership without touching file ownership (files stay root:root, writes still denied), runAsGroup only sets the processes' primary group, and the image can't fix ownership of files that come from a volume.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod sets runAsUser: 1000 at the pod level. Its init container runs chown on a data volume and fails with "permission denied". The main app container runs fine as UID 1000. What is the fix?
options: Init containers ignore securityContext, so the failure must be something else
Pod-level securityContext applies to init containers too — set a container-level securityContext with runAsUser: 0 on the init container to override it
Init containers always run as root, so chown should have worked — check the volume driver
Add privileged: true to the pod's securityContext
explain: The pod-level securityContext is the default for every container in the pod, including init containers — the chown failed because the init ran as UID 1000. A container-level securityContext overrides the pod-level one, so runAsUser: 0 on just the init container restores its privileges. A and C misstate init container semantics, and D is overkill (and pod-level privileged doesn't exist as a field).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A namespace is labeled pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted and pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest. After upgrading the cluster from 1.29 to 1.31, Deployments that passed admission for months start getting rejected on new ReplicaSets, with zero manifest changes. What happened?
options: The upgrade wiped the namespace labels, dropping the namespace to privileged
The restricted profile now requires signed images
"latest" tracks the newest PSS profile, and each Kubernetes release can add checks — pods compliant under 1.29 can fail under 1.31; pin enforce-version (e.g. v1.29) and migrate deliberately
All manifests must be re-applied after every cluster upgrade
explain: Pinning enforce-version exists precisely because profiles gain checks over releases: with "latest", a cluster upgrade can newly reject previously-compliant pods, turning a routine upgrade into a surprise outage. Labels survive upgrades (not A), PSS has no image-signing concept (not B), and re-applying unchanged manifests changes nothing (not D).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod sets seccompProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: "profiles/audit.json"}. The profile file exists on two of three nodes. Pods land on all three nodes. What happens on the third node?
options: The scheduler detects the missing profile and avoids the node
The containers fall back to the RuntimeDefault profile
The API server rejects the pod at admission
The containers fail to start (CreateContainerConfigError — profile not found); the scheduler doesn't check profile presence, so the profile must be distributed to every node
explain: Localhost seccomp profiles live on the node's filesystem, and nothing validates their presence at scheduling time — the kubelet fails container creation on nodes lacking the file. There is no fallback to RuntimeDefault (not B) and no admission check (not C), so the operational fix is distributing the profile to all nodes (DaemonSet, config management, or image baking).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ConfigMap volume must deliver app.yaml (readable by the app) and hooks/deploy.sh (executable, mode 0755). The whole volume currently mounts 0644. How do you make just the script executable?
options: items: [{key: hooks/deploy.sh, path: deploy.sh, mode: 0755}] — per-item mode overrides defaultMode for that file only
defaultMode: 0755 on the volume — it applies to every file equally
A postStart hook running chmod +x on the script
An init container that chmods the script before the app starts
explain: items[].mode sets permissions per file, so only deploy.sh becomes executable while app.yaml stays 0644. B would make every file executable (and the auditor won't love that). C and D both fail because ConfigMap volumes are mounted read-only — chmod inside the container returns "read-only file system".
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod mounts a Secret named tls-certs as a volume with optional: true. The Secret doesn't exist in the namespace. What does the pod do?
options: It stays Pending until someone creates the Secret
It starts; the mount directory exists but is empty — optional volumes tolerate the missing source
It CrashLoops trying to read the missing files
It starts with the files present but containing empty content
explain: optional: true on a volume source means the kubelet won't fail the mount when the Secret is absent — the directory is mounted empty and the pod runs. A describes the default non-optional behavior, C invents a crash loop (mount failures block start, they don't crash-loop), and D invents placeholder files.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: On a 1.28 cluster you create ServiceAccount ci/deployer, then kubectl get secrets shows no token Secret for it. A teammate says to wait for the tokens controller to catch up. What is actually going on?
options: The controller is slow — the Secret appears within a few minutes
The ServiceAccount manifest is malformed
Since 1.24 the tokens controller no longer auto-creates Secret objects for ServiceAccounts — mint a token on demand with kubectl create token ci/deployer
You must hand-create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token
explain: Kubernetes 1.24 removed auto-generated ServiceAccount token Secrets; the modern path is short-lived tokens via the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token), optionally projected into pods. A waits for something that will never arrive, B is a guess without evidence, and D revives the legacy long-lived pattern the change was designed to retire.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create a RoleBinding in namespace prod that binds the ClusterRole deployer (verbs: create, delete on pods) to a ServiceAccount. What can that ServiceAccount do?
options: Create and delete pods in every namespace — ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped
Nothing — a ClusterRole can only be referenced by a ClusterRoleBinding
Read pods cluster-wide, since bindings downgrade verbs
Create and delete pods, but ONLY in prod — a RoleBinding scopes even a ClusterRole's permissions to its own namespace
explain: The binding type sets the scope, not the role type: a RoleBinding grants the referenced ClusterRole's permissions only within the binding's namespace. ClusterRoleBinding is what would go cluster-wide (not A), ClusterRoles are perfectly valid in RoleBindings (not B), and nothing downgrades the verbs (not C).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A namespace has ResourceQuota hard: {pods: "5"}. kubectl get pods shows 8 pods: 5 Completed (old Job runs) and 3 Running. Creating a 4th Running pod succeeds. Why didn't the quota block it?
options: ResourceQuota counts only non-terminal pods — the 5 Completed pods don't consume the pods quota, so only 3 count
ResourceQuota never applies to pods created by Jobs
kubectl describe quota shows stale numbers until the next resync
Completed pods are automatically exempted by the Job controller
explain: Quota accounting for pods (and their CPU/memory) covers only non-terminal phases — Succeeded/Failed pods are done consuming and don't count, which is why 3 Running + 1 new fits under 5. B is false (Job pods count while running), C blames caching for correct behavior, and D credits the wrong component — it's the quota evaluator's phase filter, not the Job controller.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A LimitRange sets defaultRequest: {memory: 256Mi} for containers. A pod has two containers: app (no resources set) and sidecar (explicit requests.memory: 64Mi). What is admitted?
options: The sidecar is bumped up to 256Mi to match the default
The app gets requests.memory: 256Mi; the sidecar keeps its explicit 64Mi — LimitRange defaults apply per container, only where the field is unset
The pod is rejected — all containers must use the default
Both containers get 256Mi regardless of what was specified
explain: LimitRange defaults fill in only what a container omits, container by container — the app's missing request becomes 256Mi while the sidecar's explicit 64Mi is untouched. A, C, and D all wrongly assume the default overwrites or invalidates explicit values.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A frozen image must prefix every metric with the namespace it runs in, with no code changes and no API access. Which env entry gives the app its own namespace?
options: valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.nodeName}}
valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.namespace}} — the downward API exposes the pod's namespace as an env var
valueFrom: {configMapKeyRef: {name: ns-config, key: namespace}}
explain: The downward API's fieldRef exposes metadata.namespace directly — no ConfigMap to maintain per namespace, no RBAC, no code. A gives the pod's name, B gives the node's name, and D requires a ConfigMap that must be kept in sync in every namespace.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Each replica needs a unique identity for leader election that survives container restarts but changes whenever the pod itself is recreated. Which downward API field is the right primitive?
options: metadata.name — names are unique forever
status.podIP — IPs are unique per replica
spec.hostname — set from the pod name
metadata.uid — assigned at pod creation, stable across container restarts, and never reused for a new pod
explain: The pod UID is the cluster's unique-identity primitive: fixed for the pod's lifetime (survives container restarts) and never recycled, so a recreated pod can't collide with its predecessor's election state. Names can be reused by a new pod with the same generated name pattern (not A), IPs are recycled (not B), and hostname mirrors the name (not C).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container has a postStart hook: exec: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 60 && /ready.sh"]. Thirty seconds after creation, kubectl get pod shows the pod Pending and the container Waiting with reason ContainerCreating — yet exec into the container shows the app process already running. What is going on?
options: The postStart hook blocks the container's status (and the start of the next container) until the handler returns — the app runs alongside the hook, but Kubernetes doesn't mark the container Running until postStart completes
The hook runs before the entrypoint, so the app cannot start until the 60 seconds elapse
The pod is stuck because postStart hooks may not exceed 30 seconds
FailedPostStartHook fired immediately and the kubelet is backing off
explain: postStart runs asynchronously beside the entrypoint, but the kubelet's management of the container blocks until the handler returns: status stays Waiting/ContainerCreating, the pod stays Pending, probes don't start, and the next container waits. B reverses the ordering (there is no before-guarantee), C invents a time limit, and D only happens if the hook itself fails.

q: An inherited image ends its Dockerfile with: ENTRYPOINT python app.py --workers=4 (shell form, no brackets). You set args: ["--workers=8"] in the Deployment, roll out cleanly, and the app still runs 4 workers. Why did the override silently fail?
options: Pod args always override ENTRYPOINT — the rollout must not have happened; check the ReplicaSet
Shell-form ENTRYPOINT becomes /bin/sh -c "python app.py --workers=4"; the pod's args are appended as $0 and ignored — still 4 workers
The API server rejects args combined with a shell-form ENTRYPOINT
Both flags apply — the app runs 12 workers
explain: Only exec-form ENTRYPOINT gets clean command/args override semantics; the shell form wraps everything in sh -c, where extra args become the $0 positional parameter and are silently dropped. A assumes exec-form behavior, C invents a validation rule, and D invents flag accumulation.

q: A pod sets hostname: api-0 and subdomain: api. A headless Service named api exists in the same namespace. What DNS name resolves to this pod?
options: api-0 — the hostname alone is registered
Nothing — custom DNS names require a StatefulSet
A CNAME pointing at the api Service's cluster IP
api-0.api.default.svc.cluster.local — but only because the headless Service api exists; without a matching Service, no DNS record is created
explain: hostname + subdomain produce <hostname>.<subdomain>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, resolved via the headless Service's DNS — the Service is what makes CoreDNS publish the record, so a typo'd or missing Service name means no record. A omits the domain construction, B invents a StatefulSet requirement, and D confuses A records with CNAMEs.

q: A fluent-bit DaemonSet runs on every node with nodeSelector {log: enabled}. You change the DaemonSet's nodeSelector to {disktype: ssd}, which only half the nodes have. What does the DaemonSet controller do?
options: Nothing until you manually delete the pods on non-matching nodes — pod template changes never affect running pods
It performs a rolling update honoring maxUnavailable

It adds pods to newly matching nodes and promptly deletes pods from nodes that no longer match — the controller reconciles node matching continuously, so pods on HDD nodes are deleted and pods appear on SSD nodes with no manual step
The change is rejected — nodeSelector is immutable on a DaemonSet
explain: Per the Kubernetes docs, when node labels or the DaemonSet's nodeSelector change, the controller promptly adds pods to newly matching nodes and deletes pods from newly not-matching nodes. A confuses this with pod-template updates (which indeed don't touch running pods), B invents a rolling-update flow for selector changes, and D invents immutability.

q: A pod sets nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd} AND a nodeAffinity requiring topology zone east. A node has disktype=ssd but is in zone west and has spare capacity. Is the pod scheduled there?
options: No — nodeSelector and nodeAffinity must BOTH match (AND semantics); the zone mismatch disqualifies the node
Yes — either condition is sufficient (OR semantics)
Yes — nodeAffinity overrides nodeSelector when both are present
The pod is rejected — the two fields are mutually exclusive
explain: All node-selection mechanisms on a pod are conjunctive: nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, and any other constraints must all be satisfied. B invents OR semantics, C invents precedence, and D invents mutual exclusivity — the fields compose, they don't conflict.

q: A mixed cluster has arm64 and amd64 nodes. Your image is built for arm64 only, and pods keep landing on amd64 nodes with ImagePullBackOff (exec format error). What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Add a toleration for the amd64 nodes' taint
A nodeAffinity (or nodeSelector) on kubernetes.io/arch: arm64 — schedule only where the image can execute
Set imagePullPolicy: Always so the right image is pulled
Set runtimeClassName to an arm64 runtime
explain: Nodes carry the well-known kubernetes.io/arch label precisely for this: constrain the pod to arm64 nodes. A toleration doesn't steer scheduling toward the right arch (not A), repulling can't fix an architecture mismatch (not C), and RuntimeClass selects the container runtime, not the CPU architecture (not D).

q: A frozen image must include the ServiceAccount name it runs as in every audit log line, with no code changes and no RBAC grants. Which env entry provides it?
options: valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
An envFrom referencing the kube-system ConfigMap
valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.serviceAccountName}} — the downward API exposes the pod's ServiceAccount name
A downwardAPI volume mounting the token file
explain: spec.serviceAccountName is a downward-API field, injected with zero code and zero API access. A gives the pod's name, B invents a ConfigMap that doesn't exist, and D mounts the token (which contains the identity but not as a clean env var, and parsing JWTs in a frozen image is not the idiomatic path).

q: Migrating from a scheduler that supports seconds-precision cron, a developer writes schedule: "0 */2 * * * *" (six fields) expecting runs every 2 hours. kubectl apply fails with a parse error. What is the smallest fix?
options: Quote the value — the parser requires quotes around schedules
Change it to "*/2 * * * *" — the seconds field shifts everything
Add a timeZone — precision requires a timezone
Drop the seconds field → "0 */2 * * *" — Kubernetes cron is strictly 5-field (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week)
explain: The CronJob parser accepts exactly five fields; there is no seconds field, so six fields is a syntax error. A confuses this with the YAML-alias quoting trap, B changes the cadence to every 2 minutes, and C is irrelevant to field count.

q: A legacy app exchanges data with a host-level daemon through System V shared memory (/dev/shm). The pod must see the HOST's IPC namespace. Which pod field does this?
options: hostIPC: true — the pod joins the host's IPC namespace, sharing /dev/shm and IPC objects with host processes
hostPID: true
shareProcessNamespace: true
privileged: true on the container
explain: hostIPC joins the host's IPC namespace, which is exactly what System V shared memory and a shared /dev/shm need. hostPID shares the process ID namespace (not B), shareProcessNamespace only shares processes between the pod's own containers (not C), and privileged grants capabilities but doesn't join the host IPC namespace (not D).

q: A node is tainted maintenance=true:NoExecute. A pod tolerates it with tolerationSeconds: 0. The taint is applied while the pod is running. What happens?
options: The pod tolerates the taint forever — 0 means unlimited
The pod is evicted immediately — tolerationSeconds: 0 means it tolerates the taint for zero seconds
Only new pods are blocked; running pods are unaffected
The toleration is ignored because seconds must be positive
explain: tolerationSeconds is a countdown: 0 means the toleration expires instantly, so the kubelet evicts the pod as soon as the taint lands. A confuses 0 with unset (unset = tolerate forever), C describes NoSchedule behavior, and D invents a validation rule — 0 is legal and meaningful.

q: During a DaemonSet rolling update, each new fluent-bit pod reports Ready, but the app needs 30 more seconds to warm its buffers — the old pod is killed immediately and logs are lost on every node. Which field paces the update?
options: A longer readinessProbe period — the probe already gates the update
maxUnavailable: 0
spec.minReadySeconds: 30 — the controller waits that long after a pod becomes Ready before moving to the next node
progressDeadlineSeconds: 60
explain: minReadySeconds exists on DaemonSets too: the new pod must stay Ready for that duration before the controller considers it available and proceeds. A is wrong because the probe gates traffic/endpoints, not the update pacing; B only controls how many can be down at once; D is the watchdog for stuck rollouts, not warmup pacing.

q: Pods labeled app: web run in namespaces prod (6 pods across 2 zones) and staging (0 in zone-a, 6 in zone-b). A new prod pod carries topologySpreadConstraints: {maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, labelSelector: {app: web}}. How does the scheduler compute skew for this pod?
options: It counts web pods in every namespace — 6 per zone in each, so skew is 0
It counts no pods, because the selector can't match across namespaces
The constraint is invalid — selectors can't reference other namespaces
It counts only prod web pods — the labelSelector matches only pods in the incoming pod's own namespace
explain: Topology spread constraints are namespace-scoped: only pods holding the same namespace as the incoming pod are matching candidates, so staging's imbalance is invisible and the prod pod spreads against prod's 6. A assumes cluster-wide counting, B assumes zero matches, and C invents a validation error.

q: A Job with a broken image sets backoffLimit: 0. What happens when the pod fails?
options: Exactly one pod is attempted; with zero retries allowed, the Job is marked Failed immediately after that pod fails
The Job retries 6 times — 0 means the default
The Job retries forever until it succeeds
The Job stays Active with no pods, waiting for a manual retry
explain: backoffLimit: 0 is the explicit 'no retries' setting: the single pod failure exhausts the budget and the Job goes Failed. B confuses 0 with unset (unset defaults to 6), C describes no known setting, and D invents a limbo state.

q: A ConfigMap volume uses items: [{key: app.conf, path: "conf/app.conf"}]. The key contains slashes in the path. What lands in the container?
options: The API server rejects it — item paths must be single filenames
The volume contains conf/app.conf — item paths may include subdirectories, which the kubelet creates
The path is flattened to app.conf at the mount root
It requires subPath instead of items
explain: items[].path is a relative path, not just a filename — the kubelet creates intermediate directories, so conf/app.conf appears as nested. A invents a restriction (that restriction applies to ConfigMap KEYS, not item paths), C invents flattening, and D confuses the per-item rename mechanism with subPath mounts.

q: A Job pod runs to successful completion, but its preStop hook — which deregisters the pod from an external inventory — never executed. The hook works fine when pods are deleted mid-run. Why didn't it fire?
options: Jobs don't support container lifecycle hooks
The grace period was too short for the hook to run
preStop fires only when a container is TERMINATED — successful completion is not termination, so the hook is skipped
preStop only supports httpGet, not exec
explain: Kubernetes sends preStop only on termination; a container that runs to completion (exit 0) never receives it. This is a documented limitation, which is why completion-time cleanup belongs in the main process or a follow-up Job. A is false (hooks work in Job pods), C is irrelevant on the success path, and D invents a handler restriction.

q: A node carries the taint dedicated=gpu:NoExecute. A pod's toleration reads {key: dedicated, operator: Exists} with NO effect field set. Is the pod evicted when the taint is applied?
options: Yes — without an effect, the toleration matches nothing
Yes, but only for NoSchedule; NoExecute still evicts it
The toleration is invalid — effect is required
No — an empty effect matches all effects (NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute), so the pod tolerates the taint
explain: An unset effect is a wildcard across effects: the toleration matches the taint regardless of whether it's NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, or NoExecute. A and C wrongly treat effect as required, and B invents a partial match.

q: During a cluster-wide maintenance, nodes get various taints (disk-pressure, maintenance, gpu-reserve). One critical pod must tolerate ALL of them regardless of key, value, or effect. Which toleration does this?
options: tolerations: [{key: "", operator: Exists}] — an empty key with Exists matches every taint
tolerations: [{key: "*", operator: Exists}]
One toleration per taint — there is no wildcard
tolerations: [{operator: Exists, effect: NoExecute}]
explain: Empty key + Exists is the documented wildcard: it matches all keys, values, and (with empty effect) all effects. B invents glob syntax that doesn't exist, C denies the wildcard, and D only covers NoExecute taints.

q: Nodes are named node-1 through node-5 with no distinguishing labels. A pod must NEVER land on node-3 (being decommissioned) but may go anywhere else. nodeName can't express negation. What can?
options: nodeSelector: {metadata.name: NotIn(node-3)}
nodeAffinity with matchFields: [{key: metadata.name, operator: NotIn, values: [node-3]}] — node affinity can match on node FIELDS, not just labels
nodeName: "!node-3"
A taint on node-3 with effect PreferNoSchedule
explain: Node affinity supports matchFields against node object fields like metadata.name, including set operators like NotIn — the escape hatch when nodes lack useful labels. nodeSelector only matches labels (not A), nodeName is a single exact name (not C), and a PreferNoSchedule taint is soft — pods could still land there (not D).

q: A container sets env: [{name: SA_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.serviceAccountName}}}, {name: AUDIT_ID, value: "sa-$(SA_NAME)"}]. What does the app see for AUDIT_ID?
options: The literal string "sa-$(SA_NAME)" — valueFrom variables can't be referenced
"sa-" — valueFrom variables resolve after expansion
"sa-<the-sa-name>" — SA_NAME is defined earlier and valueFrom is resolved before expansion, so the later reference expands
The pod is rejected — mixing value and valueFrom across entries is forbidden
explain: Expansion sees every variable defined earlier in the list, regardless of whether it came from value or valueFrom — valueFrom sources resolve first, then $(VAR) expansion runs top-down. A confuses this with forward references (which do stay literal), B reverses the resolution order, and D invents a restriction (only setting both on the SAME entry is forbidden).

q: You run kubectl scale daemonset/fluent-bit --replicas=2 to halve log collection costs. What happens?
options: The DaemonSet scales to 2 pods on the first two nodes
It works, but only with --current-replicas set
The DaemonSet adopts 2 nodes and ignores the rest
It errors — DaemonSet exposes no scale subresource; replica count is meaningless for a controller whose job is one pod per matching node
explain: kubectl scale works through the scale subresource, which DaemonSets (like Jobs and bare pods) don't implement — the concept doesn't apply to a controller defined as 'one pod per matching node'. To collect fewer logs you change node selection or delete the DaemonSet, not its replica count. A, B, and C all assume DaemonSets are replica-counted like Deployments.

q: You bump the chart from 1.0 to 2.0 and run helm upgrade api ./chart --reuse-values. The upgrade fails with a nil-pointer template error on a value that 2.0's values.yaml defines by default. Your old values never mentioned it. What happened?
options: --reuse-values merges your new flags onto the STORED values from the previous release and ignores the new chart's defaults entirely — the new key was never populated; use --reset-then-reuse-values (3.14+) or an explicit -f file
The chart 2.0 is buggy and its default is malformed
--reset-values alone would have preserved your old overrides
Helm caches values.yaml and served the 1.0 copy
explain: This is the classic --reuse-values trap: it reuses the last release's values and merges only your new --set/-f on top, so defaults added by the new chart version are never picked up. --reset-then-reuse-values resets to the new chart's defaults first, then re-applies your overrides. B blames the chart, C is wrong (--reset-values discards old overrides), and D invents caching.

q: A helm upgrade fails with: Deployment.apps "web" is invalid: spec.template.spec.containers[0].ports[0].containerPort: Invalid value — the field is immutable. You must push the change through anyway. Which flag forces the upgrade past immutable-field errors?
options: --atomic — it rolls the release back instead
--force — it deletes and recreates resources whose fields can't be patched in place
--cleanup-on-fail — it removes the new resources but doesn't force anything
--no-hooks
explain: --force tells Helm to replace (delete + recreate) resources when the normal three-way merge can't apply, which is exactly the escape hatch for immutable fields. --atomic would roll back rather than force (not A), --cleanup-on-fail only garbage-collects resources a failed upgrade created (not C), and --no-hooks skips hooks, which is unrelated (not D).

q: A helm upgrade fails halfway, leaving stray new resources. You want those half-created resources cleaned up automatically, but you do NOT want an automatic rollback — the team needs the failed state preserved for debugging. Which flag gives exactly this?
options: --atomic — it cleans up AND rolls back
--wait — it only extends the readiness wait
--cleanup-on-fail — it deletes resources the failed upgrade created, without rolling back to the previous release
helm uninstall --keep-history after the failure
explain: --cleanup-on-fail removes new resources created by the failed release but leaves the release in failed state for inspection, unlike --atomic which additionally rolls back (not A). --wait only affects how long Helm waits for readiness (not B), and uninstalling destroys the evidence you wanted to keep (not D).

q: A chart ships test pods annotated helm.sh/hook: test that verify the database migration after install. The release installed cleanly. How do you execute those tests?
options: kubectl test api — kubectl runs chart tests
They run automatically right after every install
helm verify api — it checks the provenance file
helm test api — it runs the chart's test hooks on demand
explain: helm test executes the release's test hooks (pods with the test-hook annotation) whenever you ask — they don't run by themselves after install. A invents a kubectl subcommand, B confuses test hooks with install hooks, and C is about chart provenance signatures, not tests.

q: An HPA targets 60% CPU on a pod running an app container plus an idle logging sidecar. The app container runs at 95% of its request while the pod average sits at 50%, and the HPA never scales. What is the precise fix?
options: metrics: [{type: ContainerResource, containerResource: {name: cpu, container: app, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60}}}] — scale on the app container alone instead of the diluted pod average
Lower the target to 30% so the average trips sooner
Switch to type: Object with the Deployment as the described object
Remove the CPU request from the sidecar so it stops diluting the average
explain: HPA averages CPU across ALL containers in the pod, so an idle sidecar masks a hot app — the ContainerResource metric type (stable since 1.30) scopes the signal to the named container. B just moves the goalposts without fixing the dilution, C is for metrics on arbitrary objects like Ingresses, and D breaks the sidecar's scheduling guarantees.

q: You must scale the workers when the TOTAL queue depth across all pods reaches 5000 messages — not 5000 per pod. Which HPA metric target expresses a cluster-wide total?
options: target: {type: AverageValue, averageValue: 5000} — it sums across pods
target: {type: Value, value: 5000} — Value is the absolute total; AverageValue would divide it per pod and scale far too late
target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 5000}
metrics: [{type: Pods, pods: {target: {type: Value, value: 5000}}}] — Pods type already sums
explain: Value compares the raw metric total against the threshold, while AverageValue divides by pod count first — with 10 pods, AverageValue: 5000 wouldn't fire until 50,000 messages. C misuses Utilization (a percentage), and D's Pods type is inherently per-pod (its target must be AverageValue).

q: You apply an HPA with scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: v1, kind: Pod, name: web-abc}. The object is accepted, but kubectl describe hpa shows FailedGetScale events and it never scales. Why?
options: metrics-server isn't installed, so no metrics exist
scaleTargetRef apiVersion must be apps/v1 for all targets
The HPA was accepted but can never work — it scales through the scale subresource, which Pods don't expose; point it at the Deployment instead
minReplicas defaults to 0, so the HPA has nothing to manage
explain: The API server doesn't validate that the target is scalable, so the HPA persists and then fails at runtime: the controller can't GET the scale subresource of a Pod because it doesn't exist. Point scaleTargetRef at the Deployment (or StatefulSet/ReplicaSet). A would show a different symptom (unknown metrics, not FailedGetScale), B is false (v1 is correct for Pods), and D is false (minReplicas defaults to 1).

q: You must scale the API on requests-per-second as reported by the Ingress object web-ingress (a single cluster-wide number, not per pod). Which HPA metric type fits?
options: type: Pods — it reads custom metrics per pod
type: Resource — it covers ingress objects too
type: External — for anything outside the cluster
type: Object with describedObject: {apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1, kind: Ingress, name: web-ingress} — Object metrics describe a single arbitrary object
explain: Object metrics target one specific object (here, the Ingress) and its reported metric — exactly the 'single cluster-wide number' shape. Pods metrics are per-pod averages or sums (not A), Resource is only cpu/memory (not B), and External is for metrics with no Kubernetes object at all (not C).

q: New pods pass their readiness probe, but the app needs 20 more seconds to warm its cache — the rollout races ahead and clients hit cold pods. Lengthening the probe's periodSeconds just delays traffic. Which field paces the ROLLOUT itself, and why is it different from the probe?
options: spec.minReadySeconds: 20 — the probe gates traffic via Endpoints; minReadySeconds gates how fast the rollout advances to the next pod
A longer initialDelaySeconds on the readiness probe
progressDeadlineSeconds: 60
maxSurge: 0
explain: The two knobs gate different things: the readiness probe controls when a pod receives traffic (Endpoints membership), while minReadySeconds forces the Deployment controller to wait after a pod becomes Ready before considering it available and moving on. B delays traffic without pacing the rollout, C is the stuck-rollout watchdog, and D only limits extra pods.

q: A pod lists two readinessGates: example.com/warmup and example.com/db-ready. The warmup controller sets its condition True; the db controller hasn't reported yet. The readiness probe passes. Does the pod receive Service traffic?
options: Yes — a passing readiness probe is sufficient
No — every readiness gate must be True (AND semantics); one pending gate keeps the pod NotReady and out of Endpoints
Yes — one satisfied gate is enough
The pod is rejected at admission — gates must be pre-satisfied
explain: Readiness gates are ANDed with each other and with the probe: all listed conditions must be True before the kubelet marks the pod Ready. A ignores the gates entirely, C assumes OR semantics, and D invents an admission check — gates are expected to flip after admission.

q: Your kustomize overlay must generate the Ingress TLS Secret from tls.crt and tls.key files, producing type kubernetes.io/tls (not Opaque). Which generator stanza does this?
options: secretGenerator: [{name: web-tls, files: [tls.crt, tls.key]}] — the type defaults to TLS for .crt files
secretGenerator: [{name: web-tls, literals: [tls.crt=..., tls.key=...]}]
secretGenerator: [{name: web-tls, type: kubernetes.io/tls, files: [tls.crt, tls.key]}] — the type field sets the Secret type while files supply the keys
configMapGenerator with type: kubernetes.io/tls
explain: secretGenerator accepts a type field, so the generated Secret carries kubernetes.io/tls with the file contents under tls.crt/tls.key. Without it you'd get Opaque (not A — there is no filename-based type inference), literals would embed the PEM on the command line (not B), and configMapGenerator can't produce Secrets at all (not D).

q: A kustomization has two configMapGenerator entries both named app-config: the first defines keys A and B, the second (with behavior: replace) defines key C. What does the generated ConfigMap contain?
options: Keys A, B, and C — entries with the same name always merge
The API server rejects the duplicate generator names
Both ConfigMaps are kept, distinguished by their content hashes
Only key C — behavior: replace discards the earlier entry's keys (behavior: merge would have combined them)
explain: The behavior field controls same-name generator collisions: replace overwrites the earlier content, merge (the more common choice) unions the keys. A describes merge, B invents a rejection, and C misunderstands the hash suffix (it versions one ConfigMap, not two).

q: Your kustomization.yaml contains helmCharts: [{name: redis, version: 17.x, repo: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami, releaseName: cache}]. No helm CLI runs in CI. What happens on kustomize build?
options: Kustomize renders the Helm chart's templates inline during the build — the helmCharts inflator needs no helm binary
It shells out to helm template at build time
It only works with unpacked local chart directories
The build fails — Helm charts require Tiller
explain: The helmCharts field is kustomize's built-in chart inflator: it fetches and renders the chart as part of kustomize build, so CI needs no helm CLI. B describes the manual helm-template-pipe alternative, C is false (remote repos work), and D is years out of date — Tiller died with Helm 2.

q: You must scale Deployment web to 5 replicas imperatively with a JSON patch, no YAML editing. Which command does it?
options: kubectl set replicas deploy/web 5 — the set subcommand handles replica counts
kubectl patch deploy web --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":5}]'
kubectl patch deploy web --type=merge -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":5}]' — merge understands op/path
kubectl edit deploy/web and change the number by hand
explain: RFC 6902 JSON patches (op/path/value) require --type=json; the path addresses the scalar directly. There is no kubectl set replicas (not A — that's what scale is for), merge patches don't understand op/path syntax (not C), and edit defeats the 'imperative, no editor' requirement (not D).

q: Your CI pipeline must block until the web Deployment's Available condition becomes True (up to 3 minutes), then run smoke tests. Which command waits on that specific condition?
options: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s deploy/web
kubectl wait --for=condition=Complete --timeout=180s deploy/web
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available --timeout=180s deploy/web — Deployments expose an Available condition; Ready is a pod condition
kubectl rollout status deploy/web --timeout=180s — it checks the Available condition
explain: Available is the Deployment-level condition (minimum replicas up to date and ready); kubectl wait watches it directly. Ready is a pod condition (not A), Complete belongs to Jobs (not B), and while rollout status is a fine alternative in practice, the question asks for the command that waits on the Available condition itself (not D).

q: Your repo has flags.env (KEY=value per line, 40 feature flags). The kustomize base must turn it into a ConfigMap without listing 40 literals. Which generator stanza does this?
options: configMapGenerator: [{name: flags, files: [flags.env]}] — each line becomes a key
configMapGenerator: [{name: flags, literals: [...]}] — paste all 40 lines
kubectl create configmap flags --from-env-file=flags.env — but that's kubectl, not kustomize
configMapGenerator: [{name: flags, envs: [flags.env]}] — envs parses KEY=value files into individual keys
explain: The envs field is kustomize's equivalent of kubectl's --from-env-file: each KEY=value line becomes its own key. files would store the whole file under one key named flags.env (not A), literals means hand-listing all 40 (not B), and C is the right kubectl command but doesn't belong in a kustomization.

q: You run helm upgrade api ./chart --reuse-values --reset-values -f fix.yaml. An old --set replicaCount=5 from the previous install is no longer wanted. What values does the release end up with?
options: --reset-values wins and --reuse-values is ignored — the release gets the new chart's defaults plus fix.yaml; the stale replicaCount=5 is gone
All three merge — the old --set replicaCount=5 survives
--reuse-values wins and --reset-values is ignored
The command is rejected — the two flags are mutually exclusive
explain: Helm documents the precedence explicitly: when --reset-values is specified, --reuse-values is ignored — values reset to the chart's defaults, then fix.yaml applies. B assumes a three-way merge that doesn't happen, C reverses the precedence, and D invents mutual exclusivity.

q: You need to pin the web image to web:v2 inside the kustomization, imperatively — no editor, no hand-edited YAML. Which command does it?
options: kubectl set image deploy/web web=web:v2 — it updates the kustomization too
kustomize edit set image web=web:v2 — it edits the kustomization's images stanza in place
Hand-edit base/deployment.yaml and change the tag
kustomize edit add image web=web:v2
explain: kustomize edit set image is the imperative editor for the images transformer — it writes the stanza into kustomization.yaml. kubectl set image touches live cluster objects, not your kustomization (not A); C abandons the imperative requirement (and edits the base, which overlays shouldn't do); D invents a subcommand.

q: You run kubectl apply -f . --prune -l app=web --prune-allowlist=apps/v1/Deployment. What does the allowlist buy you?
options: Prune refuses to run without it
It speeds up the apply by skipping discovery
It restricts pruning to the listed group-version-kinds — a safety rail so a broad label selector can't delete kinds you didn't intend
It allows pruning MORE types than the default
explain: --prune-allowlist whitelists which resource types prune may delete, containing the blast radius of a label selector that matches more than you expected. It isn't required (not A), isn't a performance flag (not B), and it narrows rather than widens the default prune set (not D).

q: You run helm upgrade api ./chart --wait --timeout=10m. The release is marked successful, but the post-upgrade migration Job was still running when Helm returned. What is missing?
options: Nothing — --wait covers Jobs
--wait only waits for hooks, not Jobs
--timeout applies per-resource, so the Job timed out silently
--wait-for-jobs — plain --wait doesn't wait for Job/hook completion; the flag adds it
explain: --wait waits for Pods, PVCs, Services, and Deployment minimums — but not for Jobs to complete; --wait-for-jobs extends the wait to Job completion. A states the misconception directly, C reverses what's covered, and D misstates timeout semantics (it's per-operation, and expiry fails the release rather than succeeding silently).

q: A NetworkPolicy in namespace backend allows ingress from: [{namespaceSelector: {}, podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}]. Which pods may reach the selected backends?
options: Pods labeled app: web in ALL namespaces — an empty namespaceSelector matches every namespace (omitting the selector entirely would mean only the policy's own namespace)
Pods labeled app: web, but only in the backend namespace
No pods — an empty selector is invalid
All pods in all namespaces, regardless of labels
explain: In Kubernetes selectors, {} means 'match everything': an empty namespaceSelector selects all namespaces, ANDed with the podSelector. Omitting namespaceSelector (not B) would scope to the policy's namespace. C invents invalidity, and D drops the podSelector half of the AND.

q: A NetworkPolicy sets policyTypes: [Egress] with egress: [{}] — a single empty rule. What is the effect on the selected pods?
options: All egress is denied — empty rules deny everything
All egress is explicitly allowed — an empty egress rule is an allow-all (contrast: an empty egress LIST, egress: [], would deny all)
The rule is ignored as a no-op
The API server rejects the policy — rules may not be empty
explain: An empty rule object matches all peers, all ports: it's the idiomatic allow-all. The trap is the list-vs-rule distinction — egress: [] (no rules) with policyTypes Egress denies everything, while egress: [{}] (one empty rule) allows everything. C and D deny the well-defined semantics.

q: A NetworkPolicy declares both ingress: [...] and egress: [...] rules but omits policyTypes entirely. Which directions are enforced?
options: Ingress only — the default is always Ingress
Egress only — the last rule type wins
Both — when policyTypes is omitted, the API defaults it from the rules present: ingress rules imply Ingress, egress rules imply Egress
Neither — policyTypes is required
explain: The API server defaults policyTypes based on which rule sections exist: ingress rules add Ingress, egress rules add Egress, both present means both enforced. A and B each assume a single default, and D invents a required field.

q: You create Service oracle-db with no selector for the external Oracle database at 10.0.5.20:1521. Which Endpoints object makes oracle-db resolve and route?
options: An Endpoints named oracle-db-ips with endpoints: [10.0.5.20]
An Endpoints named oracle-db with data: {ip: 10.0.5.20, port: 1521}
An EndpointSlice — Endpoints objects are no longer accepted
An Endpoints named oracle-db with subsets: [{addresses: [{ip: 10.0.5.20}], ports: [{port: 1521}]}] — the name must match the Service, and addresses/ports live under subsets
explain: A selectorless Service needs a same-named Endpoints object with the subsets/addresses/ports shape — that's the contract the endpoints controller would otherwise fill in. A breaks the name match (covered in the earlier oracle-db question), C invents a data field, and D is wrong: Endpoints still work, EndpointSlice is just the modern mirror.

q: One Ingress rule defines path /api (Prefix) → svc-a and path /api/v2 (Prefix) → svc-v2. A request arrives for /api/v2/users. Where does it go?
options: svc-v2 — when multiple Prefix paths match, the longest match wins
svc-a — the first defined path wins
It depends on the order the paths are listed
404 — overlapping prefixes are rejected at admission
explain: Ingress path matching is longest-prefix-wins, independent of list order — /api/v2 is more specific than /api. B and C assume first-match ordering (that's not how the spec works), and D invents an admission rejection for overlaps.

q: A Service sets port: 80 and targetPort: "8080" (quoted as a string). The pods listen on 8080 with no named ports. Endpoints are populated, but traffic to the Service fails. Why?
options: Quoted and unquoted targetPorts behave identically — the problem is elsewhere
No traffic flows — a string targetPort is a port NAME lookup, and no containerPort is named "8080", so kube-proxy can't resolve a backend
The API server rejects quoted targetPorts
It defaults to port 80 on the pods
explain: targetPort is an IntOrString: integers are port numbers, strings are port NAMES. The quoted "8080" looks for a containerPort literally named 8080 and finds nothing. A states the exact misconception, C invents a rejection (the API accepts it), and D invents a fallback.

q: Via the Gateway API, only requests carrying the header x-tenant: acme may reach Service api-v2; everything else goes to api-v1. Which HTTPRoute construct expresses the header match?
options: matches: [{queryParams: [{name: x-tenant, value: acme}]}]
A backendRefs filter on the header
matches: [{headers: [{name: x-tenant, value: acme}], path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /}}] — HTTPRoute matches support header conditions natively
An Ingress annotation — Gateway API can't match headers
explain: HTTPRouteMatch has first-class headers matching (name/value, exact or regex) — no annotations needed. A confuses headers with query params, B puts matching logic in the wrong stanza (backendRefs select backends; matches select requests), and D denies a core Gateway API feature.

q: Via the Gateway API, every plain-HTTP request through the api route must be redirected to HTTPS with a 301, at the route level (no ingress annotations). Which filter does this?
options: filters: [{type: URLRewrite}] — it changes the scheme
filters: [{type: ResponseHeaderModifier}]
An nginx ssl-redirect annotation on the HTTPRoute
filters: [{type: RequestRedirect, requestRedirect: {scheme: https, statusCode: 301}}] — RequestRedirect issues the redirect before any backend is contacted
explain: RequestRedirect is the Gateway-native redirect filter: scheme/statusCode produce the 301 to HTTPS. URLRewrite rewrites the request forwarded upstream (no redirect to the client — not A), ResponseHeaderModifier only tweaks headers (not B), and ingress annotations don't apply to Gateway API routes (not C).

q: A Gateway listener sets allowedRoutes: {namespaces: {from: Same}}. An HTTPRoute in another namespace lists this Gateway as a parentRef. What happens?
options: The route can never attach — only routes in the Gateway's own namespace are permitted; cross-namespace attachment needs from: All or a namespace Selector
The route attaches — parentRefs override allowedRoutes
The route attaches to all namespaces by default
The Gateway is rejected at apply time
explain: from: Same is the restrictive setting: listeners only accept routes from their own namespace. All (the default) opens every namespace, and Selector opens matching ones. B reverses the precedence (allowedRoutes gates parentRefs, not vice versa), C describes All, and D invents an apply-time rejection.

q: A Gateway must terminate TLS for shop.example.com on port 443 using the kubernetes.io/tls Secret web-tls. Which listener configuration does this?
options: listeners: [{protocol: HTTPS, port: 443, hostname: shop.example.com, tls: {certificateRefs: [{name: web-tls}]}}] — Gateway listeners terminate TLS via tls.certificateRefs, not an Ingress-style secretName
listeners: [{protocol: HTTPS, tls: {secretName: web-tls}}] — the Ingress field name, which doesn't exist on Gateway listeners
spec.tls: [{hosts: [shop.example.com], secretName: web-tls}] — the Ingress tls section, pasted onto a Gateway
An annotation on the Gateway
explain: Gateway API listeners carry their own tls stanza with certificateRefs pointing at the kubernetes.io/tls Secret — there is no secretName field on a listener. B uses the Ingress field name, C pastes the entire Ingress spec.tls section onto a Gateway, and D invents an annotation.

q: A custom TCP protocol (not HTTP) needs TLS passthrough: the NGINX Ingress must NOT terminate TLS, just forward TCP 443 to the pods. Which configuration does this?
options: The annotation alone: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: "true"
A standard Ingress handles TCP passthrough natively
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: "true" on the Ingress AND the controller started with --enable-ssl-passthrough — the annotation does nothing unless the controller enables the feature
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"
explain: ssl-passthrough is a two-part opt-in: the per-Ingress annotation plus the controller-level --enable-ssl-passthrough flag (it requires Lua/TCP proxying the controller doesn't do by default). A misses the controller flag, B contradicts the documented Ingress limitation (L7 HTTP only), and D terminates at the edge and re-encrypts upstream — not passthrough.

q: The API must be throttled to 10 requests per second per client at the NGINX Ingress. Which annotation does this?
options: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "10" — it caps requests per second
A ResourceQuota on the ingress namespace
An HPA targeting the ingress controller
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "10" — requests per second per client IP
explain: limit-rps is the per-client requests-per-second throttle. limit-connections caps CONCURRENT connections, not rate (not A); ResourceQuota caps object counts and compute, not request rates (not B); and autoscaling the controller adds capacity instead of throttling clients (not C).

q: An Ingress rule sets path: /api/ with pathType: Exact, routing to the monitor Service. A request arrives for exactly /api (no trailing slash). What happens?
options: It routes to the monitor — Exact still ignores trailing slashes
