No match — Exact is a literal string comparison; /api/ and /api are different strings
The controller redirects /api to /api/
It matches /api/* underneath
explain: Exact means byte-for-byte equality: /api/ matches only /api/. The trailing-slash leniency people expect comes from Prefix semantics, not Exact (not A/B), and no redirect is implied (not C).

q: Via the Gateway API, paths like /api/v2/users and /api/v10/status must route to svc-api, but /api/internal/* must not. Which HTTPRoute path match expresses the version pattern?
options: path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api/}
path: {type: RegularExpression, value: "/api/v[0-9]+/.*"} — HTTPRoute supports RegularExpression path matching natively
path: {type: Exact, value: "/api/v[0-9]+/.*"}
pathType: ImplementationSpecific with an nginx use-regex annotation
explain: HTTPRoutePathMatch types are Exact, PathPrefix, and RegularExpression — the regex type handles the version pattern directly. PathPrefix can't express the character class (not A), Exact treats the pattern as a literal string (not C), and ImplementationSpecific/use-regex is Ingress-controller machinery, not Gateway API (not D).

q: Via the Gateway API, the backend expects /users but clients call /api/users — the /api prefix must be stripped at the route, with no ingress annotations. Which filter does this?
options: filters: [{type: RequestRedirect}] — it redirects the client
filters: [{type: RequestHeaderModifier}]
filters: [{type: URLRewrite, urlRewrite: {path: {type: ReplacePrefixMatch, replacePrefixMatch: /}}}] — the backend receives the rewritten path
The nginx rewrite-target annotation on the HTTPRoute
explain: URLRewrite with ReplacePrefixMatch rewrites the path forwarded upstream (/api/users → /users) without telling the client. RequestRedirect would 301 the client instead (not A), RequestHeaderModifier only touches headers (not B), and rewrite-target is an NGINX Ingress annotation that doesn't apply to Gateway routes (not D).

q: A NetworkPolicy selects app: api with policyTypes: [Ingress] and a single rule: ingress: [{ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8080}]}] — no from peer is listed. Which sources can reach port 8080 on the api pods?
options: None — a rule without a from peer denies all traffic
Only pods in the same namespace
The rule is invalid without a from peer
All sources — an omitted from peer is a wildcard, so the listed ports are reachable from anywhere
explain: In a NetworkPolicy rule, an omitted from/to peer matches every source: the rule allows the listed ports from anywhere. This is different from an empty RULE LIST (ingress: []), which under policyTypes Ingress denies everything. B invents a namespace restriction, C invents a required field, and A confuses 'no peer listed' with 'no rules'.

q: A Service declares port: 80 with NO targetPort. The pods listen on 8080. Service DNS resolves, endpoints exist, but connections fail. What is the backend port?
options: 80 — when targetPort is omitted it defaults to the port value, so the Service forwards to pod port 80, where nothing listens
8080 — the Service auto-detects the containerPort
It load-balances across all exposed container ports
The Service is invalid without targetPort
explain: targetPort defaults to the value of port when unset — here, pod port 80. There is no auto-detection of containerPorts (not B) and no multi-port fan-out (not C); the manifest is valid but misconfigured, which is why everything looks fine until traffic flows (not D).

q: A Gateway listener sets hostname: shop.example.com. An HTTPRoute with hostname: api.example.com lists that listener as its parent. What happens?
options: The route attaches and serves api.example.com
The route never attaches — a route's hostnames must intersect the listener's hostname; disjoint names bind to nothing
The route applies to all hosts on the listener
kubectl apply rejects the route
explain: Attachment requires hostname intersection between route and listener: api.example.com doesn't intersect shop.example.com, so the route binds to no listener and programs nothing. A assumes attachment is automatic, C describes an empty route hostname (which would inherit), and D invents an apply-time rejection — the failure is silent at the route's status level.

q: Via the Gateway API, only POST requests to /orders/* may reach svc-orders; GETs to the same paths go elsewhere. Which match expresses this?
options: matches: [{headers: [{name: method, value: POST}]}]
matches: [{queryParams: [{name: method, value: POST}]}]
matches: [{method: POST, path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /orders}}] — HTTPRouteMatch has a first-class method field
Two separate HTTPRoutes are required — method can't be matched
explain: HTTPRouteMatch.method matches the request method directly, combinable with path/header/query matches in one rule. A misuses headers, B misuses query params, and D denies a standard field.

q: An Ingress rule sets host: "*.example.com". Requests arrive for the bare apex example.com (no subdomain). Do they match?
options: Yes — the wildcard covers the apex too
Yes, but only over HTTPS with a wildcard certificate
They fall through to the defaultBackend automatically
No — the wildcard covers exactly one DNS label (bar.example.com matches; example.com does not); the apex needs its own rule or host entry
explain: Per the Ingress spec, a wildcard host matches a single DNS label: *.example.com matches bar.example.com but never the bare apex. A states the common misconception, B confuses TLS certificate scope with host matching, and C assumes a fallback that only happens if no rule matches AND a defaultBackend exists — the point is the rule itself doesn't match.

q: A container exits 1 and writes nothing to /dev/termination-log, but its last log lines contain the fatal stack trace. The container sets terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError. What does kubectl describe pod show under the terminated container's message?
options: The last chunk of the container's log output (capped at 2048 bytes or 80 lines) as the termination message — the fallback only kicks in when the message file is empty AND the exit was an error
Nothing — the message file is empty
The container's entire log output, uncapped
The fallback only works if terminationMessagePath is also customized
explain: FallbackToLogsOnError is exactly this safety net: empty termination file + error exit → kubelet surfaces the log tail (2048 bytes / 80 lines max) in the container status. B describes the default File policy, C ignores the documented cap, and D invents a co-requirement.

q: A pod has crashed and restarted 5 times. You run kubectl logs -p web-abc to see why. Which crashed instance's logs do you get?
options: All five, concatenated oldest-first
Only the most recently terminated instance — --previous never reaches further back than the last one
The oldest — the first crash is usually the root cause
A merged interleaving of all five
explain: --previous reads the last terminated container instance only; earlier crashes are gone from this view (and eventually from the node). A, C, and D all assume deeper history than the flag provides — for older crashes you need centralized logging.

q: Your forensics runbook says 'pull yesterday's container logs from the node'. The logs stop at this morning's rotation. What happened to yesterday's logs?
options: They're in etcd — query the API with --show-all
kubectl caches them client-side for 7 days

The kubelet rotates container logs (default 10Mi per file, 5 files retained) — node log files are ephemeral by design, so anything older than the rotation window is gone unless shipped to central logging
Log rotation must be configured in the pod spec — without it, logs persist forever
explain: Container logs live as files under /var/log/pods and the kubelet rotates them (container-log-max-size/files, default 10Mi × 5) — they are not archived anywhere by default. A invents etcd storage, B invents client caching, and D reverses the default (rotation is on unless tuned at the kubelet/node level, not in the pod spec).

q: An incident review needs a full offline snapshot: cluster objects, pod logs, and node state, packaged for analysis without further cluster access. Which single command collects it?
options: kubectl get all -A -o yaml — it captures every object
kubectl describe nodes and pods, saved to files
kubectl logs --all-containers -A piped to a file
kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=./dump — it snapshots cluster state plus logs (scrub Secrets before sharing)
explain: cluster-info dump is the purpose-built forensics collector: API objects, logs, and node info in one directory tree. get all misses logs and many resource types (not A), describe is per-object and manual (not B), and logs alone miss all cluster state (not C).

q: The readiness probe hits the pod IP directly, but the app serves the health endpoint only on the virtual host app.example.com — the probe gets the default vhost's 404. The probe must keep dialing the pod IP. How do you present the right Host header?
options: readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080, httpHeaders: [{name: Host, value: app.example.com}]}} — the probe dials the pod IP but sends the vhost's Host header
readinessProbe: {httpGet: {host: app.example.com, ...}} — cleaner, same result
Point the probe at a Service instead of the pod IP
Switch the probe to scheme: HTTPS
explain: httpHeaders overrides the Host header while the connection still goes to the pod IP — the documented pattern (the docs explicitly steer you to httpHeaders over the host field for this). B's host field changes connection semantics rather than just the header, C adds a Service dependency the probe doesn't need, and D changes TLS, not vhost routing.

q: You run kubectl delete pod web-abc --wait=false, then immediately run kubectl get pod web-abc — the pod is still listed, now with a deletionTimestamp. Did the delete fail?
options: Yes — the delete was silently dropped; retry without the flag
No — --wait=false only detaches the client; the pod stays in Terminating until its grace period elapses, then disappears
The pod is stuck — you must use --force to finish it
--wait=false is ignored for single-pod deletes
explain: --wait=false changes client behavior, not server behavior: the API still honors the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds. The pod lingers in Terminating by design. A misreads the async state as failure, C reaches for the last-resort flag unnecessarily, and D denies the flag's documented effect.

q: You must change a bare debug pod's hostname, but spec.hostname is immutable on a running pod. kubectl apply and kubectl patch are both rejected. What is the way through?
options: kubectl apply --force — it overrides immutability
kubectl patch --type=json with a replace op — JSON patches bypass validation
kubectl replace --force -f pod.yaml — it deletes and recreates the pod, the standard path for immutable pod fields
kubectl edit and save — the editor bypasses the API
explain: Immutable pod fields can't be patched in place by any method — replace --force deletes and recreates the object so the new spec takes effect. --force isn't an apply flag (not A), JSON patches go through the same validation (not B), and edit saves through the identical API path (not D).

q: CI must block until the nightly export Job is fully complete (up to 5 minutes), then archive its outputs. Which command waits on the Job's completion?
options: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready --timeout=300s job/export
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available --timeout=300s job/export
kubectl rollout status job/export — rollout tracks Jobs
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete --timeout=300s job/export — Jobs expose Complete/Failed conditions
explain: Jobs report the Complete (and Failed) conditions, which kubectl wait watches directly. Ready is a pod condition (not A), Available belongs to Deployments (not B), and rollout status doesn't support Jobs at all (not C).

q: You must drain node-2 but ONLY evict pods labeled app=web; everything else stays put. Which drain invocation does this?
options: kubectl drain node-2 --pod-selector app=web — --pod-selector filters pods on the node (note: -l/--selector on drain filters NODES, not pods)
kubectl drain node-2 -l app=web — the familiar label flag
kubectl drain node-2 --force app=web
kubectl cordon node-2, then kubectl delete pods -l app=web --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-2
explain: drain has a dedicated --pod-selector for this; the generic -l/--selector selects which NODES to drain, so -l app=web would try to drain nodes carrying that label (not B). C invents flag syntax, and D is a manual multi-step workaround for what one flag does.

q: kubectl describe pod shows the pod was Evicted with message "The node was low on resource: memory". The containers show no OOMKilled. What happened, and where do you look next?
options: The container was OOMKilled — raise its memory limit
Node-pressure eviction by the kubelet — the node ran out of memory, so the kubelet evicted pods by QoS/priority; check node pressure and the pod's QoS class, not the container's limit
The app has a memory leak — profile the heap
The memory request was set too low
explain: Evicted at the POD level with a node-resource message is kubelet node-pressure eviction, a different mechanism from container OOMKilled (which appears under containerStatuses with exit 137). Raising the container limit (not A/C/D) doesn't address node exhaustion — the fix space is node capacity, QoS class, and requests.

q: During a deploy you must stream (follow) the sidecar container's logs from every web pod at once, each line tagged with its pod name. Which single command does this?
options: kubectl logs -l app=web -f — the container is implied
kubectl logs -l app=web -c sidecar --all-containers -f --prefix
kubectl logs -l app=web -c sidecar -f --prefix — -c names the container (required with multiple containers), -f streams, --prefix tags pod names
kubectl logs deploy/web -c sidecar -f
explain: Multi-container pods require -c with a selector; -f follows all matched pods' streams and --prefix tags each line. A fails outright ('a container name must be specified'), B conflicts (--all-containers can't combine with -c), and D misuses the Deployment as a log source.

q: A drain hangs because a strict PDB blocks eviction, and your maintenance window is 5 minutes. You want the drain to fail fast instead of hanging forever. Which flag bounds the whole operation?
options: kubectl drain node-1 --grace-period=300 — it caps the drain
kubectl drain node-1 --skip-wait-for-delete-timeout
--disable-eviction=true — it speeds up the drain
kubectl drain node-1 --timeout=300s --ignore-daemonsets — --timeout bounds the entire drain; the PDB block then surfaces as an error instead of hanging
explain: --timeout caps the whole drain operation (default is infinite), so a PDB-blocked drain errors out instead of hanging past your window. --grace-period only overrides per-pod termination grace (not A), --skip-wait-for-delete-timeout tweaks post-delete waiting (not B), and --disable-eviction bypasses PDBs entirely — a different, riskier action (not C).

q: You attach a debug container to a pod in a namespace enforcing the restricted PSS, but the debugger needs elevated privileges (sysadmin-level syscalls). The ephemeral container is rejected by the policy. Which kubectl debug flag grants the needed profile?
options: kubectl debug -it pod/web-abc --image=busybox --profile=sysadmin --target=app — the profile sets the debug container's security posture
kubectl debug --privileged — the privileged flag
--profile=baseline — it grants sysadmin rights
Annotate the pod to opt out of PSS
explain: --profile selects a predefined security profile for the ephemeral container (sysadmin, netadmin, baseline, restricted, legacy) — the supported way to get elevated debugging rights. There is no --privileged kubectl flag (not B), baseline is the restrictive end (not C), and annotations can't waive Pod Security admission (not D).

q: A pod has a 3-minute init container. CI must wait until the init phase finishes (not until the app is Ready) before seeding test data. Which condition does kubectl wait watch?
options: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready --timeout=240s pod/web-abc
kubectl wait --for=condition=Initialized --timeout=240s pod/web-abc — Initialized becomes True when all init containers complete
kubectl wait --for=condition=ContainersReady --timeout=240s pod/web-abc
kubectl wait --for=condition=PodScheduled --timeout=240s pod/web-abc
explain: Initialized is the pod condition tracking init-container completion — True once every init container has run to completion, before app containers start. Ready and ContainersReady wait for the app too (not A/C), and PodScheduled only means placement (not D).

q: After a rollout, CI must block until EVERY pod labeled app=web is Ready (up to 3 minutes), regardless of how many replicas exist. Which command does this without hardcoding pod names?
options: kubectl get pods -l app=web -w and eyeball the READY column
kubectl rollout status deploy/web — it waits on pod conditions
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=web --timeout=180s — wait accepts a label selector over pods
A bash loop over kubectl get pod names
explain: kubectl wait takes resource types plus -l selectors, blocking until all matched pods satisfy the condition (or the timeout). get -w is manual watching (not A), rollout status tracks a Deployment's progress rather than an arbitrary pod set (not B), and D reinvents what the flag does natively.

q: kubectl logs -l app=web fails: the selector matches 50 pods and the request errors out on concurrency limits. What raises the cap?
options: --tail=50 — fewer lines per pod
--limit-bytes=1048576
--prefix=false
--max-log-requests=50 — the flag defaults to 20 concurrent log streams; raise it to cover the matched pods
explain: --max-log-requests caps how many pods' logs kubectl fetches concurrently (default 20); exceeding it errors instead of queuing. --tail and --limit-bytes shrink volume per pod but don't change the concurrency cap (not A/B), and --prefix only affects line formatting (not C).

q: kubectl logs -p web-abc returns an error instead of logs. The pod is Running and has never restarted. What is the most likely reason?
options: It errors — --previous needs a terminated instance, and this pod has never crashed, so there is nothing previous to show
You must also pass -c with --previous
The logs were rotated away
The pod name is wrong
explain: --previous reads the last TERMINATED container instance; a pod that never restarted has none, so kubectl errors rather than falling back to current logs. B invents a flag requirement, C is possible but far less likely than the never-restarted explanation, and D would error differently ('pods not found').

q: kubectl get pod shows web-abc with STATUS Init:0/2. The app container hasn't started. Where is the problem, and what do you check first?
options: The app container crashed — check kubectl logs -c app
An init container is failing or still running (0 of 2 done) — check the init containers' status and logs with kubectl logs -c <init-name>, not the app container
The scheduler can't place the pod
The image is still pulling
explain: Init:0/2 means zero of two init containers have completed — the pod is stuck in the init phase, so the app container legitimately hasn't started. The investigation targets the init containers (describe shows which, logs -c <init> shows why). A looks at a container that never ran, C would show Pending, and D would show ContainerCreating/ImagePullBackOff.

q: kubectl logs cronjob/report fails with an error. The CronJob exists and ran last night. Why can't you read its logs this way?
options: You forgot -c — CronJobs have multiple containers
The CronJob is suspended, so it has no logs
A CronJob has no pods or containers of its own — read the logs from its Jobs' pods (kubectl logs job/report-<timestamp>)
CronJob logs are only available via the events API
explain: kubectl logs needs a pod with containers; a CronJob is just a schedule + Job template — the actual log-producing pods belong to the Jobs it created. B is irrelevant (past runs still have logs), A misdiagnoses the error, and D invents an events-only restriction.

q: A cleanup script deletes pod web-abc, but the pod may already be gone — and the script must not fail when it is. Which kubectl-native flag makes the delete idempotent?
options: kubectl delete pod web-abc --wait=false
kubectl delete pod web-abc --force
kubectl delete pod web-abc || true — the shell idiom
kubectl delete pod web-abc --ignore-not-found — a missing object is treated as success
explain: --ignore-not-found makes the delete a no-op success when the object doesn't exist — the idempotent kubectl-native pattern. --wait=false changes blocking behavior, not missing-object errors (not A); --force is the stuck-deletion last resort (not B); and while || true works, the question asks for the kubectl-native flag (not C).

q: You convert a log-shipping sidecar to a native sidecar: an initContainer with restartPolicy: Always. How does the kubelet order it relative to the app container, and what happens if the sidecar process exits mid-life?
options: The sidecar starts before the app container (it does not block on the sidecar completing), it keeps running alongside the app, it is restarted if it exits, and it is terminated only after all regular containers exit
The sidecar runs to completion like a normal init container, then the app starts — so a long-lived sidecar process would block the app forever
The sidecar starts concurrently with the app container with no ordering guarantee, exactly like a second entry in containers:
The sidecar starts first but is killed as soon as the app container becomes ready, to free resources
explain: A native sidecar is an init container with container-level restartPolicy: Always. It starts in init order before app containers (waiting only for it to be running, not to complete), survives for the pod's lifetime, restarts independently on failure, and gets SIGTERM after the regular containers exit. The classic trap is treating it like a regular init container that must exit (B) or like an unordered containers: entry (C); the ordering guarantee is precisely why native sidecars replaced wait-for-it hacks.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You add a livenessProbe to a regular init container that downloads a dataset. kubectl apply rejects the pod spec. What is the rule, and what is the compliant fix?
options: Init containers accept only exec probes — rewrite the httpGet probe as an exec probe

Probes are forbidden on regular init containers (liveness, readiness, and startup); only native sidecars (restartPolicy: Always init containers) support probes — move the health check into the app container or convert the helper to a native sidecar
Probes are allowed but only with initialDelaySeconds: 0, which you omitted
The probe is fine — the rejection is because init containers cannot use imagePullPolicy: Always
explain: The API forbids all probe types on regular init containers: init containers run to completion before app start, so liveness/readiness semantics don't apply — kubelet startup ordering is the health gate. The single exception is native sidecars, which are long-lived and do support probes. Rewriting the probe type (A) or tweaking delays (C) can't fix a field the API schema rejects; the compliant fix is to probe the app container that actually serves, or make the helper a native sidecar.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod has two containers. The app container sets cpu/memory requests equal to limits. The logging sidecar sets only memory and cpu requests, with no limits. What QoS class does the pod get, and why?
options: Guaranteed — the main container is fully pinned, and sidecars are excluded from QoS classification
BestEffort — any container without limits drags the whole pod to BestEffort
Burstable — Guaranteed requires every container to have requests == limits for both cpu and memory, and the sidecar's missing limits break that
Guaranteed — QoS looks only at requests, and both containers have requests set
explain: QoS is a pod-level verdict over ALL containers: Guaranteed needs requests == limits for cpu AND memory on every container. One container with requests but no limits makes the pod Burstable (requests exist somewhere, but the equality condition fails). BestEffort (B) requires zero requests/limits anywhere, and (D) misstates the rule — limits are exactly what the equality test checks.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container has memory request 256Mi and limit 512Mi. It steadily grows to 600Mi on a node with plenty of free RAM. What happens?
options: Nothing — free node RAM means the limit is advisory only and the container keeps its 600Mi
The container is CPU-throttled until usage drops back under 512Mi
The container is evicted with status Evicted and rescheduled elsewhere
The kernel OOM-killer terminates the container (OOMKilled, exit code 137) because limits are hard cgroup caps enforced regardless of node headroom
explain: Memory limits are hard cgroup ceilings: exceeding the limit triggers the OOM killer on that container even if the node has gigabytes free — the exam's favorite 'but the node wasn't full!' trap. CPU limits throttle (B describes cpu behavior, not memory); eviction (C) is the kubelet's response to node-level pressure against requests, a different mechanism from the per-container OOM kill.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create a PriorityClass batch-low with value 1000 and preemptionPolicy: Never, and assign it to overnight ETL pods. The cluster is full when an ETL pod is submitted. What happens, precisely?
options: The ETL pod is queued ahead of lower-priority pods but waits for capacity to free naturally — it never evicts running pods; however, a higher-priority pod submitted later may still preempt the ETL pod once it is running
The ETL pod immediately evicts the lowest-priority running pod, because value 1000 outranks the default priority 0
preemptionPolicy: Never makes the pod unschedulable — it stays Pending forever even after capacity frees
The ETL pod can never be preempted by anyone, because Never is absolute in both directions
explain: preemptionPolicy: Never is one-directional: the pod jumps the scheduling queue ahead of lower-priority pods but cannot trigger preemption — it waits for natural capacity. It is NOT itself immune: higher-priority preempting pods can still evict it. (B) describes the default PreemptLowerPriority behavior, (C) confuses non-preempting with unschedulable, and (D) invents bidirectional immunity the API doesn't offer.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A Java app takes 90s to warm its cache. Its liveness probe (failureThreshold 3, periodSeconds 10) keeps killing the pod during startup. Which probe fixes this correctly, and how do the probes interact once it succeeds?
options: Add a startupProbe with a generous window (e.g. failureThreshold 30 x periodSeconds 10 = 300s). While the startup probe runs, liveness and readiness are disabled; once it succeeds, it steps aside permanently and liveness/readiness take over
Raise the liveness probe's initialDelaySeconds to 120 — simplest and equivalent to a startup probe
Add a second liveness probe with a longer period; Kubernetes ORs the results
Set the readiness probe's failureThreshold higher — readiness gates liveness, so a lenient readiness probe protects startup
explain: The startup probe exists for exactly this: it suspends liveness/readiness until the app signals it has started, then hands control back. initialDelaySeconds (B) is the blunt alternative — it delays every restart's probing, slowing genuine failure detection after fast restarts. (C) is invented (one liveness probe per container), and (D) reverses the relationship: readiness never gates liveness; the probes are independent.

q: During a database failover, your readiness probe starts failing on all pods. Which statement about the blast radius is true?
options: All pods restart simultaneously, causing a full outage until the database returns
Pods are removed from the Service endpoints and stop receiving traffic, but keep running — when the database recovers, the same pods become ready again with no restarts
The Deployment scales the ReplicaSet to zero because zero pods are ready
The kubelet deletes the pods after failureThreshold is exceeded
explain: Readiness failure only detaches the pod from endpoints — the process keeps running, so recovery is instant when the dependency returns. That is the whole point of separating readiness (can I serve?) from liveness (is the process broken?): a down database must stop traffic, not trigger restarts. (A) and (D) describe liveness-probe consequences; (C) invents autoscaler behavior that doesn't exist.

q: You write a Job manifest with restartPolicy: Always in the pod template because you want failed pods retried. kubectl rejects it. What is the rule?
options: Jobs require restartPolicy: Never — OnFailure is also rejected
Always is fine for Jobs; the error must be a typo in the image name
Job pod templates must use restartPolicy: Never or OnFailure; Always is rejected because the Job controller (not the kubelet) owns retry semantics
restartPolicy is immutable on Jobs, so you must delete and recreate the Job with a different policy
explain: The Job controller manages retries via backoffLimit, so the kubelet-level Always policy is forbidden in Job templates — only Never or OnFailure are accepted. (A) over-restricts (OnFailure is the common choice for Jobs). The rejection is API validation of the policy value itself, not a typo, and the fix is a one-word change, not a delete/recreate cycle.

q: A Job has activeDeadlineSeconds: 600. It is created with suspend: true, stays suspended for an hour, then is resumed and starts running. When can the system first terminate it for exceeding the deadline?
options: 600 seconds after the Job object was created — the clock starts at creation regardless of suspension
600 seconds after the Job's startTime, because the deadline is measured relative to startTime and the timer is stopped and reset while the Job is suspended
600 seconds after the first pod's container starts executing user code
The deadline is voided entirely once a Job has been suspended
explain: Per the API, activeDeadlineSeconds is relative to .status.startTime, and suspension stops the timer — resuming resets it, so the hour-long suspension doesn't consume the budget. (A) is the trap: creation time is irrelevant. (C) over-specifies (startTime is when the controller starts the Job, not first user code), and (D) invents a voiding rule — the timer simply pauses.

q: A batch step exits with code 42 when input data is corrupt — retrying never helps, but the Job burns all 6 backoffLimit retries over several minutes before failing. Which podFailurePolicy rule fails the Job immediately on that exit code?
options: podFailurePolicy: rules: - action: FailJob, onExitCodes: {operator: In, values: [42]} — the whole Job is marked Failed and running pods are terminated instead of retrying
podFailurePolicy: rules: - action: Ignore, onExitCodes: {operator: In, values: [42]}
podFailurePolicy: rules: - action: Count, onPodConditions: [{type: DisruptionTarget}]
Set backoffLimit: 0 — the Job then fails on the first pod failure of any kind
explain: FailJob + onExitCodes In [42] matches the corrupt-data signature and fails the entire Job at once, skipping pointless retries. Ignore (B) does the opposite — the failure wouldn't count and a replacement pod would be created. (C) matches disruption conditions, not exit codes, and Count is just the default. (D) fails fast but for every failure type, losing the selective 'known-bad exit code' semantics.

q: A PV offers 10Gi with accessModes [ReadWriteOnce]. A PVC requests 5Gi with accessModes [ReadWriteOnce]. What happens?
options: The PVC binds to the PV and the PV is wholly consumed by the claim — PVCs bind whole PVs even when the request is smaller than capacity, and the PV's modes must cover every mode the PVC asks for
Binding fails — capacity must match exactly
Binding fails — a PVC can only bind a PV in the same namespace, and PVs are cluster-scoped
The PVC binds and the remaining 5Gi stays available for a second PVC
explain: Binding needs PV capacity >= request and PV accessModes to include all requested modes; exact size match is not required. The binding is 1:1 and exclusive — the whole 10Gi PV is consumed by the 5Gi claim, so (D)'s leftover-sharing is wrong. (C) invents a namespace rule: PVs are cluster-scoped and PVCs bind across that boundary by design.

q: A PVC sets storageClassName: "" in a cluster that has a default StorageClass. The PVC stays Pending even though the default class could provision storage. Why?
options: Empty string is invalid — the API server rejects the PVC
storageClassName: "" explicitly opts out of dynamic provisioning: the PVC will only bind to a pre-provisioned static PV and ignores the default StorageClass
The default StorageClass only applies to PVCs created with kubectl create, not kubectl apply
Pending means the provisioner is broken; the empty string is irrelevant
explain: An explicit empty storageClassName means 'no dynamic provisioning' — the claim waits for a manually created PV with a matching (empty) class. Omitting the field entirely is what triggers the default class. (A) is wrong: "" is valid and meaningful. The create-vs-apply distinction in (C) is invented, and (D) misreads Pending, which here is the expected 'waiting for a static PV' state.

q: You patch a PVC's spec.resources.requests.storage from 10Gi to 20Gi, and the API rejects the change. The most likely cause is:
options: PVC size is immutable — you must delete and recreate the PVC, losing the data
You can only shrink PVCs, never grow them
The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion unset/false — expansion is gated on that field, so set it (or use a class that allows it) and retry
The PV must be edited first — the control plane refuses to resize a claim beyond its bound PV's capacity
explain: Volume expansion is allowed only when the StorageClass sets allowVolumeExpansion: true; without it the resize is rejected at the API. (A) is the old myth — growth is supported. (B) is backwards: shrinking is what's unsupported. (D) reverses the flow: you resize the PVC and the control plane grows the PV, never the reverse (editing the PV directly can even suppress the automatic resize).

q: A Deployment has 4 replicas and the default RollingUpdate strategy. During a rollout, what are the hard bounds on unavailable and extra pods?
options: Up to 4 pods may be unavailable and up to 4 extra may run — defaults are 100%
Zero pods may be unavailable and at most 1 extra may run
At most 1 pod unavailable (maxUnavailable 25% of 4) and at most 1 extra pod (maxSurge 25% of 4), so between 3 and 5 pods total during the rollout
The percentages apply to the new ReplicaSet only, so bounds are 1 unavailable and 0 extra
explain: Defaults are maxUnavailable 25% and maxSurge 25% of desired replicas: 25% of 4 = 1 each (maxSurge rounds up, maxUnavailable rounds down). So at least 3 old pods stay up and at most 1 new pod runs ahead — 3 to 5 total. (A) invents 100% defaults, (B) describes maxUnavailable: 0 which you must set explicitly, and (D) misapplies the percentages to only one ReplicaSet.

q: A StatefulSet uses volumeClaimTemplates with a 10Gi claim. It runs 3 replicas, then you delete the StatefulSet. What happens to the three PVCs?
options: The PVCs (and their data) survive — deleting a StatefulSet never deletes its volumeClaimTemplate PVCs; you must delete them explicitly
The PVCs are deleted automatically with the StatefulSet, but the PVs are retained
The PVCs and PVs are all deleted immediately, wiping the data
The PVCs are kept only if the StatefulSet had an ownerReference; otherwise they are garbage-collected
explain: volumeClaimTemplates creates one PVC per replica, and StatefulSet deletion deliberately orphans them — this is the data-safety design, since auto-deleting volumes on a scale-down typo would be catastrophic. (B)/(C) describe the opposite of the documented behavior, and (D) invents an ownerReference condition; the rule is unconditional: StatefulSets never delete PVCs.

q: You create a Service with clusterIP: None and a selector matching 3 pods. What does DNS return for the service name, and what handles load balancing?
options: A records with the IPs of all 3 pods (one answer per pod); kube-proxy does no load balancing — the client picks from the returned set, typically round-robin
A single A record with a virtual cluster IP, load-balanced by kube-proxy as usual
SRV records only — headless services have no A records
NXDOMAIN — clusterIP: None disables DNS for the service
explain: Headless means no virtual IP: DNS returns the pod IPs directly (one A record per backing pod), and there is no kube-proxy load balancing — clients consume the set themselves. (B) describes a normal ClusterIP service. (C) is wrong: A records exist for headless services; SRV records additionally require named ports. (D) invents a DNS blackout that doesn't happen.

q: A Service exposes port 80 with no port name. A client queries _http._tcp.web.default.svc.cluster.local for an SRV record and gets NXDOMAIN, though A-record lookups work. Why?
options: SRV queries require the trailing dot; without it CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN
SRV records are only created for named ports — without a name on the port, Kubernetes creates no SRV record
The service needs type: LoadBalancer for SRV records
SRV records are created only for headless services
explain: The SRV name is built from the port NAME (_<port-name>._<protocol>.<svc>...); an unnamed port yields no SRV record at all, so the fix is naming the port (e.g. name: http). The trailing-dot claim (A) confuses FQDN search behavior with record existence, (C) invents a type requirement, and (D) is backwards — SRV records are created for named ports on both normal and headless services.

q: You define a Service with type: ExternalName and externalName: db.example.com so pods can reach the managed database as db.prod.svc.cluster.local. Which statement is true?
options: Pods must connect through the service's clusterIP, which kube-proxy DNATs to the external address
The service needs a selector matching the database pods for the CNAME to be programmed
DNS returns a CNAME pointing at db.example.com — it works purely at the DNS level, with no proxying, no selectors, and no port remapping
ExternalName services only work for HTTP; database TCP connections bypass the CNAME
explain: ExternalName is DNS-only: the service name resolves to a CNAME for the external target, and the client then resolves that itself. There are no selectors, no endpoints, no kube-proxy involvement, and no port remapping — the app connects to whatever port it dials on the resolved name. (A) describes ClusterIP proxying, (B) invents a selector requirement, and (D) invents a protocol restriction.

q: An Ingress has two Prefix rules for the same host: path /api → svc-a and path /api/v1 → svc-b. A request arrives for /api/v1/users. Which backend serves it?
options: svc-a — the shortest matching path wins
Whichever rule was created first — creation order decides ties
The request is duplicated to both backends — overlapping Prefix rules fan out
svc-b — when multiple paths match a request, the longest matching path takes precedence
explain: Ingress precedence is longest-match-wins: /api/v1/users matches both rules, but /api/v1 is the longer (more specific) match, so svc-b serves it. (A) reverses the documented precedence, (B) invents order-dependence (matching is deterministic, not positional), and (C) invents request fan-out — a request goes to exactly one backend.

q: An Ingress has two rules for the same host: path /api with pathType Exact, and path /api with pathType Prefix. A request arrives for exactly /api. Which backend serves it?
options: The Exact rule's backend — when multiple paths match, the longest match wins, and on a tie Exact takes precedence over Prefix
The Prefix rule's backend — Prefix always outranks Exact
Whichever rule appears first in the YAML — order decides ties
The request is rejected with 400 — duplicate paths are invalid
explain: Ingress precedence: longest matching path wins; if still tied, Exact beats Prefix. Both rules match /api at equal length, so the Exact rule serves it. (B) reverses the documented tiebreak, (C) invents order-dependence (the API sorts this deterministically), and (D) is wrong — same-path different-type rules are legal.

q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs web shows only the latest container's startup lines, which contain nothing useful. How do you see the output from the previous crashed instance?
options: kubectl logs web --previous — shows the terminated previous container instance's logs, which is where the crash evidence lives
kubectl logs web --all-containers — merges logs from every restart
kubectl logs web --since=24h — extends the window to include earlier instances
Restarted container logs are gone — you must reproduce the crash with a debug container
explain: --previous targets the last terminated instance of the container — the one that actually crashed — while plain logs show the current (just-restarted, often empty) instance. (B) merges across containers, not across restarts of one container. (C) only filters by time within the current instance's logs, and (D) is defeatist: kubelet keeps the previous instance's logs precisely for this.

q: kubectl top pods returns 'Metrics not available for pod default/web, age: 30s'. The pod has been running for an hour. What is the most likely cause, and what is true about the data source?
options: The pod needs resources.requests set before metrics appear
The metrics-server is not installed or not healthy — kubectl top reads from it, and it only serves point-in-time snapshots with no history
kubectl top reads from Prometheus; the Prometheus adapter is misconfigured
Metrics appear only for pods in the kube-system namespace
explain: kubectl top is a thin client over the metrics-server API; 'Metrics not available' with a healthy old pod points at a missing/broken metrics-server, not the pod. And metrics-server keeps no history — it scrapes kubelets and serves the current snapshot only, so you can't graph yesterday from it. (A) confuses HPA requirements with top, (C) names the wrong backend, and (D) invents a namespace restriction.

q: An incident happened at 3 AM. At 9 AM you run kubectl get events to reconstruct the timeline, but events from 3 AM are gone while 8 AM events exist. What is the explanation?
options: Events are namespaced and you queried the wrong namespace
The API server retains events for 1 hour by default (--event-ttl), then garbage-collects them — overnight forensics need an external event exporter
kubectl get events only shows events from currently-running pods; the 3 AM pods are gone
Events are stored in etcd forever; your cluster's etcd must have been compacted manually
explain: The default event TTL is one hour: the API server deletes events older than that, so a 3 AM incident is unrecoverable from the API at 9 AM. This is why production clusters run event exporters to external storage. (A) would hide all events, not just old ones; (C) misstates scope — events cover many object types and persist independently of the pods; (D) contradicts the documented TTL.

q: Your inventory script needs every pod's IP address and node name in one tabular shot. Which command provides both?
options: kubectl describe pods — node and IP appear, but buried in verbose per-pod sections
kubectl top pods — shows CPU/memory usage, but neither pod IPs nor node names
kubectl get pods -o yaml and grep for podIP and nodeName — scriptable, but heavy for a simple table
kubectl get pods -o wide — adds NODE and IP columns to the standard table in one call
explain: -o wide is the purpose-built tabular view: NAME, READY, STATUS plus IP and NODE columns in one shot. describe (A) has the data but as verbose per-object prose, top (B) reports resource usage only, and (C) works but is the clumsy path when the CLI already renders the exact table.

q: kubectl describe pod shows a container with 'Exit Code: 137' and Reason OOMKilled, while another pod shows Exit Code 143 after a rollout. What do these mean?
options: 137 = the container was SIGKILLed after exceeding its memory limit (128 + signal 9); 143 = SIGTERM (128 + 15), the normal graceful termination signal during rollouts and deletes
137 = CPU throttling kicked in; 143 = the node ran out of disk
Both are application bugs — exit codes above 128 always mean the app crashed
137 = liveness probe failure; 143 = readiness probe failure
explain: Exit codes above 128 are 128 + signal number: 137 is SIGKILL (the OOM killer's signature when a container breaches its memory limit), 143 is SIGTERM (graceful shutdown — expected during rollouts, deletes, and preemption). (B) invents meanings for both, (C) ignores that 143 is usually platform-initiated and healthy, and (D) misattributes probe failures, which surface as restarts/unready states rather than these codes.

q: The service account deployer sets automountServiceAccountToken: false, but a pod using that SA still gets /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token mounted. The pod spec contains automountServiceAccountToken: true. Which setting wins and why?
options: The ServiceAccount setting wins — pod-level fields cannot re-enable what the SA disabled
The pod-level automountServiceAccountToken: true wins — the pod spec overrides the ServiceAccount default, so the token is mounted
Both must agree — the mount happens only if both are true, so this pod should have no token and something else is wrong
The kubelet ignores both and always mounts the token for pods with imagePullSecrets
explain: The pod spec's automountServiceAccountToken takes precedence over the ServiceAccount's setting: unset at pod level inherits the SA value, but an explicit pod-level value overrides it either way. That's why the token appears despite the SA default. (A) reverses the precedence, (C) invents an AND rule, and (D) ties token mounting to imagePullSecrets, which are unrelated.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A projected service account token volume sets expirationSeconds: 600 and audience: vault. What does the kubelet do with this token over the pod's lifetime?
options: The token is valid for the pod's entire lifetime — expirationSeconds only affects the initial issue
The token is a legacy long-lived secret and never rotates
The kubelet issues a bound token for audience 'vault' and proactively rotates it before the 600s expiry, so the mounted file is refreshed automatically
The token expires after 600s and the pod must be restarted to get a new one
explain: Projected service account tokens are short-lived and audience-bound; the kubelet rotates them ahead of expiry and updates the mounted file in place (the default expirationSeconds is 3600s when unset). (A) confuses this with static secrets, (B) describes the legacy auto-generated SA secrets, and (D) misses the rotation — no restart is needed precisely because the kubelet refreshes the projection.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You update a ConfigMap that feeds an app two ways: LOG_LEVEL as an environment variable, and /etc/app/config.yaml as a mounted file. After the edit, what does the running pod see?
options: Both update within a minute — ConfigMaps propagate to env and volumes identically
Neither updates — pods always need a restart to see ConfigMap changes
The mounted file is eventually updated by the kubelet (on its sync period), but the environment variable keeps its startup value for the container's lifetime — only new pods get the new env value
The env var updates but the mounted file is frozen at pod creation
explain: Environment variables are snapshotted at container start and never refreshed; mounted ConfigMap volumes are eventually consistent via the kubelet's sync loop (up to its sync period plus cache TTL). (A) wrongly equates the two paths, (B) is over-pessimistic about volumes, and (D) reverses the actual behavior — it's the file that updates, not the env var.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: An app mounts a single ConfigMap key with subPath: config.yaml at /etc/app/config.yaml so it can coexist with other files in /etc/app. After a ConfigMap update, the file never changes. Why, and what is the fix that preserves the coexistence?
options: subPath mounts bind-mount a single file and are excluded from the kubelet's atomic volume update — the file is frozen until the pod is recreated; use a full-directory mount with items: mapping, or roll the pods after ConfigMap changes
subPath requires readOnly: false to receive updates
The ConfigMap needs immutable: false set explicitly
subPath mounts update only on node reboot — drain and reboot the node
explain: The Kubernetes docs call this out explicitly: a container using a ConfigMap as a subPath volume mount will not receive ConfigMap updates, because the kubelet's atomic symlink-swap update path only works for whole-volume mounts. (B) invents a writability condition (ConfigMap volumes are always readOnly anyway), (C) confuses the immutable flag (which freezes the ConfigMap itself, the opposite direction), and (D) invents a reboot requirement — a pod recreate (e.g. rollout restart) suffices.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Two pods use the same image: web:2.4 in one, web:latest in the other. Neither sets imagePullPolicy. Which image does each pod pull on node assignment?
options: Both use IfNotPresent — the policy defaults uniformly regardless of tag
web:2.4 defaults to IfNotPresent (pinned tag), web:latest defaults to Always (:latest or untagged images always pull)
Both default to Always — Kubernetes never trusts the local cache
web:2.4 defaults to Never since the tag is pinned; web:latest defaults to IfNotPresent
explain: The defaulting rule keys on the tag: :latest (or no tag) → Always; any other tag → IfNotPresent. That's why pinning versions is both a reproducibility and a pull-storm control. (A) ignores the tag-dependent default, (C) claims no caching ever happens, and (D) invents a Never default that only exists when explicitly set.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A container has a startupProbe (failureThreshold 20, periodSeconds 5) that keeps failing because the dependency it checks is down. What does the kubelet do?
options: It removes the pod from Service endpoints but leaves the container running indefinitely
It waits out the 100s budget, then kills and restarts the container per its restart policy — a failed startup probe is fatal like a failed liveness probe
It keeps the pod in Pending until the probe passes
It escalates to the Job controller to recreate the pod
explain: A startup probe that exhausts its failure budget kills the container exactly like a liveness failure — the kubelet then applies the pod's restart policy. It never just detaches endpoints (A confuses startup with readiness) and never parks the pod in Pending (C confuses probe failure with scheduling). (D) invents Job-controller involvement in plain pod probing.

q: An exec liveness probe runs /bin/check-health, which prints 'OK' and exits 1 on a degraded-but-alive state. The container keeps restarting. What is the probe verdict, and what is the minimal fix?
options: The probe succeeds — any output containing 'OK' counts as success regardless of exit code
The probe reads only stdout; exit codes are ignored for exec probes

The probe fails — exec probes judge solely by exit code (0 = success, anything else = failure). Fix the script to exit 0 when the state is acceptable, or move the degraded check to the readiness probe
Exit code 1 means success for exec probes; the restarts must come from the readiness probe
explain: exec probes are exit-code-only: 0 succeeds, non-zero fails — stdout content is irrelevant to the verdict. The script's 'OK'-but-exit-1 is a failure, hence the restarts. The fix is semantic: exit 0 for acceptable states, or probe degraded-ness via readiness (which detaches traffic without restarting). (A) and (D) invent output/code rules that don't exist.

q: A Job sets completions: 5 and parallelism: 2. How many pods run at once at most, and when is the Job complete?
options: 5 pods at once; complete when any 2 succeed
At most 2 pods concurrently; the Job completes after 5 pods have succeeded in total
At most 2 pods concurrently; the Job completes when 2 pods succeed
Exactly 2 pods total are created; completions is ignored when parallelism is set
explain: parallelism caps concurrent pods (2 max at a time); completions is the success target (5 successful pods total, across retries). The Job controller keeps creating replacement pods until 5 have succeeded. (A) swaps the two fields' roles, (C) mistakes the concurrency cap for the success target, and (D) invents an either/or relationship — the fields compose.

q: A CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid has a run still executing when the next schedule fires. What happens to the newly scheduled run?
options: It is skipped entirely — Forbid means the new run is dropped if the previous Job hasn't finished, with no queueing
It queues and starts as soon as the previous run finishes
It replaces the running Job — the old one is deleted and the new one starts
The CronJob is suspended until manually resumed
explain: Forbid drops the overlapping run — it is never queued and never retried; the schedule simply misses that tick. (B) describes a queue that doesn't exist, (C) describes Replace (which kills the running Job and starts fresh), and (D) invents a suspension side effect. The default Allow would have started the overlapping run concurrently.

q: Your team in New York wants a CronJob to run at 9 AM Eastern. The cluster's controller-manager runs on UTC. Which is the correct, supported configuration?
options: schedule: "TZ=America/New_York 0 9 * * *" — embed the zone in the cron string
spec.timeZone: "America/New_York" alongside the plain schedule — stable since 1.27; CRON_TZ/TZ prefixes inside the schedule string are rejected by validation
schedule: "0 9 * * *" and set the pod's TZ environment variable to America/New_York
CronJobs always run in UTC; convert the schedule to 14:00/13:00 UTC manually and document the DST switch
explain: The supported mechanism is the spec.timeZone field (GA since 1.27); embedding TZ/CRON_TZ in the schedule string is explicitly unsupported and fails validation. (C) confuses the cron evaluation timezone (controller-side) with the pod's runtime TZ env. (D) was the pre-1.24 workaround, obsolete now that timeZone is stable.

q: A Deployment has 3 replicas with strategy rollingUpdate: {maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1}. What availability does a rollout guarantee?
options: At least one pod is always down — maxSurge 1 forces a termination first
Zero downtime by definition — no old pod is ever terminated before its replacement is ready, and at most one extra pod runs (up to 4 total)
Up to 3 extra pods may run during the rollout
Rollouts are paused until maxUnavailable is raised above 0
explain: maxUnavailable: 0 means the controller never takes a desired pod offline voluntarily — new pods come up (maxSurge 1 allows one extra, 4 total) and only then do old ones terminate. (A) inverts the semantics, (C) mistakes maxSurge 1 for 100%, and (D) invents a pause — 0 is a legal, common zero-downtime setting.

q: A rollout to revision 8 is misbehaving; revision 7 was good. What is the correct rollback command, and what does it do under the hood?
options: kubectl rollout undo deployment/api — always returns to revision 7 automatically
kubectl delete replicaset api-<hash-of-8> — deleting the bad ReplicaSet rolls back
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=7 — scales the revision-7 ReplicaSet back up and the revision-8 one down, preserving the revision history
kubectl rollout pause deployment/api — pausing reverts to the previous revision
explain: --to-revision targets the known-good ReplicaSet explicitly; undo works by rescaling ReplicaSets, keeping history intact for further undos. Plain undo (A) goes to the previous revision, which isn't always 7. (B) orphans pods and fights the deployment controller, and (D) confuses pause (freezes the rollout mid-flight) with rollback.

q: A DaemonSet uses the default update strategy. During an image update, how many pods per node may be simultaneously unavailable?
options: 25% of the DaemonSet pods, like Deployments
All pods on a node at once — DaemonSets have no rolling controls
0 — DaemonSets always use the Recreate strategy
1 — DaemonSet RollingUpdate defaults maxUnavailable to 1 (an absolute number, not a percentage)
explain: DaemonSet rolling updates default to maxUnavailable: 1 — a plain count, not a percentage, so one pod at a time may be down during the update. (A) wrongly imports the Deployment 25% default. (B) ignores the strategy controls that exist, and (C) invents a Recreate default — DaemonSets do support RollingUpdate (and OnDelete) with 1 as the default budget.

q: A 5-replica StatefulSet must restart all pods simultaneously after a config change, but they restart one at a time (pod-0, then pod-1, ...). Which field changes this, and what is the trade-off?
options: podManagementPolicy: Parallel — starts/stops all pods concurrently instead of the default OrderedReady sequential rollout; you lose the ordered, one-at-a-time safety
updateStrategy: Recreate — deletes all pods first
partition: 0 — forces all pods to update at once
podManagementPolicy applies only to Deployments, so this behavior cannot be changed on StatefulSets
explain: OrderedReady (default) brings pods up strictly in ordinal order, waiting for each to be Ready; Parallel removes the ordering for speed. The trade-off is real: parallel restarts can violate quorum/leader-election assumptions the ordering protected. (B) names a Deployment strategy that doesn't exist for StatefulSets (they use RollingUpdate/OnDelete), (C) misuses partition (which pins ordinals >= N to the old version), and (D) is flatly wrong about the field's scope.

q: A PV has persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain. The bound PVC is deleted. What is the PV's state and the data's fate?
options: The PV is deleted immediately along with the data — Retain only delays deletion by the termination grace period
The PV goes to Released, the data is preserved, and the PV cannot be bound again until an admin clears spec.claimRef (then it becomes Available)
The PV is automatically recycled and bound to the next pending PVC
The PV stays Bound forever, leaking the storage
explain: Retain keeps the volume and its data after the claim is deleted; the PV sits in Released with a stale claimRef, and rebinding requires manually removing that claimRef. (A) describes Delete, (C) describes the long-removed Recycle policy, and (D) misstates the phase — it transitions to Released, not stuck Bound, precisely so an admin can inspect and reclaim it.

q: You create a Service with ports but no selector, intending to point it at an external appliance. kubectl get endpoints shows <none>. What must you do, and why?
options: Add a selector — Services without selectors are invalid and never get endpoints
Manually create an Endpoints (or EndpointSlice) object with the same name — without a selector there is no endpoints controller syncing pod IPs, so you supply the addresses yourself
Change the type to ExternalName — selectorless services only work as ExternalName
Wait — endpoints for selectorless services are created after the first DNS lookup
explain: The endpoints controller only populates Endpoints for Services with selectors; a selectorless Service is the documented pattern for custom endpoints, but you must create the Endpoints object yourself with the matching name. (A) is wrong — selectorless Services are valid. (C) conflates two different patterns (ExternalName needs no ports/endpoints at all), and (D) invents lazy endpoint creation.

q: A Service defines port: 80, targetPort: 8080. The container actually listens on 8080, but clients get connection refused. The container logs show it never receives traffic. What is the most likely misconfiguration?
options: port and targetPort are swapped in meaning — port is the container port and targetPort is the service port
Nothing is wrong with the Service — connection refused means the container's readiness probe is failing

The port/targetPort pair is correct; the refusal likely comes from the container listening on 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, or a selector mismatch — verify the pod actually listens on all interfaces and the endpoints exist
The Service is fine; the issue is that the pod's containerPort field doesn't match — containerPort must equal targetPort or traffic is dropped
explain: port (80) is the Service's virtual port, targetPort (8080) is where kube-proxy forwards — that pairing is correct as written. containerPort is purely documentary and never gates traffic, so (D) is a myth. The real suspects with a correct Service are: the app bound to localhost inside the container (unreachable from outside its netns) or no endpoints behind the selector — check kubectl get endpoints first.

q: You set nodePort: 8080 explicitly on a NodePort Service and the API rejects it. Why?
options: 8080 is reserved for the Kubernetes API server
nodePort can only be auto-assigned, never set explicitly
NodePort services cannot specify nodePort and port at the same time
nodePort must be in the 30000–32767 range (unless the cluster's service-node-port-range is customized) — 8080 is outside it
explain: Explicit nodePorts must fall inside the configured service-node-port-range, default 30000–32767; out-of-range values are rejected at admission. (B) is wrong — explicit assignment is allowed within range. (C) invents a mutual-exclusion rule, and (A) invents a reservation (the API server default is 6443, and nodePort conflicts are about the range, not specific ports).

q: An Ingress terminates TLS for app.example.com with a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls. Which two things must be true for browsers to get a clean HTTPS connection?
options: The Secret must contain tls.crt/tls.key, and spec.tls[].hosts must include app.example.com matching the rule's host — plus the cert must actually be valid for that name
Any Opaque secret works as long as it has the cert data under any key names
The hosts entry must list the Service name, not the DNS hostname
TLS termination requires the annotation nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true" or the secret is ignored
explain: TLS Secrets use the fixed keys tls.crt and tls.key (type kubernetes.io/tls), and the tls.hosts list selects which SNI hostnames get this certificate — it must cover the rule's host with a genuinely valid cert. (B) is wrong: key names are fixed, not freeform. (C) confuses hosts (DNS names) with backend service names, and (D) confuses the redirect annotation (HTTP→HTTPS redirect) with termination itself.

q: You apply an Ingress with rules but no ingressClassName, in a cluster where no IngressClass is marked default. The Ingress gets no address and serves nothing. Why?
options: Ingress is deprecated — you must use the Gateway API instead
Without ingressClassName (and no default class), ingress controllers that watch only their own class ignore the Ingress — nothing implements it
The Ingress needs a loadBalancerIP to get an address
Rules without ingressClassName are rejected by the API server
explain: Controllers reconcile only Ingresses naming their class (or all, if they watch unclassed ones); with no class set and no default, a class-scoped controller like nginx simply ignores it — the Ingress is valid but unimplemented. (A) is wrong: Ingress is GA/frozen, not removed. (C) invents a required field, and (D) is wrong — the API accepts classless Ingresses happily.

q: You need the last 20 lines of logs from every pod labeled app=web, with each line prefixed by its pod name. Which command does this in one shot?
options: kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=20 — aggregates automatically across the selector
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=20 --prefix=true — selector-based multi-pod logs with pod-name prefixes
kubectl logs --all-pods --tail=20
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=20 -c web — the -c flag enables multi-pod mode
explain: -l selects all matching pods and streams their logs together; --prefix adds the pod (and container) name to each line so the merged stream stays attributable. Plain -l (A) works but without prefixes the lines are unattributable. (C) invents a flag, and (D) misreads -c, which selects a container within pods, not multi-pod mode.

q: You want only Warning events, newest first, across the namespace. Which command is correct?
options: kubectl describe events --filter=Warning
kubectl get events | grep Warning | sort -k5
kubectl get events --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events --selector type=Warning --order=newest
explain: --field-selector filters server-side on the type field, and --sort-by orders by the timestamp field — the precise, scriptable combo. (B) is a client-side hack that breaks on wrapped columns, (A) invents a describe subcommand/flag, and (D) invents --selector/--order flags that don't exist for events.

q: You run kubectl create -f svc.yaml twice. The second run fails with 'AlreadyExists'. Your colleague runs kubectl apply -f svc.yaml repeatedly with no errors. What is the underlying difference?
options: create is broken in recent kubectl versions — always use apply
create requires --save-config on the second run to succeed
apply deletes and recreates the object each time, which is why it never conflicts
create is a pure create-only call that errors if the object exists; apply does a declarative three-way merge and is idempotent, so repeats are safe
explain: create maps to a POST that fails when the object exists; apply computes a patch (using the last-applied annotation) and is safe to repeat — the core imperative-vs-declarative distinction the exam probes constantly. (A) is nonsense, (C) describes replace --force, not apply, and (B) invents a flag requirement (--save-config mattered for old apply flows, not for create retries).

q: In a CI pipeline you must block until a Job named migration completes, timing out after 5 minutes. Which command expresses exactly that?
options: kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/migration --timeout=300s — waits for the Complete condition with a bounded timeout
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready job/migration --timeout=300s
kubectl get job migration -w | grep Complete
kubectl logs job/migration --follow and watch for the last line
explain: Jobs expose a Complete condition (and Failed); kubectl wait --for=condition=complete blocks until it appears or the timeout hits — the scriptable gate. (B) uses Ready, a pod condition Jobs don't publish. (C) and (D) are fragile watch-the-stream hacks with no timeout semantics and ambiguous completion detection.

q: You run kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80 from your laptop, then a teammate on another machine tries to reach your laptop's port 8080 and can't connect. Why?
options: port-forward only works for pods, not services
kubectl port-forward binds to 127.0.0.1 by default — it is only reachable from your own machine unless you pass --address 0.0.0.0 (and consider the security implications)
The teammate must use the service's clusterIP, not your laptop's IP
port-forward requires --address to be set even for local use
explain: By default port-forward listens on localhost only; remote machines can't reach it without --address 0.0.0.0 (which exposes it on all interfaces — a deliberate security default). (A) is wrong: svc/ targets are supported. (C) misunderstands the topology — the forward originates at your laptop. (D) inverts the default: local use needs no flag.

q: A PodSecurity admission policy requires a seccomp profile on every pod. Which pod-level setting satisfies 'use the container runtime's default profile' without shipping a custom profile file?
options: seccompProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: default.json}
securityContext: {seccompProfile: null} — null means 'use defaults'
seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} — the kubelet applies the runtime's default seccomp profile; Localhost would require a profile file present on every node
Omitting seccompProfile entirely — the kubelet always applies RuntimeDefault when the field is absent
explain: type: RuntimeDefault selects the CRI runtime's built-in default profile — no files to distribute. Localhost (A) references a JSON profile that must exist on the node's filesystem, an operational burden. (B) invents null semantics, and (D) is wrong: an absent seccompProfile means the container runs unconfined (or per-runtime default behavior), not the Kubernetes RuntimeDefault — you must set it explicitly to satisfy the policy.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod sets securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true, but its image has no USER directive (runs as root by default). What happens at pod startup?
options: The container starts as root anyway — runAsNonRoot is advisory
The image's default user is remapped to UID 65534 automatically
The pod is admitted but the container runs with reduced capabilities instead
The kubelet refuses to start the container — with runAsNonRoot: true and no non-root user configured (via runAsUser or image USER), startup fails the validation
explain: runAsNonRoot is enforced, not advisory: if the effective UID would be 0, the kubelet fails the container with a 'container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root' error. The fix is setting runAsUser to a non-zero UID or building the image with USER. (A) treats it as a hint, (B) invents automatic remapping, and (C) invents a capabilities fallback — none happen.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You need a sidecar to read the pod's labels without RBAC calls to the API server. Which downwardAPI approach works, and what is its update behavior?
options: A downwardAPI volume with items mapping metadata.labels to a file — the kubelet projects labels/annotations into files and refreshes them on its sync loop when they change
Downward API can only expose the pod name and namespace, never labels
Labels are only available via environment variables, which never update
Mounting labels requires a projected service account token volume
explain: The downwardAPI volume can project metadata.labels, metadata.annotations, name, namespace, and more into files, and the kubelet keeps them refreshed (same eventual-consistency as ConfigMap volumes). (B) understates the field list — labels and annotations are supported. (C) is half-true for env but ignores the volume path, and (D) confuses projected token volumes with the downwardAPI projection.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod mounts an emptyDir with medium: Memory for a high-throughput cache, with no memory limits set on the container. Under load the node starts evicting pods. What is the mechanism?
options: tmpfs emptyDir has a fixed 1Gi cap and the cache hit it

medium: Memory mounts a tmpfs backed by node RAM/swap, and its usage counts against the container's memory — with no limit set, the pod is Burstable/BestEffort and becomes an eviction candidate under node memory pressure
emptyDir with medium Memory is stored on disk, so disk pressure caused the eviction
The kubelet never evicts pods for emptyDir usage — the evictions must be CPU-related
explain: medium: Memory means tmpfs: fast, but every byte counts against the container's memory usage and therefore against node memory pressure accounting. Without a memory limit the pod can't be Guaranteed and is evictable when the node is squeezed. (A) invents a 1Gi cap (sizeLimit is optional), (C) reverses the medium semantics — Memory is RAM, not disk — and (D) denies the documented accounting.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A DaemonSet mounts a hostPath for node logs. On some nodes the /var/log/app directory doesn't exist yet. Which hostPath type handles both cases correctly?
options: type: Directory — it creates the directory if missing
type: File — it works for directories too
type: DirectoryOrCreate — mounts if the directory exists, creates it (as a directory) if it doesn't; plain Directory fails when the path is absent
hostPath always creates missing paths regardless of type
explain: DirectoryOrCreate is the tolerant variant: use the existing directory or create it. Plain Directory (A) errors when the path doesn't exist — the exam trap. (B) is wrong: File expects a file, and mounting a directory as File fails. (D) overgeneralizes: only the *OrCreate variants create anything.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: An httpGet liveness probe hits /healthz. During deploys the endpoint briefly returns 301 redirects, and pods restart. The app team insists 301 is healthy. Who is right per the probe contract?
options: The app team — redirects prove the server is alive, so the kubelet follows them
The kubelet treats any 3xx as failure — only 200 is success
The kubelet treats HTTP 200–399 as success, so a 301 passes the probe — the restarts must have another cause (e.g. the redirect target failing, or timeouts)
httpGet probes require the exact body 'ok' regardless of status code
explain: The kubelet counts any status in 200–399 as probe success and does not follow redirects — a 301 alone cannot fail the probe. So the restarts come from elsewhere: timeouts, connection errors, or 5xx from the redirect chain. (A) is wrong about following redirects (it doesn't), (B) narrows success to 200 only, and (D) invents a body check httpGet never performs.

q: A Job sets ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 120. It completes successfully at 10:00:00. What happens and when?
options: The Job is deleted immediately at completion — the TTL only applies to failed Jobs
The finished Job (and its pods, via cascading deletion) is automatically deleted around 10:02:00 — the TTL controller cleans up completed Jobs after the delay
The TTL is ignored unless backoffLimit is also set
The pods are deleted at 10:02:00 but the Job object is kept forever for audit
explain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished schedules automatic deletion of the finished Job after the delay, and the Job's pods are cascade-deleted with it — the standard finished-Job hygiene. (A) invents a success/failure split (the TTL applies to both), (C) invents a backoffLimit dependency, and (D) splits the cleanup that actually happens together.

q: A CronJob nightly-backup runs at 2 AM. You need to run it once right now to validate a config change, without altering the schedule. What is the correct command?
options: kubectl create job manual-test --from=cronjob/nightly-backup — instantiates a one-off Job from the CronJob's jobTemplate
kubectl run manual-test --image=<same image> — equivalent and simpler
kubectl rollout restart cronjob/nightly-backup — triggers an immediate run
Edit the schedule to '* * * * *' temporarily, then change it back
explain: --from=cronjob/<name> clones the CronJob's jobTemplate into a standalone Job — the exact template, one run, schedule untouched. (B) hand-rolls a pod and loses the template's env/volumes/resources. (C) invents rollout support for CronJobs, and (D) is the risky hack: editing the live schedule can fire unintended runs and race the controller.

q: A busy CronJob's namespace is filling with old Job objects. Which defaults govern how many finished Jobs are kept, and how do you keep fewer?
options: successfulJobsHistoryLimit defaults to 3, failedJobsHistoryLimit defaults to 1 — lower them (even to 0) to keep fewer
CronJobs keep all history by default — set the limits to enable pruning
History is governed by ttlSecondsAfterFinished, which defaults to 3600
Old Jobs are never pruned — you must delete them by hand
explain: The CronJob controller prunes finished Jobs to the history limits: 3 successful and 1 failed by default; setting either to 0 keeps none of that class. (B) is wrong — defaults exist and prune automatically. (C) confuses the optional Job TTL (a different cleanup mechanism, unset by default) with history limits, and (D) ignores the built-in pruning.

q: A container's preStop hook flushes buffers to disk, but during node drains the flush is cut off mid-write. The hook needs ~20s; terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30s. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: preStop hooks are best-effort and may be skipped entirely — move the flush to a sidecar
The preStop hook runs after SIGTERM, so the app is already dead — hooks must be postStart instead

preStop must complete within the grace period or the kubelet sends SIGKILL when it expires — the drain likely used a shorter grace period override, or the hook plus app shutdown exceeded it; raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds and ensure drains honor it
preStop only runs on kubectl delete, not on drains — this is expected
explain: preStop runs before SIGTERM and blocks termination, but only until terminationGracePeriodSeconds expires — then SIGKILL ends everything mid-flush. Drains can also pass a shorter --grace-period. The fix is sizing the grace period to cover hook + app shutdown. (A) is wrong: preStop is synchronous, not best-effort. (B) reverses the order (preStop precedes SIGTERM), and (D) invents a delete-only trigger — preStop fires on any pod termination.

q: Two PVs match a PVC's class and access modes. You must bind the PVC to pv-data-2 specifically (it holds the legacy dataset). How?
options: Label the PV and use nodeSelector on the PVC
Set spec.volumeName: pv-data-2 on the PVC — the claim pre-binds to that PV instead of letting the binder choose
Rename the PV to match the PVC name — binding is by name convention
Delete pv-data-1 so only pv-data-2 remains available
explain: spec.volumeName on the PVC pins the binding to that exact PV (it must still satisfy class/mode/capacity). (A) confuses PV binding with pod scheduling (nodeSelector is a pod field). (C) invents name-convention binding, and (D) is the destructive workaround — volumeName exists precisely to avoid it.

q: After resizing a PVC from 10Gi to 20Gi, kubectl describe pvc shows the condition FileSystemResizePending and the PV already reports 20Gi. The pod using it is running. What does this condition mean?
options: The resize failed — the condition indicates an error that requires recreating the PVC

The block device is expanded but the filesystem inside hasn't been grown yet — the kubelet completes filesystem expansion when a pod is using the PVC (online for drivers/filesystems that support it), then clears the condition
The StorageClass needs allowVolumeExpansion added retroactively before the condition clears
The pod must be deleted — FileSystemResizePending never clears on a running pod
