explain: FileSystemResizePending is a normal intermediate state: controller-side expansion is done (PV shows 20Gi), and the kubelet now grows the filesystem — online while the pod runs if the driver/filesystem supports it, otherwise at next pod start. (A) misreads a progress condition as an error, (C) is too late (the class gate was already passed — the PV grew), and (D) is wrong for online-capable drivers, which clear it without restarts.

q: A pod needs /etc/app/config.yaml from a ConfigMap but must not hide the other files already in /etc/app. Which mount achieves this, and what is its update caveat?
options: Mount the ConfigMap at /etc/app with subPath: config.yaml — the single file lands without masking the directory; caveat: subPath mounts don't receive ConfigMap updates
Mount the whole ConfigMap at /etc/app/config.yaml directly — Kubernetes merges the files
Use envFrom — it writes files into /etc/app
Mount at /etc/app; Kubernetes always merges volume content with existing directory content
explain: subPath mounts one key as one file at the given path, leaving sibling files intact — the standard trick for injecting a single config file into a populated directory. Its documented caveat: subPath mounts skip the kubelet's atomic update, so ConfigMap edits won't propagate. (B) is invalid (mountPath must be a directory for whole-volume mounts; mounting a volume 'at a file' without subPath fails), (C) confuses env injection with files, and (D) is wrong — a volume mount masks the underlying directory.

q: You create an HPA targeting CPU utilization for a Deployment whose containers set no resources.requests. The HPA shows <unknown> for current CPU and never scales. Why?
options: HPA requires requests to compute utilization as usage/requests — without requests the percentage is undefined; set cpu requests on the containers
HPA only works with memory, not CPU
The HPA needs the metrics-server in the same namespace as the Deployment
<unknown> means the pods are idle — HPA will scale once traffic arrives
explain: Utilization-type HPA targets divide actual usage by the requested amount; with no requests there's no denominator, so the HPA can't compute a percentage and reports <unknown>. Setting requests fixes it. (B) is flatly wrong (CPU is the classic HPA metric), (C) invents a namespace co-location rule, and (D) misreads <unknown> — it's a configuration gap, not idleness.

q: Which imperative command creates an HPA scaling a Deployment between 2 and 6 replicas at 70% CPU, and what object does it create?
options: kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=2 --max=6 --cpu-percent=70 — creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler object
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=2-6 --cpu=70%
kubectl create hpa web --min=2 --max=6 --cpu-percent=70
kubectl autoscale can only target StatefulSets, not Deployments
explain: kubectl autoscale is the imperative HPA generator: it creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler with min/max replicas and the CPU utilization target (default target kind Deployment when you name one). (B) invents a scale-with-range syntax — scale sets an absolute replica count. (C) invents a create subcommand that doesn't exist, and (D) invents a target restriction — Deployments are the most common HPA target.

q: You need 'no pod in namespace api accepts ingress traffic unless explicitly allowed' as a baseline. Which NetworkPolicy expresses a default-deny ingress for the whole namespace?
options: A policy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress] and no ingress rules — the empty selector matches all pods, and no rules means deny all
A policy with podSelector: {matchLabels: {}} and an ingress rule with an empty from:
NetworkPolicies can't express default-deny — you need a ServiceMesh
A policy with policyTypes: [Egress] only — that denies ingress too
explain: podSelector: {} selects every pod in the namespace; policyTypes: [Ingress] with zero ingress rules isolates all of them from incoming traffic (egress stays open unless also listed). (B) is wrong: an ingress rule with empty from: actually allows all sources — the opposite. (C) denies a bread-and-butter NetworkPolicy use case, and (D) confuses direction: Egress-only policies leave ingress untouched.

q: A NetworkPolicy allows egress to the database pods and to cluster DNS on port 53. Pods reach the database fine, but every DNS lookup times out. The DNS egress rule specifies port: 53 with no protocol field. What is wrong?
options: NetworkPolicy cannot filter DNS traffic — the timeouts must come from CoreDNS itself
DNS requires an ingress rule back from kube-dns — egress-only rules break the reply path
The rule must use port 5353 — 53 is the inbound CoreDNS port, not the query port
The rule allows only TCP 53 (the default protocol) — DNS queries go over UDP first, so add protocol: UDP (or a second rule) for port 53
explain: Port rules default to TCP when protocol is omitted, but DNS resolution primarily uses UDP 53 (falling back to TCP only for large/truncated responses) — so the 'allow DNS' rule allowed the wrong protocol and all UDP queries died. The fix is an explicit protocol: UDP rule. (A) is wrong: DNS is ordinary UDP/TCP traffic and is absolutely filtered. (B) invents an ingress-reply requirement (established traffic isn't separately policed), and (C) invents a port number.

q: From a pod, curl db works but curl db.prod.svc.cluster.local also works while curl db.prod.svc.cluster.local. (trailing dot) behaves differently in a packet capture. What does the trailing dot change?
options: The trailing dot makes it a fully-qualified name — the resolver skips the ndots:5 search-domain expansion and queries the name as-is
The trailing dot forces TCP instead of UDP for the DNS query
The trailing dot selects the SRV record instead of the A record
Nothing — trailing dots are stripped by CoreDNS before processing
explain: A trailing dot marks the name as absolute (FQDN): the stub resolver bypasses the search list (svc.cluster.local, etc.) that ndots:5 would otherwise trigger for short names. That's why packet captures differ — fewer queries. (B) confuses name syntax with transport, (C) confuses it with record-type selection (_tcp prefixes do that), and (D) is wrong: the dot is semantically meaningful to the resolver.

q: A StatefulSet of etcd needs each member to discover its peers via DNS before any member is Ready. The headless Service uses the default settings and dig returns only ready pods. Which Service field fixes peer discovery?
options: publishNotReadyAddresses: true — includes not-yet-ready pods in DNS/endpoint records so peers can find each other during bootstrap
sessionAffinity: ClientIP — pins discovery traffic per client
externalTrafficPolicy: Local — preserves source IPs for discovery
clusterIP: None is not enough; you must also set type: Headless
explain: Endpoints (and thus headless DNS) normally include only ready addresses; publishNotReadyAddresses: true publishes unready pods too — the standard etcd/ZooKeeper/Kafka bootstrap requirement. (B) is about stickiness, irrelevant to discovery. (C) concerns external traffic source IP, not DNS membership. (D) invents a type value — clusterIP: None IS the headless mechanism; there is no type: Headless.

q: A stateful web app keeps per-client in-memory carts, and users lose carts when kube-proxy rebalances them across pods. Which Service setting preserves client-to-pod stickiness, and what is its scope?
options: sessionAffinity: ClientIP — routes a client IP to the same backend pod consistently (best-effort, with a configurable timeout)
externalTrafficPolicy: Local — pins clients to pods on their node
publishNotReadyAddresses: true — keeps the client on the same pod
Change the Service type to LoadBalancer — cloud LBs are always sticky
explain: sessionAffinity: ClientIP gives kube-proxy client-IP-based stickiness (sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds tunes it) — the built-in answer to in-memory session state. (B) preserves source IP for external traffic, it doesn't pin backends. (C) is about DNS/endpoints for unready pods, unrelated. (D) is wrong twice: stickiness isn't a type property, and cloud LBs aren't sticky by default either.

q: kubectl exec -it web -- /bin/bash fails with 'executable file not found in $PATH' although the pod is Running. What is the situation and the CKAD-appropriate workaround?
options: The pod is crashing — exec only works on ready pods
The image is distroless/minimal with no shell — use kubectl debug -it web --image=busybox --target=web to attach an ephemeral debug container sharing the target's process namespace
exec requires the containerPort to be declared — add it and retry
Use kubectl attach instead — attach works without a shell in the image
explain: Minimal images (distroless) ship no shell, so there's nothing to exec — the pod itself is fine. kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container with your chosen troubleshooting image alongside the target (--target shares its process namespace). (A) is wrong: exec works on running-but-unready containers too. (C) repeats the containerPort myth, and (D) is wrong: attach connects to the main process's stdio, it doesn't conjure a shell.

q: You run kubectl rollout restart deployment/api with no manifest changes. What happens, and why does the Deployment roll?
options: Nothing — without template changes the command is a no-op
The Deployment scales to zero and back — restart is implemented as scale-down/up
kubectl adds/updates a kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation on the pod template, which changes the template hash and triggers a rolling update with identical containers
It deletes all pods simultaneously and recreates them
explain: rollout restart stamps the restartedAt annotation into the pod template; any template change — even annotation-only — creates a new ReplicaSet and rolls. That's the sanctioned way to bounce pods for ConfigMap/Secret env changes without editing the manifest. (A) misses the annotation mechanism, (B) describes a manual scale dance, and (D) describes Recreate strategy, not what restart does.

q: You delete a Job with kubectl delete job payroll. What happens to its pods?
options: They are deleted too — Job deletion cascades to its pods by default (foreground cascading deletion)
They are orphaned and keep running — Jobs never cascade
They are orphaned only if you pass --cascade=orphan; default is orphan for Jobs
The pods are deleted but the Job object is kept for history
explain: kubectl delete defaults to foreground cascading deletion: dependents (the Job's pods) are removed along with the owner. --cascade=orphan exists for the opposite behavior. (B) and (C) invert the default — orphaning is opt-in, not default. (D) invents selective retention; if you want history you keep the Job and let TTL/history limits manage it.

q: A production pod's app container is misbehaving but you must not restart it. You need strace and curl inside its network namespace right now. Which command does this without touching the running container?
options: kubectl exec -it pod/app -- strace — runs inside the existing container
kubectl debug -it pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app — adds an ephemeral container sharing the target container's namespaces (process, network) without restarting anything
kubectl cp the binaries into the container, then exec them
Ephemeral containers require pod recreation — instead delete and recreate the pod with a debug image
explain: kubectl debug with --target spins up an ephemeral container in the same pod sharing the target's process (and pod's network) namespace — full observability with zero disruption to the app container. (A) fails if the tools aren't in the image (that's the whole problem). (C) mutates the running container's filesystem, and (D) is wrong: ephemeral containers are the mechanism designed to avoid exactly that recreation.

q: kubectl cp /tmp/report.txt web:/tmp/report.txt fails with 'tar: not found' style errors. What is the requirement, and the workaround for images without it?
options: kubectl cp requires tar inside the container image — for images without tar, use kubectl exec with redirection (e.g. kubectl exec -i web -- sh -c 'cat > /tmp/report.txt' < /tmp/report.txt) or a debug container
kubectl cp only works for directories, not files
The destination directory must be an emptyDir volume
kubectl cp requires the pod to be in the same namespace as your kubectl context's default
explain: kubectl cp shells out to tar on both ends to stream the file tree — no tar in the image, no copy. The workarounds are exec-with-stdin-redirection or a debug container carrying tar. (B) is wrong: cp handles files and directories. (C) invents a volume-type requirement, and (D) invents a namespace restriction — cp takes -n like everything else.

q: A node gets a new taint: dedicated=gpu:NoExecute. A running pod on that node has no tolerations at all. What happens to the pod?
options: Nothing — NoExecute only affects scheduling of new pods, like NoSchedule
The pod keeps running but is never rescheduled there again
The pod is evicted after the default 300s toleration grace period
The pod is evicted immediately — NoExecute evicts existing non-tolerating pods, and with no tolerationSeconds the eviction is immediate
explain: NoExecute is the only taint effect that evicts running pods; without a matching toleration the pod is removed right away (tolerationSeconds, when set, grants a grace window — unset means zero). (A) describes NoSchedule, (B) invents a keep-running-but-tainted state, and (C) invents a 300s default — there is no default grace; immediate is immediate.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A teammate creates a second PriorityClass with globalDefault: true, saying 'every team should have their own default.' What happens?
options: The API rejects it — only one PriorityClass in the cluster may have globalDefault: true; pods without priorityClassName get priority 0 (or the single global default's value)
Both are accepted and pods without a class get the higher of the two values
Both are accepted and pods without a class get the lower of the two values
The second one silently overwrites the first as the default
explain: globalDefault is cluster-singleton by API validation — a second one is rejected. Pods naming no PriorityClass get priority 0 unless exactly one global default exists, in which case they inherit its value. (B) and (C) invent merge semantics, and (D) invents silent replacement — the API fails the create instead.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You try to create a PriorityClass with value: 2000000000 for a 'galaxy-critical' tier. What happens?
options: It is accepted — PriorityClass values have no upper bound
It is rejected — user PriorityClass values are capped at 1,000,000,000; values above that are reserved for system classes like system-node-critical (2000001000)
It is accepted but treated as 1000000000 silently
Values above 1 billion are allowed only with preemptionPolicy: Never
explain: The API caps PriorityClass value at 1 billion (1,000,000,000); higher values are rejected because the 2-billion range is reserved for system classes (system-node-critical at 2000001000, system-cluster-critical at 2000000000). (A) ignores the documented ceiling, (C) invents silent clamping, and (D) invents a preemption-policy exception that doesn't exist.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod in namespace team-a references imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}] where regcred exists only in namespace team-b. The pod's image is private. What happens?
options: The kubelet finds regcred cluster-wide — secrets are visible across namespaces for pulls
The pod falls back to anonymous pull automatically
Image pull fails — imagePullSecrets must exist in the pod's own namespace; create the secret in team-a (e.g. re-run kubectl create secret docker-registry there)
The secret is copied automatically on first use
explain: Secrets are namespace-scoped, and imagePullSecrets resolve only in the pod's namespace — a cross-namespace reference fails the pull with an auth error. The fix is creating the docker-registry secret in team-a. (A) invents cluster-wide secret visibility, (B) invents an anonymous fallback (private registries reject it), and (D) invents auto-copying that Kubernetes never does.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ConfigMap must carry a small binary license file (non-UTF8 bytes). What is the correct field, and how do text fields handle encoding?
options: Put it in data: — Kubernetes base64-encodes data values automatically
Use binaryData: for the non-UTF8 file (values are base64-encoded); data: values must be UTF-8 strings, exposed to containers as UTF-8 files
Binary content is not allowed in ConfigMaps — use a Secret instead
Store it with a .bin suffix in the key name — the suffix triggers binary handling
explain: binaryData exists exactly for non-UTF8 payloads (values supplied base64-encoded); data is UTF-8 strings only, and mounted files are written as UTF-8. (A) is wrong: data values are not base64-encoded (that's Secrets). (C) is wrong — binaryData is the sanctioned path, no Secret needed. (D) invents suffix-triggered behavior; the field name, not the key name, decides.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: An Indexed Job has completions: 4. How do the pods know which work item to process, and how is completion tracked?
options: Pods are named job-0..job-3 explicitly and the Job completes when those names all exist
Each pod gets the annotation batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index (0 to 3) and hostname <job>-<index>; the Job completes when every index has one successful pod
The Job controller passes the index as the first CLI argument automatically
Indexed mode is just a label — completion is tracked by counting successful pods like NonIndexed
explain: With completionMode: Indexed, each pod carries its index in the batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index annotation (and hostname), letting the workload shard by index; the Job is complete only when each index 0..3 has succeeded. (A) invents explicit naming control, (C) invents automatic CLI injection (you read the annotation/downward API yourself), and (D) denies the mode's whole purpose.

q: You create a Job with spec.suspend: true. What is the observable effect, and how do you start it?
options: The Job starts immediately — suspend is only meaningful on CronJobs
No pods are created until you set suspend: false (e.g. kubectl patch job/<name> --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}') — the Job waits in suspended state
The Job is created in Failed state and must be recreated
Suspended Jobs are deleted after the activeDeadlineSeconds expires
explain: suspend: true tells the Job controller to create no pods; the Job sits Suspended until unsuspended via patch/edit, then proceeds normally. (A) is wrong — suspend is a first-class Job field (used for staging Jobs and CronJob-spawned runs alike). (C) invents a Failed state, and (D) invents TTL behavior tied to the deadline.

q: A Job's pods keep failing on a flaky external API. With the default backoffLimit, how many pod failures are tolerated before the Job is marked Failed, and what spaces the retries?
options: 3 failures, retried immediately in a tight loop
1 failure — any pod failure fails the Job immediately by default
Unlimited — Jobs retry forever unless activeDeadlineSeconds is set
6 failures, with exponential backoff between retries (10s, 20s, 40s... capped at 6 minutes)
explain: backoffLimit defaults to 6: the Job tolerates 6 pod failures, spacing retries with exponential backoff (10s doubling, capped at six minutes) to avoid hammering the dependency. (A) understates the default, (C) confuses Jobs with Deployments' endless pod restarts, and (B) describes backoffLimit: 0, the opt-in fail-fast setting.

q: A CronJob has startingDeadlineSeconds: 120. The controller is down for 10 minutes and misses a scheduled run. When the controller recovers, what happens to that missed run?
options: It runs immediately — missed runs are always made up
It runs immediately only if suspend was true during the outage
The missed start counts as a failure against the deadline and no Job is created for it — startingDeadlineSeconds bounds how late a start may be; beyond it the run is skipped
The CronJob is permanently disabled after any missed deadline
explain: startingDeadlineSeconds sets the lateness budget: if the controller can't start the Job within 120s of schedule, that occurrence is counted as missed/failed and no Job is created for it. (A) is true only within the deadline (the 'missed Jobs scheduled immediately' behavior applies to short outages and suspend toggles). (B) invents a suspend condition, and (D) invents permanent disablement.

q: A pod runs an app container and a metrics exporter container. The exporter must be reachable at localhost:9090 from the app, and both must start in a defined order. Which statements are true?
options: Containers in a pod share the network namespace, so localhost:9090 works between them; but regular containers: entries have no startup ordering — use a native sidecar (initContainer with restartPolicy: Always) for the exporter if order matters
Each container gets its own loopback interface, so localhost never works pod-internally
containers: entries start in list order, so ordering is already guaranteed
A Service is required for any container-to-container communication in a pod
explain: Pod containers share net/IPC namespaces: localhost works, and they can share volumes — but startup order among regular containers is undefined, so an order-sensitive helper belongs in initContainers as a native sidecar. (B) denies the shared loopback, (C) invents list-order startup (that's init containers, not regular ones), and (D) is wrong: Services route to pods, they aren't needed for intra-pod traffic.

q: You need to move deployment/api to image api:2.0 imperatively and trigger a rollout. Which command does exactly this?
options: kubectl set image deployment/api api=api:2.0 — updates the container image in the pod template and rolls out a new ReplicaSet
kubectl edit deployment/api and change the image — the only way; set image doesn't exist
kubectl replace --force -f api.yaml — required for image changes
kubectl rollout restart deployment/api — restarts with the new image automatically
explain: kubectl set image patches the named container's image in the pod template, which changes the template and triggers the rolling update — the standard imperative image bump. (B) denies the subcommand's existence, (C) is overkill (replace --force deletes/recreates; image edits roll fine), and (D) only restarts existing pods with the current image — it never changes the image.

q: A Deployment uses strategy: {type: Recreate}. During an image update, what is the availability profile?
options: All existing pods are terminated before any new pods are created — simple and safe for singleton workloads, but there is downtime between the old and new sets
New pods start first, then old pods terminate — identical to RollingUpdate
Half the pods are replaced at a time — Recreate is just RollingUpdate with 50%
Recreate only works with a single replica
explain: Recreate kills the entire old ReplicaSet before creating the new one: no version mixing (good for singletons/migrations), but guaranteed downtime. (B) describes RollingUpdate, (C) invents a 50% variant, and (D) invents a replica restriction — Recreate works at any scale, it just takes everything down first.

q: Before a risky database migration, you want a crash-consistent point-in-time copy of the data volume. The cluster has a CSI driver with snapshot support. Which objects are involved?
options: Create a PersistentVolumeClaim with snapshot: true — PVCs snapshot themselves

Create a VolumeSnapshot object referencing the PVC (via source.persistentVolumeClaimName); the snapshot controller + CSI driver capture the point-in-time copy, which can later seed a new PVC via dataSource
Take an etcd snapshot — it includes all volume data
Copy the data with kubectl cp — snapshots require manual copies
explain: VolumeSnapshot is the API: it points at the source PVC, the external-snapshotter and CSI driver take the storage-level copy, and a later PVC can restore from it via spec.dataSource. (A) invents a PVC self-snapshot flag, (C) confuses etcd snapshots (cluster state only — never volume bytes), and (D) is the manual path snapshots exist to replace.

q: Two pods on the same node need read-write access to one ReadWriteOnce PVC. Is this allowed, and what does ReadWriteOnce actually restrict?
options: Forbidden — RWO means exactly one pod cluster-wide
Allowed on any nodes — RWO is just a hint and not enforced
Only allowed if the pods are in the same Deployment
Allowed — ReadWriteOnce restricts mounting to a single node, not a single pod; multiple pods on that node may mount it read-write
explain: The 'Once' in ReadWriteOnce is about nodes: the volume can be mounted read-write by one node at a time (block storage can only attach once). Pods co-located on that node share it freely. (A) over-restricts to one pod, (B) denies enforcement that the attach/detach controller performs, and (C) invents a workload-type condition.

q: A StorageClass sets volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer. A PVC using it stays Pending even though matching PVs exist, until a pod is scheduled. Why is this mode used?
options: It is the workaround for clusters without a provisioner

It delays binding (and dynamic provisioning) until a pod using the PVC is scheduled, so topology constraints (zone, node affinity) are known — avoiding a volume provisioned in a zone the pod can't reach
It speeds up binding by skipping the capacity check
Pending is a bug — WaitForFirstConsumer should bind immediately like Immediate
explain: WaitForFirstConsumer defers PV selection/provisioning until scheduling places the pod, so the binder can honor the pod's node/zone constraints — the fix for the classic 'volume provisioned in zone-a, pod scheduled in zone-b' failure of Immediate mode. (A) invents a provisioner workaround, (C) invents a skipped check, and (D) misreads the intentional Pending state as a bug.

q: A headless Service selects 2 ready pods. What do kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> and a DNS A query for the service return?
options: EndpointSlices list the pod IPs; DNS returns one A record per pod IP — the two views agree because both derive from the same ready-endpoint set
EndpointSlices are empty for headless services; DNS still returns pod IPs
EndpointSlices list the clusterIP; DNS returns the clusterIP
Both return NXDOMAIN until a ClusterIP is assigned
explain: Headless services still get EndpointSlices (the endpoints controller works off selectors, not clusterIP), listing ready pod IPs — and DNS A queries return those same pod IPs. The two are consistent views of one endpoint set. (B) wrongly empties EndpointSlices, (C) describes a normal ClusterIP service, and (D) invents a dependency on clusterIP that headless services by definition lack.

q: Which imperative command creates an Ingress routing host shop.example.com, path /api to service api:8080, and what pathType does it produce?
options: kubectl create ingress shop --rule='shop.example.com/api*=api:8080' — the trailing * produces pathType: Prefix for /api
kubectl expose deployment api --hostname=shop.example.com — creates the Ingress with pathType Exact
kubectl create ingress shop --rule='shop.example.com/api=api:8080' — produces pathType Exact
Imperative Ingress creation is not supported — write YAML
explain: kubectl create ingress --rule='HOST/PATH*=SVC:PORT' is the imperative form; the /* suffix maps to pathType: Prefix (no suffix maps to Exact). (B) invents an expose flag, (C) misstates the mapping (bare /api without * yields Exact, not Prefix), and (D) denies a real subcommand.

q: An Ingress defines two host rules but a request arrives with a Host header matching neither. What happens?
options: The request is rejected at the TCP level — no matching rule means no connection
It is routed to spec.defaultBackend if defined; otherwise the controller returns 404
It is routed to the first rule's backend alphabetically
The Ingress controller crashes — every request must match a rule
explain: Unmatched requests fall through to spec.defaultBackend (the catch-all); with no default backend the controller answers 404. (A) confuses L7 routing with TCP rejection, (C) invents alphabetical fallback, and (D) is nonsense — non-matching traffic is routine (scans, wrong Host headers) and handled gracefully.

q: You change a Service from type ClusterIP to type LoadBalancer. Which statements about the resulting Service are true?
options: It keeps its clusterIP and also gets a nodePort on every node, plus the cloud load balancer — LoadBalancer builds on NodePort builds on ClusterIP
The clusterIP is removed — LoadBalancer replaces it entirely
No nodePort is allocated — cloud LBs bypass node ports
The change requires deleting and recreating the Service — type is immutable
explain: Service types nest: LoadBalancer = ClusterIP + NodePort + external LB (unless you opt out via allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false). The clusterIP stays for in-cluster traffic and each node gets a nodePort the LB forwards to. (B) wrongly drops the clusterIP, (C) denies the nodePort the cloud LB actually targets, and (D) is wrong — type is mutable on update for this transition.

q: A pod with IP 10.244.1.5 in namespace prod needs its DNS name for a peer that resolves pod IPs directly. What is the pod's DNS A record name (default cluster domain)?
options: 10.244.1.5.prod.pod.cluster.local — dots are kept as-is
pod-10-244-1-5.prod.pod.cluster.local — IPs get a pod- prefix
10-244-1-5.prod.pod.cluster.local — dots in the IP are replaced with dashes
Pods don't get DNS A records — only Services do
explain: Pod IPs are published under <ip-with-dashes>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local — dots become dashes because dots are DNS label separators. (A) keeps dots, producing invalid labels. (B) invents a pod- prefix. (D) is wrong: pods do get A records in the .pod subdomain (used by headless-service peer discovery).

q: You need logs from the last 10 minutes with timestamps for a postmortem. Which flags compose this correctly?
options: kubectl logs web --since=10m --timestamps — time-bounded logs with per-line timestamps
kubectl logs web --tail=10m --timestamps
kubectl logs web --since-time=10m
kubectl logs web --previous --timestamps=10m
explain: --since=10m bounds the window to the last ten minutes and --timestamps prepends RFC3339 timestamps to each line — the postmortem combo. (B) misuses --tail (line count, not duration), (C) misuses --since-time (needs an RFC3339 timestamp, not a duration), and (D) misuses --previous (previous container instance) with a bogus timestamps value.

q: kubectl top pod shows a pod using 900Mi against a 100Mi memory request (900% utilization). The node has 8Gi free. Is the pod in danger, and what does the percentage actually mean?
options: The pod will be OOM-killed immediately — utilization over 100% is fatal

The percentage is usage ÷ request (scheduling reservation), not usage ÷ limit — the pod is fine unless it breaches its memory limit; but the 9x ratio signals a badly under-set request that will mislead the scheduler and HPA
The node will evict the pod for exceeding its request
kubectl top percentages are usage ÷ node capacity
explain: top's percentage divides by the request — a scheduling-time reservation, not a runtime ceiling. Only the limit triggers OOM kills; exceeding requests just means the pod uses unreserved headroom (fine on a quiet node). But 900% means the request lied to the scheduler (bin-packing, QoS, HPA math all skew). (A) confuses request with limit, (C) invents request-based eviction, and (D) misstates the denominator.

q: A pod is stuck Pending. Which single command surfaces the scheduler's reason (e.g. Insufficient cpu, unbound PVC, untolerated taint) fastest?
options: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler — read the scheduler logs
kubectl describe pod <name> — the Events section carries the scheduler's FailedScheduling messages with the specific reason
kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml — the reason is in spec.schedulerName
kubectl top node — pending reasons show as resource pressure there
explain: describe's Events section aggregates the FailedScheduling events with human-readable reasons (insufficient CPU, persistentvolumeclaim not found, taints) — the fastest diagnostic. (A) works but means digging through component logs. (C) points at the wrong field (schedulerName just names the scheduler), and (D) shows node usage, not why this pod can't schedule.

q: You want to validate a manifest against the API server (catching schema errors and admission rejections) without creating anything. Which flag does this?
options: kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f app.yaml — validates against the API server
--dry-run=server — sends the object to the API server for full validation including admission webhooks, but does not persist it
kubectl create --validate=false — validates without persisting
kubectl diff -f app.yaml — validates the schema server-side
explain: --dry-run=server submits the object through the API server's validation and admission chain without persisting it — catching what client-side validation misses (CRD schemas, webhooks, quota). --dry-run=client (A) only checks locally. (C) does the opposite of validating (it skips validation), and (D) diffs against live state rather than validating the object itself.

q: You need to check whether the CI service account can create deployments in namespace staging, without using its actual credentials. Which command answers this?
options: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:builder -n staging — impersonates the SA for an authorization check; no real credentials needed
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n staging — checks your own permissions, which answers it if you share the SA's roles
Look at the CI pod's mounted token and decode it — the token lists allowed verbs
RBAC can't be queried — you must attempt the create and watch for Forbidden
explain: auth can-i with --as impersonates the service account for a SubjectAccessReview — the exact 'what can X do' query, no credentials required. (B) checks your own rights, which proves nothing about the SA. (C) is wrong: tokens carry identity, not the permission set (that's RoleBindings). (D) ignores the discovery API built for this — trial-and-error is the slow path.

q: The team wants Vault secrets mounted into pods with no PVCs and no Kubernetes Secrets — the volume should live and die with the pod, defined entirely in the pod spec. The cluster runs the Secrets Store CSI driver. Which volume stanza does this, and what must the CSIDriver declare?
options: volumes: [{name: vault, csi: {driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io, volumeAttributes: {secretProviderClass: vault-tls}}}] — inline CSI ephemeral volumes are declared in the pod spec and follow the pod lifecycle; the CSIDriver must list Ephemeral in volumeLifecycleModes
Create a PVC with storageClassName: secrets-store and reference it — inline CSI volumes still require a PersistentVolumeClaim
Use an emptyDir plus a sidecar that fetches the secrets — CSI drivers cannot be referenced inline in a pod spec
volumeAttributes are admin-only; end users can never pass them in a pod spec
explain: CSI ephemeral inline volumes (GA since 1.25) embed driver plus volumeAttributes directly in the pod spec — no PVC, and the volume's lifecycle is the pod's lifecycle. The CSIDriver object must explicitly declare Ephemeral in volumeLifecycleModes or the pod is rejected. They are not covered by the pod's storage resource limits, and they cannot use snapshots, cloning, or expansion — the traps are reaching for a PVC or assuming persistence.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A PVC uses VolumeAttributesClass "silver" (3000 IOPS). Load testing shows the database needs 6000 IOPS, and the storage admin has created a "gold" class. How do you move the live volume to gold without recreating the PVC?
options: Patch spec.storageClassName to gold — the storage class is mutable after provisioning

kubectl patch pvc db-data -p '{"spec":{"volumeAttributesClassName":"gold"}}' — unlike storageClassName, volumeAttributesClassName is mutable; the external-resizer works with the CSI driver to modify the volume in place, and PVC status tracks current versus desired class
Delete and recreate the PVC — volumeAttributesClassName is immutable like storageClassName
Edit the PersistentVolume directly — the PVC field is read-only
explain: VolumeAttributesClass (storage.k8s.io/v1) is the mutable sibling of StorageClass: changing volumeAttributesClassName on the PVC triggers an in-place volume modification via the CSI driver. The class's own parameters and driverName are immutable — new attributes mean a new class, then repoint the PVC. storageClassName can never be changed after provisioning, which is the trap.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod runs two containers: "trainer" needs a GPU, "logger" needs none. The cluster has a DRA driver with a ResourceClaimTemplate named gpu-template. How do you give ONLY the trainer container the GPU?
options: Put resources.claims under the pod spec — claims are pod-wide, so both containers share the GPU
Reference the template directly in the container: resources: {claimTemplateName: gpu-template}

Pod spec resourceClaims: [{name: gpu, resourceClaimTemplateName: gpu-template}], plus in the trainer container resources: {claims: [{name: gpu}]} — the pod declares claims, each container opts in by name; logger lists no claims and gets no device
DRA claims are always shared by every container in the pod — split into two pods
explain: Dynamic Resource Allocation splits declaration from consumption: pod-level spec.resourceClaims names each claim (from a template or an existing ResourceClaim), and each container's resources.claims selects which claims it gets by name. A template gives every pod its own claim instance; referencing a named ResourceClaim shares one instance across pods. The trap is assuming claims are automatically pod-wide.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You need a 2GB ML model stored as an OCI artifact mounted read-only into the inference container — no PVC, no initContainer download step. Which volume source does this, and what is its mount behavior?
options: A ConfigMap with binaryData — ConfigMaps handle multi-gigabyte binaries efficiently
An OCI registry cache sidecar that copies the model into an emptyDir at startup
image volumes are writable scratch space shared like emptyDir

volumes: [{name: model, image: {reference: registry.example.com/model:v3, pullPolicy: IfNotPresent}}] — the image volume source mounts the OCI object read-only at mountPath; it is resolved at pod startup, and a pull failure blocks containers from starting (retried with volume backoff)
explain: The image volume source mounts any OCI object as a read-only volume — no PVC, no download sidecar. It resolves at pod startup honoring pullPolicy, and resolution failure blocks container start and surfaces on the pod's reason/message. subPath mounts on image volumes need v1.33+. The traps: treating it as writable, or assuming it behaves like a container image layer.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A mutating admission webhook injects a logging sidecar. During a webhook outage, pods are rejected and the incident escalates. The sidecar is nice-to-have, not required for correctness. Which failurePolicy keeps the cluster usable, and what is the trade-off?
options: failurePolicy: Ignore — if the webhook is unreachable or errors, the API server skips it and admits the object; the trade-off is pods land WITHOUT the sidecar during the outage, so audit for missing injections afterward
failurePolicy: Fail — the default, and it keeps admitting objects during webhook outages
failurePolicy: Ignore — the API server drops the pod instead of admitting it
failurePolicy only applies to validating webhooks, not mutating ones
explain: Fail is the default: a dead webhook blocks writes (safe for policy enforcement, bad for availability). Ignore favors availability — objects are admitted unmutated/unvalidated while the webhook is down. The operational cost is silent non-injection, so you must reconcile afterward. The trap is thinking Ignore retries or queues the mutation.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your Dockerfile builds a Go binary in a golang:1.22 image, then ships the result. The final image is 900MB because the SDK and build cache leak into it. Which pattern fixes the image size?
options: Multi-stage build: FROM golang:1.22 AS builder ... RUN go build ./..., then a second FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 with COPY --from=builder /app/server /server — only the final stage becomes the image; compilers and caches never ship
Add more RUN layers that rm -rf the SDK — deleted files still occupy earlier layers
COPY --from only works between separate Dockerfiles, not stages
Switch ADD for COPY — ADD strips build tools automatically
explain: In a multi-stage build only the last stage defines the final image; COPY --from=<stage> pulls just the artifact across. Deleted-in-a-later-layer files still bloat the image because layers are additive — the trap is rm -rf cleanup instead of stage separation.

q: docker build spends minutes on "sending build context to Docker daemon" and once shipped a .env containing production secrets into the image. What is the single fix for both symptoms?
options: Add a .dockerignore excluding .env, .git, and node_modules — the entire context directory is sent to the daemon before the build starts; ignoring files shrinks the context and keeps secrets out of image layers
Pass --no-context to docker build
Move the secrets into Dockerfile ARG instructions — ARGs are never persisted
Build with --network=none so secrets cannot leak
explain: .dockerignore filters what is sent as build context — smaller context, faster builds, and excluded files can never land in a layer via COPY/ADD. ARG values are visible in image history (docker history) and baked into layers that use them, so ARG is not a secrets mechanism — that is the trap.

q: You build on an ARM laptop and push myapp:v1; on the AMD64 cluster the pod fails with "exec format error". What happened, and what is the proper fix?
options: Set imagePullPolicy: Always — the pull negotiates the architecture
Add a nodeSelector for ARM nodes and relabel the cluster
Registries transcode architectures automatically on pull
Build a multi-arch image (e.g. docker buildx) producing an OCI image index that lists one manifest per architecture — the runtime then pulls the manifest matching the node's architecture
explain: The pushed image is a single-arch ARM manifest; the AMD64 runtime cannot execute it. A multi-arch build publishes an OCI image index (manifest list), and the kubelet/runtime selects the manifest for the node's platform. imagePullPolicy has nothing to do with architecture — the trap is treating this as a pull problem.

q: CI applies a Deployment with --field-manager=ci --server-side while Helm manages the same release. CI's apply fails with a conflict naming the "helm" manager. What does this mean?
options: Helm deleted the Deployment out from under CI
Conflicts are warnings only — the apply actually succeeded
Delete .metadata.managedFields to clear the conflict

Server-side apply tracks per-field ownership in managedFields; CI tried to change a field Helm owns. Resolve by dropping the field from CI's manifest (yielding ownership), matching the live value (shared management), or re-running with --force-conflicts to take ownership
explain: SSA records which manager owns each field. A conflict (HTTP 409) means another manager claims a field you tried to set — last-writer-wins is replaced by explicit ownership. managedFields is API-server-managed and must not be hand-edited. The three resolutions are: force (take), drop the field (give up), or converge the value (share).

q: You are taking over a Deployment from a decommissioned tool whose manager "old-ci" still owns spec.replicas in managedFields. Your server-side apply keeps conflicting. Which flag completes the takeover, and what does it do to old-ci's entry?
options: kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f deploy.yaml — forces the change and removes the field from old-ci's managedFields entry, making you the sole manager
Add --overwrite — the client-side apply conflict flag, which also works server-side
Use --force — deletes and recreates the resource, clearing all managers
Use --prune — garbage-collects the stale manager entry
explain: --force-conflicts sets force=true on the apply: the write succeeds, the value is yours, and the field is stripped from every other manager's entry. --overwrite is the client-side-apply equivalent and does not apply here; --force on apply means delete-recreate semantics, a different flag entirely — the classic lookalike trap.

q: You rotated the database password in the Secret; the Deployment's pods still use the old value from their env vars. What is the fastest way to roll the new value out?
options: kubectl rollout restart deploy/api — it adds/updates a pod-template annotation, changing the template hash and triggering a rolling restart; the new pods inject the fresh Secret value
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api — restores the previous Secret value
Delete the ReplicaSet — the Deployment will not recreate pods on its own
Wait — env-var Secrets update in running pods automatically within a minute
explain: rollout restart bumps a pod-template annotation (kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt), which changes the pod template and starts a normal rolling update. Env-var values are snapshot at container start and never refresh — only volume-mounted Secrets/ConfigMaps update in place (and the app must re-read them). The trap is expecting automatic env refresh.

q: A legacy app holds a file lock on a ReadWriteOnce volume and can never run two copies at once. Which Deployment strategy fits, and what does it cost?
options: RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 — zero downtime and no overlap
strategy: {type: Recreate} — kills all old pods before creating new ones; the cost is downtime during the rollout because old and new never overlap
Recreate keeps the old pods until the new ones are ready — it is the zero-downtime option
Only a blue-green pair of Deployments can do this
explain: Recreate tears everything down first, then brings the new version up — the only safe choice for single-writer RWO volumes or apps that cannot coexist with themselves. RollingUpdate always overlaps old and new (even maxUnavailable: 0 still runs both briefly), which is the trap.

q: You must change a Deployment's selector, which the API server rejects as immutable. Which command performs the change, and what actually happens to the pods?
options: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml — apply patches immutable fields in place
kubectl replace -f deploy.yaml — replace handles immutable fields without disruption
kubectl replace --force -f deploy.yaml — deletes the object (cascading to its pods by default) and recreates it; there is a window with no pods, and a brand-new ReplicaSet starts up
kubectl edit — the editor bypasses immutability checks
explain: --force turns replace into delete-then-create: the Deployment, its ReplicaSets, and pods are removed and rebuilt from the file. It is disruptive by design — the trap is expecting rolling-update behavior. Plain replace still fails the immutability check.

q: You strategic-merge-patch a Deployment, listing only ONE container in the containers array to change its image. What happens to the other containers?
options: They are deleted — a patched list replaces the whole list
The patch is rejected — strategic merge requires complete lists
Strategic merge only works on maps, so the patch fails
They are preserved — strategic merge patch merges lists by their merge key (name for containers), so the named container is updated in place
explain: Strategic merge uses per-type merge keys (containers merge on name, ports on port, etc.), so a partial list patches matching elements instead of replacing the array. A JSON merge patch (RFC 7386, --type=merge) WOULD replace the whole list — confusing the two patch types is the trap.

q: You must add the label team=payments to Deployment web using an RFC 6902 JSON patch, without editing YAML. Which command is correct?
options: kubectl patch deploy web --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/metadata/labels/team","value":"payments"}]' — JSON Patch uses op/path/value with JSON-pointer paths
kubectl patch deploy web -p='{"metadata":{"labels":{"team":"payments"}}}' — that is the default strategic merge patch, not JSON Patch
kubectl patch deploy web --type=merge -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/metadata/labels/team"}]' — merge type accepts JSON-pointer operations
kubectl patch deploy web --type=json -p='{"metadata.labels.team": "payments"}' — JSON Patch uses dotted paths
explain: RFC 6902 (--type=json) expresses changes as operations: add/replace/remove with JSON-pointer paths (/metadata/labels/team). The default patch type is strategic merge, which takes a partial object instead. The traps are mixing the two syntaxes and using dotted paths.

q: You need a headless Service for an EXTERNAL database, so no selector is possible. What must you create by hand, and what DNS do pods get?
options: Create an Endpoints object with the SAME name as the Service listing the database IPs — with no selector the controller creates no endpoints; pods then resolve db.ns.svc.cluster.local to those IPs directly (clusterIP: None returns endpoint IPs, no virtual IP)
Nothing — headless Services auto-discover external IPs from the cloud provider
An EndpointSlice is auto-created for selector-less Services
Only an ExternalName Service can point outside the cluster
explain: A Service without a selector gets no automatic endpoints — you must create the Endpoints object yourself with the identical name. Combined with clusterIP: None, DNS returns the endpoint IPs as A records. The trap is expecting the controller to populate endpoints without a selector.

q: A 2000-endpoint Service shows both an Endpoints object and many EndpointSlices. Which one does kube-proxy actually consume at scale, and why do both exist?
options: kube-proxy reads the Endpoints object; EndpointSlices are informational only
kube-proxy consumes EndpointSlices — sharded (≈100 endpoints each), scalable discovery with topology hints; the legacy Endpoints object is kept as a mirror for older consumers
EndpointSlices only exist for headless Services
You must delete the Endpoints object to activate slice-based proxying
explain: EndpointSlices are the scalable replacement for the monolithic Endpoints object (which becomes a bottleneck past a few hundred endpoints). The Endpoints resource is still mirrored for backward compatibility. The trap is treating slices as a headless-only or optional feature.

q: A Cassandra StatefulSet needs pods to discover peers via DNS BEFORE they pass readiness (gossip bootstrap). Which Service field enables DNS records for not-ready pods?
options: readinessGates: [cassandra-ready] — gates make DNS appear sooner
minReadySeconds: 0 on the StatefulSet
publishNotReadyAddresses: true on the headless Service — DNS then returns A records for all pods regardless of readiness
sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service
explain: publishNotReadyAddresses flips the headless Service's DNS to include unready pods — the standard peer-discovery pattern for gossip/clustering systems. readinessGates delay readiness further (the opposite direction), which is the trap.

q: Two clusters in a ClusterSet both run a Service named "api" in namespace "shop". How do you expose them as ONE logical service reachable from any cluster?
options: A ServiceExport in one cluster is enough — the import side is automatic without any object
Merge the kubeconfigs with kubectl config use-context — federation is client-side
Create an Ingress with the same host in each cluster — Ingress federates automatically

Create a ServiceExport (multicluster.x-k8s.io API) with the SAME name and namespace as the Service in each exporting cluster — the MCS controller builds ServiceImports merging all endpoints, reachable at api.shop.svc.clusterset.local
explain: The MCS API is presence-based: a ServiceExport named exactly like the Service marks it for export, and the controller creates ServiceImports that merge endpoints across clusters under the clusterset.local domain. Same name+namespace is mandatory — that matching rule is the trap.

q: On a dual-stack cluster you need Service web with IPv4 primary and IPv6 secondary. Which fields do you set, and what can you never change afterward?
options: ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack with ipFamilies: [IPv4, IPv6] — the first entry is the primary family used for the legacy .spec.clusterIP; you may add or remove the secondary family later but can never change the primary
ipFamilies is fully immutable once set
Dual-stack requires two separate Services, one per family
ipFamilyPolicy: DualStack — the single value covering both stacks
explain: ipFamilyPolicy (SingleStack/PreferDualStack/RequireDualStack) plus the ordered ipFamilies list. ipFamilies is conditionally mutable: secondary families can be added/removed, but the primary (first entry, backing .spec.clusterIP) is fixed. RequireDualStack fails creation on single-stack clusters while PreferDualStack falls back — and DualStack is not a valid value, the trap.

q: The worker pod was OOMKilled and restarted clean. You need the killed instance's last log lines, and the runbook abbreviates the flag. Which command shows them?
options: kubectl logs worker-abc -p — -p is the short form of --previous: logs of the last TERMINATED container instance
kubectl logs worker-abc --prev — the abbreviated long flag
Container logs are lost on OOMKill — only the event survives
kubectl logs worker-abc --since=1h — reaches back across restarts
explain: -p/--previous targets the last terminated instance of the container — the one that actually printed the failure. Plain kubectl logs follows the current (possibly clean) instance. The traps are inventing a --prev flag and assuming logs are deleted with the container.

q: A pod runs containers "app" and "sidecar". kubectl logs pod-x errors out asking for a container. What are the correct invocations?
options: kubectl logs pod-x --all — streams every container
kubectl logs pod-x -c app for one container, or kubectl logs pod-x --all-containers=true to stream both
kubectl logs pod-x -c app,sidecar — -c takes a comma-separated list
kubectl logs only supports single-container pods — use stern instead
explain: With multiple containers -c is mandatory to pick one; --all-containers streams them all. --all is not a logs flag and -c takes exactly one name — the two lookalike traps.

q: You want only the events for pod web-abc, newest first. Which command does it?
options: kubectl describe pod web-abc — the only way to see a single pod's events
kubectl get events --selector involvedObject.name=web-abc — label selectors filter events
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=web-abc --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp — field selectors match the involved object; sort-by orders the output
kubectl logs --events web-abc
explain: Events are filtered server-side with --field-selector on involvedObject.name (label selectors don't target the involved object), and --sort-by orders them. describe shows a pod's events but isn't filterable/sortable output — the trap is reaching for -l.

q: The distroless "api" container has no shell, and you need to inspect its filesystem and live processes. Which debug invocation shares its namespaces?
options: kubectl exec -it api-pod -- sh — distroless images always include sh
kubectl debug -it api-pod --image=busybox — an ephemeral container always shares the target's namespaces by default
Ephemeral containers are PID-isolated by design and can never share
kubectl debug -it api-pod --image=busybox --target=api — the ephemeral container shares the target container's process namespace, so you can inspect its /proc and filesystem
explain: --target attaches the ephemeral debug container to the named container's namespaces (notably PID). Without --target the debug container gets its own namespaces and cannot see the target's processes. exec is hopeless on a shell-less image — the trap.

q: You suspect a CNI misconfiguration on node-3 and need a root shell on the node itself through kubectl. Which command gets you there?
options: kubectl debug node/node-3 -it --image=busybox — schedules a privileged pod on the node; run chroot /host inside it to access the node's filesystem
kubectl exec into any pod already running on node-3 — equivalent access
kubectl debug node opens an SSH session to the node
kubectl node-shell node-3 — the built-in node shell subcommand
explain: kubectl debug node creates a privileged HostPID pod on that node; chroot /host pivots into the node's root filesystem. There is no node-shell subcommand and no SSH involved — the traps are inventing either.

q: A kata-containers RuntimeClass pod requests 2 CPU / 2Gi but stays Pending on a node with 2.2 CPU free. kubectl get pod shows spec.overhead {cpu: 250m, memory: 120Mi}. Why is it Pending, and who set that overhead field?
options: Overhead is informational — the real cause is elsewhere

The scheduler accounts requests PLUS overhead (2.25 CPU needed > 2.2 free); the RuntimeClass admission controller injects spec.overhead at admission time — and rejects the pod if you try to set it yourself
Set spec.overhead: {cpu: 0} in your manifest to fix scheduling
Overhead only counts against limits, never against scheduling
explain: Pod overhead covers the runtime/sandbox cost (VM-based runtimes like Kata). The scheduler and ResourceQuota both count requests + overhead, and the RuntimeClass admission controller sets the field — a manually set overhead is rejected. The trap is treating overhead as cosmetic or trying to zero it.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Security wants a forensic snapshot of a suspected-compromised container WITHOUT stopping or alerting it. Which mechanism captures it, and what does it produce?
options: kubectl checkpoint pod/container — the built-in checkpoint subcommand
kubectl exec tar of the filesystem — captures memory too

The kubelet Checkpoint API: POST https://<node>:10250/checkpoint/<ns>/<pod>/<container> (ContainerCheckpoint feature gate, CRIU installed) — writes a tar under /var/lib/kubelet/checkpoints containing memory pages, process state, open files, and filesystem deltas; the container keeps running, unaware
Checkpointing freezes the container permanently — plan for the restart
explain: Forensic container checkpointing is a node-local kubelet API (alpha 1.25, beta 1.30): kubelet → CRI → runc → CRIU. There is deliberately no kubectl-level command and no restore API — analysis happens offline with tools like checkpointctl. The trap is assuming a cluster-level subcommand exists.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The liveness probe exec: {command: ["curl -f http://localhost/health || exit 1"]} always fails even though curl works in the container. What is wrong?
options: curl is not on the probe's PATH — probes run with an empty environment
exec probes require the command to be a script file on disk
Probes cannot use exit codes — only stdout matters
exec probes run the command directly with NO shell — pipes, ||, and && are not interpreted. Wrap it: command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -f http://localhost/health || exit 1"]
explain: An exec probe execs the binary directly (like Docker exec), so shell metacharacters are passed literally as arguments. Explicitly invoking sh -c restores shell semantics. The trap is assuming probe commands run under a shell.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The /healthz endpoint requires the header X-Probe: kube (it 401s without it). How do you attach that header to the readiness probe?
options: readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080, httpHeaders: [{name: X-Probe, value: kube}]}} — httpHeaders is a list of name/value pairs on the httpGet probe
HTTP probes cannot set headers — switch to an exec probe with curl
httpGet: {headers: {X-Probe: kube}} — headers take a map
Inject the header via the container's env vars
explain: httpGet supports httpHeaders as a list (not a map) of custom headers — also available on the deprecated httpGet path used by startup probes. The trap is inventing a map-shaped field or abandoning HTTP probes.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You want the Secret manifest to carry the PLAINTEXT password (the repo itself is encrypted by external tooling) and let Kubernetes do the base64 encoding. Which field, and what is its read behavior?
options: data: {password: s3cr3t} — data accepts plaintext and encodes it
stringData: {password: s3cr3t} — a write-only convenience field; the API server base64-encodes it into data, and it is never returned on read (GET shows only data)
stringData is stored unencoded in etcd — convenient but insecure
kubectl create secret --from-plaintext — the imperative equivalent
explain: stringData lets you write secrets as plaintext in manifests; the API server merges it into data as base64 and never serves stringData back. data always requires you to encode. The traps: thinking data takes plaintext, or that stringData skips encoding in etcd.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The chart uses the lookup function to read the existing tls-secret Secret. helm template renders an empty string for it, but helm install works fine. Why?
options: The lookup function is broken in Helm 3 — avoid it

lookup needs cluster access — helm template is purely client-side and returns empty for lookups; to validate against the real cluster (admission webhooks, API schemas, lookups) use helm install/upgrade --dry-run=server, which submits without persisting
helm template evaluates lookup against values.yaml instead
Use --dry-run=client — it evaluates lookups server-side
explain: helm template never contacts the cluster, so lookup (and any server-side validation) cannot work there — it renders empty. dry-run=server exercises the real API machinery without creating anything. The trap is assuming template is a faithful dry run.

q: Chart defaults set image.tag: v1, -f prod.yaml sets v2, and --set image.tag=v3 is also passed. Which value wins, and what is the full precedence?
options: v2 — values files always beat command-line flags
v1 — chart defaults are authoritative
v3 wins — precedence is --set > --set-file > -f/--values > chart defaults (and among -f files, later files override earlier ones)
--set-file beats --set
explain: Helm's value precedence: --set highest, then --set-file, then -f/--values files in order, then chart defaults. The classic exam trap is the file-beats-flag intuition — flags win.

q: Chart.yaml lists a dependency on the bitnami/postgresql chart, but helm install fails with a missing-dependency error. What step did you skip?
options: Nothing — Helm fetches dependencies automatically on install
Move the dependency into values.yaml instead of Chart.yaml
Run helm repo update — that downloads chart dependencies
helm dependency update ./chart — downloads the subchart into charts/ per Chart.yaml (after helm repo add bitnami <url>)
explain: Dependencies declared in Chart.yaml must be vendored with helm dependency update (into charts/) before install; the repo providing them must be added first. Neither install nor repo update performs this step — the trap.

q: You installed with --set image.tag=v1. Months later the chart's default tag moved to v9, and you run helm upgrade -f prod.yaml (which never mentions the tag). Which flag keeps v1, and what happens without it?
options: helm upgrade --reuse-values — merges your new flags over the PREVIOUS release's values, ignoring the chart's new defaults (keeps v1); without it the release resets to chart defaults and you silently get v9
--reuse-values resets everything to the new chart defaults
--reuse-values and a plain upgrade behave identically
Values are immutable after install — you must uninstall first
explain: --reuse-values carries forward the last release's computed values and ignores changed chart defaults — the source of the classic 'why didn't the new default apply' surprise. A plain upgrade (or --reset-values) recomputes from current chart defaults. The trap is expecting defaults to refresh under --reuse-values.

q: Compliance requires the app's ConfigMap to be unchangeable underneath running pods. Which field enforces this, and what is the update path?
options: readOnly: true on the volumeMount — locks the ConfigMap object
immutable: true on the ConfigMap — the API server rejects ANY data change; to update, create a new ConfigMap under a new name and roll the pods to it (the versioned-config pattern)
immutable applies only to Secrets, not ConfigMaps
Set a resourceVersion on the ConfigMap to lock it
explain: immutable: true (available on ConfigMap and Secret) makes the API server reject data updates outright, eliminating the whole class of mid-run config drift. Updates become new-object + rollout. A readOnly mount only protects the file inside the container, not the object — the trap.

q: Your CRD serves both v1 and v2. Which version actually stores objects in etcd, and what happens to a v2-only field when the object is read as v1?
options: Every served version gets its own etcd storage — v1 and v2 store independently
Exactly ONE version has storage: true and etcd stores that; the API server converts on read, so a v2-only field is pruned when served as v1 (unless a conversion webhook preserves it)
storage: true may be set on multiple versions simultaneously
Fields are never pruned between versions — conversion is lossless by default
explain: A CRD has exactly one storage version; all served versions convert to/from it. Structural-schema pruning drops fields unknown to the requested version. The trap is imagining per-version etcd storage or lossless downgrades.

q: You want the API server itself to reject a Database custom resource that is missing spec.engine. Where does this rule live, and when is it enforced?
options: In the operator's RBAC Role — the API server checks it on write
Client-side only: kubectl validates before sending

In the CRD's openAPIV3Schema (spec.versions[].schema.openAPIV3Schema with required: [engine] under spec properties) — enforced by the API server at write time; invalid objects are rejected before reaching etcd
CRDs cannot validate natively — you must write a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
explain: Structural schemas give CRDs native server-side validation: required fields, types, patterns, and pruning of unknown fields all happen in the API server. Webhooks are for logic schemas can't express. The trap is assuming CRDs are schema-less without a webhook.

q: kubectl scale mydb/postgres-1 --replicas=3 fails with "the server doesn't have a resource type 'scale'". The target is a custom resource. What is missing from the CRD?
options: Custom resources can never be scaled — use the operator's own CLI
Only the status subresource needs enabling for scale to work
kubectl scale only works on built-in workload types

The scale subresource: spec.versions[].subresources.scale with specReplicasPath (.spec.replicas), statusReplicasPath (.status.replicas), and labelSelectorPath — without it there is no /scale endpoint, so neither kubectl scale nor an HPA can drive the resource
explain: The scale subresource maps the autoscaling/v1 Scale shape onto JSONPaths inside your CR, exposing /scale. Both paths are required and must use dot notation under .spec/.status. The trap is assuming kubectl scale works on any CR by default.

q: In one sentence, what does an operator's controller actually do inside its reconcile loop?
options: It watches its custom resources and continuously drives actual cluster state toward the desired state declared in the CR's spec — creating, updating, or deleting child objects and reporting back via status
It runs kubectl apply on a timer against a Git repo
It mutates the CRD's OpenAPI schema whenever a spec changes
Operators only validate objects — they never create child resources
explain: Operators are level-driven, not edge-driven: every reconcile compares desired (spec) with actual (observed children/status) and acts to close the gap, requeueing as needed. The trap is picturing a cron-like imperative script rather than continuous convergence.

q: The metrics.k8s.io API (metrics-server) is not a CRD. How is it attached to the main Kubernetes API?
options: It is compiled into kube-apiserver at build time
Via an APIService object (the aggregation layer) — the API server proxies /apis/metrics.k8s.io to the extension API server's Service; kubectl get --raw /apis lists it alongside native APIs
Via a CRD with the aggregation annotation
Aggregated APIs require replacing kube-apiserver with a custom build
explain: API aggregation lets an APIService register an extension API server (a real Deployment+Service) under a new group/version; the main API server reverse-proxies matching requests. That is how metrics-server and service-catalog-style extensions appear native. The trap is confusing aggregated APIs with CRDs.

q: Your Ingress terminates TLS but browsers get the controller's fake certificate even though the Secret exists. What is the most likely manifest error?
options: The Secret must be type Opaque — kubernetes.io/tls is deprecated

The Secret must be type kubernetes.io/tls with keys tls.crt and tls.key (not server.crt/server.key), live in the SAME namespace as the Ingress, and be referenced by spec.tls[].secretName with matching spec.tls[].hosts
TLS Secrets must live in kube-system
spec.tls[].hosts is optional when secretName is set — the mismatch is elsewhere
explain: Ingress TLS demands the exact type, the exact key names, namespace locality, and host coverage. Opaque secrets or renamed keys are silently ignored and the controller falls back to its default cert. The trap is assuming any secret with certificate-ish keys works.

q: You want requests matching NO rule (unknown hosts/paths) to hit a custom 404 Service instead of the ingress controller's built-in default backend. Which Ingress field does this?
options: A rule with host: "*" — the wildcard-only host catches everything
Set the default on the IngressClass object
spec.defaultBackend — serves all requests that match no rule; per-rule backends only handle their own matches
Only an annotation can define the fallback — the Ingress API has no such field
explain: spec.defaultBackend is the catch-all for unmatched hosts/paths. Note host: "*" is invalid — a wildcard must be a single leading label like *.example.com. The trap is inventing a wildcard-host rule.

q: The game server needs UDP ports 30000-30100 open to 10.0.0.0/8. Which single NetworkPolicy ports entry covers the whole range?
options: List all 101 ports as separate entries — ranges are not supported
port: "30000-30100" — port accepts a string range
endPort works with named ports, so port: game-port plus endPort: 30100
ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 30000, endPort: 30100}] — endPort defines an inclusive range; it requires port to be set, both numeric, endPort >= port (stable since 1.25)
explain: endPort extends a numeric port into an inclusive range in one entry. Restrictions: port must be set, both must be numbers (no named ports), endPort >= port, and the CNI must support it. The traps are string ranges and named-port combinations.

q: Service port 80 forwards to the container port named "http" (currently 8080). Which targetPort form survives renumbering the container port to 9090 with NO Service edit?
options: ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: http}] — targetPort by NAME resolves against the pod's named containerPort, so renumbering the container needs no Service change
targetPort: 8080 — names are cosmetic, numbers are what matter
Named targetPorts only work on headless Services
kube-proxy requires targetPort to be numeric
explain: A named targetPort is resolved per-pod against container port names — the Service decouples from the actual number. Hard-coding 8080 re-couples them and forces a Service edit on renumber. The trap is dismissing names as cosmetic.

q: An Ingress has rules for host api.example.com and host *.example.com. A request arrives with Host: deep.api.example.com. Which rule matches?
options: *.example.com matches — wildcards cover any depth
Neither rule matches by default — the wildcard covers exactly ONE DNS label (api.example.com yes; deep.api.example.com no; example.com no), and precise matches require exact host-header equality
The precise rule api.example.com matches by suffix
Both match — the first rule in the list wins
explain: Ingress wildcards are single-label: *.example.com matches api.example.com but not deep.api.example.com and not the bare domain. Precise hosts need an exact header match. The trap is treating * like a glob.

q: kubectl get pods -o jsonpath={.items[*].metadata.name} prints garbage or nothing in bash. What went wrong?
options: {.items[*]} requires --all-namespaces to work
Double quotes fix it the same way — quoting style is irrelevant
jsonpath only supports single-index access like {.items[0]}
Always single-quote the template: -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' — bash brace expansion mangles the unquoted braces before kubectl ever sees them
explain: Bash performs brace expansion on unquoted {a,b}-style text, corrupting the template. Single quotes protect the whole expression (they also block $ expansion, unlike double quotes). The trap is blaming jsonpath syntax for a shell quoting bug.

q: You need a compact table of pod NAME, node, and restart count across ALL namespaces. Which output flag does it in one command?
options: -o wide — it includes restart counts
Pipe -o yaml through grep and awk
-o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount combined with -A — arbitrary columns from JSONPaths
custom-columns cannot span namespaces
explain: custom-columns projects any JSONPath expressions as table columns; -A covers all namespaces. -o wide shows node and IPs but not restarts. The trap is assuming wide is the maximal table.

q: The HPA scales on the app container's CPU via a ContainerResource metric. Before tuning the target you want that container's current CPU — not the pod total. Which command isolates it?
options: kubectl top containers web-abc — the containers subcommand
kubectl top pod web-abc --containers — per-container metrics (metrics-server required either way)
--containers only works with kubectl top node
top cannot show containers — exec in and read /proc
explain: --containers splits the pod's metrics per container on both top pod and top node. There is no top containers subcommand — the trap is inventing one.

q: SLO: a deadlocked container must be restarted within 60s of the deadlock. The liveness probe uses periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3, timeoutSeconds: 2. Does it meet the SLO?
options: Yes — worst case is roughly failureThreshold x periodSeconds = 30s to mark the container failed (plus restart time), comfortably under 60s; each hanging probe only adds its timeout if probes actually hang
No — liveness probes only evaluate once per minute regardless of periodSeconds
No — failureThreshold counts successful probes, not failed ones
initialDelaySeconds dominates, so the math above is irrelevant
explain: Time-to-restart ≈ failureThreshold × periodSeconds (timeouts add only when a probe hangs the full timeout). 3×10s = 30s worst case here. The trap is ignoring the multiplication and reading periodSeconds as the total detection time.

q: You must drain node-3 for kernel patching. It runs a DaemonSet collector and a pod with an emptyDir cache. Which drain command is correct, and what does each flag do?
options: kubectl drain node-3 — bare drain handles DaemonSets and emptyDir automatically
kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data — DaemonSet pods are skipped (their controller recreates them per node anyway) and emptyDir pods are evicted despite losing local data
kubectl drain node-3 --delete-emptydir-data — the flag deletes the node object afterward
Drain never evicts DaemonSet pods, so no flag is needed for them
explain: Bare drain refuses to evict DaemonSet pods and pods using emptyDir (data loss). --ignore-daemonsets skips them (safe: the DaemonSet controller owns that lifecycle); --delete-emptydir-data acknowledges the local-data loss. The trap is assuming drain just works.

q: A ConfigMap must carry a non-UTF8 binary blob (a compiled protobuf descriptor). Which field holds it, and how do you write the value?
options: data: {descriptor.pb: <raw bytes>} — data accepts arbitrary bytes
ConfigMaps cannot hold binary data — you must use a Secret
binaryData: {descriptor.pb: <base64>} — like data but for non-UTF8 bytes; you base64-encode, the API stores raw bytes; data would reject invalid UTF-8
binaryData takes plaintext like stringData — no encoding needed
explain: binaryData is the non-UTF8 sibling of data: base64 in, raw bytes stored. data requires valid UTF-8 strings; stringData is the plaintext convenience for data, not for binary. The trap is assuming ConfigMaps are text-only.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod writes 5Gi of temp files to an emptyDir while its ephemeral-storage limit is 2Gi. What does the kubelet do?
options: Nothing — emptyDir is exempt from ephemeral-storage accounting
The container gets OOMKilled for exceeding its storage limit
ephemeral-storage only affects scheduling, never runtime
The kubelet EVICTS the pod once it exceeds its ephemeral-storage limit (container-level enforcement); if the disk itself fills, the node reports DiskPressure (nodefs/imagefs)
explain: ephemeral-storage limits are enforced by eviction, not OOM (OOM is memory-only). Writes beyond the limit get the pod evicted; node-level disk exhaustion surfaces as DiskPressure. The trap is mapping every limit breach to OOMKill.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: An app needs a Vault-scoped token (audience "vault") that expires in 10 minutes and rotates automatically. Which volume projection does this, and what are the lifetime bounds?
options: projected: {sources: [{serviceAccountToken: {path: vault-token, audience: vault, expirationSeconds: 600}}]} — the kubelet fetches the token via the TokenRequest API and rotates it at ~80% of TTL; expirationSeconds defaults to 3600 and must be at least 600
Create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token — the legacy non-expiring kind, which rotates automatically
audience defaults to the pod name, so no audience field is needed
expirationSeconds accepts any value down to 1 second
