explain: Bound service-account tokens are projected volumes: audience-scoped, time-bound, kubelet-rotated. The legacy Secret-based tokens never expire and don't rotate — the trap is reaching for them. Minimum lifetime is 600s (10 minutes).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You run kubectl label pod web-abc tier=canary on a running pod. The pod exposes its labels BOTH as env vars and as downwardAPI volume files. What changes where?
options: Both update immediately — the downward API is fully live
The volume files update (the kubelet rewrites them via the atomic ..data symlink on its sync loop); the env vars stay frozen at pod-start values — env injection is snapshot-only
Neither updates — pod metadata is immutable after creation
The env vars update but the files do not — files are snapshot-only
explain: Downward API volumes are refreshed by the kubelet (labels/annotations are patchable on live pods), while env vars are injected once at container start and never change. The trap is assuming symmetric behavior — and note subPath mounts never receive updates at all.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Two Pending pods compete for one free slot: pod-a has priorityClassName: high (value 10000), pod-b has no class (cluster default). Who gets the slot, and can pod-a displace a RUNNING lower-priority pod?
options: pod-b wins — the cluster default outranks named classes
Priority only orders the queue; it can never evict running pods
pod-a wins the slot, and with the default preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority it can also evict running lower-priority pods to make room — higher value means higher priority
Lower values win — pod-a's 10000 makes it the LOWEST priority
explain: Priority is a plain integer ordering: higher value = higher priority = scheduled first and, with PreemptLowerPriority (the default), allowed to preempt lower-priority pods. preemptionPolicy: Never would disable only the eviction half. The trap is inverting the value ordering.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: After kubectl apply -k, the ConfigMap is named app-config-7d9f4b6h2k instead of app-config. Why the suffix, and how does the Deployment find it?
options: The suffix is random — update the Deployment's configMap name by hand
It is a bug in kubectl apply -k — file an issue

configMapGenerator appends a content hash so that config changes produce a NEW object name, which triggers a rollout; kustomize's nameReference transformer rewrites the reference in the Deployment automatically
disableNameSuffixHash is enabled by default and malfunctioning
explain: Content hashing turns config edits into new object names, and the name change is what rolls the pods (a same-name data edit would not). The nameReference transformer keeps all referrers in sync. The trap is hand-editing the generated name.

q: An external backup tool addresses the ConfigMap by its stable name app-config, but kustomize keeps appending a content hash. Which kustomization field restores the stable name, and what do you lose?
options: namePrefix: "" — strips generated suffixes
Content hashing cannot be disabled
generatorOptions: {disableNameSuffixHash: true} — keeps the stable name; the cost is that config edits no longer auto-trigger rollouts (same-name update), so you must restart or roll pods yourself
behavior: replace on the generator — disables hashing
explain: disableNameSuffixHash trades the automatic rollout-on-config-change for a stable name. With hashing off, editing the ConfigMap updates data in place and running pods keep the old mounted/env values until restarted. The trap is expecting both stability and auto-rollouts.

q: In CI you gate the pipeline on the exit code of kubectl diff -f app.yaml. What do exit codes 0, 1, and greater than 1 mean?
options: 0 = differences found, 1 = no differences, >1 = warning
0 = no differences, 1 = differences present, >1 = error (cluster unreachable, invalid manifest, etc.)
kubectl diff always exits 0 — gate on stdout instead
Exit codes are nondeterministic — do not gate on them
explain: kubectl diff follows diffutils convention: 0 clean, 1 differences, >1 error. The trap is inverting 0/1 or assuming diff never fails — an unreachable cluster exits >1, which a naive 'nonzero means changes' gate would misread as a diff.

q: Someone hand-edited a live Deployment's image with kubectl; ArgoCD now shows the app OutOfSync. What does that mean, and what restores Git as the source of truth?
options: OutOfSync means the Git repo is corrupted — reclone it
OutOfSync means live state drifted from Git; a Sync reapplies the Git manifests over the live objects (automated sync/self-heal does this continuously), wiping the manual edit
ArgoCD deletes manually changed resources without any sync
Drift is impossible — the API server blocks out-of-band edits on managed resources
explain: GitOps compares desired (git) with live (cluster); OutOfSync is the drift signal, and Sync is the convergence action that overwrites hand edits. The trap is assuming the manual edit persists or that ArgoCD somehow prevents it — it detects, then corrects on sync.

q: Your multi-stage Dockerfile has stages base, test, and prod. CI must run the test stage WITHOUT building prod. Which flag does that?
options: --stage test — selects the build stage
A build arg like --build-arg STAGE=test selects stages
docker build --target test . — stops the build at the named stage
Comment out the prod stage in CI with sed
explain: --target builds only up to the named stage (and its dependencies). There is no --stage flag, and build args don't select stages — the traps are inventing either.

q: After a traffic spike ends, the HPA takes about 5 minutes to scale back down even though metrics are low. Which default causes this, and how do you shorten it?
options: behavior.scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds defaults to 300 — lower it
The HPA only evaluates metrics every 5 minutes

behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds defaults to 300s — the controller holds the highest recommendation over the window before scaling down; set it lower (e.g. 60) to react faster, accepting more flapping risk
Stabilization windows are hardcoded and cannot be configured
explain: The defaults are deliberately asymmetric: scaleUp stabilizes 0s (immediate), scaleDown 300s (flap protection). Setting scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds lower speeds scale-down at the cost of oscillation. The trap is assuming symmetric cooldowns.

q: The nightly-report CronJob must run RIGHT NOW for a backfill, without waiting for its schedule. Which command triggers it?
options: kubectl run backfill --image=<same> --restart=Never — rebuilds the job by hand
Edit the CronJob schedule to "* * * * *" temporarily
CronJobs cannot be triggered manually — wait for the next schedule
kubectl create job backfill-2026 --from=cronjob/nightly-report — clones the CronJob's jobTemplate into a one-off Job
explain: --from=cronjob/<name> instantiates the jobTemplate as an ad-hoc Job, leaving the schedule untouched. Hand-rebuilding with kubectl run risks diverging from the template; schedule-hacking risks forgetting to revert. The trap is thinking manual triggers don't exist.

q: For canary analysis you want v2 held at a small fraction while you check metrics, then continue the rollout. Which commands gate the progression?
options: kubectl rollout pause deploy/web to freeze the rollout mid-progression, then kubectl rollout resume deploy/web to continue — pause halts ReplicaSet scaling at the current step
kubectl rollout stop deploy/web — the stop subcommand
Pause deletes the new ReplicaSet and resume recreates it
Rollouts cannot be paused — use an HPA to hold replica counts
explain: rollout pause/resume freezes and resumes the Deployment controller's progression — the manual gate for canary analysis. There is no rollout stop subcommand. The trap is inventing one or assuming pause destroys progress.

q: New pods pass readiness in 2 seconds but crash at 20 seconds under real traffic, causing flapping rollouts that never settle. Which Deployment field forces each pod to prove itself before the rollout proceeds?
options: progressDeadlineSeconds: 30 — marks the rollout failed sooner
minReadySeconds: 30 — the pod must remain Ready for 30s before the rollout counts it available and moves on
readinessProbe.periodSeconds: 30 — probes less often
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 — gives crashing pods more shutdown time
explain: minReadySeconds is the 'soak' timer: a pod must stay Ready for that long before the Deployment considers it available and continues the rollout. It is distinct from probe timing (how often to check) and progressDeadlineSeconds (how long before the rollout is declared stuck). The trap is tuning the probe instead.

q: A 50-replica StatefulSet rolls painfully slowly because pods start strictly one at a time. Which field parallelizes startup, and what guarantee do you give up?
options: updateStrategy: {type: Parallel} — StatefulSets accept a Parallel strategy
rollingUpdate: {partition: 0} — partition parallelizes the rollout
podManagementPolicy: Parallel — starts, updates, and deletes pods concurrently; you give up the default OrderedReady guarantees (strict ordinal order, at most one unavailable)
StatefulSets are always ordered — split into smaller StatefulSets
explain: podManagementPolicy: Parallel drops the ordered, one-at-a-time semantics of OrderedReady (the default) for speed — appropriate when pods are truly independent. There is no Parallel updateStrategy type for StatefulSets; the only strategies are RollingUpdate and OnDelete. The trap is inventing strategy names.

q: An Ingress routes /shop/* to a Service whose app serves content at / (so /shop/cart 404s in the app). With the nginx ingress controller, which annotation strips the prefix?
options: pathType: Rewrite — the native rewrite path type
spec.rewriteTarget: / — a native Ingress API field

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2 with a path like /shop(/|$)(.*) and pathType: Prefix — controller-specific annotation using capture groups; the rewrite is implementation-specific and not portable across controllers
The app's base path must change — annotations cannot rewrite paths
explain: Path rewriting is not in the Ingress API — it lives in controller annotations (nginx's rewrite-target with regex capture groups). pathType: Rewrite and spec.rewriteTarget don't exist. The portability cost is the trap: the manifest only works on nginx.

q: Your cloud load balancer targets pods directly, and you want NO NodePorts allocated (to conserve the node-port range). Which Service field does that?
options: type: LoadBalancer never allocates NodePorts — nothing to do
Set nodePort: 0 on each port — disables allocation
externalTrafficPolicy: Local implies no NodePorts
allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false — skips NodePort allocation; requires the cloud LB to route to pods directly (some controllers need NodePorts for health checks, so verify yours)
explain: LoadBalancer Services allocate NodePorts by default (the cloud LB typically forwards to them). allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false opts out, but only works if the LB implementation targets pods directly. The trap is assuming no NodePorts are involved by default.

q: For headless Service "db" with 3 ready pods, what does a DNS lookup of db.default.svc.cluster.local return, and why is that useful?
options: Three A records — one pod IP each; clients can implement their own load balancing or peer discovery without kube-proxy in the path
A single A record for the Service's ClusterIP
Only SRV records — A records are never returned for headless Services
NXDOMAIN — headless Services have no DNS entries
explain: Headless (clusterIP: None) Services return the endpoint pod IPs as A records instead of a virtual IP — the basis for client-side balancing and gossip discovery. The trap is expecting a ClusterIP that doesn't exist.

q: Imperatively expose Deployment web (container port 8080) as a NodePort Service listening on port 80. Which command is correct?
options: kubectl create service nodeport web --port=80 — the declarative-style imperative form
kubectl expose deploy web --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=8080 --name=web-svc — --port is the Service port, --target-port is the container port
kubectl run web --expose --port=80 — run exposes existing Deployments
Imperative NodePort creation is not supported — write YAML
explain: kubectl expose builds the Service from the workload; --port vs --target-port is the classic mix-up (swapping them exposes the wrong port or fails). kubectl create service exists but with different syntax (clusterip/nodeport/loadbalancer subcommands) — the trap is blending the two CLIs.

q: A legacy monitoring agent must be reachable on each node's port 9100, so you set hostPort: 9100 on its container. What is the scheduling landmine?
options: hostPort pods are pinned to the node forever — they can never be rescheduled
hostPort requires hostNetwork: true or it is silently ignored
Only ONE pod using hostPort 9100 can run per node — a second such pod cannot schedule (port conflict); prefer a DaemonSet plus hostPort, or a NodePort Service
There is no landmine — hostPorts are virtualized per pod
explain: hostPort binds the node's real port, so it is exclusive per node — a second replica on the same node stays Pending with a port conflict. The standard pattern is DaemonSet + hostPort (exactly one per node by design). The trap is treating hostPort like the virtualized containerPort.

q: kubectl exec -it debug-pod -- bash fails with "executable file not found". The image is alpine-based. What is the fastest working shell invocation?
options: apt-get install bash inside the running container, then retry
alpine images have no shell at all — use kubectl debug instead
kubectl exec -it debug-pod -- sh — alpine ships busybox sh; bash is simply not installed
Use kubectl attach — it provides a shell automatically
explain: Alpine-based images include sh (busybox) but not bash. Installing packages into a running prod container is the trap — slow, ephemeral, and often blocked by read-only filesystems.

q: You run kubectl cp web-abc:/app/config/ ./config (note the trailing slash). Where do the files land, and what must the container provide?
options: Always in ./config/config/ — cp preserves the source directory name
kubectl cp does not use tar — it needs only the kubelet
The trailing slash is ignored — behavior is identical either way
The trailing slash copies the directory's CONTENTS into ./config (files land directly, no extra nesting); the container must have tar in PATH because kubectl cp streams through tar
explain: kubectl cp follows rsync-like trailing-slash semantics: slash = contents, no slash = the directory itself. And it shells out to tar inside the container — distroless/tar-less images fail with 'tar: command not found'. The traps are assuming fixed nesting and forgetting tar.

q: HPA is misbehaving and you want the RAW metrics API output, not kubectl top's table, to see what the autoscaler sees. Which command gets it?
options: kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/pods — bypasses kubectl formatting and proves whether the metrics API itself is serving
kubectl top pod --raw — the raw output flag
curl the kubelet's /metrics endpoint — same data
metrics.k8s.io cannot be queried directly — it is internal only
explain: kubectl get --raw passes the request straight through to the API server, returning the raw JSON the HPA consumes. If this 404s or is empty, metrics-server (or the aggregation layer) is the problem — top's table would hide that. The trap is inventing a --raw flag on top.

q: You need the pod's logs starting at the exact deploy finish time, 2026-10-18T14:00:00Z. Which flag accepts an RFC3339 timestamp?
options: --since=2026-10-18T14:00:00Z — since accepts timestamps
--since-time=2026-10-18T14:00:00Z — absolute RFC3339 time; --since takes only a relative duration like 2h
Neither — use --tail and count backwards
kubectl logs cannot filter by time at all
explain: --since-time is the absolute timestamp; --since is the relative duration. Swapping them is the classic flag-confusion trap — --since with a timestamp errors or misbehaves.

q: A pod sits in Pending with no obvious cause. What is the fastest diagnostic, and where exactly do you look in its output?
options: kubectl logs — Pending pods still produce startup logs
kubectl get pods -o wide — the wide columns explain scheduling
kubectl describe pod <name> — the Events section at the bottom shows the scheduler's decisions (Insufficient cpu/memory, unbound PVC, taint/toleration mismatch, affinity conflicts)
Restart kube-scheduler — it is probably stuck
explain: describe aggregates the pod's Events, which is where the scheduler (and kubelet) explain Pending: resource shortfalls, volume binding, image pull, taints. Logs don't exist for unscheduled pods — the trap is reaching for logs first.

q: A sidecar must send SIGHUP to the main app's nginx process on config change, but it cannot see the app's PIDs. Which pod field enables this, and what is the visibility scope?
options: SYS_PTRACE capability on the sidecar — sufficient without any pod field
Containers in a pod always share the PID namespace — no field needed
Add hostPID: true — shares PIDs pod-wide
shareProcessNamespace: true on the pod spec — ALL containers in the pod share one PID namespace, so the sidecar sees and can signal the app's processes (and /proc is shared)
explain: shareProcessNamespace merges the pod's PID namespaces — purpose-built for sidecar signaling and debugging. hostPID shares the NODE's PID namespace, a far bigger blast radius and a common overreach trap. Containers are PID-isolated by default.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You expose the container's memory limit as an env var via valueFrom: {resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.memory}}. The container sets NO memory limit. What value does the env var get?
options: The node's allocatable memory — the kubelet's documented fallback when the limit is unset; set explicit limits if the app needs its real cgroup ceiling
An empty string — unset resources inject nothing
Pod creation fails — resourceFieldRef requires the resource to be set
The env var is set to 0
explain: When limits/requests are absent, the downward API's resourceFieldRef falls back to the node's allocatable value for that resource — a documented gotcha that silently gives the app a wrong number. The trap is assuming empty or zero.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Pods must reach the legacy monitoring server at mon.legacy (10.20.30.40), but the platform team has locked the CoreDNS config. Which pod field adds the name, and where does the entry land?
options: A postStart lifecycle hook that appends to /etc/hosts
hostAliases: [{ip: 10.20.30.40, hostnames: [mon.legacy]}] — the kubelet appends these entries to the pod's /etc/hosts after its managed entries
hostAliases REPLACES the entire /etc/hosts — use it carefully
An ExternalName Service named mon.legacy
explain: hostAliases adds static /etc/hosts entries per pod without touching DNS. It appends after kubelet-managed entries (it does not replace the file). ExternalName only creates a DNS CNAME inside the cluster for a Service name — it cannot mint arbitrary external hostnames, the trap.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Every pod gets dozens of injected FOO_SERVICE_HOST env vars you don't use, and one collides with an application variable. How do you disable the injection?
options: Delete the Services — no Services, no variables
envFrom cannot be disabled once Services exist
enableServiceLinks: false in the pod spec — stops the kubelet from injecting the Docker-links-style service env vars; cluster DNS is unaffected
Set dnsPolicy: None — that controls env injection too
explain: enableServiceLinks toggles the legacy service env-var injection (SERVICE_HOST/PORT). DNS-based discovery keeps working. The trap is conflating env injection with DNS — disabling links never breaks DNS resolution.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You edit a ConfigMap that is mounted as a volume. The app re-reads the file every 30s but still sees the old value minutes later. Why isn't the update instant?
options: ConfigMap volumes are immutable — you must restart the pod
The app must re-mount the volume to see changes
Volume updates are instant — the application must be caching aggressively

The kubelet syncs projected volume contents on its sync loop (up to ~a minute by default) plus propagation delay — updates are eventually consistent, not instant; and subPath mounts never receive updates at all
explain: Mounted ConfigMaps/Secrets update via the kubelet's periodic sync (atomic ..data symlink swap), so there's an inherent delay of up to the sync period. subPath mounts are frozen at container start — the sharper trap for anyone who 'fixed' it with subPath.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: helm history shows revisions 1, 2, 3 for release web (revision 3 deployed and broken). You run helm rollback web 1. What does helm history show afterward?
options: Revision 3 is deleted and revision 1 is marked deployed again
The history is rewritten to end at revision 1
helm rollback web 0 would roll to a revision 0 — revisions start at 0
A NEW revision 4 (deployed) whose content mirrors revision 1 — rollback never rewrites history; revisions 1-3 remain as superseded records
explain: Helm's release history is append-only: every install, upgrade, and rollback creates a new revision. rollback web 1 records revision 4 with revision 1's content. (helm rollback RELEASE 0 means 'the previous revision', not revision zero.) The trap is the git-revert mental model.

q: The Dockerfile needs VERSION at build time to stamp the binary, but it must NOT persist as an environment variable in the final image. Which mechanism, and what is its secrecy caveat?
options: ARG VERSION with docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.2 — build-time only and not persisted as an env var; caveat: the value IS visible in image history/layers, so never use build args for secrets
ENV VERSION=1.2 — identical to ARG for this purpose
--build-arg values are secret-safe because they are not stored
ARG cannot be referenced in RUN instructions
explain: ARG is build-time-only (unlike ENV, which persists into the image environment), but build args are baked into layer history — visible via docker history. The trap is using ARG/ENV for secrets; real secrets need BuildKit secret mounts or multi-stage exclusion.

q: In CI you want ONE idempotent command that installs the release if missing, upgrades it if present, and creates the namespace when needed. Which flags combine to do this?
options: helm install --upgrade — install accepts upgrade semantics
helm upgrade --install web ./chart --namespace shop --create-namespace — --install makes upgrade idempotent; --create-namespace creates shop if absent
--create-namespace works standalone without --install
Two separate commands are always required — no single idempotent form exists
explain: helm upgrade --install is the idempotent form (installs when absent, upgrades when present), and --create-namespace handles the namespace. Plain helm install fails if the release exists — the trap is assuming install is idempotent.

q: The base kustomization pins image api:1.0; the prod overlay must ship api:2.0 WITHOUT editing any base files. Which command records that in the overlay?
options: Edit the base deployment.yaml — overlays cannot change images
kustomize edit set image only works in the base, not overlays
cd overlays/prod && kustomize edit set image api=api:2.0 — writes an images: transformer entry into the overlay's kustomization.yaml, overriding the base tag
Images cannot be transformed — use a JSON patch instead
explain: kustomize edit set image manages the images transformer (api=api:2.0 or old=new form) in whichever kustomization you run it against — overlays included. The trap is hand-editing base files that the overlay is supposed to leave alone.

q: The Dockerfile uses ADD https://example.com/tool.tar.gz /opt/ to fetch a remote tarball. It works, but the reviewer flags it. What is the preferred pattern and why?
options: ADD is the preferred instruction for remote files — the reviewer is wrong
COPY supports remote URLs too — just swap the instruction
ADD's auto-extraction is always desirable — keep it

Fetch explicitly with curl/wget in a RUN step (or a multi-stage build) and COPY the result — ADD's magic (remote URLs, silent tar auto-extraction) is opaque and hurts reproducibility and layer-cache auditing
explain: Best practice: COPY for local files, explicit RUN curl for remote fetches. ADD's implicit behaviors (URL download, auto-untar) make builds harder to audit and cache correctly. The trap is treating ADD as a superset convenience.

q: You add nodeSelector: {disk: ssd} to a RUNNING DaemonSet. What happens to the existing pods?
options: Nothing — nodeSelector is immutable on DaemonSets after creation
All pods are recreated on every node regardless of labels
Only future nodes get pods — existing pods are never touched
Pods on nodes that no longer match are deleted, and new pods are created on all matching nodes (gated by the updateStrategy) — the DaemonSet controller continuously reconciles desired node coverage
explain: DaemonSets are level-driven: any change to the node-selection criteria re-reconciles coverage — non-matching pods are removed, matching nodes gain pods. The trap is assuming nodeSelector is a create-time-only constraint.

q: You want to canary a StatefulSet: update only pods with ordinal 3 and above, keeping ordinals 0-2 on the old version. Which field does that?
options: updateStrategy: {rollingUpdate: {partition: 3}} — only pods with ordinal >= partition are updated; ordinals below stay put; set partition: 0 to complete the rollout
podManagementPolicy: Parallel — partitions the rollout by ordinal
StatefulSets cannot canary — all pods update together
replicas: 3 — scales the canary instead
explain: The partition field gates RollingUpdate by ordinal: >= partition updates, < partition holds. It is the built-in StatefulSet canary mechanism. The trap is confusing partition with podManagementPolicy (ordering vs gating).

q: Two CI jobs might scale Deployment web concurrently, and yours must only apply if the Deployment currently has exactly 3 replicas. How do you make the scale conditional?
options: kubectl scale always overwrites safely — concurrency is handled internally
kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5 --current-replicas=3 — the API rejects the scale unless the current count is 3 (optimistic concurrency)
Run with --dry-run=client first — that eliminates the race
Scales cannot conflict — the last writer wins harmlessly
explain: --current-replicas makes scale a compare-and-swap: it fails if the live count differs. A dry-run check-then-act still races — the trap is thinking a pre-check is race-free.

q: kubectl rollout history shows bare revision numbers with no context. How do you attach human-readable causes to FUTURE revisions?
options: Rename the ReplicaSets — history shows their names
change-cause is recorded automatically from commit messages

Set the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation on the Deployment (e.g. kubectl annotate deploy web kubernetes.io/change-cause="v2.1 for PAY-42", or use --record on the mutating command) — the annotation is copied into each new revision and shown in rollout history
Rollout history cannot display causes — use external docs
explain: The kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation is the intended channel: whatever value it holds when a rollout happens is stamped on that revision and displayed by rollout history. --record auto-sets it from the command (deprecated but still functional). The trap is assuming history is self-describing.

q: Update ONLY the "api" container's image in Deployment web to api:v2, without editing YAML. Which command does it?
options: kubectl set image deploy/web api:v2 — the container name is inferred
kubectl edit is required — set image cannot target one container
kubectl set image updates every container in the pod template
kubectl set image deploy/web api=api:v2 — the container-name=image form targets one container and triggers a rolling update
explain: kubectl set image takes name=image pairs (multiple allowed), updating just the named containers. Omitting the name is a syntax error, not an all-containers update — the trap.

q: You must allow ingress ONLY from pods labeled role: api that are ALSO in namespaces labeled env: prod. A teammate wrote two separate from-entries (one per selector) and it over-permits. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Selectors inside one peer entry are ORed — splitting them was correct
Two entries are required for AND semantics — the policy is fine
namespaceSelector cannot be combined with podSelector at all
Separate list entries are ORed — the teammate allowed every role: api pod cluster-wide PLUS every pod in env: prod namespaces; put both selectors in ONE peer entry to AND them
explain: Peer semantics: AND within a single from/to entry, OR across entries. Splitting the selectors into two entries unions the two groups instead of intersecting them. The fix is one entry carrying both selectors. The trap is reading a list of peers as an intersection.

q: The nginx controller must route the regex path /api/v[0-9]+/.* to the API Service. Which pathType handles this, and what is the portability cost?
options: pathType: ImplementationSpecific — regex interpretation is controller-specific; the Ingress is not portable to other controllers
pathType: Prefix — Prefix supports regular expressions
pathType: Exact with the regex — Exact matches patterns
Regex paths are standardized — every controller interprets them identically
explain: Prefix is element-wise path matching and Exact is literal — neither does regex. ImplementationSpecific delegates interpretation to the controller (nginx supports regex there). The cost is lock-in: the same manifest means something different (or nothing) on another controller.

q: You create a NodePort Service without specifying nodePort. What port does it get, and what is the valid range for manual selection?
options: It defaults to the Service's port (e.g. 80) on every node
The API server auto-allocates a free port from 30000-32767; manually chosen nodePorts must fall in that range or creation is rejected
Any port 1-65535 is valid for manual nodePort selection
nodePort is mandatory — creation fails without it
explain: NodePorts auto-allocate from the configured range (default 30000-32767) when unset; out-of-range explicit values are rejected by the API server. The trap is assuming well-known ports are usable as NodePorts.

q: You need to change Service web's clusterIP. kubectl apply with a new clusterIP fails validation. Why, and what is the fix?
options: clusterIP can be patched freely — the failure is a different field
kubectl edit bypasses the check — edit it in place
spec.clusterIP is immutable after creation — delete and recreate the Service (or drop the field and let the API server allocate a new one)
ClusterIPs are permanent — the Service must keep it forever
explain: clusterIP (like several networking-assigned fields) is immutable: the API server rejects changes. The fix is delete + recreate, which naturally gets a fresh IP. kubectl edit hits the same validation — the trap.

q: Two IngressClasses exist (nginx, traefik). Your Ingress sets no class and traefik unexpectedly picks it up. How do you make nginx the default class?
options: The earliest-created IngressClass is the default automatically
Set the default in the kube-controller-manager flags
Defaults are not supported — every Ingress must set spec.ingressClassName
Annotate the nginx IngressClass with ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" — exactly one default is allowed; an explicit spec.ingressClassName on an Ingress always overrides the default
explain: The is-default-class annotation designates the default IngressClass (only one permitted). Ingresses without spec.ingressClassName (and without the legacy annotation) use it. Explicit class always wins — the trap is assuming creation order or controller flags decide.

q: A node reports DiskPressure. How do you determine whether container IMAGES or writable container layers/logs are filling the disk?
options: DiskPressure never distinguishes — treat all disk pressure the same
kubectl top node — it breaks down disk by consumer
Only image pulls can cause DiskPressure — evict images

kubectl describe node — kubelet tracks imagefs (image storage) separately from nodefs (kubelet root: emptyDir, logs, writable layers); eviction thresholds (--eviction-hard) are configured per filesystem
explain: The kubelet splits disk accounting into imagefs and nodefs with independent pressure signals and thresholds. describe node exposes both. The trap is treating disk as monolithic — the remediation differs (image GC vs evicting heavy writers).

q: You want to watch pods but SKIP the initial full list — only deltas from the moment the command starts. Which flag does that?
options: kubectl get pods --watch-only — streams only changes occurring after the command starts; plain --watch first dumps the current state, then streams
--watch already skips the initial list
The two flags are identical — watch-only is an alias
--watch-only prints the initial list and then exits
explain: --watch = list then watch; --watch-only = watch without the initial list. Useful for tailing changes without the snapshot noise. The trap is assuming they are aliases.

q: Every app=web pod runs containers "app" and "sidecar". You need the last 20 lines of ONLY the app containers across all pods, each line prefixed with its pod name. Which command?
options: kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=20 — pod and container names are shown by default
kubectl logs -l app=web -c app --tail=20 --prefix=true — selects all matching pods, filters to the app container, and prefixes each line with pod/container names
-l label selectors do not work with kubectl logs
--prefix is the default — the flag is unnecessary
explain: logs accepts -l selectors across pods, -c picks the container in each, --tail bounds each stream, and --prefix attributes the interleaved lines — without it (and without -c) you get an unattributable mix of both containers. The traps are assuming prefixes or single-container defaults.

q: kubectl get events shows COUNT 47 on an ImagePullBackOff event row. What does COUNT mean?
options: 47 pods are affected by the same event
The event occurred on 47 nodes
The event was aggregated — 47 similar occurrences folded into one row (same reason/message); firstTimestamp/lastTimestamp bound the window instead of printing 47 rows
Events are never aggregated — COUNT is always 1
explain: The event API deduplicates: identical events increment count and update lastTimestamp rather than creating rows. COUNT 47 means one recurring condition, not 47 pods. The trap is reading COUNT as a blast radius.

q: A pod went CrashLoopBackOff right after a config change. What is the systematic debug order?
options: Delete the pod immediately — the ReplicaSet will make a clean one
Raise the memory limit first — most crashes are OOM
Restart kubelet on the node — the runtime is probably wedged

kubectl describe (Events: why it cannot start) → kubectl logs --previous (the crashed instance's output) → kubectl get events --sort-by (timeline) → verify the config change itself (diff the ConfigMap/Secret, check mounts and env names)
explain: Describe-first surfaces scheduler/kubelet reasons; --previous captures the dead container's last words; sorted events build the timeline; then validate the actual change. The traps are reflexive deletion, blind resource bumps, and node-level restarts before reading any output.

q: Your Dockerfile needs a private package registry token during the build to install dependencies. A teammate suggests passing it with --build-arg and an ARG instruction. Why is that unsafe, and what is the correct BuildKit pattern?
options: ARG values passed at build time are baked into an image layer and visible in docker history — use RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token with docker buildx build --secret id=token,src=token.txt so the secret is only mounted during that RUN step and never persisted in any layer
ARG is fine as long as you unset it with a second ARG before the final stage — the value is dropped from the image
--build-arg values are encrypted by the daemon automatically, so ARG is the recommended pattern
Put the token in a .env file and COPY it in, then delete it in the same RUN — deletion in the same layer removes all traces
explain: Build args are recorded in the image config/history, so anyone with the image can read the token — secrets must never travel via ARG/ENV. RUN --mount=type=secret exposes the secret only for the duration of that single RUN step and leaves nothing in the layer. Deleting a copied file in a later layer does not remove it from the earlier layer that still ships in the image.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A security audit flags that your pods run with privilege escalation allowed. You never set allowPrivilegeEscalation anywhere. The pods are rejected by the restricted Pod Security Standard. What is the actual default, and the fix?
options: allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to false — the audit tool is misreporting, no change needed
allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to true when not set — set it explicitly to false in the container securityContext to satisfy the restricted standard
The field only exists on the pod-level securityContext, so your container-level setting was ignored
Privilege escalation is controlled by runAsNonRoot alone — set that and the flag becomes irrelevant
explain: The trap is assuming 'not set' means 'off': allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to true, so a process that gains more privileges (e.g. via setuid binaries or file capabilities) keeps them. The restricted PSS requires it explicitly false. It is a container-level field, and runAsNonRoot is a separate control — neither implies the other.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You harden a pod with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and the app immediately crashes writing its PID file to /tmp. What is the minimal fix that keeps the root filesystem read-only?
options: Drop readOnlyRootFilesystem — it is incompatible with any app that writes files
Mount an emptyDir volume at /tmp (optionally with medium: Memory to make it a tmpfs) so the app has a writable scratch area while the container root filesystem stays read-only
Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: false only on the init container — the setting propagates to app containers
Move the PID file path into an env var — read-only filesystems still allow writes through env indirection
explain: readOnlyRootFilesystem only locks the container's root filesystem; mounted volumes remain writable by design, so an emptyDir at /tmp restores scratch space without weakening the control (medium: Memory makes it a tmpfs that never touches disk). Removing the flag throws away the hardening, and the flag is per-container — nothing propagates from init containers.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A namespace enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard. You deploy a pod with runAsNonRoot: true, but the image's Dockerfile ends with USER root. The pod never starts. Why?
options: runAsNonRoot is advisory — the kubelet warns but still runs the container, so the real problem must be the image pull
The container runtime ignores USER when runAsNonRoot is set and picks a random UID, which breaks file ownership

runAsNonRoot: true makes the kubelet validate the effective UID at admission/startup — because the image runs as UID 0, the container is rejected and never starts; fix by building the image with a non-root USER or setting runAsUser to a non-zero UID
Restricted PSS forbids runAsNonRoot entirely — remove the field and the pod will run
explain: runAsNonRoot is enforced, not advisory: with the image defaulting to UID 0, the check fails and the container is refused. The fix is at the image or the securityContext — a non-root USER in the Dockerfile or an explicit runAsUser. The restricted standard requires runAsNonRoot; it is the root USER in the image that collides with it.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create an imagePullSecret in namespace team-a, then reference it in a pod in namespace team-b. The pod fails with ErrImagePull and an authentication error. The secret data is correct. What is wrong?
options: imagePullSecrets are namespaced — the secret must exist in team-b, the pod's own namespace; cross-namespace references are never resolved. Also note a ServiceAccount's imagePullSecrets are merged with (not replaced by) the pod's list
The secret type must be Opaque for image pulls — recreate it as Opaque
imagePullSecrets only work with public registries — private registries need the credentials in an env var
You must restart the kubelet on the node before new pull secrets take effect
explain: Pull secrets are looked up in the pod's namespace only; a secret in team-a is invisible to pods in team-b, so duplicate (or move) it into team-b. The exam's second trap is the merge rule: imagePullSecrets from the pod's ServiceAccount are combined with the pod-level list, not overwritten. The correct secret type is kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, and no node restart is involved.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your multi-stage Dockerfile copies the dependency manifest first, installs packages, then copies source code last. A teammate reorders it to COPY the source first 'for readability'. What is the build-cache consequence?
options: None — BuildKit caches by instruction text, and the same instructions produce the same layers regardless of order

Every layer after the first changed layer is invalidated: because source files change far more often than the manifest, the expensive package-install layer rebuilds on every code change — keep the rarely-changing COPY first so the install layer stays cached
COPY layers are never cached, so only the RUN layer timing matters
BuildKit automatically reorders COPY instructions for optimal caching, so readability ordering is safe
explain: Layer caching is order-dependent: any change invalidates that layer and every layer after it. Source files change constantly, so putting the source COPY ahead of the dependency install forces the expensive install layer to rebuild on every commit. Keep the rarely-changing manifest COPY and install first, volatile source last — that is the whole point of the pattern.

q: Your Dockerfile starts with ARG GO_VERSION=1.24 before the first FROM, and you reference $GO_VERSION in a RUN instruction two stages later. The build prints an empty value. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: ARG values are only visible inside the FROM line that follows their declaration — the scope resets at each FROM, so re-declare ARG GO_VERSION (no value needed) inside each stage that uses it; the global default is inherited
ARG is a runtime-only instruction — convert it to ENV to use it in RUN
Build args cannot have default values — remove =1.24 and always pass --build-arg
Each FROM starts a fresh Dockerfile, so ARGs must be passed again with --build-arg per stage
explain: An ARG declared before the first FROM lives in the global scope and is only usable in FROM lines; each FROM resets the scope, so a stage that needs the value must re-declare the ARG name (it then inherits the global default or the --build-arg override). ARG is build-time-only — ENV is the runtime one, which is exactly backwards from the distractor's claim.

q: You ship a distroless-based image with no shell. During an incident you need to inspect the running container's filesystem, but kubectl exec fails — there is no shell to exec into. What is the supported approach?
options: Rebuild the image with a shell baked in — there is no way to inspect a shell-less running container
kubectl logs --shell drops you into the container's mount namespace

Use kubectl debug to attach an ephemeral container with a debugging image (e.g. busybox), optionally with --target to share the app container's process namespace — the debug container brings its own shell and tools without changing the app image
Copy the image's layers with docker save and inspect them locally — live inspection is impossible
explain: kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container carrying its own toolbox image alongside the shell-less app container, and --target shares its process namespace. There is no --shell flag on kubectl logs, and rebuilding the image mid-incident is the slow path the exam wants you to reject.

q: You build FROM scratch and set ENTRYPOINT ./app --serve. The container exits immediately with 'executable file not found in $PATH' even though /app exists in the image. What is the breakage?
options: scratch images cannot run binaries at all — use distroless instead
The binary needs a CMD, not an ENTRYPOINT — scratch ignores ENTRYPOINT
Files copied into scratch images lose their executable bit — chmod in a RUN step

You used the shell form of ENTRYPOINT, and scratch has no shell to interpret it — use the exec form ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] with an absolute path, since there is no shell and no PATH resolution without one
explain: The shell form wraps the command in /bin/sh -c, which does not exist in scratch, and relative-path lookup fails without a shell's PATH handling; the JSON exec form with an absolute path launches the binary directly. The other options invent nonexistent scratch limitations.

q: Your build context is 2 GB because the repo directory contains datasets and old artifacts, and every docker build takes minutes just to start. Which change actually fixes the slow start, and why?
options: Switch from COPY to ADD — ADD streams files lazily during the build
Add more RUN layers — finer layers build faster
Use --no-cache — stale cache entries are what slow the start
Add a .dockerignore file excluding datasets, artifacts, and .git — the entire build context is sent to the daemon/builder before the build starts, so shrinking it removes the minutes-long upload
explain: .dockerignore prunes the context that is tarred and shipped to the builder on every build — that upload is the slow start, not the layer count. ADD vs COPY changes nothing about context transfer, more layers add overhead rather than removing it, and --no-cache makes builds slower, not faster.

q: A Deployment has 4 replicas with the default rolling update settings. During a rollout, how many pods can be unavailable and how many extra pods can exist, and why do the defaults produce whole numbers?
options: maxUnavailable rounds 25% of 4 (=1) down to 1, maxSurge rounds 25% (=1) up to 1 — maxUnavailable rounds DOWN and maxSurge rounds UP when converting percentages, so small Deployments still get at least one surge pod and never more unavailability than the percentage allows
Both round up: 1 unavailable and 2 extra pods
Both round down: 0 unavailable and 0 extra, so the rollout serializes one pod at a time
Percentages are truncated to integers, so 25% of 4 is 0 for both — you must set absolute numbers
explain: The rounding rules are the exam point: maxUnavailable rounds down (never exceed the allowed disruption) and maxSurge rounds up (always allow at least the surge). With 4 replicas both compute to 1. The 'both round the same way' distractors and the '0/0 serialization' claim are the standard traps — and note both values also cannot be 0 simultaneously.

q: You need to apply a risky multi-resource change but want to stage the Deployment update first, verify it, then let the rollout proceed — without the change going live the moment you apply. Which sequence does this safely?
options: kubectl apply the change, then immediately kubectl rollout undo if it looks wrong
Set replicas to 0, apply, then scale back up — pausing is not a real kubectl feature

kubectl rollout pause deployment/api before applying, apply the change (the new ReplicaSet is created but the rollout is held), verify, then kubectl rollout resume deployment/api to continue the rollout
Edit the Deployment with kubectl edit and leave the editor open — the rollout waits for the editor to close
explain: rollout pause freezes the rollout after the new ReplicaSet is created, so you can inspect the staged change (pod template, revisions) before resume releases it. Undo-after-the-fact is reactive rather than staged, scaling to zero causes an outage, and the editor trick only delays your own save — it holds nothing server-side.

q: After several rollouts you run kubectl rollout history deployment/api and see only the last 10 revisions, but you need to roll back to a change from 12 deployments ago. What controls this, and what is the consequence of raising it?
options: The API server keeps unlimited revisions — your cluster's etcd must be corrupted
kubectl only displays 10 by default — pass --limit=20 to see older revisions
Revision history is stored in the Deployment's annotations, which are truncated at 10 entries

spec.revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) caps how many old ReplicaSets are retained — raise it to keep more rollback targets, at the cost of more ReplicaSet objects (and their pods' metadata) lingering in etcd
explain: The Deployment controller garbage-collects old ReplicaSets down to revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) — revisions beyond that are gone, not hidden, so no flag recovers them. Raising the limit preserves more rollback targets at the cost of retained objects. The 'display limit' and 'annotation truncation' distractors invent mechanisms that don't exist.

q: You are deploying a single-instance database that uses a ReadWriteOnce PVC. Which strategy must the Deployment use, and why is the default wrong here?
options: Keep the default RollingUpdate — PVCs are automatically reattached to the new pod before the old one terminates
Use RollingUpdate with maxSurge: 0 — that is equivalent to Recreate without the downtime
Deployments cannot use PVCs at all — convert it to a StatefulSet

Use strategy: Recreate — RollingUpdate would start the new pod while the old one still holds the RWO volume (or briefly run two writers against the same data directory), and a single-instance database cannot tolerate two versions running against its data; Recreate terminates all old pods first, accepting downtime
explain: Recreate kills every old pod before any new pod starts, which is what a single-writer RWO database needs; RollingUpdate overlaps old and new pods and risks two writers or a volume stuck attached to the terminating pod. maxSurge: 0 still overlaps (it only removes the extra capacity), and Deployments absolutely can mount PVCs.

q: You need to change only the container image of a live Deployment to api:2.1. Which command is the precise, auditable one-liner, and how does it differ from the alternatives?
options: kubectl set image deployment/api api=api:2.1 — updates just the image field and records the change in the rollout revision; kubectl edit opens the full manifest (risk of accidental edits) and kubectl patch needs a correctly-typed patch document for the same one-field change
kubectl edit deployment/api — the only supported way to change an image on a live Deployment
kubectl patch requires --type=json always, so it cannot touch the image field
Images are immutable on live Deployments — you must delete and recreate it
explain: set image is the purpose-built imperative verb for exactly this one-field change and it flows through the normal rollout machinery. edit works but exposes the whole object to fat-finger edits; patch works but demands the right --type and document for a trivial change. Nothing about images is immutable on a live Deployment.

q: You set topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, across 3 zones, and scale to 6 pods. The scheduler refuses to place a 7th pod when one zone already has 3. What does maxSkew: 1 actually enforce?
options: The difference in pod count between any two matching topology domains cannot exceed maxSkew — with 6 pods evenly spread (2/2/2), a 7th pod would make its zone hold 3 vs 2 elsewhere (skew 2 > 1), so it stays Pending until the distribution allows it
maxSkew is the maximum pods per zone — with maxSkew: 1 each zone can only ever hold 1 pod
maxSkew: 1 means all pods must land in a single zone for locality
Skew is computed against node count, not pod count — the 7th pod is blocked by a taint
explain: maxSkew caps the *difference* in matching-pod counts between topology domains: 3 vs 2 is a skew of 2, which violates maxSkew: 1, so the pod stays Pending (a classic 'mysterious Pending' during scale-up). It is not a per-zone cap, and it is computed over pod counts per domain, not nodes or taints.

q: Your pod anti-affinity must spread replicas across nodes but ALSO avoid nodes running the monitoring stack, which lives in namespace monitoring while your app is in namespace payments. Which field makes the affinity term see pods in the other namespace?
options: namespaces: [monitoring] — a static list of namespaces whose pods the labelSelector matches against
Anti-affinity is always cluster-wide — no field is needed
namespaceSelector with matchLabels selecting the monitoring namespace — dynamically matches namespaces by label, so the term applies to pods in any namespace carrying those labels
topologyKey: kubernetes.io/namespace — the namespace becomes a topology domain
explain: By default affinity terms only match pods in the pod's own namespace. namespaceSelector extends the term to namespaces selected by label (the dynamic, label-driven way), while the namespaces list is the static alternative. Anti-affinity is not cluster-wide by default, and there is no kubernetes.io/namespace topology key.

q: During a node upgrade, kubectl drain evicts your pods gracefully, but when a node suffers a sudden kernel panic the pods are just gone and rescheduled — the PDB did nothing. What is the PDB's actual scope?
options: PDBs protect against both — your PDB selector must be misconfigured
PDBs only apply to Deployments, not to bare pods or StatefulSets
A kernel panic is a voluntary disruption because the kernel 'chose' to panic

PDBs only constrain voluntary disruptions (drain, voluntary eviction via the eviction API) — involuntary disruptions like node failure, kubelet death, or network partitions bypass PDBs entirely; the API server simply recreates the pods elsewhere
explain: PDBs gate only voluntary, API-driven evictions (drains, voluntary eviction calls); a dead node is an involuntary disruption and no budget check runs before those pods are lost — the controller simply recreates them elsewhere. PDBs work for any pods matching their selector regardless of controller, and 'misconfigured selector' is the reflexive wrong diagnosis the exam plants.

q: You drain a node but it hangs: one pod is CrashLoopBackOff and guarded by a PDB with minAvailable: 2, while only 1 of 3 pods is Ready. The drain never proceeds. Which setting explains the block, and what unblocks it?
options: PDBs never cover unhealthy pods — the drain tool is broken, use --force
minAvailable counts pod objects, not Ready pods — 3 objects exist so the budget is satisfied and drain should proceed
CrashLoopBackOff pods are exempt from PDBs by definition

unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy defaults to IfHealthyBudget — a Running-but-not-Ready pod may only be evicted while currentHealthy >= desiredHealthy; with the app already disrupted, the unhealthy pod is protected and the drain stalls. Setting it to AlwaysAllow lets the eviction proceed
explain: The IfHealthyBudget default protects Running-but-unhealthy pods when the app is already below its desired healthy count, which is exactly what wedges the drain; AlwaysAllow trades that protection for drain progress. CrashLoopBackOff pods are not exempt, minAvailable is evaluated against Ready/healthy pods, and PDBs very much cover unhealthy pods — that is what the policy is for.

q: You create a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for a StatefulSet and query its DNS name. What answer do you get, and how does it differ from a normal ClusterIP Service?
options: The headless Service name resolves to the ClusterIP like any other Service — clusterIP: None is just a validation placeholder

The Service DNS name returns A records for each ready backing pod's IP (plus per-pod hostnames like web-0.svc), instead of a single virtual IP — clients discover individual pod IPs directly rather than going through kube-proxy load balancing
Headless Services get no DNS records at all — you must use Pod IPs from the API
The DNS name resolves to the node's external IP so clients bypass the cluster network
explain: With clusterIP: None there is no virtual IP, so DNS returns the backing pods' IPs (and stable per-pod DNS names for StatefulSets) — clients discover individual pod IPs directly rather than going through kube-proxy load balancing. Headless Services absolutely get DNS records; the 'no DNS' and 'node external IP' options are fabrications.

q: You need to capture packets on a pod to diagnose intermittent connection resets. The namespace enforces the baseline Pod Security Standard, so a privileged debug container would be rejected. Which kubectl debug invocation fits?
options: kubectl debug with --profile=sysadmin — the only profile that can capture packets
--profile=general is the default and already includes NET_ADMIN
Packet capture requires hostNetwork on the debug pod — profiles cannot grant it

kubectl debug -it pod/web-0 --image=nicolaka/netshoot --profile=netadmin --target=web — the netadmin profile adds NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW (enough for tcpdump) without full privilege, and --target shares the app container's network/process context
explain: netadmin is the least-privilege profile for packet capture: NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW without going fully privileged (sysadmin), and --target puts the debugger in the target container's namespaces. general only adds SYS_PTRACE (no packet capture), and profiles absolutely can shape capabilities — hostNetwork is not required.

q: Your app container has no shell, but you need to inspect the files it sees at /etc/app from inside its own mount namespace. Which ephemeral-container flag gives the debugger the app's view?
options: --target=app — the ephemeral container shares the target container's process namespace (and you see its /proc/<pid>/root), letting you inspect what the app sees without restarting it
--share-processes is a kubectl debug copy flag, not for ephemeral containers
Ephemeral containers always run in their own namespaces — sharing is impossible
Use --copy-to and --set-image instead — ephemeral containers cannot see other containers' filesystems
explain: --target=<container> enables process namespace sharing for the ephemeral container, so /proc/<pid>/root exposes the target's filesystem view without restarting anything. --share-processes is indeed a pod-copy flag (a fine distractor), sharing is very much possible, and --copy-to is the heavier alternative for when you don't need the live pod.

q: A node is NotReady and you suspect disk pressure, but the kubelet is unresponsive so kubectl exec into any pod there fails. How do you get a shell on the node itself?
options: kubectl ssh node-3 — kubectl has a built-in SSH client for nodes
kubectl debug only works on pods — use kubectl logs on the kubelet's static pod

kubectl debug node/node-3 -it --image=ubuntu — creates a privileged pod bound to that node in the host's namespaces; chroot /host then gives you the node's real filesystem to inspect disk, logs, and kubelet state
Nodes cannot be accessed without SSH credentials — drain the node blind and hope
explain: kubectl debug node/<name> creates a debug pod on that node with host namespaces, and chroot /host pivots into the node's filesystem for inspecting disk, logs, and kubelet state. There is no kubectl ssh, blind draining is the despair option, and kubectl debug absolutely supports the node/ resource.

q: A pod's container crashed 30 seconds ago and the replacement is already running. You need the crashed instance's last log lines. Which command gets them, and what is the common failure mode of the alternative?
options: kubectl logs pod/web-0 shows both instances merged automatically

kubectl logs pod/web-0 --previous — reads the terminated instance's logs; plain kubectl logs only shows the current (new, mostly empty) container, and kubectl cp from the crashed container fails because exec/cp need a running container with tar
kubectl cp works on terminated containers — copy /var/log out of the dead one
Logs of crashed containers are deleted immediately — nothing can be recovered
explain: --previous targets the last terminated instance, which is exactly what you need when the replacement container has no useful output yet. kubectl cp/exec require a running container, and the kubelet retains terminated container logs until garbage collection — they are not instantly deleted.

q: A Deployment's pods are CrashLoopBackOff with no useful events. The current container restarted 5 seconds ago so its log is empty, and the pod has two containers (app and sidecar). Which single command sequence gives you the most signal?
options: kubectl logs deploy/api --previous -c app --tail=100 — previous-instance logs of the app container: the crash reason is in the dead instance's output, -c selects the right container in a multi-container pod, and --tail bounds the output; add kubectl logs -l app=api --all-containers --prefix to sweep every replica
kubectl describe pod — events alone always contain the crash reason
kubectl logs deploy/api without flags — defaults cover previous instances and all containers
Delete the pod and wait for a fresh crash with better logs
explain: CrashLoopBackOff diagnosis is --previous plus the right container: the live container's log is empty because it just restarted, and without -c kubectl refuses (or guesses) in multi-container pods. describe shows scheduling reasons, not app output; bare logs default to the current instance of one container; deleting evidence is never the answer.

q: Your compliance team requires the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile on all app pods. You add seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} to the pod spec and it works — but a colleague claims seccomp is already on by default since 1.27 so the field is redundant. Is he right?
options: Yes — since 1.27 the kubelet applies RuntimeDefault to every pod automatically

No — seccomp defaults to Unconfined unless the kubelet is started with --seccomp-default; the 1.27 milestone only made that opt-in flag stable. Setting the field explicitly is the portable way to guarantee the profile regardless of node configuration
Seccomp profiles can only be set via annotations, not the securityContext API field
RuntimeDefault is a Windows-only profile — on Linux it is silently ignored
explain: The default seccomp behavior is Unconfined (disabled) unless the cluster admin opts in per-node with --seccomp-default; 1.27 stabilized the mechanism, not the default. Explicit seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault in the pod spec is the only setting you control from the workload side, and it works on Linux nodes.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your tuning guide asks for net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time=600 and kernel.msgmax=65536 via pod securityContext sysctls. The pod is rejected at admission. Which of these is the unsafe one, and what does the cluster need to allow it?
options: Both are safe — the rejection must come from a Pod Security Standard, not the sysctl values
net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time is unsafe; kernel.msgmax is safe

kernel.msgmax is unsafe (it affects the whole node), net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time is namespaced-safe — unsafe sysctls require the kubelet's --allowed-unsafe-sysctls flag on the node, otherwise pods requesting them fail to start
Sysctls can only be set on the node, never in a pod spec
explain: Kubernetes splits sysctls into safe (namespaced, allowed by default — most net.* fall here) and unsafe (node-wide impact like kernel.msgmax/kernel.shm*), which need --allowed-unsafe-sysctls on the kubelet or the pod is rejected. The exam trap is treating all sysctls alike; the unsafe ones are a node-admin decision, not a pod-author one.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your container env sets APP_URL: "https://$(API_HOST):$(API_PORT)/v1" but API_HOST is defined three entries later in the same env list. At runtime APP_URL literally contains $(API_HOST). Why?
options: Variable expansion only works in args, not in env values
The $() syntax is shell syntax — Kubernetes uses ${} instead

Expansion references are resolved in list order: a variable must be defined before (above) the entry that references it, and references to undefined variables are left as the literal $(...) string rather than erroring
$$ escaping is required — single $ is treated as a literal
explain: Kubernetes expands $(VAR) against previously-defined env vars (including Service host/port vars), order matters, and undefined references are passed through literally — a silent misconfiguration trap. $$ is indeed the escape for a literal $, but escaping is not the bug here; the variable was simply defined too late in the list.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A pod mounts a 500 GB volume with thousands of files and sets fsGroup: 2000. Every pod start takes minutes in 'chmod' before the app launches. Which setting fixes the slow start, and what does it change?
options: Remove fsGroup entirely — group ownership is handled by the storage driver
Set runAsGroup instead — fsGroup is deprecated
Use supplementalGroups — they bypass the chown completely

fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch — skips the recursive ownership change when the volume root already has the expected group, eliminating the minutes-long chown on every restart (the default policy re-chowns more aggressively)
explain: The kubelet's recursive chown on every start is the slow-start culprit; OnRootMismatch only chowns when the root directory's ownership doesn't already match, so warm restarts skip it. fsGroup is not deprecated, supplementalGroups add groups without replacing this behavior, and removing fsGroup changes the permission model rather than fixing the performance.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your web container must bind to port 80 but the restricted PSS requires dropping all Linux capabilities. Which securityContext satisfies both?
options: capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]} alone — binding to port 80 needs no capabilities when running as non-root
privileged: true with drop: ["ALL"] — privileged overrides the drop list
Capabilities are pod-level only — set them under spec.securityContext
capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]} — drop everything, then add back only the single capability needed to bind privileged ports (<1024)
explain: Binding ports below 1024 requires CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE even for non-root users, so the least-privilege answer is drop ALL then add just that one. Dropping everything without the add breaks the bind; privileged: true is the opposite of the requirement; and capabilities live in the container-level securityContext, not the pod level.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your liveness probe needs to check that a log file contains 'READY': exec: command: ["grep", "READY", "/var/log/app.log"]. It works. You change it to grep READY /var/log/app.log | wc -l and the probe fails permanently. What broke?
options: exec probes run the command directly with no shell — pipes, redirects, and globs are not interpreted; wrap it as ["sh", "-c", "grep READY /var/log/app.log | wc -l"]
Pipes are forbidden in probes by the API server for security
wc is not in the probe's PATH — use the absolute path /usr/bin/wc
exec probes only accept a single binary with no arguments
explain: The exec probe handler execs the argv directly — there is no shell, so | is passed as a literal argument to grep instead of creating a pipeline. Wrapping in sh -c restores shell semantics. Pipes aren't forbidden, PATH is inherited normally, and multi-argument commands are fine.

q: You add a startup probe to a slow-starting Java app but leave the existing liveness and readiness probes untouched. During the 90-second startup, what do the liveness and readiness probes do?
options: They run in parallel with the startup probe — a slow start will still trip the liveness failureThreshold
They keep their default successThreshold of 3, so the app gets extra grace automatically

While the startup probe has not yet succeeded, liveness and readiness checks are disabled — the startup probe gates them, so tune failureThreshold x periodSeconds on the startup probe to cover the worst-case start time
The startup probe replaces the readiness probe permanently after first success
explain: That gating is the entire purpose of the startup probe: until it succeeds once, liveness/readiness are suspended, protecting slow starters from premature restarts. They don't run in parallel, successThreshold defaults to 1 (not 3), and after success the normal probes resume — nothing is permanently replaced.

q: Your pod has terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 and a preStop hook that sleeps 10 seconds to let endpoint removal propagate. After SIGTERM the app needs 25 more seconds to drain. Will it get them?
options: Yes — the grace period starts after preStop completes, so the app gets the full 30 seconds after the 10-second sleep
Yes — preStop and the grace period run on separate clocks in parallel

No — preStop runs before SIGTERM but the 30-second grace countdown starts before preStop, so the sleep consumes 10 of the 30 seconds and the app has ~20 left; raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds to cover sleep + drain
No — preStop hooks are killed the moment SIGTERM is sent
explain: There is one clock: it starts when the pod is marked terminating, preStop runs first and eats into the same budget, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL at expiry. 10s sleep + 25s drain needs a grace period comfortably above 35s. The 'separate clock' and 'grace starts after preStop' options are the classic exam traps.

q: A pod has two app containers requesting 500m CPU / 1Gi each, and one init container requesting 2 CPU / 4Gi. The scheduler refuses to place it on a node with 3 CPU allocatable free, even though the init container only runs for seconds. Why?
options: The scheduler reserves the maximum of (sum of app container requests, highest init container request) per resource — here max(1 CPU, 2 CPU) = 2 CPU and max(2Gi, 4Gi) = 4Gi effective, which exceeds what's free; init containers are not summed but their peak still counts because the node must fit the hungriest phase
Init container requests are summed with app requests: 2.5 CPU total
Init containers are ignored by the scheduler entirely — the node must have a taint
The scheduler uses limits, not requests, for init containers
explain: Effective pod request = max(highest init-container request, sum of app container requests) per resource, since init containers run sequentially before the app containers but the node must accommodate whichever phase is hungrier. Summing everything over-counts; ignoring init containers under-counts — the max-of-the-two rule is the documented middle.

q: You submit a Job with restartPolicy: Always (copied from a Deployment manifest) and the API server rejects it. What is the rule, and which policies are legal for Jobs?
options: Jobs require restartPolicy: OnFailure or Never — Always is rejected because a Job's pod is meant to terminate; with Always the kubelet would restart completed pods forever and the Job could never finish
restartPolicy is immutable after creation — set it at submit time only
Jobs only accept Never; OnFailure is for CronJobs
The field must be omitted — Jobs default it internally and reject explicit values
explain: Job pods must be allowed to terminate, so only OnFailure (retry failed pods) and Never (let the Job controller count the failure) are legal; Always would resurrect finished pods and break completion semantics. The field is settable at creation — the rejection is about the value, not about mutability.

q: A bad image went out 5 revisions ago. kubectl rollout history shows revisions 8-12 and you want revision 7's template back. Which command restores it, and what does it do under the hood?
options: kubectl rollout restart — restarts pods on the current revision
kubectl apply the old manifest — rollout history is informational only and cannot be rolled back
--to-revision only accepts the immediately previous revision

kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=7 — the Deployment controller scales the ReplicaSet of revision 7 back up and the current one down, i.e. a rollback is just another rollout to an older ReplicaSet template
explain: undo --to-revision repoints the Deployment at the stored ReplicaSet template of that revision and rolls forward to it — rollbacks are rollouts to older templates, which is why revisionHistoryLimit matters. restart only recycles pods on the current template, and any retained revision (not just the previous one) is a valid target.

q: You try to change a Deployment's selector.matchLabels from app: api to app: api-v2 to 'cleanly separate' the new version, and the API server refuses. Why is the selector immutable, and what is the correct approach?
options: Selectors are immutable to prevent a Deployment from suddenly adopting or orphaning pods it doesn't own — create the v2 as a separate Deployment (or change the pod template labels, which flow into new pods while the selector stays fixed)
Selectors can be changed with kubectl replace --force — the error means you used apply
matchLabels is deprecated — use matchExpressions which are mutable
The selector is derived from the pod template automatically, so editing it is redundant
explain: Immutability protects the controller's ownership mapping: changing the selector mid-life could orphan running pods or adopt strangers. The supported path is a new Deployment object (or just updating template labels — the selector only needs to match the template, and the template's labels can evolve as long as they still satisfy the fixed selector). --force replace doesn't bypass the validation.

q: Your readiness probe passes, the new pod gets traffic, then crashes 5 seconds later — repeatedly during rollouts, causing 500s. Which Deployment field directly mitigates this, and how does it differ from the probe?
options: minReadySeconds: 10 — the pod must stay Ready for 10s before it counts as Available, so the rollout won't proceed to the next pod (or mark the Deployment available) until the pod proves stable; the probe only samples instants, minReadySeconds demands sustained readiness
progressDeadlineSeconds — extends how long the rollout waits
activeDeadlineSeconds — caps total rollout time
terminationGracePeriodSeconds — delays the old pod's shutdown
explain: The probe answers 'ready right now'; minReadySeconds answers 'ready and stable for N seconds' before the pod counts toward availability and the rollout advances. progressDeadlineSeconds detects stuck rollouts, activeDeadlineSeconds is a Job/pod field (not Deployment), and grace period only affects shutdown timing.

q: You roll out a DaemonSet update and set updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 3. During the update, how many nodes can have the DaemonSet pod down at once, and what is the DaemonSet default strategy?
options: Up to 3 nodes' pods can be unavailable simultaneously; the default updateStrategy is RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 1
maxUnavailable is a percentage for DaemonSets — 3 means 3%
DaemonSets only support OnDelete — RollingUpdate is rejected
All nodes update at once regardless — maxUnavailable is ignored for DaemonSets
explain: DaemonSets support RollingUpdate (the default) with an integer-or-percentage maxUnavailable (default 1): the controller updates that many nodes' pods at a time. OnDelete is the opt-in alternative that waits for manual pod deletion. The 'percentage-only' and 'ignored' distractors misread the field.

q: A StatefulSet has 5 replicas (web-0..web-4). You set updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: 3 and update the pod template. Which pods get the new template, and what happens if you delete web-1?
options: All 5 pods update — partition only affects the order, not the set
Pods with ordinal <= 3 update — partition is an upper bound
Pods with ordinal >= 3 (web-3, web-4) update; web-0..web-2 stay on the old template, and even if you delete web-1 it is recreated from the previous revision until you lower the partition
The partition must be 0 for any update to roll out
explain: Partition is a canary gate: ordinals >= partition take the new template, lower ordinals pin to the old revision — deleted lower-ordinal pods come back on the old template too. Lower the partition stepwise (3 → 0) to phase the rollout. 'Affects order only' and 'upper bound' invert the documented semantics.

q: You run a 3-node etcd cluster as a StatefulSet behind a headless Service. On startup each member must discover the other members' addresses — including members that are not Ready yet. Which Service field makes DNS publish not-ready pods?
options: clusterIP: None alone is sufficient — headless Services always publish all pods
sessionAffinity: ClientIP — pins DNS answers per client
externalTrafficPolicy: Local — keeps DNS answers node-local
publishNotReadyAddresses: true — without it, DNS (and endpoints) only include Ready pods, so a bootstrapping member can never discover peers that haven't passed readiness yet
explain: Headless alone still filters to ready endpoints; publishNotReadyAddresses: true is the explicit opt-in that publishes every backing pod's address regardless of readiness — the standard quorum-bootstrap pattern. sessionAffinity and externalTrafficPolicy are traffic-routing knobs, unrelated to DNS publication.

q: A multiplayer game server keeps player state in memory per pod. You set sessionAffinity: ClientIP on its Service but players still get bounced to different pods after a few hours. What is the default stickiness duration, and how is it tuned?
options: Stickiness is permanent once set — the bounces must come from pod restarts
ClientIP affinity only works for UDP — the game uses TCP
sessionAffinity requires the Service to be headless
Default timeoutSeconds is 10800 (3 hours), set via sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds (max 86400); after it expires the client may be rebalanced
explain: ClientIP stickiness expires: the default is 10800s (3h), tunable up to 86400s (24h) under sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP. The multi-hour bounce matches the default expiry exactly. It works for TCP/UDP alike, needs no headless Service, and is emphatically not permanent.
