q: To preserve real client IPs you set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on a NodePort Service. After a rolling update, one node temporarily has zero pods and requests sent there time out instead of being forwarded elsewhere. Is this expected?
options: No — kube-proxy always forwards to a pod on another node as a fallback
Only for LoadBalancer Services — NodePort always forwards

Yes — with Local, kube-proxy drops traffic on nodes with no local endpoints instead of forwarding cross-node (that's the documented tradeoff for preserving source IP); the fix is ensuring coverage (pod on every node, e.g. DaemonSet) or accepting the health-check-driven LB behavior
The timeouts prove externalTrafficPolicy was not applied — check the Service YAML
explain: Local means strictly local: no node-local endpoints, no forwarding — packets are dropped, which is the price of avoiding the SNAT hop that hides client IPs. Cloud LBs mitigate it via health checks (nodes without local endpoints fail), but direct-to-node traffic hits the drop. It applies to NodePort and LoadBalancer alike.

q: Your audit pods must talk to the API server with their original pod IP visible for network policy logging, but externalTrafficPolicy only affects traffic from outside the cluster. Which field controls the same local-only routing for in-cluster traffic?
options: clusterIP: None — headless Services preserve source IP

internalTrafficPolicy: Local — routes in-cluster Service traffic only to node-local endpoints, preserving the client pod IP the same way externalTrafficPolicy does for external traffic (default is Cluster)
sessionAffinity: ClientIP — pins the source IP
There is no in-cluster equivalent — source IP is always SNAT'd
explain: internalTrafficPolicy is the in-cluster mirror of externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps traffic on the node and preserves the source pod IP; Cluster (default) may hop nodes and masquerade. Headless Services bypass kube-proxy but don't set policy; sessionAffinity is about stickiness, not source preservation.

q: You apply a NetworkPolicy with only an egress rule allowing DNS, expecting 'default deny all + allow DNS'. Pods can still receive traffic from anywhere. What did you miss?
options: NetworkPolicies are allow-only and additive — but policyTypes defaults to [Ingress] when only ingress rules exist; with only egress rules you wrote, policyTypes must explicitly include Egress for the egress rule to take effect AND include Ingress (with no ingress rules) to actually deny ingress
Egress rules implicitly deny ingress — your CNI must be misconfigured
You need a second policy — one policy cannot contain both directions
DNS uses TCP only — you allowed UDP so the rule never matches
explain: The defaulting trap: policyTypes is inferred from the rules present ([Egress] here), so ingress stays wide open — to deny it you must list Ingress in policyTypes with no ingress rules (an empty allow = deny all). One policy can absolutely hold both directions; the CNI is fine; and DNS needs both UDP and TCP on 53.

q: An incident spans 12 replicas of a Deployment, each with app and sidecar containers. You need the last 20 lines from every app container across all replicas, tagged with the pod name. Which command does it in one shot?
options: kubectl logs -l app=api -c app --tail=20 --prefix — label selector fans out to all matching pods, -c picks the container in each multi-container pod, --prefix prepends the pod name to every line
kubectl logs deploy/api --tail=20 — covers all replicas and containers by default
kubectl logs -l app=api --all-containers merges both containers' logs per pod automatically
--prefix only works with --previous
explain: The label-selector form is the fleet-wide log tool: -l selects pods, -c disambiguates the container (required when a pod has more than one — kubectl won't guess), --tail bounds output, --prefix tags each line with its pod. The deploy/ form targets one pod's log stream, not the fleet; --all-containers exists but concatenates both containers, which isn't what's asked.

q: You suspect the metrics.k8s.io API is down because kubectl top fails. How do you query that API group directly, bypassing kubectl's resource interpretation?
options: kubectl api-versions — shows live health of each API group
kubectl top --debug — dumps the raw API payload
Raw access to aggregated APIs is blocked by RBAC by design
kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1 — issues the HTTP request verbatim and prints the raw response, so you can see whether the API group answers at all (e.g. 404/503 vs valid JSON)
explain: get --raw is the escape hatch to the API server's HTTP surface: it shows exactly what the aggregated API returns (or whether the APIService is failing) without kubectl's decoding. api-versions only lists available groups, top has no --debug dump, and RBAC applies uniformly — raw access isn't specially blocked.

q: During an outage you need only Warning events from the last hour across the namespace, newest first. Which command expresses exactly that, and why not just grep?
options: kubectl get events --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp — server-side filtering by the type field plus chronological sort; grep on the human-readable table is brittle (message text can contain 'Warning' as a word) and can't sort
kubectl get events | grep -i warn — the standard approach
--field-selector only supports metadata.name — type filtering must be client-side
Events have no type field — they use severity instead
explain: The server-side form is precise: type is a real filterable field (Normal|Warning) and --sort-by orders by the timestamp field, immune to text-matching false positives in messages. --field-selector supports more than names (type, reason, involvedObject fields work), and 'severity' isn't the field name.

q: An incident started 3 hours ago. kubectl get events shows nothing relevant, but the deployment's rollout history confirms the bad change went out then. Why are the events gone?
options: Events are namespaced — you queried the wrong namespace

The kube-apiserver retains events for 1 hour by default (--event-ttl); after that they are garbage-collected from etcd. For anything older you need an external event exporter / log sink — events are a short debugging window, not an audit log
Events are deleted when the involved object is deleted — the ReplicaSet was garbage collected
kubectl get events only shows the last 100 events — use --limit
explain: The 1-hour default TTL is the key operational fact: events are ephemeral by design to protect etcd, so a 3-hour-old incident's events are simply gone. Exporters (event exporter, Loki, etc.) are the durable answer. Namespace scoping and object deletion are real behaviors but not the cause here, and there is no --limit paging that hides them.

q: You're on an unfamiliar cluster and need to know whether the autoscaling/v2 API (for HPA behavior) exists before writing the manifest. Which commands answer 'what APIs does this cluster serve' without guessing versions?
options: kubectl explain autoscaling/v2 — works even if the group doesn't exist
Apply the manifest and read the error — the fastest discovery method
kubectl api-versions to list API groups/versions, and kubectl api-resources to list which resource kinds each group serves — discovery before authoring, instead of trial-and-error applies
API groups are identical on every cluster — just use the docs
explain: api-versions + api-resources are the discovery commands: they report exactly what this cluster's API server (including aggregated/CRD groups) serves. explain errors on unknown types, apply-and-pray wastes cycles and can half-apply, and clusters genuinely differ (managed offerings, CRDs, disabled groups).

q: A pod needs three things mounted at /etc/app/conf: a ConfigMap, a Secret, and the pod's own name from the downward API. You could declare three volumes, but there is a cleaner single-volume approach. Which one?
options: An emptyDir volume — copy all three sources into it with an init container
A hostPath volume pointing at /etc/app/conf on the node
Use envFrom for all three — volumes aren't needed for configuration
A projected volume with three sources (configMap, secret, downwardAPI) — one volume, one mount, all three data sources merged into the same directory
explain: Projected volumes exist exactly for this: multiple volume sources (configMap, secret, downwardAPI, serviceAccountToken, clusterTrustBundle) projected into a single directory with one mount. Three separate volumes work but triple the declaration; envFrom can't produce files; hostPath ties the pod to a node.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: The cluster's default ServiceAccount has automountServiceAccountToken: true, but one specific pod must NOT get a token mounted (it talks to no API). Where do you disable it so the change is scoped to just that pod?
options: Set automountServiceAccountToken: false in the pod's spec — the pod-level field overrides the ServiceAccount's setting, scoping the opt-out to that pod alone
Delete the default ServiceAccount's token Secret — that disables mounting cluster-wide
Set it on the container's securityContext — automount is a container-level field
Tokens can't be opted out per-pod — you must create a dedicated ServiceAccount with automount disabled
explain: automountServiceAccountToken exists at both levels and the pod spec wins for that pod — the precise, minimal opt-out. Deleting the SA token is a cluster-wide hammer; the field is pod-level (not container-level); and while a dedicated SA also works, it's unnecessary when the pod-level override exists.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create a Secret with type: kubernetes.io/tls for an Ingress, providing keys cert.pem and key.pem. The Ingress controller ignores it and serves its default certificate. What is wrong with the Secret?
options: TLS Secrets must be created with kubectl create secret tls, which encrypts the values — hand-written ones are rejected
The type field is case-sensitive and must be Kubernetes.io/TLS
A kubernetes.io/tls Secret must carry exactly the keys tls.crt and tls.key — controllers look up those names; cert.pem/key.pem are ignored even though the data is valid PEM
Ingress controllers only accept Secrets in the ingress-nginx namespace
explain: The tls Secret type is a contract on key names: tls.crt and tls.key. Wrong key names mean the controller finds nothing to serve, with no error — a silent mismatch. kubectl create secret tls just builds the same object conveniently; the type string is lowercase as written; cross-namespace Secrets are the actual restriction (the Secret must be in the Ingress's namespace).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You hand-write a docker-registry Secret manifest with type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson and put the base64 credentials under key: config.json. Image pulls fail with 'no basic auth credentials'. What is the key supposed to be?
options: The key name is free-form — the failure must be bad base64 padding
username and password as separate keys — dockerconfigjson Secrets use two keys
.dockerconfigjson — the type mandates that exact key holding the Docker config JSON auth blob; any other key name is ignored by the kubelet
Docker Secrets don't use keys at all — the data section must be empty
explain: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson requires the single key .dockerconfigjson containing the Docker config auth JSON blob — that leading-dot name is the contract, and a differently-named key is silently ignored at pull time. (kubectl create secret docker-registry builds this correctly, which is why hand-written ones are the exam's failure mode.)
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A ConfigMap holding feature flags is accidentally edited several times a day, breaking the app. You want the API server to reject any update to it. Which field provides this, and what is the operational consequence?
options: Setting the ConfigMap's resourceVersion explicitly — locks the object

immutable: true — the API server rejects all updates to the data/binaryData; to change the flags you must delete and recreate the ConfigMap (which is the point: it forces a deliberate, reviewable change and also lets kubelet skip the watch)
Adding the annotation config.kubernetes.io/immutable — annotations are advisory only
ConfigMaps are immutable by default once mounted — no field needed
explain: immutable: true makes the data fields write-once: updates are rejected, so changes require delete+recreate — deliberate friction against drive-by edits, plus kubelet can close its watch. resourceVersion is concurrency control, not a lock; the annotation doesn't exist; mounted ConfigMaps update by default (the kubelet syncs them).
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You create a Job with completions: 6 and parallelism: 2 to process 6 work items. How does the Job controller schedule the pods, and what happens if one pod fails with restartPolicy: Never?
options: All 6 pods start at once — parallelism is only a hint

2 pods run at a time; as each succeeds the controller starts another until 6 have succeeded — 3 waves total; a failed pod (Never) counts against backoffLimit and is replaced so the completion count can still be reached
The Job runs 2 pods and stops — completions is capped by parallelism
One pod runs 6 times sequentially — parallelism multiplies the work per pod
explain: parallelism caps concurrent pods; completions is the success target — the controller keeps the pipeline full (2 at a time here) until 6 pods have succeeded. A failed pod with Never isn't restarted in place; the failure counts toward backoffLimit and a replacement pod is created to still reach the completion count.

q: A Job has backoffLimit: 3 and its pods keep failing. What does the limit count, and what happens between attempts?
options: It counts container restarts — three restarts across any pods fail the Job
It counts successful pods — three successes mark the Job Failed
It counts failed pods (not container restarts): once failed pods exceed backoffLimit the Job is marked Failed, and retries are spaced with exponential back-off (10s, 20s, 40s, capped at six minutes)
It counts schedule ticks — the Job fails after three CronJob schedules
explain: backoffLimit is a failed-pod counter: container-level restarts (restartPolicy: OnFailure) don't increment it, only pod failures do. Retries back off exponentially (10s, 20s, 40s… capped at 6m), and exceeding the limit marks the Job Failed. Counting restarts or successes are the standard misreads.

q: A CronJob's schedule triggers while the previous run is still going. With the default concurrencyPolicy the cluster fills with overlapping runs; you want at most one run and the old one killed when a new schedule hits. Which policy, and what do the other two do?
options: Forbid — skips the new run; the other policies are Allow (default, overlaps permitted) and Replace (the running job is deleted and a new one starts)
Suspend — pauses the schedule; Allow and Replace are node selectors
Replace — cancels the old run and starts the new one; Allow (default) permits overlaps, Forbid skips the new schedule while the previous run is active
concurrencyPolicy only accepts true/false — overlapping is unavoidable
explain: The three policies are Allow (default — overlapping runs permitted), Forbid (skip the new run while one is active), and Replace (delete the running Job, start fresh). The described need — kill the old, start the new — is Replace. 'Suspend' is a different field (spec.suspend pauses the whole schedule).

q: A CronJob missed its 2 AM run because the controller was down for 10 minutes. At 2:10 the controller is back and starts the missed job — but your backup job must never start more than 2 minutes late, or it collides with production traffic. Which field enforces that deadline?
options: activeDeadlineSeconds — caps how long the job may run
startingDeadlineSeconds: 120 — if the controller can't start the Job within 120s of its scheduled time, the start is skipped and counted as a missed (failed) schedule instead of running late
concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — prevents late starts
backoffLimit: 0 — fails the job immediately on any delay
explain: startingDeadlineSeconds is the 'start no later than' budget for a scheduled run: miss it and the Job is never started for that tick (counted as failed in status). activeDeadlineSeconds caps execution duration, not start lateness; Forbid governs overlap, not lateness; backoffLimit governs retries.

q: Your namespace accumulates hundreds of completed Jobs from a busy CronJob, cluttering kubectl get jobs and etcd. You want finished Jobs (and their pods) auto-deleted 10 minutes after completion, without a cron cleaner. Which field?
options: revisionHistoryLimit — prunes old Jobs like ReplicaSets
activeDeadlineSeconds: 600 — deletes the Job 10 minutes after it starts
Jobs are garbage-collected automatically after 1 hour — no field needed
ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600 on the Job — the TTL controller deletes the finished Job (and its pods) 600s after it completes; failed Jobs can use the same field
explain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished drives the TTL-after-finished controller: N seconds after the Job reaches Complete/Failed, the Job object (and its pods, via cascading deletion) is removed — the built-in replacement for external cleaners. revisionHistoryLimit is a Deployment field; activeDeadlineSeconds kills running pods at the deadline; there is no automatic 1-hour Job GC.

q: You need to canary a StatefulSet: update only web-3 and web-4 to the new image while web-0..web-2 stay put for now. You set updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: 3. A colleague says you also need podManagementPolicy: Parallel for the partition to work. Is he right?
options: Yes — partitions only take effect with Parallel pod management
No — but you need OnDelete updateStrategy instead of RollingUpdate
Partitions are a Deployment feature — StatefulSets don't support them

No — partition works with the default OrderedReady policy too; partition selects WHICH ordinals update (>= 3), while podManagementPolicy selects the ORDER/speed of pod creation (OrderedReady = strictly sequential 0..N, Parallel = no ordering guarantees)
explain: The two knobs are orthogonal: partition gates which ordinals take the new template; podManagementPolicy governs creation/deletion ordering (OrderedReady's strict sequencing vs Parallel's free-for-all, useful for faster scale-up). Neither requires the other, OnDelete is the manual alternative to RollingUpdate, and partitions are a StatefulSet feature.

q: You delete a StatefulSet named db with volumeClaimTemplates named data. The pods are gone but the PVCs data-db-0..2 remain, Bound, holding data. Is this a leak, and how do you reclaim or keep the data deliberately?
options: It's a leak — StatefulSet deletion always deletes its PVCs; file a bug
The PVCs are orphaned and unusable — only the StatefulSet that created them can ever mount them
Set cascading deletion with --cascade=foreground to delete PVCs too

Expected behavior — PVCs created from volumeClaimTemplates are never auto-deleted with the StatefulSet (protecting data); delete them explicitly with kubectl delete pvc -l app=db when the data is truly disposable, or leave them so a recreated StatefulSet reattaches (PVC names are <template>-<sts>-<ordinal>)
explain: volumeClaimTemplates PVCs are deliberately retained on StatefulSet deletion — data safety over tidiness. The naming convention (<claim>-<sts>-<ordinal>) means a same-named StatefulSet reattaches to the existing data. Foreground cascading affects dependents via ownerReferences, but these PVCs aren't owned that way, so explicit deletion is the cleanup path.

q: You run: helm install api ./chart -f prod.yaml --set-json '{"replicas":3}' --set replicas=2 --set-string replicas="2" --set-file replicas=count.txt (count.txt contains 5). All target the same key. Which value wins, and what is the general rule?
options: --set-json wins — JSON is the most explicit format
The values file prod.yaml wins — files beat all --set variants

--set-file wins — within the CLI flags, later-processed sources override earlier ones: files < --set-json < --set < --set-string < --set-file, and all CLI flags beat -f/--values files, which beat the chart's values.yaml
The last flag typed on the command line wins regardless of flag type
explain: Helm merges CLI value sources in a fixed order with later sources winning: -f files first, then --set-json, --set, --set-string, --set-file last — so --set-file's 5 wins here. Typing order across different flag types doesn't matter (only repeated uses of the same flag are rightmost-wins). Chart values.yaml sits below all of these.

q: Your chart template does {{ .Values.apiKey }} and renders an empty string when the key is missing, deploying a broken app. You want the render to FAIL loudly instead, but only for this one required value. Which function, and how does it differ from default?
options: {{ .Values.apiKey | default "" }} — fails when empty
{{ required .Values.apiKey }} — required takes the value first
{{ .Values.apiKey | required "apiKey is required" }} — required aborts template rendering with your message when the value is empty/missing; default silently substitutes a fallback value instead
required only works in values.schema.json — templates can't enforce it
explain: required "message" value is the fail-fast guard: empty/missing input aborts the render with your message, while default quietly substitutes. Note the pipeline order — the message comes first, then the value. values.schema.json validates types/coercion at a different layer; required is the template-level enforcement.

q: Your chart has two pre-install hooks: a Secret (weight "-5") and a Job (weight "10"). In what order do they run, and after a successful install the Job object is still in the cluster — why?
options: Job first (higher weight runs first), and hooks are always deleted automatically

Secret first — hooks sort by weight ascending (-5 before 10); the Job remains because the default hook-delete-policy is before-hook-creation, which only removes the previous hook instance before the next run — add hook-succeeded to delete it after success
Weights are strings so they sort alphabetically: "10" before "-5"
Hooks run in parallel — weight only affects deletion order
explain: Weights sort numerically ascending (lower first): the Secret (-5) runs before the Job (10). The leftover Job is the default deletion policy at work — before-hook-creation cleans the previous instance before launching a new one but doesn't remove the just-completed one; hook-succeeded (often combined as "before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded") deletes on success while keeping failed hooks around for debugging.

q: You write a NetworkPolicy with an egress rule allowing port 53 to 0.0.0.0/0, expecting DNS to work. Pods still can't resolve names. The rule allows TCP port 53 only. What is missing?
options: Nothing — DNS is TCP-only; the problem is elsewhere
Port 53 must be allowed on ingress, not egress — DNS is inbound
DNS primarily uses UDP port 53 (TCP only for large/truncated responses) — the egress rule must allow both UDP and TCP on 53, otherwise the default-deny egress policy drops the UDP queries
NetworkPolicy can't allow DNS — use a separate DNSPolicy object
explain: The classic DNS-egress trap: stub resolvers send UDP first, so a TCP-only allowance leaves name resolution broken under a default-deny egress stance. Allow both protocols on 53 (or scope the rule to the kube-dns/CoreDNS pods). DNS queries are egress from the pod's perspective, and there is no DNSPolicy object — that's a fabricated kind.

q: You need a NetworkPolicy egress rule allowing all outbound traffic EXCEPT the 10.0.0.0/8 pod CIDR (to force external traffic through a proxy sidecar). Which ipBlock form expresses 'everywhere except 10/8'?
options: ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0} — covers everything; exceptions aren't supported
Two rules: one allowing 0.0.0.0/0 and a second denying 10.0.0.0/8 — NetworkPolicy supports deny rules
Use podSelector instead — ipBlock can't express this
egress: [{to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [10.0.0.0/8]}}]}] — the except list carves exclusions out of the cidr; note NetworkPolicy is allow-only, so there are no deny rules to stack
explain: ipBlock supports except: [...] for carve-outs — the allow-only model means you express 'all but X' in a single allow rule rather than allow+deny pairs (deny rules don't exist in NetworkPolicy). The two-rule approach fails because a second 'deny' rule is invalid, and podSelector matches pods, not arbitrary CIDRs.

q: Your NetworkPolicy allows ingress to port: web on pods whose containers expose containerPort: 8080 with name: web. After a deploy renames the container port to http (still 8080), the policy stops matching and traffic is dropped. Why did the name matter?
options: It didn't — port names are cosmetic; the drop must be from the deployment's new labels

NetworkPolicy port names are resolved against the pod spec's named container ports — port: web only matches pods with a containerPort literally named web; renaming it to http (or using a numeric port: 8080) changes what matches
Named ports in NetworkPolicy refer to Service port names, not container port names
The policy caches the old port mapping — delete and recreate the NetworkPolicy
explain: Named ports in a NetworkPolicy are looked up in the destination pods' container port definitions — the name is a live reference, not a label. Renaming the containerPort breaks the match even though the number is identical. Using the numeric 8080 in the policy would have been immune to the rename; no caching is involved.

q: Your app makes thousands of external API calls (api.stripe.com) and CoreDNS is saturated. You notice each lookup generates multiple upstream queries. The pod's resolv.conf shows options ndots:5. What is happening, and what is the targeted fix?
options: ndots:5 means names with fewer than 5 dots are tried against every search domain first (api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local, ...svc..., ...cluster.local) before the bare name — 3+ wasted NXDOMAIN queries per lookup; set dnsConfig.options ndots: "1" (or use FQDNs with a trailing dot) for external-heavy workloads, keeping in mind short service names then need full qualification
ndots:5 limits DNS to 5 queries per second — raise it to 50
The search domains are the problem — delete them with dnsPolicy: None
CoreDNS caches for 5 seconds because of ndots — lower it to cache longer
explain: ndots:5 is the threshold below which the resolver walks the whole search list first: a 2-dot external name burns a query per search suffix before the real lookup. Lowering ndots (via dnsConfig) or using trailing-dot FQDNs skips the fanout — at the cost that bare short names like 'db' may no longer expand, so internal callers must use FQDNs. dnsPolicy: None requires full manual dnsConfig; it's not a shortcut.

q: You deploy a monitoring agent with hostNetwork: true and it can't resolve in-cluster Service names (db.monitoring resolves nowhere), though node-level DNS works. Which DNS policy does a hostNetwork pod need, and why?
options: dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst — the default, which should already work
dnsPolicy: None with manual nameservers — the only supported option for hostNetwork
dnsPolicy: Default — hostNetwork pods share the host's network stack, so ClusterFirst's cluster-DNS resolv.conf is wrong for them; Default makes the pod inherit the node's DNS configuration instead
DNS doesn't work with hostNetwork at all — run the agent as a sidecar instead
explain: ClusterFirst writes the cluster DNS IP into resolv.conf, which is unreachable/meaningless from the host network namespace in many setups; Default inherits the node's resolver (correct for host-networked pods, at the cost of losing cluster Service discovery — use node IPs or hostnames). None+manual config also works but isn't the only option.

q: You run kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f deploy.yaml and it succeeds, but the real apply fails with a validation error. What did client dry-run miss that server dry-run would have caught?
options: Nothing — client and server dry-run are identical; the cluster must have changed between runs
Client dry-run requires --validate=true to do anything — by default it's a no-op
Server dry-run actually applies the object — it's not a dry run at all

--dry-run=client only renders and validates locally without contacting the API server — it misses server-side validation, defaulting, admission webhooks, and quota checks; --dry-run=server sends the object through the full API pipeline (validation, mutation, admission) without persisting it
explain: Client dry-run is kubectl-side only: schema rendering with no server round-trip. Server dry-run exercises the real admission chain (API validation, defaulting, mutating/validating webhooks, quota) and returns what would be persisted — which is why it catches the errors client mode waves through. It persists nothing.

q: Before applying a big refactor you want to see exactly what would change server-side, as a diff. Which command does this, and what is it actually comparing?
options: kubectl diff -f refactor/ — performs a server-side dry run of the apply and diffs the live objects against the would-be-applied state, showing the precise field-level changes before anything is persisted
kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f refactor/ --diff — client-side only and shows nothing useful
kubectl get --raw — shows raw objects but no comparison
git diff — the cluster state isn't in git, so this is meaningless
explain: kubectl diff is the pre-apply preview: it dry-runs the apply server-side and renders the field-level delta vs live state. Client dry-run can't show server-defaulted changes; --raw shows objects without comparison; and the git joke is the distractor for people who version everything except the cluster.

q: You want a ResourceQuota that caps only the batch workloads (Jobs/CronJobs with activeDeadlineSeconds set), leaving long-running services uncapped. Which scope expression does this, and what does it match?
options: scopes: [BestEffort] — matches pods without resource requirements
scopes: [NotTerminating] — matches batch workloads
scopeSelector matching Terminating — matches pods where spec.activeDeadlineSeconds is set (>= 0), i.e. time-bounded pods; pair it with the pod/cpu/memory resources the quota should count
Quotas can't distinguish batch from services — split them into separate namespaces
explain: The Terminating scope matches exactly pods with activeDeadlineSeconds >= 0 — the time-bounded batch population — while NotTerminating matches everything else. (The naming is historical: it predates Jobs and refers to pods with a deadline.) With a scope set, the quota only counts matching pods' cpu/memory/pods. Separate namespaces also work but the scope is the precise tool.

q: A LimitRange sets default request 100m/128Mi and default limit 500m/512Mi. A developer submits a pod requesting 400m CPU with a 300m limit. It is rejected. Which LimitRange mechanism fired, and why?
options: The defaults overrode the pod's values — defaults always win
min/max constraints — 400m exceeds the max request

The pod is invalid on its face — a container's limit (300m) may never be below its request (400m), so no LimitRange ratio is even evaluated; maxLimitRequestRatio is the separate knob that caps how large limit/request may be
LimitRange can't reject pods — it only fills in defaults
explain: The rejection is the universal invariant, not a ratio: a container's limit may never be below its request (300m < 400m is invalid on any cluster). maxLimitRequestRatio is the related but distinct knob — it caps how large limit/request may be (e.g. ratio 4 blocks a 100m request with a 1 CPU limit). LimitRange absolutely can reject, via min, max, and maxLimitRequestRatio.

q: You create two PriorityClasses, both with globalDefault: true, expecting 'either one applies when pods don't specify a class'. The second one is rejected. What is the rule?
options: PriorityClass names must be unique — you reused a name
Only one PriorityClass in the cluster may have globalDefault: true — the admission check rejects a second; pods without an explicit priorityClassName get the single global default's value
globalDefault requires value: 0 — nonzero defaults are rejected
PriorityClasses are namespaced — create them in the same namespace
explain: globalDefault is a cluster-singleton flag: exactly one PriorityClass may claim it, so unscheduled pods without a class get a deterministic value. Name uniqueness is a separate rule; the value can be any integer (higher = more important, preemption order); PriorityClasses are cluster-scoped, not namespaced.

q: You need a ConfigMap to carry a small binary license file (non-UTF8). kubectl create configmap lic --from-file=license.bin succeeds, but the app reading it as text gets garbage. Where did the binary land, and how should the app consume it?
options: In data.license.bin — ConfigMaps transparently handle binary; the app has a bug
kubectl rejects binary files for ConfigMaps — use a Secret instead
ConfigMaps can't hold binary data at all — mount it from a PVC
In binaryData.license.bin — kubectl base64-encodes non-UTF8 files into binaryData automatically; the app (or a volume mount) gets the decoded bytes, while data is strictly UTF-8 strings
explain: ConfigMap has two maps: data (UTF-8 strings) and binaryData (base64-encoded bytes); --from-file routes non-UTF8 content to binaryData automatically. Mounted as a volume, the file materializes as the original bytes. Secrets aren't required for non-sensitive binary, and PVCs are overkill.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Two containers in one pod (app as UID 1000, log-shipper as UID 2000) share an emptyDir volume, but the shipper gets 'permission denied' reading files the app wrote (mode 640, group 3000). Which pod-level field grants the shipper group access without changing either image's USER?
options: supplementalGroups: [3000] — adds the group to every container's group list, so the shipper's processes gain group-3000 read access to the shared files
fsGroup: 3000 — changes file ownership on the volume, but only for volume types that support it
runAsGroup: 3000 — sets the primary group of both containers, breaking the app's expectations
Share the volume as readOnly — read-only mounts bypass permission checks
explain: supplementalGroups appends extra groups to all containers' supplementary group sets — the standard fix for cross-container shared-volume access when UIDs differ. fsGroup chowns volume files (works here too but changes ownership rather than granting access); runAsGroup replaces the primary group; readOnly doesn't bypass Unix permissions.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your pod spec sets securityContext.runAsUser: 1000 at pod level, but one container needs runAsUser: 0 for a privileged setup task, and you want to drop ALL capabilities on the app container. Where do these settings live, and what wins?
options: Everything must be pod-level — per-container securityContext is not allowed

Container-level securityContext overrides pod-level for the same fields, and capabilities (add/drop) exist ONLY at container level — so set runAsUser: 0 on the setup container (overriding the pod's 1000) and capabilities.drop on the app container
Pod-level always wins — the setup container cannot run as root if the pod says 1000
Capabilities are pod-level — set them once for all containers
explain: The container-level securityContext overrides the pod-level one field-by-field, and the capabilities stanza is container-only (there is no pod-level capabilities field). So the setup container gets runAsUser: 0 while the app keeps the pod's 1000 plus its own dropped capabilities. 'Pod always wins' inverts the precedence.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: You expose the container's CPU limit to the app via the downward API resourceFieldRef, and the app expects millicores as an integer. The raw value comes through as '2' (meaning 2 CPUs). Which divisor setting gives the app '2000'?
options: divisor: 1000 — divides the value by 1000
No divisor is needed — resourceFieldRef always reports millicores
The downward API can't expose limits — only requests
divisor: 1m — scales the quantity to millicores, so a 2-CPU limit is exposed as 2000
explain: resourceFieldRef supports divisor to rescale the quantity: divisor: 1m expresses CPU in millicores (2 → 2000). divisor: 1 is the default (2 → '2'); 1000 would divide the wrong way. Both requests and limits are exposable via resourceFieldRef — the 'only requests' claim is false.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: Your app needs its own pod name and namespace as env vars for log correlation. Which downward API fieldRefs provide them, and what is a common mistake when referencing labels instead?
options: fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name} and fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.namespace} — both are supported; for labels the path is metadata.labels['app'] and the value is captured at pod creation (it does NOT live-update if labels change later, unlike volume-mounted downward API files which are refreshed)
env vars can't use the downward API — only volume mounts
metadata.name isn't available — use spec.nodeName instead
Label values live-update in env vars automatically
explain: metadata.name and metadata.namespace are first-class downward API fields for env injection. The subtlety is labels/annotations: env-var values are frozen at container start, while downwardAPI volume files are periodically refreshed by the kubelet — so label changes propagate to files but never to already-injected env vars. Downward API works for both env and volumes.
domain: Domain 1: Application Environment, Configuration and Security

q: A CronJob's next run is hours away but you need to test tonight's batch job RIGHT NOW with the exact same template. What is the one-liner, and what does it create?
options: kubectl create job manual-test --from=cronjob/nightly-batch — creates a standalone Job from the CronJob's jobTemplate, running immediately with an independent lifecycle (the CronJob's schedule is untouched)
kubectl run manual-test --image=batch:latest — equivalent as long as you pass the same env vars
Edit the CronJob's schedule to '* * * * *' temporarily — the only way to trigger it
CronJobs can't be triggered manually — wait for the schedule
explain: --from=cronjob/<name> clones the jobTemplate into a regular Job you can run, watch, and delete independently — the purpose-built manual trigger. kubectl run rebuilds the spec by hand (drift risk); editing the schedule fires the real recurring job and risks double-runs.

q: Your app speaks only HTTP, but the mesh requires all outbound traffic as mTLS. Instead of changing the app, you add a sidecar that accepts the app's plain HTTP on localhost and forwards it as mTLS. Which multi-container pattern is this?
options: Adapter — normalizes the app's output format
Init container — runs before the app starts
Sidecar logging — ships logs to a collector
Ambassador — a proxy sidecar that represents the app to the outside world (or vice versa), letting the app stay simple while the ambassador handles cross-cutting concerns like mTLS, retries, or auth
explain: Ambassador = proxy on behalf of the main container: the app talks plain localhost HTTP, the ambassador handles the complex protocol outward. Adapter transforms data formats (e.g. log normalization); init containers run to completion before app start; neither describes a localhost proxy.

q: Your app writes logs to /var/log/app/*.log (files, not stdout). You add a log-shipper sidecar in the same pod. How do the two containers share the log files, and what is the key volume property?
options: They can't — containers in a pod have isolated filesystems with no sharing mechanism
An emptyDir volume mounted at /var/log/app in both containers — emptyDir is pod-scoped storage shared by all containers in the pod for its lifetime; the app writes, the shipper tails and forwards
A ConfigMap mounted in both — ConfigMaps are writable shared storage
Use hostPath — the only shareable volume type
explain: emptyDir is the pod-local shared filesystem: both containers mount it at the same path, the app writes files, the sidecar reads them — the textbook sidecar-logging pattern. Container filesystems are otherwise isolated; ConfigMaps are read-only config, not scratch space; hostPath works but ties the pod to a node unnecessarily.

q: You need to pause a CronJob over a maintenance weekend without losing its schedule definition, history, or Jobs. Which field does this, and how does it differ from deleting the CronJob?
options: Delete the CronJob and recreate it Monday — suspend isn't a real field
Scale the CronJob to 0 — CronJobs support replicas
Set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — pauses scheduling

spec.suspend: true — the CronJob controller stops creating Jobs while the object, its schedule, and its history stay intact; set it back to false to resume. Deleting would lose the schedule and successful-Job history
explain: suspend is the pause switch: no new Jobs are scheduled, everything else is preserved, and flipping it back resumes cleanly. CronJobs have no replicas to scale; Forbid only prevents overlapping runs; delete+recreate loses successfulJobHistoryLimit-tracked history and risks spec drift.

q: You try to set a custom selector on a Job (spec.selector.matchLabels) to group batch workloads, and the API server rejects it. Why, and how do you select a Job's pods instead?
options: Selectors are forbidden on Jobs entirely — Jobs can't be selected

The Job controller auto-generates an immutable selector (controller-uid based) — you must not set it manually; select the pods with the job-name=<job> label that the controller applies, e.g. kubectl logs -l job-name=nightly-batch
Custom selectors are allowed but must match the pod template exactly including the controller-uid label
Use spec.template.metadata.labels — the selector is derived from them automatically
explain: Job selectors are system-managed (a unique controller-uid hash) and immutable — manual selectors are rejected to guarantee the 1:1 Job↔pods mapping. The controller labels every pod job-name=<jobname>, which is the supported selector for logs/describe. Template labels don't derive the selector; they're matched against it.

q: Your chart ships a smoke-test Job annotated helm.sh/hook: test. After helm install, the test never ran. A teammate says tests run automatically post-install. Who is right?
options: The teammate — test hooks run automatically after every install and upgrade
helm test only runs on helm upgrade, not install

Test hooks run ONLY when you explicitly invoke helm test <release> — they are on-demand validation Jobs/Pods, never part of the install/upgrade lifecycle; that's what distinguishes them from pre/post-install hooks
Test hooks were removed in Helm 3 — use pre-install hooks instead
explain: helm.sh/hook: test marks resources for the helm test command exclusively — install/upgrade ignore them. That's the design: lifecycle hooks automate the release flow, test hooks are a manual verification step you run when you choose. They were not removed; they're a core Helm feature.

q: You find a chart with type: library in Chart.yaml. What does that mean for helm install, and what are library charts for?
options: It's installed like any chart — type is informational only

Library charts cannot be installed directly — they provide reusable named templates/helpers that application charts include as dependencies; helm install on one fails because there is nothing to render into the cluster
Library charts are OCI-only — they can't live in a repo directory
type: library means the chart is deprecated
explain: Library charts are helper-only: type: library tells Helm there's no releasable workload here, just _helpers.tpl-style templates for other charts to consume via dependencies. Installing one errors out. They're the DRY mechanism for chart authors, unrelated to OCI packaging or deprecation.

q: Your umbrella chart needs TWO independent Redis instances (cache and sessions) from the same redis subchart. How do you declare this in Chart.yaml dependencies?
options: List the redis dependency twice — Helm deduplicates identical entries automatically
Use the alias field: two dependency entries with the same chart/version but different alias values (redis-cache, redis-sessions) — each alias gets its own values subtree and release resources
Aliases are only for values files — dependencies can't be duplicated
Install redis twice with two helm install commands — umbrella charts support one instance per subchart
explain: alias is the multi-instance mechanism: same chart, two dependency entries, two aliases → two independent sub-releases with separate .Values.redis-cache / .Values.redis-sessions subtrees. Duplicate entries without alias are deduplicated; two separate helm installs break the umbrella's single-release management.

q: You need to patch a Deployment's container image AND remove an env var in one kubectl patch call. The JSON patch --type=json with remove operations works, but --type=strategic fails on the CRD-based operator object nearby. What is the actual difference between the patch types?
options: They're identical — strategic is just an alias for json

strategic merge patch (default for built-in types) understands Kubernetes list-merge semantics (patchStrategy tags like merge on name key), so it can merge lists intelligently; json patch (RFC 6902) is positional op-based and works on any object including CRDs; plain merge patch replaces whole lists
json patch only works on CRDs — built-in types require strategic
kubectl patch always uses strategic — --type is ignored
explain: Three distinct semantics: strategic (default where supported) merges lists by merge key using the type's patchStrategy metadata; JSON patch applies explicit add/remove/replace ops by path (universal, hence the CRD-safe choice); merge patch (RFC 7386) replaces maps and whole lists. The strategic failure on the CRD is expected — CRDs lack patchStrategy metadata, so fall back to --type=json or merge.

q: You manage a namespace declaratively: kubectl apply -f manifests/ plus --prune to delete objects you removed from git. The first prune run wants to delete half the namespace, including resources you never managed. What guard did you miss?
options: --prune is a no-op without --all — it never deletes anything

You must scope the prune: --prune -l <selector> limits deletion to objects carrying your label, and --prune-allowlist restricts which GroupVersionKinds may be pruned — unscoped prune matches everything previously applied (and can surprise you via the last-applied annotation inventory)
Prune only works with kustomize, not plain manifests
Apply --prune requires --force — otherwise it's a dry run
explain: Unscoped --prune is the footgun: always pair it with -l to select your managed set and --prune-allowlist to bound the kinds (core/v1 Pod, apps/v1 Deployment, etc.). The prune inventory comes from last-applied-configuration annotations, so anything ever applied with the same tooling is a candidate — scope it or lose things.

q: You create a Service with no selector to front an external database (10.0.5.44:5432). kubectl get endpoints shows <none> and the Service has no backends. What must you create manually, and why doesn't the controller do it?
options: A Deployment with the database image — Services require pod backends

An Endpoints (or EndpointSlice) object with the same name as the Service, listing 10.0.5.44:5432 — the endpoints controller only auto-populates endpoints when the Service HAS a selector; selector-less Services leave endpoint management to you
An Ingress — selector-less Services only work behind Ingress
Nothing — ClusterIP Services work without endpoints
explain: No selector → no automatic endpoints: you hand-write the Endpoints/EndpointSlice (name must match the Service) pointing at the external IP:port, and kube-proxy routes the ClusterIP there. This is the standard 'external service behind a cluster IP' pattern. A ClusterIP with no endpoints blackholes traffic.

q: Your Service maps port 80 to the pods, but the app team changes the container port from 8080 to 9090. You want the Service manifest to survive that change untouched. Which targetPort form gives you that indirection?
options: targetPort: 8080 — numeric ports auto-track container port changes
Omit targetPort — it defaults to following the container's port
targetPort: http — a named port resolved against the pod's containerPorts; the Service keeps pointing at the logical name while the pod team renumbers the actual port freely
targetPort must equal port — the indirection isn't supported
explain: Named targetPorts are the decoupling mechanism: the Service references the logical name (http), the pod defines which number that name means today. Renumbering the containerPort no longer requires a Service edit. Numeric targetPorts are literal; omitting targetPort defaults it to the Service port value, not the container's.

q: Your cloud load balancer needs to know which Services speak HTTP vs raw TCP to configure L7 routing. Which Service port field carries that protocol hint, and what are typical values?
options: protocol: TCP/UDP — that's the L4 protocol, not the app protocol
appProtocol: http — a free-form (but conventionally standardized) hint like http, https, grpc, or kubernetes.io/ws that LB controllers and meshes read; it doesn't change kube-proxy behavior itself
targetPort — the name implies the protocol
Annotations only — there is no API field for this
explain: appProtocol is the dedicated hint field: it tells controllers/meshes the application-layer protocol (http, https, grpc, mysql...) without affecting kube-proxy's L4 forwarding. protocol is TCP/UDP/SCTP only. Standardized values (kubernetes.io/h2c, kubernetes.io/ws) exist but the field is a hint, not enforcement.

q: kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80 works from your laptop, but a teammate on another machine can't reach your forwarded port. What is the binding behavior, and the fix?
options: port-forward binds 127.0.0.1 only — add --address 0.0.0.0 to listen on all interfaces (and mind the security implications of exposing it to the network)
port-forward requires --address even for localhost — your command should have failed
Forwarded ports are only reachable via the pod IP — use that instead
port-forward doesn't work with Services — forward to a pod
explain: Default bind is localhost-only; --address 0.0.0.0 opens it to the LAN (convenient for demos, risky on untrusted networks — anyone who can reach your machine gets your cluster access). port-forward supports the svc/ prefix fine; the pod IP is cluster-internal and not the answer.

q: You request nodePort: 80 on a NodePort Service and the API server rejects it. What is the allowed range, and what happens if you omit nodePort entirely on a LoadBalancer Service you don't want NodePorts for?
options: NodePorts must be in 30000-32767 (default range) — 80 is rejected; omit nodePort to get one auto-allocated, or set allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false on a LoadBalancer Service to skip NodePort allocation entirely
Any port 1-65535 is valid — 80 was rejected for another reason
Omitting nodePort disables the Service — nodePort is required
LoadBalancer Services never allocate NodePorts
explain: The default NodePort range is 30000-32767 (configurable via the API server's --service-node-port-range); out-of-range values are rejected. Unspecified nodePorts are auto-allocated — and LoadBalancer Services allocate them too by default, unless allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false opts out (for LB controllers that target pods directly).

q: A node hits memory pressure and the kubelet starts evicting pods. Which pods go first, and which eviction signal fired?
options: Alphabetical by pod name — the signal is memory.available dropping below the eviction threshold
Guaranteed pods first — they hold the most memory

BestEffort pods first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed (only if needed) — QoS class sets the eviction order; the signal is memory.available (also nodefs.available, imagefs.available, nodefs.inodesFree, pid.available for other pressures)
Eviction is random — QoS only affects scheduling
explain: Node-pressure eviction follows QoS: BestEffort (no requests/limits) are the first sacrificed, then Burstable exceeding their requests, Guaranteed last. The kubelet watches eviction signals — memory.available, nodefs.available, imagefs.available, pid.available — against --eviction-hard thresholds. QoS is very much an eviction concept, not just scheduling.

q: A pod is evicted with 'ephemeral storage exceeded limit' though its memory and CPU are fine. What counts toward ephemeral-storage, and how do you bound it?
options: Only the container image layers — pull smaller images
ephemeral-storage can't be limited — it's informational only
Only emptyDir counts — move logs to stdout

The container writable layer + logs + emptyDir volumes (everything on the node's ephemeral disk for that pod) — set ephemeral-storage requests/limits like any other resource; exceeding the limit evicts the pod, exceeding available disk triggers node-pressure eviction
explain: Ephemeral storage = writable layer + logs + emptyDir: all pod data that lives on the node's local disk. It takes real requests/limits (e.g. 2Gi), the kubelet enforces the limit by evicting violators, and node-level disk pressure (nodefs.available) evicts by QoS. Image layers don't count against the pod.

q: You delete a namespace and it sits in Terminating for an hour. kubectl get ns shows it stuck; the resources inside are mostly gone. What is the most likely blocker, and the safe fix direction?
options: The API server is down — wait for it to recover

A finalizer on the namespace (or on a remaining resource like a PVC) is blocking completion — some controller that should remove it is gone or failing; identify the holder via the finalizers list and either fix/remove the blocking resource or, as a last resort, edit the finalizers out through the API
Namespaces always take an hour — the 1h events TTL applies here too
Delete it with --force --grace-period=0 — namespaces support force deletion
explain: Terminating namespaces are finalized: the object isn't removed until every finalizer is cleared, and a dead/misconfigured controller (or a stuck resource like a bound PVC) holds the list forever. The fix is at the finalizer level — clear the blocking resource or patch the finalizers list — not --force (namespaces don't take it) and not waiting out a nonexistent timer.

q: You delete a Deployment and its ReplicaSets and pods vanish too, but the PVCs created by a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates survive its deletion. What controls whether dependents are garbage-collected?
options: Nothing — it's random per resource type
The --cascade flag defaults differ between kubectl versions
Finalizers decide everything — ownerReferences are informational

ownerReferences with cascading deletion: dependents carrying an ownerReference to the deleted object are collected (foreground or background per the deletion propagation policy); volumeClaimTemplates PVCs intentionally lack that ownerReference so data survives — protection by design, not accident
explain: Garbage collection follows ownerReferences: delete the owner and dependents with that reference are cascade-deleted (background default; foreground waits for dependents first). StatefulSet PVCs deliberately have no such ownerReference — that's the data-protection design, consistent with the retained-PVC behavior. Finalizers gate timing; they don't select the dependent set.

q: A Job finished 2 hours ago but its pods are still listed, and the namespace has a LimitRange. A teammate blames the LimitRange for keeping finished pods around. What actually controls finished-Job pod retention, and is the teammate right?
options: The teammate is right — LimitRange retains pods for quota accounting

Finished Job pods are kept until the Job is deleted — retention is governed by the Job object's lifetime (ttlSecondsAfterFinished for automatic cleanup, or manual kubectl delete job); LimitRange only defaults/validates resources on pod creation and retains nothing
Pods are deleted immediately on Job completion — something is broken
The kubelet's --terminated-pod-gc-threshold deletes them after 2 hours exactly
explain: Pod retention after Job completion is a Job-lifetime question: pods live as long as the Job object does (visible for logs/inspection), cleaned by ttlSecondsAfterFinished or explicit deletion. LimitRange mutates/validates at admission and has no retention role. (The kubelet's terminated-pod GC threshold only bounds how many dead pods linger per node — 12500 by default, not a 2-hour timer.)
